<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{theorem:mainpaperreverseOUsummary}
    If $\pi$ is the pushforward of $\gamma_d$ by a ResNet of depth $\Theta(d)$ and width $O(1)$ with bounded weights and two-layer blocks using activation $\phi$, then $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \lesssim d$. However, the following hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{(Theorem \ref{theorem:mainpaperrepresentaitonlowerbound}).} There exists such a ResNet (with some $\phi$) for which  $\int_0^1 \|v_t^\pi\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}dt \gtrsim 2^d$, even though we have $\|v_t^\pi\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} < \infty$ for all $t$.
        \item \textbf{(Corollary \ref{corollary:mainpaperintegratedlowerbound}).} There exists such a ResNet (with $\phi = \operatorname{ReLU}$)\footnote{Our construction provides similar results for other activations. For example, if $\phi = \tanh$ then we get $d^{\Omega(\log(1/\varepsilon)^2)}$ lower bounds, see Remark \ref{remark:mainpaperapproximationtanhscaling}.} such that for \textbf{any} approximate drifts $\hat{v}_t$ there is the implication
        \begin{equation}
            \int_0^1 \|\hat{v}_t(x) - v_t^\pi(x)\|^2 d\rho_t^\pi(x) dt\leq \varepsilon^2 \implies \int_0^1 \|\hat{v}_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}dt \gtrsim d^{\Omega(\varepsilon^{-4/5})}~,
        \end{equation}
        and moreover if each $\hat{v}_t$ is a two-layer neural network then the largest width is at least $d^{\Omega(\varepsilon^{-4/5})}$ in such cases. 
       Here, $\rho_t^\pi$ are the marginals along the ground truth denoising path.
    \end{itemize}
    In words, exact shallow representation of the denoising drifts can require exponential width, and shallow $L^2$-approximation to accuracy $\varepsilon$ can require $d^{\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ width.\footnote{Early-stopping does not fix this. Indeed, we show in Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixearlystoppingforresnets} that if one $\varepsilon$-approximates scores up to an OU time whose marginal has $\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon)$ error in either $\operatorname{TV}$, $W_1$, or $\operatorname{KL}$, then our $d^{\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ width lower bound still applies.}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theorem:mainpaperfeaturelearningsummary}
    Let $\gamma_d \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ be the standard Gaussian and let $k: {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d}$ be rotation-equivariant (see Definition \ref{def:rotationequivariantkernel}). Define $\pi_\varepsilon$ as the time-$\varepsilon$ marginal of a flow initialized from $\gamma_d$ with single-index drifts with activation $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$.\footnote{In other words $\pi_\varepsilon = \operatorname{Law}(X_\varepsilon)$, where $\dot{X}_t = v(X_t)$ with $X_0 \sim \gamma_d$ and $v: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ is a single-index vector field $v(x) = \sigma u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)$ for some $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and $\sigma > 0$.} 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{(Examples \ref{example:nonlinearshearrkhs} and \ref{example:nonlinearshearrkhssmoothed}).} For each activation $\phi$, denote
        \begin{equation}
            Q_\phi(d) := \inf_{\substack{\text{$k$ rotation-equivariant}}} \left\{\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x)d\gamma_d(x)}\cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon)}\right\}.
        \end{equation}
        Then, we have the scalings $Q_{\operatorname{ReLU}}(d) = +\infty$, $Q_{\tanh}(d) \asymp d^{d/4}$, $Q_{\sin}(d) \asymp e^{\sqrt{d}}$ as $d \to \infty$.
        \item \textbf{(Example \ref{example:mainpapernonperturbativefeaturelearning}).}  There exists a rotation-equivariant $k_\star$ s.t. for each fixed $\varepsilon > 0$
        \begin{equation}
            \left(\sup_{t \in [0, 1]}\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k_\star(x, x)d\rho_t^\star(x)}\right)\cdot  \frac{\int_0^1 \|v_t^\star\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_\star}}dt}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon)} \lesssim \operatorname{poly}(d)
        \end{equation}
        as $d \to \infty$, where $(v_t^\star, \rho_t^\star)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ satisfies (\ref{eqn:introcontinuityequation}) with $\rho_0^\star = \gamma_d$ and $\rho_1^\star = \pi_\varepsilon$.
    \end{itemize}
    In words, the separation between $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$ and rotation-equivariant $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}$ is made superpolynomially-large by perturbative single-index flows, but not by nonperturbative ones.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- assumptionp-1: body_md -->
{$k$}
\label{assumption:kernel}
    Throughout the rest of this paper, we assume the kernel $k: {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d}$ is jointly continuous (w.r.t. the operator norm).
<!-- end assumptionp-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:rotationequivariantkernel}
A matrix-valued kernel $k$ is {\em rotation-equivariant} if
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:prelimrotationequivariant}
    k(Qx,Qy)
    =
    Qk(x,y)Q^\top \quad (\forall x, y \in {\mathbb{R}}^d)
\end{equation}
for every orthogonal matrix $Q\in O(d)$. We denote the class of such kernels by $\mathcal K_{\operatorname{rot}}$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:abstractmetric}
    Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a Banach space of functions from ${\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ which satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:main}. For every $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, define the quantity
    \begin{equation}
        D_\mathcal{B}(\mu, \nu) := \inf_{\mu \to \nu} \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_\mathcal{B} dt,
    \end{equation}
    where the infimum is over $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ transporting $\mu$ to $\nu$ via the continuity equation (\ref{eqn:prelimcontinuity}).
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:abstractmetricsmainpaper}
     $(\mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d), D_\mathcal{B})$ is an extended metric space (i.e. the metric may take the value $+\infty$), and convergence in $D_\mathcal{B}$ implies narrow convergence of measures.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
See Section \ref{subsec:appendixproofofabstractmetrics}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{remark:barronasinfoverRKHS}
    Note that since $\|\mu\|_{\operatorname{TV}} = \inf_{\substack{\eta \in \mathcal{P}(\Theta):\; \mu \ll \eta}} \|\frac{d\mu}{d\eta}\|_{L^2(\eta)}$, if for each $\eta \in \mathcal{P}(\Theta)$ we define the random feature kernel $k^{(\eta)}(x, y) := \int_\Theta \phi_\theta(x) \phi_\theta(y) d\eta(\theta) \cdot \1_d$, then for all $w$ we have
    \begin{equation}\|w\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \inf_{\substack{\eta \in \mathcal{P}(\Theta)}} \|w\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k^{(\eta)}}},\end{equation}
    see \cite[Proposition 3]{weinan}.
    In this way, the Barron norm is an infimum over random feature RKHS norms, and the optimal distribution over features is allowed to depend on $w$. Hence,
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\mu, \nu) \leq \inf_{\eta \in \mathcal{P}(\Theta)} D_{\mathcal{H}_{k^{(\eta)}}}(\mu, \nu) \quad (\forall \mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)).\end{equation}
    This need not be an equality, since the choice of the optimal $\eta$ need not be the same for all drifts along an optimal flow.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- assumptionp-2: body_md -->
{$\phi$}
\label{assumption:activationfunciton}
    Throughout the rest of this paper, we assume the activation $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuous and either bounded or positively $s$-homogeneous for some $s > 0$ (i.e. $\phi(\lambda z) = \lambda^s\phi(z)$ for all $\lambda \geq 0$).
<!-- end assumptionp-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:barronspaces}
    Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be continuous and bounded, and let $R \in (0, \infty]$.
        We denote by $\mathcal{B}_\phi^R$ the Banach space of vector fields $v: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ with norm
        \begin{equation}\|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi^R} = \inf_\mu \left\{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}} (1 + \|a\| + |b|) d|\mu|(a, b):\; v(\cdot) = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d  \times {\mathbb{R}}} \phi(\left\langle a, \cdot\right\rangle + b)d\mu(a, b)\right\}\end{equation}
        where $\mu$ ranges over signed vector-valued measures on $ {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}$ s.t. $\|a\| + |b| \leq R$ for $\mu$-a.e. $(a, b)$. If $R = \infty$ we denote this space by $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ for simplicity.
        
        In particular, the finite two-layer neural network with $\mu_j, a_j \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$ and $b_j \in {\mathbb{R}}$ given by
        \begin{equation}v(\cdot) = \sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j \phi(\left\langle a_j, \cdot\right\rangle + b_j)\end{equation}
        has Barron norm $\|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \sum_j \|\mu_j\| (1 + \|a_j\| + |b_j|)$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:barronspaceshomogeneous}
    Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be continuous and positively $s$-homogeneous for some $s > 0$. We denote by $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ the Banach space of vector fields $v: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ with norm
        \begin{equation}\|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \inf_\mu \left\{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}} (\|a\| + |b|)^s d|\mu|(a, b):\; v(\cdot) = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d  \times {\mathbb{R}}} \phi(\left\langle a, \cdot\right\rangle + b)d\mu(a, b)\right\}\end{equation}
        where $\mu$ ranges over signed vector-valued measures on $ {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}$.
        
        In particular, the finite two-layer neural network with $\mu_j, a_j \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$ and $b_j \in {\mathbb{R}}$ given by
        \begin{equation}v(\cdot) = \sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j \phi(\left\langle a_j, \cdot\right\rangle + b_j)\end{equation}
        has Barron norm $\|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \sum_j \|\mu_j\| ( \|a_j\| + |b_j|)^s$.
        
    Note that if $\phi(z) = z$ is the identity then every $v \in \mathcal{B}_\phi$ must be affine $v(x) = Mx + c$, in which case $\|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \|M\|_* + \|c\|$ with $\|\cdot\|_*$ the nuclear norm.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
We will abuse notation and use $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ to denote both of these Banach spaces, where we implicitly use the correct definition depending on whether $\phi$ is bounded or positively $s$-homogeneous. We will only ever refer to $\mathcal{B}_\phi^R$ in the bounded case, and unless otherwise stated we always use $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ (i.e. the $R = \infty$ case).
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
One could also define a finite-depth distance via $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}^{(L)}(\mu, \nu) := \inf \frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell = 1}^L \|v_\ell\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$, where the infimum is over blocks $(v_\ell)_{\ell = 1}^L$ s.t. $F_\# \mu = \nu$ with $F := (\1 + \frac{1}{L}v_L) \circ \ldots \circ (\1 + \frac{1}{L}v_1)$. Quantifying the convergence $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}^{(L)} \to D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$ as $L \to \infty$ is useful to transfer our $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$ results to real-world ResNets, which we leave for future work.
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The relaxation to measures may also be useful beyond generative modeling in the study of ResNet approximation theory. For example, any infinitely-deep and infinitely-wide ResNet (i.e. a neural ODE) with bounded activations which interpolates a dataset whose inputs have marginal distribution $\mu$ and whose outputs have marginal distribution $\nu$ must have norm at least $ D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\mu, \nu)$ (which is $\gtrsim W_2(\mu, \nu)$). By using the results of \cite{chizat2026hiddenwidthdeepresnets}, one should be able to get an analogous statement for ResNets of finite depth and width which have been trained for finite time. Alternatively, by using the results of \cite{jacot2026deeplearningconvexparadigm} one can hope to understand the minimal circuit complexity needed for such a task. This offers an approach to ResNet approximation lower bounds in terms of the geometry of the data distributions themselves, which we leave for future work.\footnote{Note that such an approach discards information about any coupling between inputs and outputs. Lower bounds would therefore be weaker, as they would capture the difficulty of transforming one distribution into another (as opposed to transforming each input into its corresponding output). The power of this perspective is that by relaxing to measures, we can naturally encode model depth through continuity equation dynamics while still using simple Barron technology.}
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:wassersteinkllowerbound}
    Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfy Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} and suppose that $\|\phi\|_\infty\leq M < \infty$. Then, there is the Wasserstein lower bound
    \begin{equation}
        D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\mu, \nu) \geq \frac{W_\infty(\mu, \nu)}{M} \quad (\forall \mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)).
    \end{equation}
    If we assume further that $\phi$ is $M$-Lipschitz then there is the KL lower bound
\begin{equation}
        D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \geq \frac{1}{4M} \cdot \min\left\{\frac{\operatorname{KL}(\pi \| \gamma_d)}{\sqrt{d}},\; \sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(\pi \| \gamma_d)}\right\} \quad (\forall \pi \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
See Section \ref{subsec:proofofWassersteinKLlowrbounds}. Similar lower bounds hold for any $D_\mathcal{B}$ metric with $\mathcal{B} \hookrightarrow L^\infty$ and $\mathcal{B} \hookrightarrow W^{1,\infty}$, respectively, as well as with $\gamma_d$ replaced by any log-smooth measure with sufficient tail control, see Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixwassersteinandKLcontrol}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:optimalgaussiantogaussian}
    Let $\pi := \mathcal{N}(m, \Sigma)$ with $\Sigma \succ 0$. Then, the following hold up to universal constants:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{(Wasserstein). }$W_2(\gamma_d, \pi) = \sqrt{\|m\|^2 + \|\Sigma^{1/2} - \1_d\|_F^2}$.
        \item \textbf{(Stein).} $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi) \asymp \log(1 + \|m\|) + \|\log \Sigma\|_F$ for $k(x, y) = (1 + \left\langle x, y\right\rangle)\1_d$.
        \item \textbf{(Barron).} $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \asymp \log(1 + \|m\|) + \|\log \Sigma\|_*$ for $\phi(z) = z$.
    \end{itemize}
    Here, $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius norm and $\|\cdot\|_*$ is the nuclear norm.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
This follows from Lemmas \ref{lemma:W2distancebetweengaussians}, \ref{lemma:steingaussiantogaussian}, and \ref{lemma:barrongaussiantogaussian}. Interestingly, the transports realizing the upper bounds for linear Stein and linear Barron are almost the same. They move the mean and covariance in separate motions: the mean movement uses a spatial preconditioning by $mm^\top$ to get the logarithmic dependence, while the log-covariance linearly interpolates from $0$ to $\log \Sigma$. See Remark \ref{remark:steinbarronlineargaussiantogaussianmeanmovement} for more details.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Note that by Proposition \ref{prop:wassersteinkllowerbound}, if $\|\phi\|_\infty < \infty$ then $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) = +\infty$ whenever $\Sigma \neq \1_d$, and when the covariances are equal we have $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi)  \gtrsim \|m\|$. By contrast, Proposition \ref{prop:optimalgaussiantogaussian} shows that an activation with linear growth allows a logarithmic cost of translation and can connect two Gaussians of different covariance. Hence, using an activation with linear growth instead of a bounded one makes an affine shift exponentially easier to implement via a neural network flow (at least in the Gaussian case).
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma:reverseOUsuboptimality}
Let $\pi \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ and $\mathcal{B}$ a Banach space of functions from ${\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$, and define
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}}(\pi) := \int_0^\infty \left\|\nabla \log \frac{P_\tau^* \pi}{\gamma_d}\right\|_{\mathcal{B}}d\tau,
\end{equation}
where $(P_\tau)_{\tau > 0}$ is the OU semigroup. If $(v_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ is any time-reparameterization\footnote{By this we mean that $v_t =  \frac{\dot\alpha(t)}{\alpha(t)} \nabla\log \frac{\rho_{\alpha(t)}}{\gamma_d}$, where $\rho_s = P_{-\log s}^* \pi$ and $\alpha: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ is any absolutely continuous, strictly increasing function with $\alpha(0) = 0$, $\alpha(1) = 1$.} of the reverse OU transport from $\gamma_d$ to $\pi$, then 
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}}(\pi) = \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}}dt \geq D_{\mathcal{B}}(\gamma_d, \pi).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This follows from reparameterizing from transport time $t \in [0, 1]$ to OU time $\tau \in [0, \infty)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:reverseOUgaussiantogaussian}
    Let $\pi := \mathcal{N}(m, \Sigma)$ with $\Sigma \succ 0$. Then, the following hold up to universal constants:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{(Wasserstein).} $\mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) \asymp W_2(\gamma_d, \pi)$.\footnote{Here, we denote $\mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) := \int_0^\infty \|\nabla \log \frac{P_\tau^* \pi}{\gamma_d} \|_{L^2(P_\tau^*\pi)}d\tau$ to be the unsquared Benamou-Brenier kinetic energy of the reverse OU transport.}
        \item \textbf{(Stein).} 
        If $k(x, y) = (1 + \left\langle x, y\right\rangle)\1_d$ then
\begin{equation}
        \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}\left(\pi\right) \gtrsim \frac{\|m\|}{\max\{1, \;\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\}} + \frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_F.\end{equation}
        However, if $m = 0$ and $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(e^{d/\sqrt{1}}, \ldots, e^{d / \sqrt{d}})$ then $\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}\left(\pi\right) \gtrsim \sqrt{\log d} \cdot D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi)$.
        \item \textbf{(Barron).}
        If $\phi(z) = z$ then
\begin{equation}
        \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left(\pi\right) \gtrsim \frac{\|m\|}{\max\{1, \;\|\Sigma\|_{\operatorname{op}}\}} + \frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_*.\end{equation}Furthermore, if $m = 0$ then $\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left(\pi\right) \asymp D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi)$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
This follows from Lemma \ref{lemma:reverseOUgaussiantogaussian} and Example \ref{example:reverseOUsteinGaussiansuboptimality}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{example:reverseOUsingleindexflowsandtilts}
    Fix a globally-Lipschitz $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ which is bounded below, and fix any $\sigma \in (0, \infty)$ and $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ s.t. $|\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle| < 1$. For $\varepsilon > 0$ define the flow perturbation
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:flowsandtiltsexampleflow}\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}} := \operatorname{Law}(X_\varepsilon), \quad \dot{X}_t = \sigma u \phi(\left\langle X_t, \theta\right\rangle), \quad X_0 \sim \gamma_d
    \end{equation}
    and for $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough that $1 + \varepsilon h_\phi \geq 0$ define the tilt perturbation
    \begin{equation}
        \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}} := (1 + \varepsilon h_\phi) \gamma_d, \quad h_\phi(x) := \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} [\phi(\xi)].
    \end{equation}
    If $\phi \in \{\operatorname{ReLU},\tanh, \sin\}$ then it holds that
    \begin{equation}
        \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left({\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}}\right)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}})} = +\infty,\quad 
        \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left({\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}}}\right)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}})} \leq 23.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
See Section \ref{subsec:proofofreverseOUsingleindexflowsandtilts}. Morally, the measure $\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}$ from (\ref{eqn:flowsandtiltsexampleflow}) has a reverse OU transport whose drifts have a term like $\theta \left\langle \cdot, u\right\rangle \phi'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)$; this is a product of two neurons, and it is not representable by two-layer networks for the activations we consider. This obstruction does not occur in the case of tilts, in which the reverse OU transport has a term like $\theta \phi'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theorem:mainpaperrepresentaitonlowerbound}
    Fix $d \geq 4$ and let $\phi(t) := \max\{0, t\}^3$ be the $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ activation. Then, there exists a ResNet $T_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ of depth $\Theta(d)$ and width $O(1)$ (which uses a smoothed $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ activation) s.t. if $\pi^\theta := (T_\theta)_\# \gamma_d \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ then 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:mainpaperrepresentationseparation}
        \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi^\theta) \gtrsim 2^d, \quad D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi^\theta) \lesssim d.
    \end{equation}
    Furthermore, the OU scores $s_\tau^\theta := \nabla \log P_\tau^* \pi^\theta$ and $b_\tau^\theta := \nabla \log \frac{P_\tau^* \pi^\theta}{\gamma_d}$ are in $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ for every $\tau \in [0, \infty)$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The precise statement is given in Proposition \ref{prop:appendixrepresentaitonupperlowerbounds}.
The hard instance constructs a triangular shear $T_\theta(z, u) = (z, \psi(u) + \Psi_\theta(z))$, where $\Psi_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^{d-1} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a deep narrow network of the form
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:mainpaperformofrepresentationlowerbound}
   \Psi_\theta(z) = \omega\left(z_{d-1} + \Lambda_\omega \omega\left(z_{d-2} + \Lambda_\omega \omega\left( \cdots + \Lambda_\omega \omega\left(z_1\right)\right)\right)\right)
\end{equation}
for a scalar function $\omega \in C^5_b({\mathbb{R}})$ with $\Lambda_\omega$ a constant depending only on $\omega$. Alternatively, this can be viewed as a scalar readout (from the $d^{th}$ coordinate) of a ResNet where each hidden layer $\ell$ has width 1, input feature $e_\ell$, output feature $e_{\ell + 1}$, and activation $\Lambda_\omega \omega$.  

The lower bound shows the third derivative of $\Psi_\theta$ is large and uses some OU stability estimates to imply the same for $s_\tau^\theta, b_\tau^\theta$ for small $\tau$ (see Corollary \ref{corollary:representationlowerbound}). 
The upper bound simply computes (\ref{eqn:mainpaperformofrepresentationlowerbound}) using an ODE with single-index drifts (namely, the layers of $\Psi_\theta$), writes the result to the $u$ coordinate, and then reverses the computation to return $z$ to its initial state. The function $\psi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is designed in order to have the right polynomial tails, which is needed to ensure the OU scores are in $\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^3}$. 
The teacher activation implementing $T_\theta$ is a smoothed $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ function, which is chosen so that both $\omega$ and $\psi$ can be represented using $O(1)$ width.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The exponential separation result of (\ref{eqn:mainpaperrepresentationseparation}) is fairly general: $\omega$ can be essentially any nondegenerate $C^5_b$ function, $\psi$ can have any tail behavior, $\phi$ can be any activation with bounded third derivatives which can represent $\omega$ and $\psi_\theta$, the features need not be an orthonormal set (though they must be chained so that the output feature of each layer is the input feature of the next layer), and the lower bound is exponential in the depth (see Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationlowerboundresnets} for a general statement). 
    
    However, our proof that the scores are Barron relies heavily on the $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ structure (since we use a weighted-Sobolev-to-Barron embedding, see Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixsobolevtobarron}). This requires the right tails for $\psi$, which in turn requires choosing a teacher activation that can implement both $\omega$ and $\psi$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The cascade-across-coordinates structure in (\ref{eqn:mainpaperformofrepresentationlowerbound}) is akin to the Gibbs scan, which is known in sampling theory as a way to sample complicated measures via simple iterated conditioning. These are the types of measures from which an algorithm like chained Langevin \cite{cheng2025hardnesssamplingmixturedistributions} is designed to sample. Our result shows that denoising models can fail to take advantage of this structure.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{theorem:mainpaperapproximationlowerbound}
Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ smaller than a universal constant. Then, there exists $d_0 = d_0(\varepsilon)$ s.t. for each $d \geq d_0$ there exists a ResNet $T_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ of depth $\Theta(d)$ and width $O(1)$ with ReLU activations with the following property for a universal $c > 0$:

If $0 \leq \tau \lesssim \varepsilon^{4/3}$ and $\hat{s}_\tau: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ is any two-layer neural network of width $m$ (i.e. a sum of $m$ ridge functions) for which
\begin{equation}
    \|s_\tau^\theta - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^\theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} \leq \varepsilon,
\end{equation}
then it holds that $m \gtrsim d^{c\varepsilon^{-4/3}}$ and $\|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \gtrsim \varepsilon d^{\frac{c}{2}\varepsilon^{-4/3}}$ for all $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}.
The same statements hold with $s_\tau^\theta$ replaced by $b_\tau^\theta$, and the implied constants are independent of $\varepsilon, d, \tau, \hat{s}_\tau,m$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
The ResNet $T_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ also does not depend on $\varepsilon$. In other words, for each dimension $d \in {\mathbb{N}}$ there is a fixed ResNet pushforward s.t. for any $\varepsilon > 0$ the reverse OU scores are hard to $\varepsilon$-approximate by shallow networks in dimension $\geq d_0(\varepsilon)$. Moreover, $D_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}}}(\gamma_d, \pi^\theta) \lesssim \sqrt{d}$ with a universal constant.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The hard instance constructs a triangular shear $T_\theta(z, u) = (z, u + \Psi_\theta(z))$, where $\Psi_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^{d-1} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a wide three-layer network of the form
    \begin{equation}
        \Psi_\theta(z) = \chi\left(z_{d-1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{d-2}}\sum_{\ell = 1}^{d-2} g(z_\ell)\right)
    \end{equation}
    for scalar functions $\chi, g: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$. Note that $T_\theta$ can be also expressed as a deep narrow ResNet, see Section \ref{subsec:appendixresnetapproximation}. In this ResNet each layer is a shear (i.e. the input and output features are orthogonal) and so it can be implemented by a ReLU flow; since the weights are $\frac{1}{\sqrt{d-2}}$, this means that  $D_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}}}(\gamma_d, \pi^\theta) \lesssim \sqrt{d}$.

    
    By Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermitedecayforapproximation}, with $\chi(t) = \max\{0, t\} - \max\{0, t-1\}$ and any centered non-affine Lipschitz $g$ we get $\mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K, 2K) \gtrsim K^{-3/2}$ with constants depending only on $g$, and hence $K(\varepsilon) \gtrsim \varepsilon^{-4/3}$.
    We choose $g(t) = \max\{0, t\} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ for simplicity.
    The claim follows by applying Corollary \ref{corollary:approximationlowerbound} with $L = d-2$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{remark:mainpaperapproximationtanhscaling}
The same construction with $\chi = g = \tanh$ yields a similar result:
for $0 \leq \tau \lesssim \varepsilon$,  we get that $m \gtrsim d^{c \log(1/\varepsilon)^2}$ and $\|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \gtrsim \varepsilon d^{\frac{c}{2}\log(1/\varepsilon)^2}$. To show this, we apply the other result from Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermitedecayforapproximation} to see that $K(\varepsilon) \gtrsim \log(1/\varepsilon)^2$, after which we use Corollary \ref{corollary:approximationlowerbound}. In this case, getting the first two terms of (\ref{eqn:mainerrordecomposition}) to $\lesssim \delta$ using shallow score networks requires width $\gtrsim d^{\Omega(\log(1/\delta)^2)}$.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{corollary:mainpaperintegratedlowerbound}
        Fix $T > 0$ and $0 < \varepsilon < \varepsilon_0(T)$. Then, for each $d \geq d_0(\varepsilon)$ there exists a ResNet $T_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ of depth $\Theta(d)$ and width $O(1)$ with ReLU activations with the following property for a universal $c > 0$:

        If $(\hat{s}_\tau)_{\tau \in [0, T]}$ is a measurable family of two-layer neural networks of width $m(\tau)$ for which
        \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:mainpaperintegratederrorassumption}
            \int_0^T \|s_\tau^\theta - \hat{s}_\tau\|^2_{L^2(\rho_\tau^\theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}d\tau \leq \varepsilon^2,
        \end{equation}
        then $\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\tau \in [0, T]}m(\tau) \gtrsim d^{c\varepsilon^{-4/5}}$ and for all $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} we have
        \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:mainpaperintegratederrorclaim}
            \int_0^T \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}d\tau \gtrsim \varepsilon^{7/5} d^{\frac{c}{2}\varepsilon^{-4/5}} \quad \text{and}\quad \int_0^T \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}^2d\tau \gtrsim \varepsilon^{2} d^{{c}\varepsilon^{-4/5}}.
        \end{equation}
        The same statements hold with $s_\tau^\theta$ replaced by $b_\tau^\theta$, and the implied constants are independent of $T, \varepsilon, d, (\hat{s}_\tau)_{\tau \in [0, T]}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
We let $a > 0$ be the constant s.t. Theorem \ref{theorem:mainpaperapproximationlowerbound} holds for $\tau \in [0, a \delta^{4/3}]$ with pointwise accuracy parameter $\delta$. We take $\delta = (2\varepsilon^2/a)^{3/10}$ and $\tau_\delta = a\delta^{4/3}$. This implies that $\tau_\delta \delta^2 = 2\varepsilon^2$ while $\delta \asymp \varepsilon^{3/5}$ and $\tau_\delta \asymp \varepsilon^{4/5}$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, Theorem \ref{theorem:mainpaperapproximationlowerbound} applies at accuracy $\delta$ and time $\tau_\delta \leq T$. If we set $e_\tau := \|s_\tau^\theta - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^\theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}$ and $G := \{\tau \in [0, \tau_\delta]:\; e_\tau \leq \delta\}$ then by (\ref{eqn:mainpaperintegratederrorassumption}) we have 
        \begin{equation}
            |[0, \tau_\delta] \setminus G| \leq \frac{1}{\delta^2}\int_0^{\tau_\delta}e_\tau^2 d\tau \leq \frac{\varepsilon^2}{\delta^2} = \frac{\tau_\delta}{2}.
        \end{equation}
        Hence, $|G| \geq \tau_\delta / 2$. For every $\tau \in G$ we have $m(\tau) \gtrsim d^{c\delta^{-4/3}}$ and $\|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \gtrsim \delta d^{\frac{c}{2}\delta^{-4/3}}$, from which the claim (\ref{eqn:mainpaperintegratederrorclaim}) follows by integration over $G$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{example:nonlinearshearrkhs}
Let $d \geq 4$ and $\mu \in \mathcal{P}_2({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ be rotationally-invariant with $\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |x|^2 d\mu(x) > 0$. Let $\phi(z) = \max\{0, z\}$ be the ReLU activation, fix $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with $\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \neq 0$, and for $\varepsilon > 0$ define
\begin{equation}w(x) := u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle), \quad \nu_\varepsilon := (\1 + \varepsilon w)_\# \mu \in \mathcal{P}_2({\mathbb{R}}^d).\end{equation}
Then, for any rotation-equivariant $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}}$ which satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel} we have
\begin{equation}\lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)} = +\infty .\end{equation}
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
See Section \ref{subsection:generativemodelingproofs}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{example:nonlinearshearrkhssmoothed}
    Let $d\geq3$ and $\gamma_d$ be the standard Gaussian. Fix $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, and for $\varepsilon > 0$ define $\nu_\varepsilon := \operatorname{Law}(X_\varepsilon)$ using the flow
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:mainpapersingleindexflow}
    \dot{X}_t =  u\phi(\left\langle X_t, \theta\right\rangle), \quad X_0 \sim \gamma_d.\end{equation}
    For an activation $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}, define
    \begin{equation}
        Q_{\phi, d} :=  \inf_{\substack{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}} \\ k \text{ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel}}}}\left\{\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\gamma_d(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_{\phi}}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}\right\} .
    \end{equation}
    Then, the following scalings hold as $d \to \infty$:
    \begin{equation}
        Q_{\tanh, d} \asymp d^{\frac{d}{4} \cdot (1+o(1))}, \qquad Q_{\sin, d} \asymp e^{\sqrt{d} \cdot (1+o(1))}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
See Section \ref{subsection:generativemodelingproofs}.
    In Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixupperandlowerboundsforsingleindexgaussianflows} we show matching upper and lower bounds (up to constants) for Gaussian single-index flows in terms of the Hermite coefficients of the activation. In Lemmas \ref{lemma:appendixtanhhermitescaling} and \ref{lemma:appendixtsinhermitescaling} we compute the asymptotics uniformly in $u, \theta$ for $\tanh$ and $\sin$, respectively.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The use of spherical harmonics to lower bound RKHS norms of single-index functions is well-known in the field; our only contribution to this story is the application of this technique to the local geometry of the $D_\mathcal{B}$ metrics/the measure transport problem.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{example:mainpapernonperturbativefeaturelearning}
Let $d \geq 3$, fix $\phi \in C^\infty_b({\mathbb{R}})$ and $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with $\left\langle u, \theta \right\rangle = 0$, and define $\nu_T := \operatorname{Law}(X_T)$ for the flow (\ref{eqn:mainpapersingleindexflow}). 
Then, there exists a smooth rotation-equivariant $k_\star \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}}$ (depending only on $d, \phi, T$) and a transport $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ from $\gamma_d$ to $\nu_T$ using $\operatorname{poly}(d)$-Lipschitz drifts which satisfies
\begin{equation}
    \left(\sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k_\star(x, x) d\rho_t(x)}\right) \cdot \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_\star}}dt \lesssim \operatorname{poly}(d).
\end{equation}
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The precise nonasymptotic statement is given in Proposition \ref{prop:appendixnonperturbativefeaturelearning}, and it holds with $\gamma_d$ replaced by any initial $\rho_0 \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ for which $(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}|x|^d d\rho_0(x))^{1/d} \lesssim \operatorname{poly}(d)$. The method is similar to how the linear Stein metric achieves logarithmic dependence on the mean in Proposition \ref{prop:optimalgaussiantogaussian}: there is an initial compression/preconditioning phase in the direction $u$, followed by an exponentially-shrunk version of the original single-index transport, followed by a decompression phase. Since the compression/decompression phases have costs logarithmic in the compression factor, we may efficiently shrink the single-index phase to achieve polynomial total cost.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
An efficient algorithm to learn dynamical transports must somehow discretize $[0, 1]$, which relies on the regularity-in-time of the optimal transport $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$. At the current moment we do not have precise control on this (since the $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}$ and $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$ energies do not directly penalize irregularity of $t \mapsto v_t$). 
    
    A promising direction involves a priori estimates on the geodesic PDE. As an example, in the Stein case with a Matérn/Sobolev kernel $\mathcal{H}_k \cong H^s$, the PDE (\ref{eqn:prelimssteingeodesics}) and Sobolev multiplication estimates ensure that any constant-speed $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}$ geodesic has $\sup_{t \in [0, 1]}\|\partial_tv_t\|_{H^{s-1}} \lesssim D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\rho_0, \rho_1)$. This approach will be formalized and developed for the general case in \cite{companionpaper}.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
\label{question:resnetpushforwards}
    Given a teacher ResNet $F: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ and samples from its Gaussian pushforward $\pi = F_\# \gamma_d$, is there an efficient algorithm which learns a drift field $(v_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ transporting $\gamma_d$ to $\pi$? In other words, can we efficiently learn a deep ResNet/neural ODE which maps $\gamma_d$ to $\pi$?
    What properties of $F$ allow such an algorithm? 
Ideally, we want the learned transport to have path norm/Barron cost comparable to that of $F$.
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
To make this question more practical, it suffices to transport $\gamma_d$ to a measure which approximates $\pi$ in some metric or divergence. Allowing the target to be shifted within a small ball can substantially facilitate transport; this tradeoff between controlled metric displacement and dynamical transport is closely related to the shifted composition methodology of \cite{altschuler2026shifted}. In our setting, this would correspond to the quantity 
    \begin{equation}
        \widetilde{D}_{\mathcal{B},\varepsilon}( \mu, \pi) = \inf \left\{ \int_0^1 \| \hat{v}_t \|_{\mathcal{B}} dt: \; \int_0^1 \| \hat{v}_t - v_t \|_{L^2(\rho_t; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}^2 dt \leq \varepsilon^2\right\},
    \end{equation}
    where the infimum is over transports $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ satisfying $\partial_t \rho_t + \nabla \cdot( v_t \rho_t)=0$ and $ \rho_0 = \mu, \rho_1 = \pi $.
    Under mild regularity of $\hat{v}_t$ (e.g. Lipschitz regularity, see \cite[Prop. 3]{albergo2023building}), the drift approximation can be translated into Wasserstein control of the transport endpoint $W_2(\hat{\pi}, \pi) \lesssim \varepsilon$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
\label{question:multiindexpushforwards}
    Given a teacher multi-index vector field $F: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ of the form $F(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m \sigma_j u_j \phi(\left\langle x, \theta_j\right\rangle)$  and samples from its Gaussian pushforward $\pi = (\operatorname{Id} + F)_\# \gamma_d$, is there an efficient algorithm which learns a generative model for $\pi$? Which properties of $F$ allow such an algorithm (e.g. $m = O(1)$)?
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
For a fixed total depth of the generative process of a denoising model, what is the ``best" allocation between the number of neural network score evaluations and the depth of each score neural network? Here, ``best" should be measured in terms of both training complexity and sample quality.
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- assumption-1: body_md -->
\label{assumption:main}
Throughout this paper we assume that for every $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$,
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{\|v\|_\mathcal{B} \leq 1} \sup_{x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d} \left|\left\langle v(x), \nabla \varphi(x)\right\rangle\right| < \infty.
\end{equation}
We will always identify vectors $v \in \mathcal{B}$ with their representative functions $v(x)$.
<!-- end assumption-1 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:independentofp}
     For any $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, let $\mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ denote the class of pairs $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ s.t.:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] $t \mapsto \rho_t$ is narrowly continuous,
        \item[(ii)] $v_t \in \mathcal{B}$ for a.e. $t$ and the maps $t \mapsto \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} $ and $ (t, x) \mapsto v(t, x)$ are Borel measurable,
        \item[(iii)] 
        $\int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |v_t(x)| d\rho_t(x) dt < \infty,$
        \item[(iv)] the continuity equation (\ref{eqn:informalcontinuityequation}) holds in the weak sense, see (8.1.3) of \cite{ags}.
    \end{enumerate}
    For every $p \in [1, \infty)$, define the quantity
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}, p}(\mu, \nu) := \inf_{(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}} \left(\int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}}^p dt\right)^{1/p},\end{equation}
    with a value of $+\infty$ if no admissible transport of finite energy exists.
    Then, it holds that 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:independentofp}
    D_{\mathcal{B}, p}(\mu, \nu) = D_{\mathcal{B}, p'}(\mu, \nu) \quad (\forall p, p' \in [1, \infty)). \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
It suffices to prove that $D_{\mathcal{B}, p}(\mu, \nu) = D_{\mathcal{B}, 1}(\mu, \nu)$ for every $p \in [1, \infty)$. Naturally, for any admissible pair Hölder's inequality implies
    \begin{equation}\int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt \leq \left(\int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}}^p dt\right)^{1/p}\end{equation}
    and so $D_{\mathcal{B}, 1}(\mu, \nu) \leq D_{\mathcal{B}, p}(\mu, \nu)$. If $D_{\mathcal{B}, 1}(\mu, \nu) = +\infty$ then the reverse inequality is trivial, and otherwise let $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ be admissible with finite length
    \begin{equation}L := \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt < \infty.\end{equation}
    Fix $\delta > 0$ and define
    \begin{equation}a_\delta(t) := \frac{\int_0^t \|v_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}}d\tau + \delta t}{L + \delta}.\end{equation}
    Then, $a_\delta: [0, 1] \to [0, 1]$ is strictly increasing and absolutely continuous with $a'_\delta(t) = \frac{\|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} + \delta}{L+\delta} > 0$ for a.e. $t$, and so its inverse $\theta_\delta := a_\delta^{-1}$ is $\frac{L+\delta}{\delta}$-Lipschitz and therefore absolutely continuous. Define
    \begin{equation}\tilde{\rho}_\tau := \rho_{\theta_\delta(\tau)}, \quad \tilde{v}_\tau := \theta'_\delta(\tau) v_{\theta_\delta(\tau)}.\end{equation}
    For any $\varphi \in C^\infty_c((0, 1) \times {\mathbb{R}}^d)$, if we define $\psi(t, x) := \varphi(a_\delta(t), x)$ then
    testing $\psi$\footnote{Here, we may test $\psi$ by approximating $a_\delta$ in $W^{1,1}$ by smooth functions and using dominated convergence due to (iii).} against
    the original continuity equation (\ref{eqn:informalcontinuityequation}) gives
    \begin{align}0 &= \int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left(a_\delta'(\tau) \partial_t\varphi(a_\delta(\tau), x) + \left\langle v_\tau(x), \nabla_x \varphi(a_\delta(\tau), x) \right\rangle\right) d\rho_\tau(x) d\tau\\
     &= \int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left(\partial_t\varphi(t, x) + \left\langle  \theta_\delta'(t){v}_{\theta_\delta(t)}(x), \nabla_x \varphi(t, x) \right\rangle\right) d\tilde{\rho}_t(x) dt \\
    &= \int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left(\partial_t\varphi(t, x) + \left\langle \tilde{v}_t(x), \nabla_x \varphi(t, x) \right\rangle\right) d\tilde{\rho}_t(x) dt,
    \end{align}
    where the second line uses the absolutely continuous time change $t =a_\delta(\tau) $ along with the chain rule. Similarly, change of variables implies
    \begin{equation}\int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |\tilde{v}_t| d\tilde{\rho}_t dt = \int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \theta_\delta'(t) |v_{\theta_\delta(t)}| d\rho_{\theta_\delta(t)} dt = \int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |v_\tau| d\rho_\tau d\tau < \infty\end{equation}
    and so $(\tilde{v}_t, \tilde{\rho}_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$. Furthermore, for a.e. $t \in [0, 1]$ we know
    \begin{equation}\|\tilde{v}_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} = \theta'_\delta(t) \|v_{\theta_\delta(t)}\|_{\mathcal{B}} = \frac{L+\delta}{\|v_{\theta_\delta(t)}\|_{\mathcal{B}} + \delta} \cdot \|v_{\theta_\delta(t)}\|_{\mathcal{B}} \leq L + \delta\end{equation}
    and therefore
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}, p}(\mu, \nu) \leq \left(\int_0^1 \|\tilde{v}_t\|_{\mathcal{B}}^pdt\right)^{1/p} \leq L + \delta.\end{equation}
    Taking $\delta \downarrow 0$ and taking the infimum over all finite-length admissible pairs proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:dbpmetrics}
For $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we denote the class $\mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ as in Proposition \ref{prop:independentofp} and we denote the shared quantity (\ref{eqn:independentofp}) by
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:defofDb}
    D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu) :=   \inf_{(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}} \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt,\end{equation}
    with a value of $+\infty$ if no admissible transport of finite length exists.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:quasimetric}
$D_{\mathcal{B}}$ is an extended metric (i.e. a metric which may take the value $+\infty$). In particular, the following hold for all $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] $D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu) = D_{\mathcal{B}}(\nu, \mu)$.
    \item[(ii)] $D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu) = \inf_{\rho \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)}\left\{ D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \rho) + D_{\mathcal{B}}(\rho, \nu)\right\}$.
    \item[(iii)] $D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu) = 0 \iff \mu = \nu$.
\end{enumerate}
Furthermore, if $(\mu_n)_{n \in {\mathbb{N}}} \subseteq \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ and $\mu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ are s.t. $\lim_{n \to \infty}D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu_n, \mu) = 0$ then we have the narrow convergence $\mu_n \rightharpoonup \mu$.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(i) follows from the observation that if $(v_t, \rho_t) \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ then $(-v_{1-t}, \rho_{1-t}) \in \mathcal{S}_{\nu \to \mu}$ and $\|-v_{1-t}\|_{\mathcal{B}} = \|v_{1-t}\|_{\mathcal{B}}$. 
    
    Our proof of (ii) is taken from \href{https://mathoverflow.net/questions/166307/pde-based-triangle-inequality-for-optimal-transportation}{this MathOverflow post}. Suppose first that
    \begin{equation}d_1 := D_{\mathcal{B},1}(\mu, \rho), \quad d_2 := D_{\mathcal{B},1}(\rho, \nu)\end{equation}
    are both finite (if not, the inequality is trivial). Fix $\varepsilon > 0$ and let $(v_t, \rho_t) \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \rho}$ and $(w_t, \eta_t) \in \mathcal{S}_{\rho \to \nu}$ be s.t.
    \begin{equation}\int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt \leq d_1 + \varepsilon, \quad\int_0^1 \|w_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt \leq d_2 + \varepsilon.\end{equation}
Note that if $\tau \in (0, 1)$ and we define
    \begin{equation}\tilde{v}_t := \begin{cases}
        v_{t/\tau}/\tau & t \leq \tau \\
        w_{(t-\tau)/(1-\tau)}/(1-\tau) & t > \tau
    \end{cases}, \quad \tilde{\rho}_t := \begin{cases}
        \rho_{t/\tau} & t \leq \tau \\
        \eta_{(t - \tau)/(1-\tau)} & t > \tau
    \end{cases},\end{equation}
    then $\tilde{\rho}_{\tau} = \rho$ and $(\tilde{v}, \tilde{\rho}) \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$. Furthermore,
    \begin{align}\int_0^1 \|\tilde{v}_t\|_{\mathcal{B}}dt &={\tau^{-1}}\int_0^{\tau} \|{v}_{t/\tau}\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt+ {(1-\tau)^{-1}}\int_{\tau}^{1} \|{w}_{(t-\tau)/(1-\tau)}\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt  \\&\leq (d_1+\varepsilon) + (d_2+\varepsilon), \end{align}
    and therefore taking the infimum over transports implies
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B},1}(\mu, \nu) \leq d_1 + d_2 + 2\varepsilon.\end{equation}
    Taking $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows the $\leq$ direction; for equality we may take $\rho = \mu$.


    For (iii), note that if $D_{\mathcal{B},1}(\mu, \nu) = 0$ then for each $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ there is some $(v_t^n, \rho_t^n) \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ s.t. 
    \begin{equation}\int_0^1 \|v_t^n\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt \leq \frac{1}{n}.\end{equation}
    For any $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, by testing against the continuity equation we find
    \begin{equation}\int \varphi d\nu - \int \varphi d\mu = \int_0^1 \int \left\langle v_t^n, \nabla \varphi\right\rangle d\rho_t^n dt.\end{equation}
    Applying Assumption \ref{assumption:main} and denoting by $C_\varphi$ the implied constant, we find
    \begin{align}\left|\int \varphi d\nu - \int \varphi d\mu\right| &\leq C_\varphi  \cdot \left(\int_0^1 \|v_t^n\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt\right) \leq \frac{C_\varphi }{n}.\end{align}
    Letting $n \to \infty$ implies $\int \varphi d\nu = \int \varphi d\mu$, and since this holds for all $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, we find $\mu = \nu$. If $\mu = \nu$ then the null drift is admissible, proving (iii).

    For the last statement, let $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ be admissible. Integrating the continuity equation against $\varphi$ yields
\begin{equation}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\nu - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu = \int_0^1 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle v_t, \nabla \varphi\right\rangle d\rho_t dt\end{equation}
and so 
\begin{align}
    \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\nu - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu\right| &\leq C_\varphi \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}} dt,
\end{align}
Taking the infimum over admissible transports,
\begin{equation}
     \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\nu - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu\right|  \leq C_\varphi D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu).
\end{equation}
Suppose now that $D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu_n, \mu) \to 0$. The above estimate implies that
\begin{equation}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu_n \to \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu \quad (\forall \varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)),\end{equation}
from which narrow convergence follows from e.g. \cite[Remark 5.1.6]{ags}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Assumption \ref{assumption:main} is satisfied in either of the following cases:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item if a kernel $k: {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d}$ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel} and $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{H}_k$.
        \item if an activation $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} and $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}_\phi$.
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, and let $K := \operatorname{spt}(\varphi)$ be its compact support set. It suffices to show that there is some $C_K < \infty$ s.t.
    \begin{equation}
        \sup_{x \in K}\|v(x)\| \leq C_K \|v\|_\mathcal{B} \quad (\forall v \in \mathcal{B}).
    \end{equation}
    In the Stein case, we know that 
    \begin{equation}
        \|v(x)\| \leq \|v\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} \cdot \|k(x, x)\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{1/2},
    \end{equation}
    and so compactness of $K$ and continuity of $k$ yield that $C_K := \sup_{x \in K} \|k(x, x)\|_{\operatorname{op}}^{1/2} < \infty$. In the Barron case, if $\phi$ is bounded then we know
    \begin{equation}
        \|v(x)\| \leq \|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \cdot \|\phi\|_\infty,
    \end{equation}
    while if $\phi$ is positively $s$-homogeneous then
    \begin{equation}
        \|v(x)\| \leq \|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \cdot \max\{|\phi(1)|, |\phi(-1)|\} \cdot (1 + \|x\|)^s.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixwassersteinandKLcontrol}
    Let $\mathcal{B}$ be a Banach space of functions from ${\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ s.t.
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:appendixboundedM0}
        \|w\|_\infty \leq M_0 \|w\|_\mathcal{B} \quad (\forall w \in \mathcal{B})
    \end{equation}
    for some $M_0 < \infty$. Then, for every $p \in [1, \infty]$ we have 
    \begin{equation}
        W_p(\mu, \nu) \leq M_0 D_\mathcal{B}(\mu, \nu) \quad (\forall \mu, \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)).
    \end{equation}
    Suppose further that $\mathcal{B} \hookrightarrow W^{1, \infty}$ continuously and
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:appendixboundedM1}\|\operatorname{div}w\|_{L^\infty} \leq M_1 \|w\|_\mathcal{B} \quad (\forall w \in \mathcal{B})
    \end{equation}
    for some $M_1 < \infty$. Let $\mu \propto e^{-V}$ be s.t. $\nabla V$ is $\beta$-Lipschitz and $S_\mu := \mathbb{E}_{\mu}\|\nabla V\| < \infty$. Then,
        \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{KL}(\nu \| \mu) \leq (M_0 S_\mu + M_1) D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu) + \frac{\beta M_0^2}{2}D_{\mathcal{B}}(\mu, \nu)^2 \quad (\forall \nu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Fix an admissible $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mu \to \nu}$ and write $L := \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_\mathcal{B} dt$. By the superposition principle for the weak continuity equation, there is a probability measure $\mathbb{Q}$ on absolutely continuous curves $\omega:[0, 1] \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ s.t. $(e_t)_\# \mathbb{Q} = \rho_t$ and $\dot{\omega}_t = v_t(\omega_t)$ for $\mathbb{Q}$-a.e. $\omega$. Hence,
\begin{equation}
    |\omega_1 - \omega_0| \leq \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_\infty dt \leq M_0 L
\end{equation}
for $\mathbb{Q}$-a.e. $\omega$, which means $(e_0, e_1)_\# \mathbb{Q}$ is a coupling of $\mu$ and $\nu$ supported on pairs with distance at most $M_0L$. Taking an infimum over transports yields $W_\infty(\mu, \nu) \leq M_0 D_\mathcal{B}(\mu, \nu)$.

Now, assume that $\mathcal{B} \hookrightarrow W^{1,\infty}$ continuously and that we take Lipschitz representatives. This means that
\begin{equation}
    \int_0^1 (\|v_t\|_\infty + \operatorname{Lip}(v_t)) dt < \infty
\end{equation}
for any finite-action drifts $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$, which ensures that the corresponding ODE has a unique flow $X_t$ with $(X_t)_\# \mu = \rho_t$; this lets us upgrade from the weak continuity equation to this ODE flow for any finite-action path. Now, the change of variables and Jacobian formulas imply
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixklchangeofvariables}
    \operatorname{KL}(\nu \| \mu) = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left(V(X_1(x)) - V(x) - \int_0^1 \operatorname{div}v_t(X_t(x)) dt\right) d\mu(x).
\end{equation}
Since $\nabla V$ is $\beta$-Lipschitz we know
\begin{equation}
    V(X_1(x)) - V(x) \leq \left\langle \nabla V(x), X_1(x) - x\right\rangle + \frac{\beta}{2}\|X_1(x) - x\|^2.
\end{equation}
We know $\|X_1(x) - x\| \leq \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_\infty dt \leq M_0 L$ as before, and also
\begin{equation}
    -\int_0^1 \operatorname{div}v_t(X_t(x))dt \leq \int_0^1 \|\operatorname{div}v_t\|_{L^\infty} dt \leq M_1 L.
\end{equation}
Plugging these into (\ref{eqn:proofappendixklchangeofvariables}) yields that
\begin{equation}
    \operatorname{KL}(\nu \| \mu) \leq M_0 L \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|\nabla V\| d\mu + \frac{\beta M_0^2}{2}L^2 + M_1L,
\end{equation}
after which the claim follows by taking an infimum over transports.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The $W_\infty$ bound follows from Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixwassersteinandKLcontrol}.
   For the KL bound, the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixwassersteinandKLcontrol} hold with $M_0, M_1 = M$, and with $\mu = \gamma_d$ we have $\beta = 1$ and $S_{\gamma_d} \leq \sqrt{d}$. Thus, with $K := \operatorname{KL}(\pi \| \gamma_d)$ and $D := D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi)$ we find
   \begin{equation}
       K \leq M(\sqrt{d} + 1) D + \frac{M^2}{2}D^2 \leq 2M\sqrt{d}D + \frac{M^2}{2}D^2.
   \end{equation}
   At least one term on the right must be at least $K/2$, and so either $MD \geq \frac{K}{4\sqrt{d}}$ or $MD \geq \sqrt{K}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma:W2distancebetweengaussians}
    $W_2(\gamma_d, \pi) = \sqrt{\|m\|^2 + \|\Sigma^{1/2} - \1_d\|_F^2}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma:steingaussiantogaussian}
    Let $\alpha > 0$ and $A \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d}$ be symmetric and positive definite, and let $k(x, y) := (\alpha + x^\top A y) \1_d$ (which implies Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel} is satisfied). 
    If we denote
    \begin{equation}D := \frac{1}{\sqrt{\|A\|_{\operatorname{op}}}} \left(\log\left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{\|A\|_{\operatorname{op}}}{\alpha}}\|m\|\right) + \frac{1}{2} \|\log \Sigma\|_F\right), \end{equation}
    for $\|\cdot\|_F$ the Frobenius norm, then with $\kappa(A)$ the condition number of $A$ it holds that
    \begin{equation}\frac{1}{2}D \leq {D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi)} \leq 2\sqrt{\kappa(A)}D.\end{equation}
    In particular, with $k(x, y) = (1 + \left\langle x, y\right\rangle)\1_d$ we have
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi) \asymp \log \left(1 + \|m\|\right) + \|\log \Sigma\|_F.\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Let us denote $a := \|A\|_{\operatorname{op}}$.
   Every $v \in \mathcal{H}_k$ is of the form $v(x) = Mx + c$ with the norm
   \begin{equation}\|v\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}^2 = \|MA^{-1/2}\|_F^2 + \frac{\|c\|^2}{\alpha}.\end{equation}
   Since these are affine, any finite-length admissible transport starting from $\gamma_d$ remains Gaussian; we write
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:prooftherhoandvofchoice}
       \rho_t = \mathcal{N}(m_t, \Sigma_t), \quad v_t(x) = M_tx + c_t
   \end{equation}
   which follow the dynamics
   \begin{equation}\label{eqn:proofmatrixdynamics}\dot{m}_t = M_t m_t + c_t, \quad \dot{\Sigma}_t = M_t\Sigma_t + \Sigma_t M_t^\top, \quad m_0 = 0, \Sigma_0 = \1_d.\end{equation}
   Let us denote
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofrkhsnorminthebilinearcase}
       \ell_t := \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} = \left(\|M_tA^{-1/2}\|_F^2 + \frac{\|c_t\|^2}{\alpha}\right)^{1/2}.
   \end{equation}
   If we let $L_t$ solve the dynamics
   \begin{equation}
       \label{eqn:proofcholeskydynamics}
       \dot{L}_t = M_t L_t, \quad L_0 = \1_d
   \end{equation}
   then $\Sigma_t = L_t L_t^\top$. If $s_1(t), \ldots, s_d(t)$ are the singular values of $L_t$ then
we may take an SVD $L_t = U_t S_t V_t^\top$ with $S_t = \operatorname{diag}(s_1(t), \ldots, s_d(t))$. In other words, $L_t v_j = s_j(t) u_j$ with $u_j, v_j$ the left and right unit singular vectors, after which the standard formula yields \begin{equation}s_j'(t) = u_j^\top \dot{L}_t v_j = u_j^\top M_tL_t v_j = s_j(t) u_j^\top M_t u_j\end{equation}
whenever singular values do not cross, and so for a.e. $t$ we have
\begin{equation}\frac{d}{dt} \log s_j(t) = u_j^\top M_t u_j.\end{equation}
Since $u_j^\top M_tu_j$ are the diagonal entries of $U_t^\top M_t U_t$ we find
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofell2estimatesingularvalues}
    \sum_{j=1}^d |u_j^\top M_tu_j|^2 \leq \sum_{i,j = 1}^d \left|(U_t^\top M_tU_t)_{ij}\right|^2 = \|U_t^\top M_tU_t\|_F^2 = \|M_t\|_F^2
\end{equation}
and therefore we have
   \begin{equation}\left(\sum_{j=1}^d \left|\frac{d}{dt}\log s_j(t)\right|^2\right)^{1/2} \leq \|M_t\|_F.\end{equation}
   Integrating over time and using that $\log s_j(0) = 0$,
    \begin{equation}\left(\sum_{j=1}^d |\log s_j(1)|^2 \right)^{1/2} = \|\log s(1)\|_2 \leq \int_0^1 \left\|\frac{d}{dt} \log s(t)\right\|_2 dt \leq \int_0^1 \|M_t\|_F dt.\end{equation}
    In particular, since the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ are $s_1(1)^2, \ldots, s_d(1)^2$ we find that
    \begin{equation}\|\log \Sigma\|_F^2 = \sum_{j=1}^d \left|\log(s_j(1)^2)\right|^2 = 4 \|\log s(1)\|_2^2\end{equation}
    and hence
    \begin{equation}\frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_F \leq \int_0^1 \|M_t\|_F dt \leq \sqrt{a} \int_0^1 \ell_t dt.\end{equation}
    For the mean, if $r_t := \|m_t\|$ then 
    \begin{equation}\dot{r}_t \leq \|M_tm_t\| + \|c_t\| \leq \sqrt{a}r_t \|M_tA^{-1/2}\|_F + \sqrt{\alpha}\frac{\|c_t\|}{\sqrt{\alpha}} \leq \sqrt{ar_t^2 + \alpha} \cdot \left(\|M_tA^{-1/2}\|_F^2 + \frac{\|c_t\|^2}{\alpha}\right)^{1/2}\end{equation}
    and so
    \begin{equation}\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}\frac{d}{dt} \left[\sinh^{-1} \left(\sqrt{\frac{a}{\alpha}}r_t\right)\right] = \frac{\dot{r}_t}{\sqrt{ar_t^2 + \alpha}} \leq \ell_t.\end{equation}
    Integrating in time and using that $r_0 = 0$, we find
    \begin{equation}\sinh^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{a}{\alpha}} \|m\|\right) \leq \sqrt{a}\int_0^1 \ell_t dt.\end{equation}
    We may now take an infimum over finite-energy transports $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ and use that $\sinh^{-1}(z) \geq \log(1+z)$ to find
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi) \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}} \max\left\{\frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_F, \; \log\left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{a}{\alpha}} \|m\|\right)\right\} \geq \frac{1}{2}D.\end{equation}
    For the upper bound, we start with the triangle inequality: with $\pi_0 := \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ the centered Gaussian with correct variance we have
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi_0) + D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\pi_0, \pi)\end{equation}
    by Proposition \ref{prop:quasimetric}(ii). To bound the first term, we take $\rho_t := \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma^t)$ and $v_t(x) := M_tx$ with $M_t := \frac{1}{2}\log \Sigma$, so that we have
    \begin{equation}\frac{d}{dt}\Sigma^t = M_t \Sigma^t + \Sigma^t M_t.\end{equation}
This is an admissible transport with time-invariant drift, and we use (\ref{eqn:proofrkhsnorminthebilinearcase}) to calculate
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:prooftriangleinequalityterm1}
    D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi_0) \leq \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}dt = \frac{1}{2}\|(\log \Sigma)A^{-1/2}\|_F \leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\lambda_{\text{min}}(A)}} \|\log \Sigma\|_F.
\end{equation}
If $m = 0$ the desired bound trivially holds; otherwise, write $u := \frac{m}{\|m\|}$. We define the affine maps
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofmeantermupperbound1}
    T_t(x) := (\1 + (s(t) - 1)uu^\top)x + h(t) u
\end{equation}
for $s: [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ and $h: [0, 1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ to be determined. We take $s(0) = s(1) = 1$, $h(0) = 0$, and $h(1) = \|m\|$ to ensure that if we define $\rho_t := (T_t)_\# \pi_0$ then $\rho_0 = \pi_0$ and $\rho_1 = \pi$. The Eulerian velocity of this path is $v_t(x) = M_tx + c_t$ for
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofmeantermupperbound2}
    M_t = \frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}uu^\top, \quad c_t = \left(h'(t) - \frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}h(t)\right)u
\end{equation}
and so by (\ref{eqn:proofrkhsnorminthebilinearcase}) we have
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:proofrkhsnorminthebilinearcase2}\|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}^2 = \beta \left(\frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}\right)^2 + \frac{1}{\alpha} \left(h'(t) - \frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}h(t)\right)^2,
\end{equation}
where we denote $\beta := u^\top A^{-1}u$.
Hence, if we change variables to
\begin{equation}y_t := \frac{1}{s(t)}, \quad z_t := \frac{h(t)}{\sqrt{\alpha \beta}s(t)}\end{equation}
then the derivatives satisfy
\begin{equation}\dot{y}_t = \frac{-s'(t)}{s(t)^2} , \quad \dot{z}_t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha \beta}} \frac{h'(t) s(t) - h(t) s'(t)}{s(t)^2}.\end{equation}
Using (\ref{eqn:proofrkhsnorminthebilinearcase2}) we find
\begin{equation}\int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} dt = \sqrt{\beta} \cdot \int_0^1 \frac{\sqrt{\dot{y}_t^2 + \dot{z}_t^2}}{y_t}dt.\end{equation}
This is exactly $\sqrt{\beta}$ times the length of the curve $w(t) := (z_t, y_t) \in \mathbb{H}$, where $\mathbb{H} := \{(x, y):\; y > 0\}$ is the Poincaré upper half-plane with metric $dw^2 = \frac{dx^2 + dy^2}{y^2}$. Using the \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poincaré_half-plane_model#Distance_calculation}{formula for the distance in the metric space $\mathbb{H}$}, if $w:[0, 1] \to \mathbb{H}$ is a geodesic then
\begin{align}\int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}dt &= \sqrt{\beta} \cdot d_{\mathbb{H}}(w(0), w(1)) \\&=\sqrt{\beta} \cdot 2 \sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{\|w(1) - w(0)\|_{{\mathbb{R}}^2}}{2\sqrt{y_0y_1}}\right)\\
&= \sqrt{\beta} \cdot 2\sinh^{-1}\left(\frac{\|m\|}{2\sqrt{\alpha \beta}}\right).
\end{align}
We take $w(t) = (z_t, y_t)$ to be any constant-speed hyperbolic geodesic from $w(0) = (0, 1)$ to $w(1) = (\|m\|/\sqrt{\alpha \beta}, 1)$ and define $s = 1/y$ and $h = \sqrt{\alpha \beta }z / y$ in order to ensure that this holds.
Since $\sinh^{-1}(z/2) \leq \log(1+z)$ and $\frac{1}{a}\leq \beta \leq \frac{1}{\lambda_{\text{min}}(A)}  $ we find
\begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\pi_0, \pi) \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{\text{min}}(A)}}\cdot 2 \log\left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{a}{\alpha}}\|m\|\right).\end{equation}
Combining this with (\ref{eqn:prooftriangleinequalityterm1}) and the triangle inequality, we find
\begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{\text{min}}(A)}} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_F + 2 \log \left(1 + \sqrt{\frac{a}{\alpha}}\|m\|\right)\right) \leq 2\sqrt{\kappa(A)} D.\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma:barrongaussiantogaussian}
    Let $\phi(z) = z$ (which satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}). Then, with $\|\cdot\|_*$ denoting the nuclear norm it holds that
    \begin{equation}\frac{1}{2}\left(\log\left(1 + \|m\|\right) + \frac{1}{2} \|\log \Sigma\|_*\right) \leq D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq 3\left(\log\left(1 + \|m\|\right) + \frac{1}{2} \|\log \Sigma\|_*\right).\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
As in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:steingaussiantogaussian}, since $v \in \mathcal{B}_\phi$ has $v(x) = Mx + c$ then any finite-length admissible transport starting from $\gamma_d$ remains Gaussian. Let $\rho_t, v_t, M_t, c_t, m_t, \Sigma_t, L_t$ be as in (\ref{eqn:prooftherhoandvofchoice}), (\ref{eqn:proofmatrixdynamics}), and (\ref{eqn:proofcholeskydynamics}), let $s_1(t), \ldots, s_d(t)$ be the singular values of $L_t$, and let us denote
    \begin{equation}\ell_t := \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \|M_t\|_* + \|c_t\|.\end{equation}
    If we replace the estimate (\ref{eqn:proofell2estimatesingularvalues}) with its $\ell_1$ version
    \begin{equation}\sum_{j=1}^d |u_j^\top M_tu_j| \leq \|M_t\|_*\end{equation}
    then we instead find that
    \begin{equation}\|\log s(1)\|_1 \leq \int_0^1 \left\|\frac{d}{dt}\log s(t)\right\|_1 dt \leq \int_0^1 \|M_t\|_* dt.\end{equation}
    In particular, since the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ are $s_1(1)^2, \ldots, s_d(1)^2$ we have
    \begin{equation}\frac{1}{2} \|\log \Sigma\|_* = \|\log s(1)\|_1 \leq \int_0^1 \ell_tdt.\end{equation}
    For the mean, with $r_t := \|m_t\|$ then
    \begin{equation}\dot{r}_t \leq \|M_tm_t\| + \|c_t\| \leq r_t \|M_t\|_{\operatorname{op}} + \|c_t\| \leq r_t \|M_t\|_* + \|c_t\| \leq (1 + r_t) \ell_t,\end{equation}
    or in other words
    \begin{equation}\frac{d}{dt} \log (1+r_t) \leq \ell_t.\end{equation}
    Integrating and applying $r_0 = 0$ yields
    \begin{equation}\log(1+\|m\|) \leq \int_0^1 \ell_t dt,\end{equation}
    and so we find
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \geq \max\left\{\frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_*,\; \log \left(1 + \|m\|\right)\right\}.\end{equation}
    For the upper bound, we apply the same triangle inequality
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_0) + D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi_0, \pi)\end{equation}
    with $\pi_0 := \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$. For the first term, we use the interpolation $\rho_t = \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma^t)$ and $v_t(x) = M_tx$ with $M_t = \frac{1}{2}\log \Sigma$ to see that
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_0) \leq \frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_*.\end{equation}
    Note that in light of our lower bound, the above is equality. 
    
    For the mean term in the upper bound, fix $s: [0, 1] \to (0, \infty)$ and $h: [0, 1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ with $s(0) = s(1) = 1$, $h(0) = 0$, and $h(1) = \|m\|$ to be determined. Define $T_t$ as in (\ref{eqn:proofmeantermupperbound1}) and $\rho_t := (T_t)_\# \pi_0$, and let $v_t(x) = M_tx + c_t$ for $M_t, c_t$ as in (\ref{eqn:proofmeantermupperbound2}). This is an admissible transport from $\pi_0$ to $\pi$ with
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofbarronnormformeanupperbound}
        \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \left|\frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}\right| + \left|h'(t) - \frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}h(t)\right|.
    \end{equation}
    If $m= 0$ then we are done, and for $m \neq 0$ we take
    \begin{equation}s(t) := \begin{cases}
        (1 + \|m\|)^{-3t} & 0 \leq t < \frac{1}{3},\\
        (1 + \|m\|)^{-1} & \frac{1}{3} \leq t < \frac{2}{3}, \\
        (1 + \|m\|)^{-3(1-t)} & \frac{2}{3} \leq t \leq 1,
    \end{cases} \qquad h(t) := \begin{cases}
       0 & 0 \leq t < \frac{1}{3},\\
       \frac{(3t-1)\|m\|}{1 + \|m\|} & \frac{1}{3} \leq t < \frac{2}{3}, \\
        \|m\|s(t) & \frac{2}{3} \leq t \leq 1.
    \end{cases} \end{equation}
    Then, we have $s(0) = s(1) = 1$, $h(0) = 0$, and $h(1) = \|m\|$. Furthermore, using (\ref{eqn:proofbarronnormformeanupperbound}) we have
    \begin{equation}\|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \begin{cases}
     \left|\frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}\right|   & 0 \leq t < \frac{1}{3},\\
       |h'(t)| & \frac{1}{3} \leq t < \frac{2}{3}, \\
        \left|\frac{s'(t)}{s(t)}\right|  & \frac{2}{3} \leq t \leq 1,
    \end{cases}\end{equation}
    where $h = 0$ on the first interval, $s' = 0$ on the second, and $h' - \frac{s'}{s}h = 0$ on the third. Hence, since $|\frac{s'}{s} | = |(\log s)'|= 3\log(1+\|m\|)$ on the first and third intervals we have
    \begin{align}
        D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi_0, \pi) &\leq \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} dt \\&\leq \frac{1}{3} \cdot (3 \log(1 + \|m\|)) + \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{3\|m\|}{1 + \|m\|} + \frac{1}{3} \cdot (3 \log(1+\|m\|)) \\&\leq 3 \log(1+\|m\|),
    \end{align}
    where we used that $\frac{z}{1+z} \leq \log(1+z)$. Thus,
    \begin{equation}D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq \frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_* + 3 \log(1 + \|m\|) .\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{remark:steinbarronlineargaussiantogaussianmeanmovement}
The transports realizing the upper bounds for linear Stein and linear Barron are almost the same: they both use the triangle inequality (i.e. they move the mean and covariance in separate steps) and they use the exact same transport to move the covariance. Furthermore, the transports which move the mean both use a compress-translate-expand strategy to achieve logarithmic dependence on $\|m\|$. This is exactly analogous to the structure of a hyperbolic geodesic, and it matches the fact that hyperbolic distance between horizontally-separated points is logarithmic in the Euclidean separation.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma:reverseOUgaussiantogaussian}
    If we denote $C_a := (1-a^2)\1_d + a^2 \Sigma$ then the following bounds hold:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{(Wasserstein).} With $\mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) = \int_0^\infty \|\nabla \log \frac{P_\tau^* \pi}{\gamma_d}\|_{L^2(P_\tau^* \pi)} d\tau$, we have
        \begin{equation}W_2(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq \mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) \leq \frac{\pi}{2} W_2(\gamma_d, \pi).\end{equation}

        \item \textbf{(Stein).} With $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{H}_k$ for $k(x, y) = (1 + \left\langle x, y\right\rangle)\1_d$, we have 
        \begin{equation}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\pi) \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left( \int_0^1 \|C_a^{-1}m\| da + \frac{1}{2} \|\log \Sigma\|_F\right).\end{equation}
        \item \textbf{(Barron).} With $\mathcal{B} = \mathcal{B}_\phi$ for $\phi(z) = z$, we have \begin{equation}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi) = \int_0^1 \|C_a^{-1}m\| da + \frac{1}{2} \|\log \Sigma\|_* .\end{equation}
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Letting $a := e^{-\tau}$, we know that
    $P_\tau^*\pi = \mathcal{N}(am, C_a)$
    and therefore that
    \begin{equation}\left(\nabla \log \frac{P_\tau^*\pi}{\gamma_d}\right)(x) = x - C_a^{-1}(x - am) = a^2 (\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}x + aC^{-1}_am.\end{equation}
    This is an affine drift, and we will now compute the respective tangent norms.

    For the Wasserstein case, if $X_a \sim \mathcal{N}(am, C_a)$ then
    \begin{equation}\left(\nabla \log \frac{P_\tau^*\pi}{\gamma_d}\right)(X_a) = am + a^2 (\Sigma - \1_d) C_a^{-1} (X_a - am)\end{equation}
    and so we use $d\tau = -da / a$ to find
    \begin{align}\mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) &= \int_0^1 \left(\|m\|^2 + a^2 \|(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1/2}\|_F^2\right)^{1/2}da \\&= \int_0^1 \left(\|m\|^2 + \sum_{j=1}^d \left|\frac{a(\sigma_j^2 - 1)}{\sqrt{1 -a^2 + a^2\sigma_j^2}}\right|^2\right)^{1/2}da,\end{align}
    where $\sigma^2_1, \ldots, \sigma_d^2$ are the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$.
    Now, for any $a \in [0, 1)$ and $\sigma > 0$ we have that
    \begin{align}
        0 &\leq (1 - a^2(\sigma + 1))^2 \\&= 1 - 2a^2(\sigma + 1) + a^4 (\sigma + 1)^2 \\&= 1 + a^2 (\sigma^2 - 1) - a^2(1-a^2)(\sigma+1)^2,
    \end{align}
    and so $1-a^2 + a^2\sigma^2  \geq a^2(1-a^2)(\sigma + 1)^2$. In other words,
    \begin{equation}\frac{a^2(\sigma + 1)^2}{{1 - a^2 + a^2\sigma^2}} \leq \frac{1}{{1 - a^2}}\end{equation}
    and so multiplying by $(\sigma - 1)^2$ implies the inequality
    \begin{align}
       \left|\frac{a(\sigma_j^2 - 1)}{\sqrt{1 -a^2 + a^2\sigma_j^2}}\right|^2 \leq \frac{(\sigma_j - 1)^2}{1 - a^2} \quad (\forall a \in [0, 1)).
    \end{align}
    By Lemma \ref{lemma:W2distancebetweengaussians} we know $W_2(\gamma_d, \pi) = (\|m\|^2 + \sum_{j=1}^d (\sigma_j - 1)^2)^{1/2}$, and so
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) \leq W_2(\gamma_d, \pi) \cdot \int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-a^2}} da = \frac{\pi}{2}W_2(\gamma_d, \pi).
    \end{align}
    The lower bound $W_2(\gamma_d, \pi) \leq  \mathcal{E}_{W_2}(\pi) $ is obvious because $W_2$ is the infimum over all transports.

    For the Stein case with $k(x, y) = (1 + \left\langle x, y\right\rangle)\1_d$, we know $d\tau = -da / a$ and so
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsteinreverseouenergygaussian}
        \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\pi) = \int_0^1 \left(\|C_a^{-1}m\|^2 + a^2 \|(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}\|_F^2\right)^{1/2}da ,
    \end{equation}
    which implies that
    \begin{equation}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\pi) \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\int_0^1 \left(\|C_a^{-1}m\| + a\|(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}\|_F \right)da.\end{equation}
    Now, since $\frac{d}{da}\log C_a = 2a(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}$ (note that $\Sigma - \1_d$ and $C_a$ commute) and $\log C_0 = 0, \log C_1 = \log \Sigma$, we have
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofthefrobeniustriangleinequalitystuff}
        \frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_F = \left\|\int_0^1 a(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}da\right\|_F \leq \int_0^1 a\|(\Sigma - \1_d)C^{-1}_a\|_F da.
    \end{equation}

    For the Barron case with $\phi(z) = z$, we have
    \begin{equation}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi) = \int_0^1 \left(\|C_a^{-1}m\| + a\|(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}\|_*\right)da,\end{equation}
after which the result follows from the equalities
\begin{align}
    \int_0^1 a\|(\Sigma - \1_d)C_a^{-1}\|_* da = \sum_{j=1}^d \int_0^1 \frac{a|\sigma_j^2 - 1|}{1 +a^2(\sigma_j^2-1)}da = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^d |\log \sigma_j^2| = \frac{1}{2}\|\log \Sigma\|_*.
\end{align}
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{example:reverseOUsteinGaussiansuboptimality}
Let $\pi = \mathcal{N}(0, \Sigma)$ for $\Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(e^{d/\sqrt{1}}, e^{d/\sqrt{2}}, \ldots, e^{d/\sqrt{d}})$. Then, with $k(x, y) = (1 + \left\langle x, y\right\rangle)\1_d$ we have
\begin{equation}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}\left(\pi\right) \geq  \frac{\sqrt{\log d}}{24} \cdot \|\log \Sigma\|_F \geq \frac{\sqrt{\log d}}{12} \cdot D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi).\end{equation}
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
In the centered case, from (\ref{eqn:proofsteinreverseouenergygaussian}) we find that if $\sigma^2_1, \ldots, \sigma_d^2 \geq 1$ are the eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ then
    \begin{equation}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}\left(\pi\right) = \int_0^1 \left(\sum_{j=1}^d \left(\frac{a(\sigma_j^2 - 1)}{1 + a^2(\sigma_j^2 - 1)}\right)^2\right)^{1/2} da.\end{equation}
    For $a \in [\sigma_j^{-1}, \sigma_{j+1}^{-1})$ and all $i \leq j$ we have $a^2(\sigma_i^2 - 1) \geq 1 - e^{-d/\sqrt{i}} \geq 1 - e^{-\sqrt{d}} \geq \frac{1}{2}$, and so
    \begin{equation}\frac{a(\sigma_i^2 - 1)}{1 + a^2(\sigma_i^2 - 1)} = \frac{1}{a} \cdot \frac{a^2(\sigma_i^2 - 1)}{1 + a^2(\sigma_i^2 - 1)} \geq \frac{1}{3a}.\end{equation}
    Plugging this in and denoting $\sigma_{d+1}^2 = e^{d / \sqrt{d+1}}$ for simplicity, we split the integral to get
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}\left(\pi\right) &\geq \sum_{j=1}^d\int_{\sigma_j^{-1}}^{\sigma_{j+1}^{-1}} \left(\sum_{i=1}^j \left(\frac{a(\sigma_i^2 - 1)}{1 + a^2(\sigma_i^2 - 1)}\right)^2\right)^{1/2} da
\geq \sum_{j=1}^d \int_{\sigma_j^{-1}}^{\sigma_{j+1}^{-1}} \frac{\sqrt{j}}{3a}da \\
    &= \frac{1}{3}\sum_{j=1}^d \sqrt{j} \cdot \log\left(\frac{\sigma_j}{\sigma_{j+1}}\right)
    = \frac{1}{6}\sum_{j=1}^d \sqrt{j} \cdot \left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{j}} - \frac{d}{\sqrt{j+1}}\right) \\
    &= \frac{d}{6} \sum_{j=1}^d \left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{j}{j+1}}\right) \geq \frac{d}{6} \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{2(1+j)} \\
    &\geq \frac{d}{24} \sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{j},
\end{align}
where we used that $1 - \sqrt{\frac{z}{1+z}} \geq \frac{1}{2(1+z)}$ for $z > 0$. On the other hand, we have
\begin{equation}\|\log \Sigma\|_F = d\left(\sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{j}\right)^{1/2}\end{equation}
and so
\begin{equation}\frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{H}_k}\left(\pi\right)}{\|\log\Sigma\|_F} \geq \frac{1}{24}\left(\sum_{j=1}^d \frac{1}{j}\right)^{1/2} \geq \frac{\sqrt{\log d}}{24}.\end{equation}
The comparison with $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \pi)$ comes from (\ref{eqn:prooftriangleinequalityterm1}).
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lemma:epsilonfirstorder}
Let $k: {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^{d \times d}$ satisfy Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel}.
    Suppose that $\varphi \in C_c^\infty({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, $\mu \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, and $w : [0, 1] \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ satisfy the following:
    \begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $L :=   
        \sup_{\|u\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} \leq 1} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle u, \nabla \varphi\right\rangle d\mu
        \in [0, \infty)$.
        \item[(ii)] $w$ is jointly measurable and each $w_t$ is globally-Lipschitz with $\int_0^1 (|w_t(0)| + \operatorname{Lip}(w_t))dt <\infty$.
    \end{enumerate}
    For each $\varepsilon > 0$ define $\nu_\varepsilon := \operatorname{Law}(X_1)$ according to the flow
    \begin{equation}\dot{X}_t = \varepsilon w_t(X_t), \quad X_0 \sim \mu.\end{equation}
    Then, with $F_1(x) := \int_0^1 w_t(x) dt$ we have
    \begin{equation}\liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{\left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi, F_1\right\rangle d\mu\right|}{L}\end{equation}
    where if $L = 0$ then the right hand side is $\infty$ if $\left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi, F_1\right\rangle d\mu\right| > 0$ and 0 otherwise.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
For $\rho \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we denote
    \begin{equation}
        g_\rho := \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} k(\cdot, x) \nabla \varphi(x) d\rho(x) \in \mathcal{H}_k, \quad G(\rho) := \|g_\rho\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}.
    \end{equation}
    By the reproducing property, we know that
    \begin{equation}
        G(\rho) = \sup_{\|u\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} \leq 1}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle u, \nabla \varphi\right\rangle d\rho
    \end{equation}
    and so $G(\mu) = L$. Moreover, the reproducing property also ensures
    \begin{equation}
        G(\rho)^2 = \iint_{{\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi(x), k(x, y) \nabla \varphi(y)\right\rangle d\rho(x) d\rho(y).
    \end{equation}
