    This integrand is bounded and continuous since $k$ is jointly continuous and $\nabla \varphi$ is compactly supported, and so $G$ is narrowly continuous. 

Assumption (ii) implies the Carathéodory conditions, yielding a unique flow. 
    Let $T_t^\varepsilon$ be the flow of $\varepsilon w_t$, so that $\nu_\varepsilon = (T_1^\varepsilon)_\# \mu$. For each $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$ we know that $T_t^\varepsilon(x) \to x$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ uniformly in $t$ by Grönwall's lemma. By integrating the continuity equation, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{\varphi(T_1^\varepsilon(x)) - \varphi(x)}{\varepsilon} = \int_0^1 \left\langle \nabla \varphi(T_t^\varepsilon(x)) , w_t(T_t^\varepsilon(x))\right\rangle dt.
    \end{equation}
    Denoting $K := \operatorname{spt}(\nabla \varphi)$, then by compactness of $K$ we know the integrand is bounded in absolute value by
    \begin{equation}
        \|\nabla \varphi\|_\infty \sup_{y \in K}|w_t(y)| \leq C_K(|w_t(0)| + \operatorname{Lip}(w_t)).
    \end{equation}
    This bound is integrable in $t$ by (ii) and is independent of $x, \varepsilon$, which by dominated convergence and integration over $\mu$ implies
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:proofdualitylowerbound}\lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\nu_{\varepsilon} - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu}{\varepsilon} = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi, F_1\right\rangle d\mu.
    \end{equation}
    If we define 
    \begin{equation}
        \omega(r) := \sup_{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \rho) \leq r} G(\rho)
    \end{equation}
    then since $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}$ convergence implies narrow convergence (Proposition \ref{prop:quasimetric}) and $G$ is narrowly continuous we have
    \begin{equation}
        \lim_{r \downarrow 0}\omega(r) = G(\mu) = L.
    \end{equation}
    Let us denote
    \begin{equation}
        \ell := \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}.
    \end{equation}
    If $\ell = \infty$ the claim is immediate, and otherwise we take $\varepsilon_n \downarrow 0$ realizing the $\liminf$ and admissible curves $(v_t^n, \rho_t^n)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ transporting $\mu$ to $\nu_{\varepsilon_n} $ for which
    \begin{equation}
        A_n := \int_0^1 \|v_t^n\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} dt \leq D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_{\varepsilon_n}) + \varepsilon_n^2.
    \end{equation}
    Hence, $A_n \to 0$ and moreover $D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \rho_t^n) \leq \int_0^t \|v_s^n\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}ds \leq A_n$. Therefore, $G(\rho_t^n) \leq \omega(A_n)$ and so
    \begin{equation}
        \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\nu_{\varepsilon_n} - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\varphi d\mu\right| \leq \int_0^1 \|v_t^n\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} G(\rho_t^n) dt \leq A_n \omega(A_n)
    \end{equation}
    by the continuity equation and duality. Dividing by $\varepsilon_n$, we find
    \begin{equation}
        \left|\frac{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\nu_{\varepsilon_n} - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\mu}{\varepsilon_n} \right| \leq \frac{A_n}{\varepsilon_n} \omega(A_n) \leq \left(\frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_{\varepsilon_n})}{\varepsilon_n} + \varepsilon_n\right) \omega(A_n).
    \end{equation}
    Taking the $n \to \infty$ limit and using $\omega(A_n) \to L$ along with (\ref{eqn:proofdualitylowerbound}) implies the claim.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma:rkhslowerboundspherical}
     Let $d \geq 3$ and $\mu \in \mathcal{P}_2({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ be rotationally-invariant and not $\delta_0$. Let $w: [0, 1] \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ be jointly measurable with each $w_t$ globally-Lipschitz with $\int_0^1 (|w_t(0)| + \operatorname{Lip}(w_t))dt < \infty$, and for $\varepsilon > 0$ define $\nu_\varepsilon := \operatorname{Law}(X_1)$ according to the flow
    \begin{equation}\dot{X}_t = \varepsilon w_t(X_t), \quad X_0 \sim \mu.\end{equation}
Then, for any $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel} with $\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x) \in (0, \infty)$ we have
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:sphericalclaimquadratic}\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \cdot \frac{ \sum_{\substack{n \in {\mathbb{N}}}} \sqrt{a_{n,d}}A_n}{\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} {|x|^2}d\mu(x)}} ,
\end{equation}
where we define
\begin{align}a_{n,d} &:= \frac{1}{n(n+d-2)} {n+d-2 \choose n},\\ A_n &:= \sup_{\substack{Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d \\ \|Y\|_{L^2(\sigma)} = 1}} \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla_x \left[|x|^2 Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right)\right], \int_0^1 w_t(x)dt\right\rangle d\mu(x)\right|\end{align}
for $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ the space of degree-$n$ spherical harmonics (see \cite[Definition 2.7]{atkinson2012spherical}) and $\sigma$ the uniform probability measure on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
Note that for any $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$ we have the spherical gradient identity
\begin{equation}\nabla_x \left[|x|^2 Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right)\right] = 2Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right) {x} + |x| \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right).\end{equation}
Alternatively, if $F_1(x) := \int_0^1 w_t(x) dt$ is $C^1$ and $DF_1$ is sufficiently integrable we can apply integration by parts to get
\begin{equation}A_n = \sup_{\substack{Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d \\ \|Y\|_{L^2(\sigma)} = 1}} \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right) \left[(d+1)x^\top F_1(x) + x^\top DF_1(x) x - |x|^2 \operatorname{div}F_1(x)\right] d\mu(x)\right|.\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
In the statement and in what follows, we set $|x|^2Y(x/|x|)$, $h(R)/R$, and quantities like it to equal 0 when $x,R=0$.
Let $F_1(x) := \int_0^1 w_t(x) dt$, which we know lies in $L^2(\mu; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ by the assumptions on $w$.
By Lemma \ref{lemma:epsilonfirstorder}, we find that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericaldageneralsteinlowerbound}
    \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \sup_{\varphi} \frac{|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d } \left\langle \nabla \varphi, F_1\right\rangle d\mu|}{\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d\times {\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi(x), k(x, y) \nabla \varphi(y)\right\rangle d\mu(x) d\mu(y)}}
\end{equation}
where the supremum ranges over $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$. We will choose $\varphi$ as a weighted sum of spherical harmonics.

Let $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ be the linear space of degree-$n$ spherical harmonics on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ (see \cite[Definition 2.7]{atkinson2012spherical}) and $N_{n, d} := \operatorname{dim}\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ its dimension, which by (2.10) of \cite{atkinson2012spherical} satisfies
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalharmonicdimscaling}
    N_{n, d} = \frac{(2n+d - 2)(n+d-3)!}{n!(d-2)!} = \frac{2n+d-2}{(d-2)!} \prod_{j=1}^{d-3}(n+j) \quad (\forall n \in {\mathbb{N}}, 
    \;d \geq 3)
\end{equation}
with $N_{0, d} = 1$ and $N_{n, 2} = 2$ for all $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$. For each $n$, let $\{Y_{n,j}:\; 1 \leq j \leq N_{n,d}\}$ be an $L^2(\sigma)$-orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$.

Since $X \sim \mu$ is rotationally-invariant we may write $X = R\Theta$ for $\Theta \sim \sigma$ drawn uniformly on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ independently of $R \in [0, \infty)$. Fix $h \in C^\infty_c((0, \infty))$ to be nonnegative with $\mathbb{E}[h(R)/R] > 0$ and set $h(0) = 0$.
We consider $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ as a representation of $O(d)$, where each $Q \in O(d)$ is represented by the automorphism $\rho_n(Q)$ on $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ sending $Y \mapsto Y \circ Q^\top$. 
For each degree $n$ we define the linear map
\begin{equation}J_n: \mathbb{Y}_n^d \to L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d), \quad (J_nY)(x) := \nabla_x \left[h(|x|) Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right) \right].\end{equation}
By the chain rule, for every $Q \in O(d)$ and $Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d$ we have
\begin{equation}J_n(Y \circ Q^\top) = Q \circ (J_n Y) \circ Q^\top.\end{equation}
Since $k$ is rotation-equivariant and $\mu$ is rotation-invariant, we know that the kernel integral operator $\mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}$ commutes with $f \mapsto Q \circ f \circ Q^\top$ and so for any $Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d$ and $Z \in \mathbb{Y}_m^d$ we have
\begin{equation}\left\langle J_n(Y \circ Q^\top), \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu} J_m(Z \circ Q^\top)\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)} = \left\langle J_nY, \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}J_mZ\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)},\end{equation}
or in other words that
\begin{equation}
    (J_n^* \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}J_m) \rho_m(Q) = \rho_n(Q) (J_n^* \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}J_m) \quad (\forall Q \in O(d)).
\end{equation}
Hence, $J_n^* \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}J_m$ is an $O(d)$-equivariant linear map from the representation $(\mathbb{Y}_m^d, \rho_m)$ to $(\mathbb{Y}_n^d, \rho_n)$. 
By \cite[Theorem 2.10]{atkinson2012spherical} these representations are irreducible. By (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalharmonicdimscaling}) and $d \geq 3$ we know that $N_{n,d}$ is strictly increasing in $n$, which means that $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$, $\mathbb{Y}_m^d$ are not isomorphic for $n \neq m$. Therefore, Schur's lemma from representation theory implies that
\begin{equation}J_n^* \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}J_m = \delta_{n,m} q_n \1_{\mathbb{Y}_n^d} \quad(\forall n, m \in {\mathbb{N}})\end{equation}
for some scalars $q_n \geq 0$. Hence,
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalschurclaim}
    \left\langle J_nY, \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}J_mZ\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)} = \delta_{n,m} q_n \left\langle Y, Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma)} \quad (\forall Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d, Z \in \mathbb{Y}_m^d).
\end{equation}
Furthermore, spherical differentiation yields
\begin{equation}(J_nY)(r\theta) = h'(r) Y(\theta) \theta + \frac{h(r)}{r}\nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Y(\theta),\end{equation}
which implies that for every $Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d, Z \in \mathbb{Y}_{m}^d$ we have
\begin{align}
    \left\langle J_nY, J_mZ\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)} &= \mathbb{E}_{R, \Theta}\left\langle h'(R) Y(\Theta) \Theta + \frac{h(R)}{R} \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y(\Theta), \; h'(R) Z(\Theta) \Theta + \frac{h(R)}{R} \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z(\Theta)\right\rangle \\
    &= \mathbb{E}_{R, \Theta}\left[h'(R)^2 Y(\Theta) {Z(\Theta)}\right] + \mathbb{E}_{R, \Theta}\left[\frac{h(R)^2}{R^2} \left\langle \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Y(\Theta), \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Z(\Theta)\right\rangle_{\mathbb{R}^d}\right],
\end{align}
where the cross-terms vanish in the second line because $\nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y(\Theta)$ (which is tangent to the sphere at $\Theta$) and $\Theta$ (which is normal to the sphere at $\Theta$) are orthogonal, and similarly for $Z$. By independence of $R, \Theta$ we find 
\begin{align}
    \left\langle J_nY, J_mZ\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)} &= \mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] \left\langle Y, Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma)} + \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h(R)^2}{R^2}\right] \left\langle \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Y, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma; \mathbb{R}^d)} \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] \left\langle Y, Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma)} + m(m+d-2)\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h(R)^2}{R^2}\right] \left\langle Y, Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma)},
\end{align}
where the second line follows from equation (3.20) of \cite{atkinson2012spherical}. Combining this with the fact that $\mathbb{Y}_n^d \perp \mathbb{Y}_m^d$ for $n \neq m$ (see \cite[Corollary 2.15]{atkinson2012spherical}), for every $Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d, Z \in \mathbb{Y}_m^d$ we find
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericalinnerproductnoTkmu}
    \left\langle J_nY, J_mZ\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)} = \delta_{n,m} \left(\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2) \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h(R)^2}{R^2}\right]\right) \left\langle Y, Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma)} .
\end{equation}
Hence, the collection
\begin{equation}\left\{\frac{J_nY_{n,j}}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2)\mathbb{E}[h(R)^2/R^2]}}:\quad n \in {\mathbb{N}},\; 1 \leq j \leq N_{n,d}\right\}\end{equation}
is an orthonormal family in $L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d)$. Therefore, since $\mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}$ is positive and trace-class we know
\begin{align}\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}) &\geq \sum_{n \in {\mathbb{N}}} \sum_{j=1}^{N_{n,d}} \left\langle \frac{J_nY_{n,j}}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2)\mathbb{E}[h(R)^2/R^2]}}, \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}\frac{J_nY_{n,j}}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2)\mathbb{E}[h(R)^2/R^2]}}\right\rangle
\\ &= \sum_{n \in {\mathbb{N}}} \frac{N_{n,d}q_n}{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2)\mathbb{E}[h(R)^2/R^2]},
\end{align}
where in the second line we applied (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalschurclaim}). In particular, using that $\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}) = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x)$ implies that 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericaltracelowerbound}
    \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\operatorname{tr} k(x, x) d\mu(x) \geq \sum_{n \in {\mathbb{N}}} \frac{N_{n,d}q_n}{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2)\mathbb{E}[h(R)^2/R^2]}.
\end{equation}
Now, for each $n$ let us write
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericalsupremumwithcutoffh}
A_n^{(h)} := \sup_{\substack{Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d \\ \|Y\|_{L^2(\sigma)} = 1}} \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle J_nY, F_1\right\rangle d\mu\right|\end{equation}
and let us take $(W_{n,\ell}^{(h)})_{\ell \in {\mathbb{N}}} \subseteq \mathbb{Y}_n^d$ to be approximate maximizers with $\|W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\|_{L^2(\sigma) }=1$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericalapproximatemaximizers}
A_{n,\ell}^{(h)} := \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle J_nW_{n,\ell}^{(h)}, F_1\right\rangle d\mu \geq A_n^{(h)} - \frac{1}{\ell},\end{equation}
where we note that $J_n$ depends on $h$.
By equation (3.20) of \cite{atkinson2012spherical} we know that
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalsobolevnormofZ}
    \|\nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\|_{L^2(\sigma; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}^2 = n(n+d-2).
\end{equation}
Now, for each degree $n$ and each $\ell$ we define the function $\varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)}: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
\begin{equation}\varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)}(r\theta) := h(r) W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}(\theta). \end{equation}
Since $h$ vanishes near $0$ and $W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}$ is a spherical polynomial we know $\varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)} \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$, and by definition we have
$\nabla \varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)} = J_n W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}$. In particular, applying (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalschurclaim}) with $n=m$ and $Y=Z=W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}$ implies
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalRKHSnorm2}
   \left\langle \nabla \varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)}, \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}\nabla \varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} = q_n \|W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^2 = q_n
\end{equation}
using that $\|W_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\|_{L^2(\sigma)} = 1$, and so the scalars $q_n$ are identified. 

We proceed by fixing a finite subset $\Lambda \subseteq {\mathbb{N}}$ with $q_n > 0$ for all $n \in \Lambda$ and defining
\begin{equation}\varphi^{(\ell, h)} := \sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{ A_{n,\ell}^{(h)}}{q_n}\varphi_{n,\ell}^{(h)} \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d).\end{equation}
By definition of $A_{n,\ell}^{(h)}$ and (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalschurclaim}),(\ref{eqn:proofsphericalRKHSnorm2}) we have
\begin{equation}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi^{(\ell, h)}, F_1\right\rangle d\mu = \sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{ (A_{n,\ell}^{(h)})^2}{q_n}= \left\langle \nabla \varphi^{(\ell, h)}, \mathcal{T}_{k, \mu}\nabla \varphi^{(\ell, h)}\right\rangle_{L^2(\mu; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} .\end{equation}
The Stein lower bound of (\ref{eqn:proofsphericaldageneralsteinlowerbound}) therefore implies that
\begin{equation}\liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \left(\sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{(A_{n,\ell}^{(h)})^2}{q_n}\right)^{1/2},\end{equation}
which we combine with (\ref{eqn:proofsphericaltracelowerbound}) to find that
\begin{align}\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}&\geq \left(\sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{(A_{n,\ell}^{(h)})^2}{q_n}\right)^{1/2}\\&\quad  \cdot \left(\sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{N_{n,d}q_n}{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2)\mathbb{E}[h(R)^2/R^2]}\right)^{1/2}.\end{align}
Applying Cauchy-Schwarz in ${\mathbb{R}}^{|\Lambda|}$, we find that
for all finite $\Lambda \subseteq {\mathbb{N}}$ with $q_n > 0$ for $n \in \Lambda$ we have
\begin{equation}
\sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{\sqrt{N_{n,d}} \left|A_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\right|}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2) \mathbb{E}[h(R)^2 / R^2]}}.
\end{equation}
If $q_n = 0$ but $A_{n,\ell}^{(h)}\neq 0$ then the left hand side must be infinite, and so this holds for all finite $\Lambda \subseteq {\mathbb{N}}$. On any such finite subset we may take $\ell \to \infty$ and apply (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalapproximatemaximizers}) to get
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalsteinlowerboundfull}
    \sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{\sqrt{N_{n,d}} \cdot A_n^{(h)}}{\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[h'(R)^2] + n(n+d-2) \mathbb{E}[h(R)^2 / R^2]}}.
\end{equation}

We will now take $h(r)$ to be smooth compactly-supported approximations to $h_\star(r) = r^2$. Indeed, we define \begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericalsupremumwithcutoffdefinitionofJstar}
J_n^\star: \mathbb{Y}_n^d \to L^2(\mu; \mathbb{R}^d), \quad (J_n^\star Y)(x) := \nabla_x \left[h_\star(|x|) Y\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right)\right] ,\end{equation}
take $\chi \in C_c^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ with $0 \leq \chi \leq 1$ equal to $1$ on $[-1, 1]$ and equal to $0$ outside $[-2, 2]$, and set
\begin{equation}
    h_j(r) := r^2 \chi(r/j) (1-\chi(jr)).
\end{equation}
Then, $|h'_j(r)| + |h_j(r)/r| \lesssim r$ uniformly in $r$ and converge pointwise to $2r$ and $r$, respectively. By dominated convergence, $h_j'/2, h_j/r \to r$ in $\operatorname{L}^2(\operatorname{Law}(R))$. Thus, if we define $A_n^{(h_j)}$ and $J_n^{(h_j)}$ analogously to (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalsupremumwithcutoffh}) and (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalsupremumwithcutoffdefinitionofJstar}) then we have $J_n^{(h_j)} \to J_n^\star$ uniformly on the unit ball of $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$. 
Therefore,
\begin{equation}A_n^{(h_j)} \to \sup_{\substack{Y \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d \\ \|Y\|_{L^2(\sigma)} = 1}} \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle J_n^\star Y, F_1\right\rangle d\mu\right| =: A_n \quad (\forall n \in {\mathbb{N}}).\end{equation}
We also find that
\begin{equation}M_2(\mu)^2 := \mathbb{E}_{X \sim \mu}|X|^2 = \frac{1}{4}\mathbb{E}[h'_\star(R)^2] = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{h_\star(R)^2}{R^2}\right],\end{equation}
which we plug into (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalsteinlowerboundfull}) to see
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalsteinlowerboundfull3}
    \sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\mu(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{1}{M_2(\mu)}\sum_{n \in \Lambda} \frac{\sqrt{N_{n,d}} \cdot A_n}{\sqrt{4+ n(n+d-2) }}.
\end{equation}
This holds for any finite subset $\Lambda \subseteq {\mathbb{N}}$, and we may increase it monotonically to hold for any subset $\Lambda \subseteq {\mathbb{N}}$. The claim (\ref{eqn:sphericalclaimquadratic}) then follows from combining (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalharmonicdimscaling}) and $2n+d-2 \geq n+d-2$ to find
\begin{equation}\frac{N_{n,d}}{4 + n(n+d-2)} \geq \frac{N_{n,d}}{5n(n+d-2)} \geq \frac{1}{5n(n+d-2)} {n+d-2 \choose d-2} \quad (\forall n \in {\mathbb{N}}, \; d \geq 3).\end{equation}
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixupperandlowerboundsforsingleindexgaussianflows}
   Fix $d \geq 3$. Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be $C^{d+2}$ with $\|\phi'\|_{C^{d+1}} < \infty$ and fix $\sigma > 0$ and $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. For each $\varepsilon > 0$ define $\nu_\varepsilon := \operatorname{Law}(X_\varepsilon)$ according to the flow 
    \begin{equation}
        \dot{X}_t = \sigma u \phi(\left\langle X_t, \theta\right\rangle), \quad X_0 \sim \gamma_d.
    \end{equation}
    If we denote the quantity
    \begin{equation}
        Q := \inf_{\substack{k \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}} \\ k \text{ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel}} \\ \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\gamma_d(x) \in (0, \infty)}} \left\{ \sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\gamma_d(x)} \cdot \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right\}
    \end{equation}
     and use the probabilist's Hermite\footnote{By this, we mean that $\{\operatorname{He}_j\}_j$ are the monic Hermite polynomials with $\left\langle \operatorname{He}_i, \operatorname{He}_j\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_1)} = \delta_{i,j} \cdot j!$. In particular, there is the decomposition $\phi = \sum_{j=0}^\infty {\hat{\phi}_j}/{j!}\operatorname{He}_j$ in $L^2(\gamma_1)$.} coefficients $\hat{\phi}_j := \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi(\xi) \operatorname{He}_j(\xi)]$ to define
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:appendixdefinitionofDpphicforthegaussianbounds}
        \mathcal{D}_\phi(c) := \sum_{n = 0}^\infty N_{n,d}  \left(\sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\n+2\ell \geq 1}}^\infty \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^{m}\ell! \Gamma(n + \ell + d/2)}\right) \cdot |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}|^2 \cdot \left(c^2 + (1-c^2) \frac{n(n + d - 2)}{m^2(d-1)}\right)\right)^{1/2}
    \end{equation}
    with $m = n+2\ell$,
    then there are the lower and upper bounds
    \begin{equation}
        \sigma \mathcal{D}_\phi(\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle) \leq Q \leq \sqrt{2} \sigma \mathcal{D}_\phi(\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle) .
    \end{equation}
    The lower bound holds under the weaker assumption that $\phi$ is globally-Lipschitz.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Fix $w : {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ globally-Lipschitz. 
    For every $m \in {\mathbb{N}}$, the $m^{th}$ scalar Hermite eigenspace $\mathcal{H}_m$ splits orthogonally as
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{H}_m = \bigoplus_{\substack{n, \ell \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\} \\ m = n + 2\ell}} \mathcal{H}_{n,\ell}
    \end{equation}
    where each $\mathcal{H}_{n,\ell}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ (here, $n$ is the angular momentum/spherical harmonic degree and $\ell$ is the radial index). Choose the orthonormal basis $\{P_{n,\ell, i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}}$ of $\mathcal{H}_{n,\ell}$ w.r.t. $L^2(\gamma_d)$
    given by 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofthe}
        P_{n,\ell,i}(r\omega) := (-1)^\ell\sqrt{\frac{\ell! \Gamma(d/2)}{2^n \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}} r^n L_\ell^{(n+d/2 - 1)} (r^2/2) Y_{n,i}(\omega)
    \end{equation}
    for $r \geq 0$ and $\omega \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, where $\{Y_{n,i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}}$ is the $L^2(\sigma)$-orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ from the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:rkhslowerboundspherical} for $\sigma$ the uniform probability measure on the sphere, and $L_\ell^{(\alpha)}$ are the generalized Laguerre polynomials. This is the standard Laguerre-spherical harmonic representation of the Hermite eigenspaces, see the $\mu=0$ case of \cite[Definition 2.1 and Theorem 2.3]{sheng2021nontensorial} after rescaling their Gaussian weight $e^{-r^2}$ to $e^{-r^2/2}$ and normalizing the Gaussian and spherical measures to be probability measures.
    For $n+2\ell \geq 1$ we set
    \begin{equation}
        E_{n,\ell, i} := \frac{1}{\sqrt{n + 2\ell}} \nabla P_{n,\ell, i}
    \end{equation}
    so that $\{E_{n,\ell, i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}}$ forms an orthonormal basis of the Gaussian gradient fields (i.e. the image of $\mathcal{H}_{n,\ell}$ under the isometry $f \mapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt{n+2\ell}}\nabla f$, equipped with the $L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ inner product).
    For each $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$, we define the operator $C_n: {\mathbb{R}}^{N_{n,d}} \to \ell^2({\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\})$ by the matrix elements
    \begin{equation}
        (C_n)_{\ell, i} := \left\langle w, E_{n,\ell, i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}
    \end{equation}
    with $\ell \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$ and $i \in \{1, \ldots, N_{n,d}\}$. For $n = 0$, we do the same but with $\ell \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and $N_{0,d} = 1$ to get $C_0: {\mathbb{R}} \to \ell^2({\mathbb{N}})$. Finally, we set
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofDtildew}
        \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \operatorname{tr} \left(\sqrt{C_nC_n^\top}\right).
    \end{equation}
    We will first obtain matching lower and upper bounds to show that $Q = \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w)$ if we define $\nu_\varepsilon$ using the more general flow $\dot{X}_t = w(X_t)$; the lower bound will hold for globally-Lipschitz $w$, while the upper bound will require extra smoothness. Afterward, we specialize to $w(x) = \sigma u\phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)$ and relate $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w)$ to our explicit quantity $\mathcal{D}_\phi(c)$. 
    
  To show that $Q$ is lower bounded by $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w)$ for any globally-Lipschitz $w$, we use the same Schur's lemma trace calculation from the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:rkhslowerboundspherical}.
   Fix any $k \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel} with $\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k(x, x) d\gamma_d(x) \in (0, \infty)$. 
    We know that for a fixed $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ the spaces $(\mathcal{H}_{n,\ell})_{\ell=0}^\infty$ are all isomorphic to $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ and transform in the same way under rotations (as do their gradient spaces). By Schur's lemma and rotational equivariance of $\mathcal{T}_{k, \gamma_d}$, there is some matrix $A_n \succeq 0$ for which
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixgaussianlowerboundschurlemma}
        \left\langle E_{n,\ell, i}, \mathcal{T}_{k,\gamma_d} E_{n', r, j}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} = \1_{n=n'} (A_n)_{\ell,r} \1_{i=j} \quad (\forall \ell, r \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\})
    \end{equation}
    for all $i \in \{1, \ldots, N_{n,d}\}$ and $j \in \{1, \ldots, N_{n', d}\}$, while if $n = 0$ the same is true for $\ell, r \in {\mathbb{N}}$. By summing over the orthonormal basis of the gradient subspace of $L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ and applying (\ref{eqn:proofappendixgaussianlowerboundschurlemma}), we find that
    \begin{align}
        \operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k, \gamma_d}) &\geq \sum_{n=0}^\infty \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\n+2\ell \geq 1}}^\infty  \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} \left\langle E_{n,\ell, i}, \mathcal{T}_{k,\gamma_d} E_{n,\ell, i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}
        \\&= \sum_{n=0}^\infty N_{n,d} \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\ n+2\ell \geq 1}}^\infty (A_n)_{\ell,\ell} \\
        &= \sum_{n=0}^\infty N_{n,d} \operatorname{tr}(A_n).
    \end{align}
    In particular, each $A_n$ is trace-class.
    Now, fix $L \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and truncate $C_{n,L} : {\mathbb{R}}^{N_{n,d}} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{L+1}$ (and $C_{0, L} : {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{L}$).
If we take any finite sequence of matrices $(Z_n)_{n=0}^N$ of the same shapes as $C_{n,L}$ supported on $\ell \leq L$ and define
    \begin{equation}
        \varphi_Z := \sum_{n = 0}^N \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\ n+2\ell \geq 1}}^L \frac{1 }{\sqrt{n+2\ell}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} (Z_n)_{\ell, i} P_{n,\ell,i}
    \end{equation}
   then we have
    \begin{equation}
        \nabla \varphi_Z = \sum_{n = 0}^N \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\n+2\ell \geq 1}}^L \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} (Z_n)_{\ell, i} E_{n,\ell,i}.
    \end{equation}
Furthermore, by definition of $(C_n)_n$ we know that
\begin{align}
    \left\langle \nabla \varphi_Z, w\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} &= \sum_{n = 0}^N \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\ n+2\ell \geq 1}}^L\sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}}  \left\langle w, E_{n,\ell, i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} \left\langle \nabla \varphi_Z, E_{n,\ell, i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}\\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top C_{n,L}\right).
\end{align}
On the other hand, by using (\ref{eqn:proofappendixgaussianlowerboundschurlemma}) and the same orthonormal basis we know that if we truncate $A_{n,L}: {\mathbb{R}}^{L+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{L+1}$ (with $A_{0,L}: {\mathbb{R}}^L \to {\mathbb{R}}^L$) then
    \begin{align}
        \left\langle \nabla \varphi_Z, \mathcal{T}_{k, \gamma_d} \nabla \varphi_Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} &= \sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top A_{n,L} Z_n\right).
    \end{align}
    If we take a cutoff $\chi_R \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ which is 1 on $B_R$ and 0 outside $B_{2R}$ with $\|\nabla \chi_R\| \lesssim 1/R$ and denote $\varphi_{Z,R} := \chi_R \varphi_Z$, then we know $\varphi_{Z,R} \in C^\infty_c$ and $\nabla \varphi_{Z,R} \to \nabla \varphi_Z$ in $L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$. By boundedness of $\mathcal{T}_{k,\gamma_d}$ we also know $\left\langle \nabla \varphi_{Z,R}, \mathcal{T}_{k, \gamma_d} \nabla \varphi_{Z,R}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} \to \left\langle \nabla \varphi_{Z}, \mathcal{T}_{k, \gamma_d} \nabla \varphi_{Z}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}$. Hence, we may apply Lemma \ref{lemma:epsilonfirstorder} to $\varphi_{Z,R}$ and take $R \to \infty$ to get
    \begin{equation}
        \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{ \left\langle \nabla \varphi_Z, w\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}}{\sqrt{ \left\langle \nabla \varphi_Z, \mathcal{T}_{k, \gamma_d} \nabla \varphi_Z\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}}} = \frac{\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top C_{n,L}\right)}{\left({\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top A_{n,L}Z_n\right)}\right)^{1/2}}.
    \end{equation}
    This holds for any $(Z_n)_{n=0}^N$ and any $N \in {\mathbb{N}}$, i.e.
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixlowerboundtraceZ_nsequence}
         \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq  \sup_{\substack{N, L \in {\mathbb{N}},\\(Z_n)_{n=0}^N}} \frac{\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top C_{n,L}\right)}{\left({\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top A_{n,L}Z_n\right)}\right)^{1/2}}. \end{equation}
    We may suppose without loss of generality that $\operatorname{im}(C_{n,L}) \subseteq \operatorname{im}(A_{n,L})$; if not, then we can choose a test direction in $\operatorname{ker}(A_{n,L})$ with nonzero numerator to make the right hand side of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixlowerboundtraceZ_nsequence}) infinite, and so the result is trivial. 
    
    To evaluate this supremum, we fix $N, L \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and first assume $A_{n,L}$ is invertible for each $n \leq N$. Put $W_n := A_{n,L}^{1/2}Z_n$ to see that $\operatorname{tr}(Z_n^\top C_{n,L}) = \left\langle W_n, A_{n,L}^{-1/2}C_{n,L}\right\rangle_F$ while $\operatorname{tr}(Z_n^\top A_{n,L} Z_n) = \|W_n\|_F^2$. Hence, this is simply the dual norm in the Frobenius inner product, i.e.
    \begin{align}
        \sup_{\substack{(Z_n)_{n=0}^N}} \frac{\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top C_{n,L}\right)}{\left({\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(Z_n^\top A_{n,L}Z_n\right)}\right)^{1/2}} &= \left(\sum_{n=0}^N \left\|A_{n,L}^{-1/2} C_{n,L}\right\|_F^2\right)^{1/2}\\& = \left(\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(A_{n,L}^{-1}C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top\right)\right)^{1/2}.
    \end{align}
    If $A_{n,L}$ is not invertible, the same holds with the pseudoinverse since $\operatorname{im}(C_{n,L}) \subseteq \operatorname{im}(A_{n,L})$. Hence, we always have
    \begin{equation}
        \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq  \sup_{N,L \in {\mathbb{N}}}\left(\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(A_{n,L}^\dagger C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top\right)\right)^{1/2}
    \end{equation}
    and since $\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k,\gamma_d}) \geq \sum_{n=0}^\infty N_{n,d}\operatorname{tr}(A_n) \geq \sum_{n=0}^N N_{n,d}\operatorname{tr}(A_{n,L}) $ for all $N,L$ we know
    \begin{align}
        \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k,\gamma_d})} \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} &\geq \left(\sum_{n=0}^N N_{n,d}\operatorname{tr}\left(A_{n,L}\right)\right)^{1/2} \cdot \left(\sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(A_{n,L}^\dagger C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top\right)\right)^{1/2} \\
        &\geq \sum_{n=0}^N \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\left(A_{n,L}\right) \operatorname{tr}\left(A_{n,L}^\dagger C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top\right)},
    \end{align}
    where the second line uses Cauchy-Schwarz $\sqrt{(\sum_n a_n)(\sum_n b_n)} \geq \sum_n \sqrt{a_nb_n}$. For $A, B \succeq 0$ with $\operatorname{im}(B) \subseteq \operatorname{im}(A)$ we know 
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{tr}(\sqrt{B}) = \operatorname{tr}(A^{1/2}A^{\dagger / 2} \sqrt{B}) \leq \|A^{1/2}\|_F \|A^{\dagger / 2}\sqrt{B}\|_F = \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(A)} \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(A^\dagger B)}.
    \end{equation}
    Taking $A = A_{n,L}$ and $B = C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top$ yields
    \begin{equation}
         \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{T}_{k,\gamma_d})} \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \sum_{n=0}^N \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \operatorname{tr}\left(\sqrt{C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top}\right).
    \end{equation}
    We first take $N,L \to \infty$ using monotone convergence and then an infimum over $k$ to arrive at the lower bound $Q \geq \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w)$.

    For the upper bound, assume further that $w \in C^{d+2}({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ with $\|Dw\|_{C^{d+1}} < \infty$. Suppose that $\widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w) < \infty$, since otherwise there is nothing to prove. Let us define the Gaussian gradient subspace
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{G} := \overline{\left\{\nabla \varphi:\; \varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)\right\}}^{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}
    \end{equation}
    with $\Pi_{\mathcal{G}}: L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d) \to \mathcal{G}$ its orthogonal projection, and denote $g := \Pi_{\mathcal{G}}w$. Since each $E_{n,\ell,i}$ is a gradient field we know that
    \begin{equation}
        \left\langle w, E_{n,\ell,i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} = \left\langle g, E_{n,\ell,i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} = (C_n)_{\ell,i}.
    \end{equation}
    Let us denote by $(\Phi_t)_{t \geq 0}$ the flow of the ODE driven by $w$ and $\nu_t := (\Phi_t)_\# \gamma_d$ the resulting trajectory of measures, and so $D\Phi_t(x)w(x) = w(\Phi_t(x))$. If we define
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofg_tflowupperbound}
        g_t(x) := D\Phi_t(\Phi_t^{-1}(x))g(\Phi_t^{-1}(x)),
    \end{equation}
    then writing $y = \Phi_t(x)$ implies $w(y) - g_t(y) = D\Phi_t(x) [w(x) - g(x)]$.
    We claim that $(g_t, \nu_t)_{t \geq 0}$ satisfies the continuity equation. Indeed, for fixed $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we have that
    \begin{align}
        \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi(y), w(y) - g_t(y)\right\rangle d\nu_t(y) &= \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi(\Phi_t(x)), D\Phi_t(x) (w(x) - g(x))\right\rangle d\gamma_d(x) \\
        &= \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla (\varphi \circ \Phi_t), w-g\right\rangle d\gamma_d \\&= 0
    \end{align}
    since $\nabla (\varphi \circ \Phi_t) \in \mathcal{G}$. This yields
    \begin{equation}
        \partial_t \nu_t + \nabla \cdot (\nu_t g_t) = 0,
    \end{equation}
    and so the drifts $(g_t)_{t \geq 0}$ generate the same trajectory of measures. In particular, for any $k$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:kernel} if $\|g_t- g\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} \to 0$ as $t \downarrow 0$ then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixthehtingtoproveforupperboundnormofg}
        \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{H}_k}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \leq \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \int_0^\varepsilon \|g_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_k} dt = \|g\|_{\mathcal{H}_k}.
    \end{equation}
    Note that $\|g\|_{W^{d+1, 4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} \lesssim \|w\|_{W^{d+1, 4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} < \infty$ since $\Pi_{\mathcal{G}}$ is a bounded operator on $W^{d+1,4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$. We claim that our smoothness assumptions imply
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:appendixproofWd12convergenceofg_t}
    \lim_{t \downarrow 0} \|g_t - g\|_{W^{d+1, 2}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} = 0.
    \end{equation}
    To see this, by Grönwall we know that if $B_t := \Phi_t^{-1}$ and $A_t := D\Phi_t \circ B_t$ then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixboundednessofderivativeshwnenneeded}
        \sup_{t \in [0, t_0]} \left\{ \|DB_t\|_{C^{d}} + \|A_t\|_{C^{d+1}}\right\} < \infty
    \end{equation}
    for some $t_0$. For any $f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$, the chain and product rules therefore imply that if $U_t f := A_t \cdot (f \circ B_t) $ then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixstupidgaussianpullbackbullshit}
        \sum_{|\alpha| \leq d+1} \|D^\alpha U_t f(x)\| \leq C \sum_{|\beta| \leq d+1} \|D^\beta f(B_t(x))\| \quad (\forall x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d)
    \end{equation}
    for a constant $C$ uniform in $x$ and $t \in [0, t_0]$. If we change variables $y = B_t(x)$ (i.e. $x = \Phi_t(y)$) and define 
    \begin{equation}
        R_t(y) := |\operatorname{det} D\Phi_t(y)| \exp\left(\frac{\|y\|^2 - \|\Phi_t(y)\|^2}{2}\right),
    \end{equation}
then Lipschitzness of $w$ implies that $R_t(y) \leq e^{C' t(1+|y|^2)}$ for some constant $C'  \in (0, \infty)$. 
In particular, after shrinking $t_0$ we know that there is some $C'' \in (0, \infty)$ for which
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{t \in [0, t_0]} \|R_t\|_{L^2(\gamma_d)} \leq C'' <  \infty.
\end{equation}
Hence,
(\ref{eqn:proofappendixstupidgaussianpullbackbullshit}) and the change of measure formula yield
    \begin{align}
        \|U_tf\|_{W^{d+1,2}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}^2 &\leq C \sum_{|\beta| \leq d+1} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|D^\beta f(B_t(x))\|^2 d\gamma_d(x)
        \\ &\leq C \sum_{|\beta| \leq d+1} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|D^\beta f(y)\|^2 R_t(y)d\gamma_d(y) \\
        &\leq C  \|f\|_{W^{d+1, 4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}^2 \cdot \|R_t\|_{L^2(\gamma_d)} \\
        &\leq CC'' \|f\|_{W^{d+1, 4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}^2,
    \end{align}
    where the second to last line applies Hölder's inequality.
    Redefining constants, this implies
    \begin{equation}
        \sup_{t \in [0, t_0]}\|U_tf\|_{W^{d+1, 2}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} \leq C \|f\|_{W^{d+1,4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} \quad (\forall f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)) 
    \end{equation}
    and so the linear operators $U_t: W^{d+1,4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d) \to W^{d+1,2}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ are uniformly bounded for small enough $t$. Furthermore, for $f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we know $U_t f \to f$ as $t \downarrow 0$ in $C^{d+1}_{\operatorname{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ by the product rule and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixboundednessofderivativeshwnenneeded}). The boundedness allows us to extend this convergence to general $W^{d+1,4}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ maps, which we apply to $g$ to prove (\ref{eqn:appendixproofWd12convergenceofg_t}).

    Let us now fix $N, L \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and define the matrices $\hat{A}_{n,L} := \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{n,d}}} \sqrt{C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top}$ and the kernel
    \begin{equation}
        k_{N,L}(x, y) := \sum_{n=0}^N \sum_{\substack{\ell,r = 0 \\ n + 2\ell \geq 1 \\ n + 2 r \geq 1}}^L (\hat{A}_{n,L})_{\ell,r} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}}E_{n,\ell, i}(x) E_{n,r,i}(y)^\top.
    \end{equation}
    This is jointly-continuous since $N,L$ are finite, it is rotation-equivariant due to the sum over $i$, and since $\hat{A}_{n,L} \succeq 0$ it is a positive kernel. Furthermore, we compute
    \begin{equation}
        \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\operatorname{tr}k_{N,L}(x, x)d\gamma_d(x) = \sum_{n=0}^N{N_{n,d}} \operatorname{tr}(\hat{A}_{n,L}) = \sum_{n=0}^N \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \operatorname{tr}\left(\sqrt{C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top}\right). 
    \end{equation}
    Moreover, if we let
    \begin{equation}
        g_{N,L} := \sum_{n=0}^N \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0\\ n+2\ell \geq 1}}^L \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} (C_{n,L})_{\ell, i} E_{n,\ell, i}
    \end{equation}
    be the truncation of $g$ then by the same calculations as before we have
    \begin{equation}
        \|g_{N,L}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{N,L}}}^2 = \sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{tr}\left(\hat{A}_{n,L}^\dagger C_{n,L}C_{n,L}^\top\right) = \sum_{n=0}^N \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \operatorname{tr}\left(\sqrt{C_{n,L} C_{n,L}^\top}\right).
    \end{equation}
    In particular, we find a sequence $(k_{N,N})_{N \in {\mathbb{N}}} \subseteq \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}}$ of jointly-continuous rotation-equivariant kernels for which
     \begin{equation}
     \label{eqn:proofappendixthingneededtoexhibitkNforupperbound}
        \lim_{N \to \infty} \sqrt{T_N} \cdot \|g_{N,N}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{N,N}}} = \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w), \quad T_N := \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\operatorname{tr} k_{N,N}(x, x) d\gamma_d(x) < \infty.
    \end{equation}
Let us define the jointly-continuous rotation-invariant scalar Sobolev kernel \begin{equation}q_{\operatorname{Sob}}(x, y) := \sum_{\alpha \in ({\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\})^d} (1+|\alpha|)^{-(d+1)} h_\alpha (x) h_\alpha(y), \quad \tau_{\operatorname{Sob}} := d\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} q_{\operatorname{Sob}}(x, x) d\gamma_d(x) < \infty\end{equation}
    with $\{h_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in ({\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\})^d}$ the normalized multivariate Hermite basis of $L^2(\gamma_d)$. Importantly, $\mathcal{T}_{q_{\operatorname{Sob}}, \gamma_d} = (\1 - \Delta_\gamma)^{-(d+1)}$ for $\Delta_\gamma = \Delta - x \cdot \nabla$ the OU generator and therefore
    \begin{equation}
        \|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}_{q_{\operatorname{Sob}}}} \asymp \|\cdot \|_{W^{d+1,2}(\gamma_d)}
    \end{equation} 
    by the Gaussian Meyer inequalities. We denote $k_{\operatorname{Sob}}(x, y) := \frac{1}{\tau_{\operatorname{Sob}}} q_{\operatorname{Sob}}(x, y) \1_{d}$ and
    \begin{equation}
        \delta_N := \|g_{N,N} - g\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\operatorname{Sob}}}}^2,
    \end{equation}
    and we note that $\delta_N \to 0$ since $g \in W^{d+1,2}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ and the Hermite truncation diagonalizes $\Delta_\gamma$. We define the modified kernel
    \begin{equation}
        \widetilde{k}_{N}(x, y) := k_{N,N}(x, y) + \left(\sqrt{\delta_N} + \frac{1}{N}\right) k_{\operatorname{Sob}}(x, y)
    \end{equation}
    and compute that
    \begin{equation}
        \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}\widetilde{k}_N(x, x) d\gamma_d(x) = T_N + \sqrt{\delta_N} + \frac{1}{N}.
    \end{equation}
    Furthermore, by the RKHS sum formula we know 
    \begin{align}
        \|g\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{k}_N}}^2 &\leq \|g_{N,N}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{N,N}}} ^2 + \|g - g_{N,N}\|^2_{ \mathcal{H}_{(\sqrt{\delta_N} + \frac{1}{N})k_{\operatorname{Sob}}}}
        \\ &= \|g_{N,N}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{N,N}}} ^2 + \frac{\delta_N}{\sqrt{\delta_N} + \frac{1}{N}}.
    \end{align}
   Putting these together, it holds that
   \begin{align}
       \limsup_{N \to \infty} {\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}\widetilde{k}_N(x, x) d\gamma_d(x)} \cdot \|g\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{k}_N}}^2 &\leq \limsup_{N \to \infty} \left(T_N + \sqrt{\delta_N} + \frac{1}{N}\right)  \cdot \left(\|g_{N,N}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{N,N}}}^2 + \sqrt{\delta_N}\right) \\&= \limsup_{N \to \infty} T_N \|g_{N,N}\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{N,N}}}^2
       \\ &= \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w)^2.
   \end{align}
   Lastly, since $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{k}_N}} \lesssim \|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{\operatorname{Sob}}}} \lesssim \|\cdot\|_{W^{d+1,2}(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)}$ for each fixed $N$ we know $\lim_{t \downarrow 0}\|g_t - g\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\widetilde{k}_N}} = 0$ by (\ref{eqn:appendixproofWd12convergenceofg_t}). The upper bound then follows from (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthehtingtoproveforupperboundnormofg}).

   Thus far, we have shown that for general flows driven by $w: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ we have
   \begin{equation}
       Q = \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w),
   \end{equation}
   where the $\geq$ direction holds if $w$ is globally-Lipschitz and the $\leq$ direction also requires $w \in C^{d+2}({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ with $\|Dw\|_{C^{d+1}} < \infty$. Furthermore, by the definition in (\ref{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofDtildew}) we have that
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofapendixalternativerepresentationofDtildew}
       \widetilde{\mathcal{D}}(w) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \cdot \|C_n\|_{\mathcal{S}_1},
   \end{equation}
   where $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{S}_1}$ denotes the sum of singular value magnitudes. 
   To finish up, we specialize to the single-index case $w(x) = \sigma u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)$ and denote $c := \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle$. We take $v \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ s.t. $\left\langle v, \theta\right\rangle = 0$ and $u = c\theta + \sqrt{1-c^2}v$. This implies that for any $n,\ell \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$ with $m := n + 2\ell \geq 1$ and $i \in \{1, \ldots, N_{n,d}\}$, if we denote $Z := \left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle$ for $\xi \sim \gamma_d$ and $s := \sqrt{1-c^2}$ then we have
   \begin{align}
       (C_n)_{\ell, i} &= \left\langle w, E_{n,\ell,i}\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{m}} \mathbb{E}\left[\phi(Z) \left\langle u, \nabla P_{n,\ell,i}(\xi)\right\rangle\right] \\&= \frac{\sigma \hat{\phi}_{m-1}}{\sqrt{m}(m-1)!} \mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{He}_{m-1}(Z) \left\langle u, \nabla P_{n,\ell,i}(\xi)\right\rangle\right],
   \end{align}
   where in the second line we used $\phi = \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{\hat{\phi}_j}{j!} \operatorname{He}_j$ and that $x \mapsto \left\langle u, \nabla P_{n,\ell ,i}(x)\right\rangle$ belongs to the $(m-1)^{th}$ Hermite chaos. For any $f \in W^{1,2}(\gamma_d)$ we have the Gaussian integration by parts identity
   \begin{equation}
       \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d}\left[\operatorname{He}_{m-1}(\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle) \left\langle u, \nabla f(\xi)\right\rangle\right] = \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \mathcal{A}_m(\theta) + \frac{1}{m}\left\langle u, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} \mathcal{A}_m(\theta)\right\rangle,
   \end{equation}
   where we define $\mathcal{A}_m(\theta) := \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d}[\operatorname{He}_m(\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle) f(\xi)]$. In the case $f = P_{n,\ell,i}$, there is the identity
   \begin{equation}
      \frac{1}{\sqrt{m!}} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d}[\operatorname{He}_m(\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle) P_{n,\ell,i}(\xi)] = \beta_{n,\ell,d} Y_{n,i}(\theta), \quad \beta_{n,\ell,d} := \sqrt{\frac{m! \Gamma(d/2)}{2^m \ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}}.
   \end{equation}
 To see this, we start from (\ref{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofthe}) and note the Laguerre polynomials have leading coefficient $L_\ell^{(\alpha)}(a) = \frac{(-1)^\ell}{\ell!} a^\ell + \text{terms of degree $<\ell$}$. Hence, the degree-$m$ homogeneous part of $P_{n,\ell,i}$, denoted $[P_{n,\ell,i}]_m$, is given by
 \begin{equation}
[P_{n,\ell,i}]_m(x) = \frac{1}{2^\ell \ell!} \sqrt{\frac{\ell! \Gamma(d/2)}{2^n \Gamma(n+\ell + d/2)}} \cdot \|x\|^m Y_{n,i}(x / \|x\|).
 \end{equation}
Applying Gaussian integration by parts $m$ times yields
 \begin{equation}
     \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim\gamma_d}[\operatorname{He}_m(\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle) P_{n,\ell,i}(\xi)] = \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d}[(\theta \cdot \nabla)^m P_{n,\ell,i}(\xi)] = \frac{m!}{2^\ell\ell!} \sqrt{\frac{\ell! \Gamma(d/2)}{2^n\Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}} Y_{n,i}(\theta)
 \end{equation}
 which implies the claimed identity.
 We find that
   \begin{align}
       (C_n)_{\ell,i} &= \frac{\sigma \hat{\phi}_{m-1} \sqrt{m!} \beta_{n,\ell,d}}{\sqrt{m}(m-1)!} \left(\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle Y_{n,i}(\theta) + \frac{1}{m} \left\langle u, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y_{n,i}(\theta)\right\rangle\right)
       \\ &= \frac{\sigma \hat{\phi}_{m-1} \sqrt{m!} \beta_{n,\ell,d}}{\sqrt{m}(m-1)!} \left(c Y_{n,i}(\theta) + \frac{s}{m} \left\langle v, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y_{n,i}(\theta)\right\rangle\right),
       \label{eqn:appendixproofformulaforCnelliwhichshowsitsrank2}
   \end{align}
   where we used that $\nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y_{n,i}(\theta)$ is tangent to the sphere at $\theta$ and therefore orthogonal to $\theta$. By differentiating the addition theorem for spherical harmonics (see \cite[Theorem 2.9]{atkinson2012spherical}), we have
   \begin{align}
       \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} Y_{n,i}(\theta)^2 = N_{n,d},
\quad \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} Y_{n,i}(\theta) \left\langle v, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y_{n,i}(\theta)\right\rangle = 0, \\ \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}} \left\langle v, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} Y_{n,i}(\theta)\right\rangle^2 = N_{n,d} \frac{n(n+d-2)}{d-1}.
   \end{align}
   In particular, for fixed $n,\ell$ we find that  
   \begin{equation}
       \sum_{i=1}^{N_{n,d}}(C_n)_{\ell, i}^2 = \frac{\sigma^2 |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}|^2 \beta_{n,\ell,d}^2 N_{n,d}}{(m-1)!} \left(c^2  + \frac{s^2}{m^2} \frac{n(n+d-2)}{d-1}\right)
   \end{equation}
   By comparing with (\ref{eqn:appendixdefinitionofDpphicforthegaussianbounds}), we find that
   \begin{equation}
       \sigma \mathcal{D}_\phi(\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle) = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \sqrt{N_{n,d}} \cdot \|C_n\|_F.
   \end{equation}
   The final claim then follows from (\ref{eqn:proofapendixalternativerepresentationofDtildew}) and the fact that $\|C_n\|_{F} \leq \|C_n\|_{\mathcal{S}_1} \leq \sqrt{2}\|C_n\|_{F}$ since each $C_n$ has rank at most $2$, see (\ref{eqn:appendixproofformulaforCnelliwhichshowsitsrank2}).
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixbarronfirstorderlowerbound}
    Let $\phi \in C^1({\mathbb{R}})$ satisfy Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} with $M := \max\{\|\phi\|_\infty, \|\phi'\|_\infty\}  \in(0, \infty)$. Fix $d \geq 2$ and $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, and for each $\varepsilon > 0$ define $\nu_\varepsilon := \operatorname{Law}(X_1)$ according to the flow 
    \begin{equation}
        \dot{X}_t = \varepsilon w(X_t), \quad w(x) := u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle), \quad X_0 \sim \gamma_d.
    \end{equation}
    Then, with $c := \left\langle u, \theta \right\rangle$ we have that
    \begin{equation}
        \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{1}{M} \sup_{a,b \in {\mathbb{R}}}\frac{\left|(a \sqrt{1-c^2}+bc)\phi(b) - c \phi'(b)\right|}{1+\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}.
    \end{equation}
    If $\phi \in \{\tanh, \sin\}$ then the right hand side is $\geq 1$ for all $c \in [-1, 1]$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Note that since $\|\phi\|_\infty, \|\phi'\|_\infty \leq M$ we know
\begin{equation}
    \|u\|_\infty, \|\operatorname{div} u\|_\infty \leq M\|u\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\phi}} \quad (\forall u \in \mathcal{B}_{\phi}).
\end{equation}
Now, let $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ be an admissible transport from $\gamma_d$ to $\nu_\varepsilon$  with \begin{equation}
    L := \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\phi}} dt < \infty.
\end{equation}
The prescribed flow has a $C^1$ bi-Lipschitz endpoint map (since $\phi$ is $C^1$ and Lipschitz), so $\nu_\varepsilon$ has a continuous positive density. Now, if we take $(Y_t^x)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ to be a characteristic ending at some $Y_1^x = x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$ then there is the change of variables formula
\begin{equation}
    \log \frac{\nu_\varepsilon}{\gamma_d}(x) = -\frac{\|Y_0^x\|^2 - \|x\|^2}{2} - \int_0^1 \operatorname{div} v_t(Y_t^x)dt;
\end{equation}
at first this holds for a.e. $x$ by Lipschitz regularity, which we extend by continuity to hold for every $x$ (note that each $\operatorname{div}v_t$ is continuous since $\phi$ is $C^1$).
Since $\|Y_0^x - x\| \leq \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_\infty dt \leq ML$ we know $\left|\frac{\|Y_0^x\|^2 - \|x\|^2}{2}\right| \leq  \frac{M^2L^2}{2}+ML \|x\| $, and so
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericaltaubarronuperbounddensityratio}
    \left|\log \frac{\nu_\varepsilon}{\gamma_d}(x)\right| \leq \frac{M^2L^2}{2} +M L(1+\|x\|).
\end{equation}
However, for the flow $\dot{X}_t = \varepsilon w(X_t)$ which generates $\nu_\varepsilon$ we know that $X_1 = X_0 + \varepsilon w(X_0) + o(\varepsilon)$ and so $\nu_\varepsilon = \gamma_d - \varepsilon \operatorname{div}(\gamma_d w) + o(\varepsilon)$.
In particular, using $\log(1+a) = a + o(a)$ we find that the log density must satisfy 
\begin{align}
  \log   \frac{\nu_\varepsilon}{\gamma_d}(x) &=\varepsilon\left( \left\langle x, w(x)\right\rangle - \operatorname{div}w(x)\right) + o_x(\varepsilon) \\
  &= \varepsilon \left(\left\langle x, u\right\rangle \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \phi'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right) + o_x(\varepsilon).
\end{align}
Combining with (\ref{eqn:proofsphericaltaubarronuperbounddensityratio}), we find that
\begin{equation}
   \varepsilon \left|\left\langle x, u\right\rangle \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \phi'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right| + o_x(\varepsilon)  \leq \frac{M^2L^2}{2}+ML(1+\|x\|)
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
    L \geq \frac{\sqrt{(1+\|x\|)^2 +  2\varepsilon \left|\left\langle x, u\right\rangle \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \phi'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right| + o_x(\varepsilon)} - (1+\|x\|)}{M}
\end{equation}
Taking an infimum over admissible paths followed by $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ with $x$ fixed implies that
\begin{equation}
    \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\frac{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{ \left|\left\langle x, u\right\rangle \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \phi'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right|}{M(1+\|x\|)}.
\end{equation}
This holds for any $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$, and so we may take a supremum over $x$. It suffices to consider $x \in \operatorname{span}\{u, \theta\}$ since otherwise the denominator is strictly suboptimal, and so we write $c = \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle$,  $u = c\theta + \sqrt{1-c^2} v$ for a unit vector $v$ orthogonal to $\theta$, and we express
$x = av + b\theta$. In this case the first claim follows due to
\begin{equation}
    \frac{ \left|\left\langle x, u\right\rangle \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \phi'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right|}{1+\|x\|} = \frac{\left|(a\sqrt{1-c^2} + bc) \phi(b) - c \phi'(b)\right|}{1 + \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}
\end{equation}
For the second claim, note first that if $\phi \in \{\tanh, \sin\}$ then $M = 1$.
Now, if $c = 0$ then the expression becomes $\frac{|a \phi(b)|}{1 + \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$, which goes to $|\phi(b)|$ as we take $a \to \infty$. Hence, the right hand side equals $\sup_b |\phi(b)| = 1$. If instead $c \neq 0$ then we take $x = R \sqrt{1-c^2}v + R c \theta = Ru$ for $R > 0$ to make the expression equal \begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixbarronfirstorderlowerboundsintanh}
\frac{|R\phi(Rc) - c \phi'(Rc)|}{1+R}.\end{equation}
For $\tanh$ we let $R \to \infty$ to find that $|\tanh(Rc)| \to 1$ while $\tanh'(Rc) = \operatorname{sech}(Rc)^2 \to 0$. For $\sin$ we take $R_j = \frac{\pi / 2 + 2 \pi j}{|c|}$ so that $|\sin(R_j c)| = 1$ while $\cos(R_j c) = 0$. In either case, (\ref{eqn:proofappendixbarronfirstorderlowerboundsintanh}) tends to 1 and so the result follows.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Let $w(x) := q\phi(\left\langle x, u\right\rangle)$ with $q, u \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ s.t. $c := \left\langle q, u\right\rangle \neq 0$ (we relabel the input and output features for notational simplicity).
We start from the ReLU-specific observation that $\1 + \varepsilon w$ is the time-1 map of the flow
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericalODEformulation}
    \dot{X}_t = \frac{\log(1+c\varepsilon)}{c} w(X_t),
\end{equation}
where $1+c\varepsilon > 0$ for small enough $\varepsilon$.
To see this, note that the induced dynamics of $a_t := \left\langle X_t, u\right\rangle$ are \begin{equation}\dot{a}_t = {\log(1+c\varepsilon)} \max\{0, a_t\}\end{equation}
and therefore $a_t = e^{\log(1+c\varepsilon) t}a_0$ if $a_0 > 0$ and $a_t = a_0$ if $a_0 \leq 0$. Hence,
\begin{equation}X_1 = X_0 + \frac{1+c\varepsilon-1}{c}\max\{0, a_0\}q = (\1 + \varepsilon w)(X_0)\end{equation}
and so (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalODEformulation}) is verified. 
Since $\|w\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq 1$ by construction (see Definition \ref{def:barronspaceshomogeneous}), and $\frac{\log(1+c\varepsilon)}{c\varepsilon} \to 1$, we get the Barron upper bound \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalbarronupperbound}
  \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\mu, \nu_\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon} \leq 1 .
\end{equation}

    For the Stein lower bound, we will show for odd $n \geq d$ that $A_n \gtrsim n^{-1}$ (which is $\gtrsim n^{1-d/2}$ whenever $d \geq 4$), after which the result will follow from Lemma \ref{lemma:rkhslowerboundspherical}. To this end, 
    let $P_{n, d}: [-1, 1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be the Legendre polynomials defined in (2.19) of \cite{atkinson2012spherical}. By the addition theorem for spherical harmonics (see \cite[Theorem 2.9]{atkinson2012spherical}), if $\{Y_{n,j}:\; 1 \leq j \leq N_{n,d}\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{Y}_n^d$ w.r.t. the normalized uniform probability measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ then 
\begin{equation}
    \sum_{j=1}^{N_{n,d}} Y_{n,j}(\xi) {Y_{n,j}(\eta)} = N_{n,d} P_{n,d}(\left\langle \xi, \eta\right\rangle) \quad (\forall \xi, \eta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}). 
\end{equation}
Let us take our input feature $u \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and define $Z_{n,u}: \mathbb{S}^{d-1} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofexampledefofZnu}Z_{n,u}(\theta) := \sqrt{N_{n,d}} P_{n,d}(\left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle),
\end{equation} and so $Z_{n, u} \in \mathbb{Y}_n^d$. By equation (2.40) of \cite{atkinson2012spherical} we know $\|Z_{n,u}\|_{L^2(\sigma)} = 1$. We will take $Y = Z_{n,u}$ as the comparator to lower bound $A_n$.


We claim that if $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is positively one-homogeneous then with $w(x) = q \phi(\left\langle u, x\right\rangle) $ and $\varphi_n(x) = |x|^2 Z_{n,u}(\frac{x}{|x|})$ we have
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalclaim1}
\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi_n,  w\right\rangle d\mu = cM_2(\mu)^2\left(2 + \frac{n(n+d-2)}{2}\right) \cdot \beta_n(\phi),
\end{equation}
where we denote $M_2(\mu) := \sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|x\|^2 d\mu(x)}$ and we define the coefficient of $\phi$ by
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofsphericalbetaintegral}
    \beta_n(\phi) := \left(\phi(1) + (-1)^{n+1} \phi(-1)\right)\int_{\{\left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle > 0\}} \left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle^2 Z_{n, u}(\theta) d\sigma(\theta).
\end{equation}
To see this, we start from
\begin{equation}\nabla \varphi_n(r\theta) = 2r Z_{n,u}(\theta) \theta + \frac{r^2}{r} \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}(\theta),\end{equation}
after which we apply positive homogeneity to find
\begin{align}
\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi_n,  w\right\rangle d\mu &=  \mathbb{E}_{R, \Theta} \left[2R^2Z_{n,u}(\Theta)\phi(\left\langle \Theta, u\right\rangle) \left\langle \Theta, q\right\rangle + R^2 \phi(\left\langle \Theta, u\right\rangle) \left\langle q, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}(\Theta)\right\rangle\right] \\
   &= cM_2(\mu)^2 \left[2\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} t\phi(t) Z_{n,u}d\sigma +  \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} \phi(t) \left\langle u, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}\right\rangle d\sigma\right],
\end{align}
where in the second line we denote $t(\Theta) := \left\langle \Theta, u\right\rangle$ and apply independence of $R,\Theta$ and symmetry about $u$ (which replaces $q$ with $cu$). Now, since $\nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}t(\theta) = u - t(\theta)\theta$ and $\nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}(\theta)$ is orthogonal to $\theta$ we find that
\begin{equation}\left\langle u, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}\right\rangle= \left\langle \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}t, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}\right\rangle.\end{equation}
We now use that $(t\phi(t))' = 2\phi(t)$ a.e. for positively one-homogeneous functions to get
\begin{align}
    \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} \phi(t) \left\langle u, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}\right\rangle d\sigma &= \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} \frac{(t\phi(t))'}{2}  \left\langle \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}t, \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}\right\rangle d\sigma \\
    &= \frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}  \left\langle \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}(t \phi(t)), \nabla_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Z_{n,u}\right\rangle d\sigma\\
    &= \frac{n(n+d-2)}{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} t \phi(t) Z_{n, u} d\sigma ,
\end{align}
where the second line uses the chain rule and the third uses equation (3.20) of \cite{atkinson2012spherical}. Thus,
\begin{equation}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi_n, w\right\rangle d\mu = cM_2(\mu)^2\left(2 + \frac{n(n+d-2)}{2}\right) \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} t\phi(t) Z_{n,u}d\sigma.\end{equation}
Now, if we let $s_+ := \phi(1)$ and $s_- := -\phi(-1)$ be the slopes then
\begin{equation}t \phi(t) = \begin{cases}
    s_+t^2, & t > 0,\\
    s_- t^2, & t < 0,
\end{cases}\end{equation}
which we combine with $Z_{n,u}(-\theta) = (-1)^n Z_{n,u}(\theta)$ to get that
\begin{align}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}t\phi(t)Z_{n,u}d\sigma &= s_+ \int_{\{t > 0\}} t^2 Z_{n,u}d\sigma + s_- \int_{\{t<0\}}t^2Z_{n,u}d\sigma\\
&= (s_+ + (-1)^ns_-) \int_{\{t>0\}} t^2 Z_{n,u}d\sigma.
\end{align}
Thus, the equality in (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalclaim1}) is proved and it remains to lower bound the integral in (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalbetaintegral}).


To this end, we claim that if $n \geq d \geq 3$ and $n$ is odd then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofsphericalhomogeneouslowerbound}
        \left| \int_{\{\left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle > 0\}} \left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle^2 Z_{n,u}(\theta) d\sigma(\theta)\right| \geq \frac{d^{1/4}n^{-3}}{6}.
    \end{equation}
    For $d\geq 3$ and $n \geq 3$ with $n$ odd
    we have
\begin{align}
   \left| \int_{\{\left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle > 0\}} \left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle^2 Z_{n,u}(\theta) d\sigma(\theta)\right| &= \frac{\Gamma(d/2)}{4\pi} \sqrt{\frac{(2n+d-2)\Gamma(n+d-2)}{\Gamma(n+1)\Gamma(d-1)}} \frac{\Gamma((n-2)/2)}{\Gamma((n+d+2)/2)}\\
   &= \frac{\pi^{-3/4}}{4\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{2n+d-2} \left(\frac{\Gamma(d/2)}{\Gamma((d-1)/2)}\right)^{1/2} \cdot \frac{\Gamma((n-2)/2)}{\sqrt{\Gamma((n+1)/2) \Gamma((n+2)/2)} }\\&\qquad  \cdot \frac{\sqrt{\Gamma((n+d-2)/2)\Gamma((n+d-1)/2)}}{\Gamma((n+d+2)/2)} \\
   &\geq \frac{\pi^{-3/4}}{4\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{2n+d-2} \cdot 2^{-3/4}d^{1/4} \cdot \frac{2^{7/4}}{n^{7/4}} \cdot \left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^{1/4} \frac{2^{7/4}}{(n+d)^{7/4}}
   \\ &\geq \frac{3^{1/4}}{2^{1/4}\pi^{3/4}} \cdot \frac{d^{1/4}}{n^{7/4}(n+d)^{5/4}}
\end{align}
where the first line is \href{https://dlmf.nist.gov/18.17#E37}{DLMF 18.17.37} with $\lambda = (d-2)/2$, the second uses the duplication formula, the third uses Wendel's inequality $(\frac{x}{x+s})^{1-s} \leq \frac{\Gamma(x+s)}{x^s \Gamma(x)} \leq 1$ for $x > 0$, $s \in (0, 1)$ on all three $\Gamma$ fraction terms along with $(n+d-2)/2 \geq 3/2$, and the fourth uses $\sqrt{2n+d-2} \geq \sqrt{n+d}$. In particular, if we take $n \geq d$ then
\begin{equation}\left| \int_{\{\left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle > 0\}} \left\langle \theta, u\right\rangle^2 Z_{n,u}(\theta) d\sigma(\theta)\right| \geq \frac{3^{1/4}}{2^{3/2}\pi^{3/4}} \cdot d^{1/4}n^{-3} \geq \frac{d^{1/4}n^{-3}}{6},\end{equation}
and so (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalhomogeneouslowerbound}) is proved.

Combining (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalclaim1}) and (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalhomogeneouslowerbound}), we use our particular choice $Y = Z_{n,u}$ and $\varphi_n = |x|^2 Z_{n,u}(\frac{x}{|x|})$ to find that for any odd $n \geq d $ and any positively one-homogeneous $\phi$ we have
\begin{align}A_n &\geq \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi_n, w\right\rangle d\mu\right| \\&\geq |c|M_2(\mu)^2 \left(2 + \frac{n(n+d-2)}{2}\right) \left|\phi(1) + \phi(-1)\right| \cdot \frac{d^{1/4}n^{-3}}{6} \\
&\geq |c|\frac{M_2(\mu)^2d^{1/4}}{12n} |\phi(1) + \phi(-1)|  .\end{align}
Thus, $A_n \gtrsim n^{-1}$ for odd $n \geq d$ and any positively one-homogeneous $\phi$ which is not a scalar multiple of the identity. Therefore,
\begin{equation}\sqrt{a_{n,d}}A_n \gtrsim \frac{d^{1/4}}{\sqrt{(d-2)!}} \cdot n^{(d-4)/2 - 1},\end{equation}
which is not summable in $n$ for $d \geq 4$. Hence, the right hand side of the lower bound in (\ref{eqn:sphericalclaimquadratic}) can be made as large as desired.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixtanhhermitescaling}
    With $\phi = \tanh$, as $d \to \infty$ we have that
    \begin{equation}
        \log \mathcal{D}_{\tanh}(c) = \frac{d}{4} \log d + O(d)
    \end{equation}
    uniformly for $c \in [-1, 1]$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Since $\tanh$ is odd, the coefficients $\hat{\phi}_{m-1}$ vanish when $m-1$ is even (i.e. when $m$ is odd). In the other cases $m=2q$, we claim that as $q \to \infty$ there is the asymptotic
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixasymptoticsfortanhhermitecoefficients}
        \log |\hat{\phi}_{2q-1}|=q \log(2q) - q - \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{q} + O(\log q).
    \end{equation}
    Before proving this, we show how it implies the main claim; from here on, universal constants are labeled $C_j$ and can change from line to line. 
Recall from (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalharmonicdimscaling}) that
\begin{equation}
    N_{n,d} = \frac{2n+d-2}{d-2} {n+d-3 \choose d-3} ,
\end{equation}
and since ${n + d - 3 \choose d- 3} \leq (\frac{e(n+d)}{d})^d$ we find that $N_{n,d} \leq C_0^d (1 + \frac{n}{d})^d$ for some $C_0 < \infty$. Moreover, 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah2}
N_{n,d} \geq {n+d-3 \choose d-3} \geq \frac{n^{d-3}}{(d-3)!} \geq \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{d-3}       \quad (\forall n \geq d).
\end{equation}
Next, with $m = n + 2\ell$ even we claim that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah1}
    |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \leq (d+m)^{C_1} \left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} \exp\left(-\frac{n^2}{4m} - C_2 \sqrt{m}\right)
\end{equation}
for some $C_1, C_2 \in (0, \infty)$. Indeed, by (\ref{eqn:proofappendixasymptoticsfortanhhermitecoefficients}) and Stirling we have for even $m$ that
\begin{align}
    \log \left( |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \right) &= \log|\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| + \frac{1}{2}\log m + \frac{1}{2}\log \Gamma(d/2) - \frac{m}{2}\log 2 \\&\quad - \frac{1}{2}\log \Gamma\left(\frac{m-n}{2}+1\right) - \frac{1}{2}\log \Gamma\left(\frac{m+n+d}{2}\right)
    \\ &= \frac{m}{2} \log m - \frac{m}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{m} - \frac{m}{2}\log 2 + \frac{d}{4}\log \frac{d}{2} - \frac{d}{4} \\&\quad - \frac{m-n}{4}\log\left(\frac{m-n}{2}\right) + \frac{m-n}{4} \\&\quad - \frac{m+n+d}{4} \log\left(\frac{m+n+d}{2}\right) + \frac{m+n+d}{4} \\&\quad + O(\log(d+m))
    \\
    &= \frac{d}{4} \log \frac{d}{m} - \frac{m-n}{4} \log\left(1-\frac{n}{m}\right)
    \label{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah3}
    \\&\quad - \frac{m+n+d}{4} \log\left(1 + \frac{n+d}{m}\right) - \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{m}\\&\quad + O(\log(d+m)),\label{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah5}
\end{align}
where we use the convention $0 \log 0 = 0$. Therefore,
\begin{align}
    \log \left( |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \right) &\leq \frac{d}{4} \log \frac{d}{m} - \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{m} + O(\log(d+m)) \\&\quad - \frac{m}{4}\left(\left(1 - \frac{n}{m}\right) \log\left(1 - \frac{n}{m}\right) + \left(1 + \frac{n}{m}\right) \log \left(1 + \frac{n}{m}\right)\right).
\end{align}
Since $(1-x) \log(1-x) + (1+x) \log(1+x) \geq x^2$ for $|x| \leq 1$, taking $x = n/m$ implies
    \begin{equation}
        \log \left( |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \right) \leq \frac{d}{4} \log \frac{d}{m} - \frac{n^2}{4m} - \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{m} + O(\log(d+m)) 
    \end{equation}
    which proves (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah1}). 

    For the upper bound, we note that $c^2 + (1-c^2) \frac{n(n+d-2)}{m^2(d-1)} \leq 1$ and that $\sqrt{\sum_\ell x_\ell} \leq \sum_\ell \sqrt{x_\ell}$, and so applying our upper bound on $N_{n,d}$ and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah1}) yields
    \begin{align}
        \mathcal{D}_{\tanh}(c) &\leq \sum_{n=0}^\infty N_{n,d} \sum_{\substack{\ell = 0 \\ n + 2\ell \geq 1}}^\infty |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m \ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \\
        &\leq C_0^d \sum_{m=1}^\infty (d+m)^{C_1} \left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} e^{-C_2\sqrt{m}} \cdot \sum_{n=0}^m \left(1 + \frac{n}{d}\right)^d e^{-\frac{n^2}{4m}} \\
        &\leq  C_0^d \sum_{m=1}^\infty (d+m)^{C_1} \left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} e^{-C_2\sqrt{m}} \cdot \sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(1 + \frac{n}{d}\right)^d e^{-\frac{n^2}{4m}}
    \end{align}
    after reorganizing the sums. Splitting the inner sum, if $n \leq d$ then $(1 + \frac{n}{d})^d \leq 2^d$ and so $\sum_{n=0}^d \left(1 + \frac{n}{d}\right)^d e^{-\frac{n^2}{4m}} \leq (d+1)2^d$. If $n > d$ then we have
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{n=d+1}^\infty \left(1 + \frac{n}{d}\right)^d e^{-\frac{n^2}{4m}} \leq \left(\frac{2}{d}\right)^d \sum_{n = 1}^\infty n^d e^{-\frac{n^2}{4m}} \leq \left(\frac{2}{d}\right)^d (C_4 dm)^{d/2} \sqrt{m} = C_5^d \left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/2} \sqrt{m},
    \end{equation}
 where the second inequality comes from comparison with the integral and Stirling. In particular,
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(1 + \frac{n}{d}\right)^d e^{-\frac{n^2}{4m}} \leq C_6^d (d+m)^{C_7} \left(1 + \left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/2}\right)
    \end{equation}
    and therefore
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{D}_{\tanh}(c) \leq C_8^d \sum_{m=1}^\infty (d+m)^{C_9} \left(\left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} + \left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/4}\right)e^{-C_2 \sqrt{m}}.
    \end{equation}
    We now split this sum into $m \leq d$ and $m > d$. If $m \leq d$ then $(\frac{d}{m})^{d/4} \leq d^{d/4}$ and $(\frac{m}{d})^{d/4} \leq 1$, and hence 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixtanhupperboundhermiteblablah}
         \sum_{m=1}^d (d+m)^{C_9} \left(\left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} + \left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/4}\right)e^{-C_2 \sqrt{m}} \leq C_{10}^dd^{d/4} .
    \end{equation}
    For $m > d$ we know $\left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} + \left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/4} \leq 2\left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/4}$ and hence
    \begin{align}
         \sum_{m=d+1}^\infty (d+m)^{C_9} \left(\left(\frac{d}{m}\right)^{d/4} + \left(\frac{m}{d}\right)^{d/4}\right)e^{-C_2 \sqrt{m}} &\leq C_{11}^d d^{-d/4} \sum_{m=d+1}^\infty m^{d/4 + C_{12}} e^{-c\sqrt{m}} \\
         &\leq C_{13}^d d^{-d/4}\Gamma\left(\frac{d}{2} + 2C_{12} + 2\right) \\
         &\leq C_{14}^d d^{d/4},
    \end{align}
    where the second line compares with the integral over $x = \sqrt{m}$ and the third uses Stirling. Combining this with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhupperboundhermiteblablah}) proves that uniformly in $c$,
    \begin{equation}
        \log \mathcal{D}_{\tanh}(c) \leq \frac{d}{4} \log d + O(d).
    \end{equation}
    For the lower bound, if we take $m \asymp d^2$ and $n \asymp d^{3/2}$ both even then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah6}
        N_{n,d} \geq \left(\frac{n}{d}\right)^{d-3} = \exp\left(\frac{d}{2}\log d - O(d)\right)
    \end{equation}
    by (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah2}), and the formula of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah3})-(\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah5}) simplifies to
    \begin{equation}
        \log \left( |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \right) = \frac{d}{4}\log\left(\frac{d}{m}\right) + O(d)
    \end{equation}
    by expanding out the logs. Since $m \asymp d^2$, this yields
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah7}
        |\hat{\phi}_{m-1}| \left(\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}\right)^{1/2} \geq \exp\left(-\frac{d}{4}\log d - O(d)\right).
    \end{equation}
    Lastly, since $c^2 + (1-c^2) \frac{n(n+d-2)}{m^2(d-1)} \geq \frac{n(n+d-2)}{m^2(d-1)} \gtrsim d^{-2}$ we may multiply (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah6}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixtanhhermiteblahblahblah7}) to lower bound this single term in the sum. Hence, the lower bound
    \begin{equation}
        \log \mathcal{D}_{\tanh}(c) \geq \frac{d}{4}\log d - O(d)
    \end{equation}
    holds uniformly in $c$.

    
We now prove the Hermite coefficient asymptotics (\ref{eqn:proofappendixasymptoticsfortanhhermitecoefficients}). Applying Gaussian integration by parts $2q-1$ times gives that if $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ then
\begin{equation}
    \hat{\phi}_{2q-1} = \mathbb{E}[\tanh(Z)\operatorname{He}_{2q-1}(Z)] = \mathbb{E}[\tanh^{(2q-1)}(Z)]. 
\end{equation}
Observe that $\tanh' = \operatorname{sech}^2$ and that the Fourier transform satisfies $\widehat{\operatorname{sech}^2}(\xi) = \frac{\pi\xi}{\sinh(\pi \xi / 2)}$ (see (3.982.1) of \cite{gradshteyn2014table}), and so
\begin{align}
    \hat{\phi}_{2q-1} &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (\operatorname{sech}^2)^{(2q-2)}(x) e^{-x^2/2}dx \\&= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{3/2}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \widehat{(\operatorname{sech}^2)^{(2q-2)}}(\xi) \widehat{e^{-x^2/2}}(\xi) d\xi \\&= \frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}} (i\xi)^{2q-2} \frac{\xi}{\sinh(\pi \xi / 2)} e^{-\xi^2/2}d\xi \\ 
    &= \frac{(-1)^{\frac{2q}{2}-1}}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{\xi^{2q-1}e^{-\xi^2/2}}{\sinh(\pi \xi / 2)} d\xi,
\end{align}
where the second line uses Parseval's identity and the fourth uses that $2q$ is even. In particular,
\begin{align}
\label{eqn:proofsphericallowerboundonLn}
    |\hat{\phi}_{2q-1}| &= \int_0^\infty \frac{\xi^{2q-1}e^{-\xi^2/2}}{\sinh(\pi \xi / 2)} d\xi = 2\int_0^\infty \frac{\xi^{2q-1}\exp\left(- \frac{\xi^2}{2} - \frac{\pi\xi}{2}\right)}{1 - e^{-\pi \xi}}d\xi.
\end{align}
Hence, since the region $\xi \in [0, 1]$ contributes $O(1)$ to this integral we find that 
\begin{equation}
    \log |\hat{\phi}_{2q-1}| = \log\left(\int_1^\infty e^{F(\xi)}d\xi\right) + O(1)
\end{equation}
where we denote $F(\xi) := (2q-1) \log \xi - \frac{\xi^2}{2} - \frac{\pi \xi}{2} $. We compute that
\begin{equation}
    F'(\sqrt{2q}) = -\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2q}} = O(1), \quad \sup_{\xi>0}F''(\xi) = \sup_{\xi>0}\left\{-\frac{2q-1}{\xi^2} - 1\right\} = -1.
\end{equation}
By Taylor's theorem, for every $\xi \geq 1$ we have $F(\xi)  \leq F(\sqrt{2q}) + O(1) - \frac{1}{4}(\xi - \sqrt{2q})^2$ and therefore
\begin{equation}
    \log\left(\int_1^\infty e^{F(\xi)} d\xi \right) \leq F(\sqrt{2q}) + O(1).
\end{equation}
For the lower bound, we note that
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{\xi \in [\sqrt{2q}, \sqrt{2q}+1]}\left\{F(\sqrt{2q}) - F(\xi)\right\} = O(1)
\end{equation}
and therefore that
\begin{equation}
    \log\left(\int_1^\infty e^{F(\xi)} d\xi \right) \geq   \log\left(\int_{\sqrt{2q}}^{\sqrt{2q}+1} e^{F(\xi)} d\xi \right) \geq F(\sqrt{2q}) - O(1).
\end{equation}
Hence,
(\ref{eqn:proofappendixasymptoticsfortanhhermitecoefficients}) follows from the computation
\begin{align}
    F(\sqrt{2q}) = (2q-1) \log(\sqrt{2q}) - q - \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{2q} 
    = q \log(2q) - q - \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{q} - \frac{1}{2}\log(2q).
\end{align}
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixtsinhermitescaling}
    With $\phi = \sin$, as $d \to \infty$ we have that
    \begin{equation}
        \log \mathcal{D}_{\sin}(c) = \sqrt{d}+ o(\sqrt{d})
    \end{equation}
    uniformly for $c \in [-1, 1]$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
First, we use the fact that
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[e^{it\xi} \operatorname{He}_j(\xi)] = (it)^j e^{-t^2/2}
    \end{equation}
    and take imaginary parts at $t=1$ to see that
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\sin(\xi)\operatorname{He}_j(\xi)] = e^{-1/2} \operatorname{Im}(i^j).
    \end{equation}
    Hence, the Hermite coefficients satisfy
    \begin{equation}
        |\hat{\phi}_j|^2 = \begin{cases}
            0 & j \text{ even}
            \\ 1/e & j \text{ odd}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    and so only even $m = n + 2\ell$ contribute (and therefore only even $n$).

    Now, for $n \geq 2$ we denote
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixsinhermiteboundsdefinitionofTn}
        T_{n,d} := N_{n,d}\left(\frac{n\Gamma(d/2)}{2^n \Gamma(n+d/2)}\right)^{1/2}.
    \end{equation}
    For $m = n + 2\ell$ we know that
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{\frac{m\Gamma(d/2)}{2^m\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)}}{\frac{n\Gamma(d/2)}{2^n\Gamma(n+d/2)}} = \frac{m}{n} \frac{1}{4^\ell \ell!} \frac{\Gamma(n+d/2)}{\Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)} \leq \frac{m}{n} \frac{1}{4^\ell \ell!}  \left(\frac{2}{d}\right)^\ell.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, the sum over $\ell$ becomes
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{\ell = 0}^\infty \frac{(n+2\ell)\Gamma(d/2)}{2^{n+2\ell}\ell! \Gamma(n+\ell+d/2)} = (1 + O(d^{-1})) \frac{n\Gamma(d/2)}{2^n\Gamma(n+d/2)},
    \end{equation}
    i.e. it is dominated by the $\ell = 0$ term. Moreover, we have
    \begin{equation}
        0 \leq c^2 + (1-c^2) \frac{n(n+d-2)}{(n+2\ell)^2(d-1)} \leq 1
    \end{equation}
    while at $\ell =0$ we have
    \begin{equation}
        c^2 + (1-c^2) \frac{n+d-2}{n(d-1)} \geq \frac{1}{n}.
    \end{equation}
    Lastly, the $n=0$ term has $\frac{\Gamma(d/2)}{ \Gamma(d/2 + 1)} \asymp d^{-1}$ and so it contributes $O(d^{-1/2})$ uniformly in $c$ after the square root.
    Therefore, uniformly in $c$ we have
    \begin{equation}
        e^{-1/2} \sum_{\substack{n \geq 2 \\ n \text{ even}}} \frac{T_{n,d}}{\sqrt{n}} \leq \mathcal{D}_{\sin}(c) \leq O(d^{-1/2}) + e^{-1/2} (1 + O(d^{-1})) \sum_{\substack{n \geq 2 \\ n \text{ even}}} T_{n,d}.
    \end{equation}
    For $n \leq d^{2/3}$ we know that
    \begin{equation}
        \log N_{n,d} = n \log d - \log(n!) + O\left(\frac{n^2}{d}+1\right)
    \end{equation}
    and that
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{1}{2} \log \left(\frac{n\Gamma(d/2)}{2^n\Gamma(n+d/2)}\right) = -\frac{n}{2}\log d + \frac{1}{2}\log n + O\left(\frac{n^2}{d}\right).
    \end{equation}
    Combining these two and using Stirling,
    \begin{align}
        \log T_{n,d} &= n\left(1 - \log \frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\right) + O\left(\frac{n^2}{d }+1\right) \\
        &= n\left(1 - \log \frac{n}{\sqrt{d}}\right) + o(\sqrt{d})
        \label{eqn:proofappendixsinhermitescalingoflogTnd}
    \end{align}
    uniformly over $n\leq d^{2/3}$. 

    For the upper bound, we split
    \begin{align}
        \sum_{\substack{n \geq 2 \\ n \text{ even}}} T_{n,d} = \sum_{\substack{2 \leq n \leq d^{2/3} \\ n \text{ even}}} T_{n,d} + \sum_{\substack{n > d^{2/3} \\ n \text{ even}}} T_{n,d}.
    \end{align}
    In the first sum, we use that $x (1-\log x) \leq 1$ with $x = n/\sqrt{d}$ to get that $T_{n,d} \leq \exp(\sqrt{d} + o(\sqrt{d}))$ for $n \leq d^{2/3}$. Since there are only $d^{2/3}$ many terms, we have
    \begin{equation}
         \sum_{\substack{2 \leq n \leq d^{2/3} \\ n \text{ even}}} T_{n,d} \leq  \exp(\sqrt{d} + o(\sqrt{d})).
    \end{equation}
