    For the second sum, we use the definition (\ref{eqn:proofappendixsinhermiteboundsdefinitionofTn}) of $T_{n,d}$ to see that
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{T_{n+1,d}}{T_{n,d}} = \frac{(n+d-2) \sqrt{2n+d}}{(2n+d-2) \sqrt{n(n+1)}}.
    \end{equation}
    If $d^{2/3} < n \leq d$ then this is $\leq \frac{\sqrt{3d}}{n} \leq \sqrt{3}d^{-1/6}$, and if $n > d$ then this is $\leq \sqrt{\frac{3}{n}} \leq \sqrt{3}d^{-1/3}$. In any case, for sufficiently large $d$ we have $\frac{T_{n+1,d}}{T_{n,d}} \leq \frac{1}{2}$ for $n > d^{2/3}$, and so this sum is geometric. Plugging these in proves the upper bound.
    For the lower bound, let $n$ be the nearest even integer to $\sqrt{d}$ and use (\ref{eqn:proofappendixsinhermitescalingoflogTnd}) to find that
    \begin{equation}
        \log T_{n,d} = \sqrt{d} + o(\sqrt{d}).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:appendixnonperturbativefeaturelearning}
    Let $d \geq 2$ and $\phi \in C^\infty_b({\mathbb{R}})$. 
    Fix $Q, R \in (0, \infty)$ and denote
    \begin{equation}
        \beta := 1 + \log(1+Q) + d\log(d+2+R+Q\|\phi\|_\infty) + \log(1 + \|\phi\|_{C^{\lceil d/2\rceil}}). 
    \end{equation}
    For every $\rho \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we also denote its $L^d$-radius by
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{rad}_d(\rho) := \left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\|x\|^d d\rho(x)\right)^{1/d}.
    \end{equation}
    Then, there exists a smooth rotation-equivariant positive kernel $k_{d,\phi, Q, R}$ with the following property:
    
    For every $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with $\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle = 0$, every $|q| \leq Q$, and every $\rho_0 \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ satisfying $\operatorname{rad}_d(\rho_0) \leq R$, there is a family of drifts $(v_t)_{t \in [0, 1]} \subseteq \mathcal{H}_{k_{d,\phi, Q, R}}$ s.t. the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] Each $v_t$ is globally-Lipschitz with
        \begin{equation}
            \sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \operatorname{Lip}(v_t) \leq 12 \beta.
        \end{equation}
        These drifts are in three phases, i.e. $t \mapsto v_t$ is piecewise-constant with three pieces. 
        \item[(ii)] If $(\Phi_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ denote the flow maps generated by $(v_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$, then
        \begin{equation}
            \Phi_1(x) = x + qu\phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle).
        \end{equation}
        \item[(iii)] If $\rho_t = (\Phi_t)_\# \rho_0$ denote the marginals along the flow (and so $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ satisfy the continuity equation), then
        \begin{equation}
            \sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \operatorname{rad}_d(\rho_t) \leq R + |q| \|\phi\|_\infty.
        \end{equation}
        \item[(iv)] There is the trace bound along the flow
        \begin{equation}
            \sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr} k_{d,\phi, Q, R}(x, x) d\rho_t(x) \leq 1 + d(R + |q| \|\phi\|_\infty)^2.
        \end{equation}
        \item[(v)] The RKHS length of this transport satisfies
        \begin{equation}
            \int_{0}^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{d,\phi, Q, R}}} dt \leq 8\beta.
        \end{equation}
    \end{enumerate}
    In particular, if  $\|\phi\|_\infty, \log (1+\|\phi\|_{C^{\lceil d/2\rceil}}) \lesssim \operatorname{poly}(d)$ then there is a smooth rotation-equivariant $k_{d,\phi} \in \mathcal{K}_{\operatorname{rot}}$ s.t. for any $T \leq d^{10000}$, any $\rho_0 \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ with $\operatorname{rad}_d(\rho_0) \leq d^{10000}$, and any single-index shear
    \begin{equation}
        \nu_T := \operatorname{Law}(X_T), \quad \dot{X}_t = u \phi(\left\langle X_t, \theta\right\rangle), \quad X_0 \sim \rho_0, \quad \left\langle u, \theta \right\rangle = 0,
    \end{equation}
there exists a transport $(v_t, \rho_t)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ from $\rho_0$ to $\nu_T$ using three phases of $\operatorname{poly}(d)$-Lipschitz drifts with an RKHS cost of
    \begin{equation}
        \sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \sqrt{\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \operatorname{tr}k_{d,\phi} (x, x) d\rho_t(x)} \cdot \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{d,\phi}}} dt \lesssim \operatorname{poly}(d).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
For notation, we define
\begin{equation}
    m := \left \lceil \frac{d}{2}\right \rceil, \quad \|\phi\|_{C^m} := \max_{0 \leq j \leq m}\|\phi^{(j)}\|_\infty, \quad C_d := \left(1 + \frac{d(d-1)}{2}m^2\right)^m \leq d^{4d}.
\end{equation}
Let $H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ be the spectral Sobolev space of index $d/2$ w.r.t. the normalized uniform measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. More precisely, if $\{Y_{n,j}:\; 1 \leq j \leq N_{n,d},\; n \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}\}$ is the orthonormal basis of $L^2(\sigma)$ composed of spherical harmonics (with $N_{n,d} = \dim \mathbb{Y}_n^d$, see (\ref{eqn:proofsphericalharmonicdimscaling})), then
\begin{equation}
    -\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}Y_{n,j} = \lambda_n  Y_{n,j}, \quad \lambda_n := n(n+d-2)
\end{equation}
and we may identify the Sobolev norm by
\begin{equation}
    \|f\|_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}^2 = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \sum_{j=1}^{N_{n,d}}(1+\lambda_n)^{d/2} |\left\langle f, Y_{n,j}\right\rangle_{L^2(\sigma)}|^2.
\end{equation}
By the addition formula \cite[Theorem 2.9]{atkinson2012spherical} we know $\sum_{j=1}^{N_{n,d}}|Y_{n,j}(\eta)|^2 = N_{n,d}$ for every $\eta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, and so the squared norm of point evaluation $f \mapsto f(\eta)$ on $H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})$ is
\begin{equation}
    E_d = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{N_{n,d}}{(1+\lambda_n)^{d/2}} \leq 1 + \sum_{n = 1}^\infty \frac{2d^{d-2}n^{d-2}}{n^{d}} = 1 + \frac{\pi^2}{3}d^{d-2} \leq 2d^d,
\end{equation}
where we used that $N_{n,d} \leq 2(n+d-1)^{d-2}\leq 2d^{d-2}n^{d-2}$ and $1+\lambda_n \geq n^2$ for $n \geq 1$ and $d \geq 2$. 

Now, for each $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d$ we define
\begin{equation}
    \Psi_x(\omega) := \phi(\left\langle x, \omega\right\rangle) \quad (\forall \omega \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1})
\end{equation}
and we claim the Sobolev bound
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativesobolevbound}
    \|\Psi_x\|_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}^2 \leq C_d (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\|x\|)^d.
\end{equation}
To show (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativesobolevbound}), we decompose $\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} = \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq d} X_{ij}^2$ for the rotation fields $X_{ij} = \omega_i \partial_{\omega_j} - \omega_j \partial_{\omega_i}$. Since $\Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}$ commutes with every $X_{ij}$, we can expand $(\1 - \Delta_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}})^m$ to get
\begin{equation}
    \|f\|_{H^m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}^2 = \|f\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^2 + \sum_{a = 1}^m {m \choose a} \sum_{1 \leq i_1 < j_1 \leq d} \cdots \sum_{1 \leq i_a < j_a \leq d} \|X_{i_1,j_1} \cdots X_{i_a,j_a}f\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^2.
\end{equation}
We have $\|\Psi_x\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^2 \leq \|\phi\|_\infty^2$ and by the chain rule we know that
\begin{equation}
    \|X_{i_1,j_1} \cdots X_{i_a,j_a}\Psi_x\|_{\infty} \leq a^a (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m}) (1+\|x\|)^a,
\end{equation}
since there are at most $a^a$ partitions of $\{1,\ldots, a\}$ and we bound the factors $\left\langle x, X_{i_1,j_1}\cdots X_{i_a,j_a}\omega\right\rangle$ by $\|x\|$. Since there are $(d(d-1)/2)^a$ such terms, we find that
\begin{align}
    \|\Psi_x\|_{H^m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}^2 &\leq (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 \left(1 + \sum_{a=1}^m {m \choose a}  \left(\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\right)^aa^{2a} (1+\|x\|)^{2a}\right) \\
    &\leq (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\|x\|)^{2m} \left(1 + \sum_{a=1}^m {m \choose a}  \left(m^2\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\right)^a \right) \\
    &=  (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\|x\|)^{2m}\left(1 + m^2\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\right)^m\\
    &= C_d (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\|x\|)^{2m}.
\end{align}
Denoting $\nu := \frac{d}{2m} \in (0, 1]$ and using the interpolation inequality
\begin{equation}
    \|f\|_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})} \leq \|f\|_{L^2(\sigma)}^{1-\nu} \|f\|_{H^m(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}^{\nu},
\end{equation}
we obtain
\begin{align}
    \|\Psi_x\|_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}^2 &\leq (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^{2(1-\nu)} \left[C_d(1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\|x\|)^{2m} \right]^\nu \\
    &= C_d^{\nu} (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\|x\|)^{2m\nu}.
\end{align}
Since $2m \nu = d$ and $C_d \geq 1$, we get (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativesobolevbound}).

Using these ingredients, we define the scalar kernel $\kappa_\phi: {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
\begin{equation}
    \kappa_\phi(x, y) := \left\langle \Psi_x, \Psi_y\right\rangle_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})}.
\end{equation}
This is positive semidefinite and since $\Psi_{Ux}(\omega) = \Psi_x(U^\top \omega)$ it is rotation-invariant. Also, since $\partial_x^\alpha \Psi_x(\omega) = \omega^\alpha \phi^{(|\alpha|)}(\left\langle x, \omega\right\rangle)$ the same Sobolev estimate shows $x \mapsto \Psi_x$ is smooth as an $H^{d/2}$-valued map; thus, $\kappa_\phi$ is smooth.
For any $\eta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, we know that
\begin{equation}
    \phi(\left\langle x, \eta\right\rangle) = \Psi_x(\eta) = \left\langle \Psi_x, e_\eta\right\rangle_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})},
\end{equation}
and so by the feature map construction of $\kappa_\phi$ we have
\begin{equation}
    \|\phi(\left\langle \cdot, \eta\right\rangle)\|_{\mathcal{H}_{\kappa_\phi}}^2 \leq \|e_\eta\|^2_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})} = E_d \leq 2d^d.
\end{equation}
Now, we set $M := (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 \left(1 + 2d^{d+1}C_d(1+R+Q\|\phi\|_\infty)^d\right)$ and define the kernel
\begin{equation}
    k_{d, \phi, Q, R}(x, y) := \left\langle x, y\right\rangle \1_d + \frac{2d^d}{1+M} \kappa_\phi(x, y) \1_d.
\end{equation}
This kernel is smooth, positive semidefinite, and rotation-equivariant. Furthermore, by construction we know $x \mapsto u \left\langle x, u\right\rangle$ has $\mathcal{H}_{k_{d,\phi,Q,R}}$ norm at most 1 while $x \mapsto u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)$ has $\mathcal{H}_{k_{d,\phi,Q,R}}$ norm $\leq \sqrt{1+M}$. Hence, if we define $r := \max\left\{1, \; \frac{|q|\sqrt{1+M}}{2}\right\}$ and
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativefeaturelearningdefinitionofdrifts}
    v_t(x) := \begin{cases}
        -3 \log r u \left\langle x, u\right\rangle & 0 \leq t < \frac{1}{3} \\
        \frac{3q}{r} u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) & \frac{1}{3} \leq t < \frac{2}{3},\\
        3\log r u \left\langle x, u\right\rangle & \frac{2}{3} \leq t \leq 1.
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
then it holds that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativefeaturelearningRKHSbound}
    \int_0^1 \|v_t\|_{\mathcal{H}_{k_{d, \phi, Q, R}}} dt \leq 2\log r + \frac{|q| \sqrt{1+M}}{r} \leq 2 + 2 \log(1+|q|\sqrt{1+M}),
\end{equation}
where the second inequality follows from definition of $r$. Next, since $\sqrt{1+M} \geq \|\phi\|_{C^m} \geq \|\phi'\|_\infty$ we know that $\operatorname{Lip}(\frac{3q}{r}u\phi(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle))\leq 6$ and so
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativefeaturelearningLipschitzbound}
    \sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \operatorname{Lip}(v_t) \leq 6 + 3 \log(1 + |q| \sqrt{1+M}).
\end{equation}
By definition of $M$ and $C_d \leq d^{4d}$ we know that
\begin{equation}
    \sqrt{1+M} \leq 2(1+\|\phi\|_{C^m}) d^{(5d+1)/2}(1 + R + Q\|\phi\|_\infty)^{d/2}
\end{equation}
from which we can bound
\begin{align}
    \log(1 + |q|\sqrt{1+M}) &\leq 1 + \log(1+|q|) + \log(1 + \|\phi\|_{C^m}) + 4d\log(d+2+R+Q\|\phi\|_\infty).
\end{align}
Combining this with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativefeaturelearningRKHSbound}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativefeaturelearningLipschitzbound}) yields (v) and (i), respectively. 
Looking back at (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativefeaturelearningdefinitionofdrifts}), we see that the first phase multiplies the $u$ coordinate by $1/r$. The second phase adds $\frac{q}{r} u \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)$ and preserves $\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle$ since $u \perp \theta$. Lastly, the third phase multiplies the resulting $u$ coordinate by $r$, which proves (ii).

It remains to prove the moment and trace estimates. Write
\begin{equation}
    x = x_\perp + \left\langle x, u\right\rangle u, \quad \left\langle x_\perp, u\right\rangle = 0.
\end{equation}
During the first phase, the absolute value of the $u$ coordinate decreases while $x_\perp$ is unchanged. During the middle phase, the displacement has magnitude at most $\frac{|q|}{r}\|\phi\|_\infty$. At the beginning of the last phase, the $u$ coordinate equals \begin{equation}
    \frac{\left\langle x, u\right\rangle + q \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)}{r}.
\end{equation}
During the final phase this coordinate is multiplied by a factor which starts at 1 and ends at $r$, and so its magnitude never exceeds $|\left\langle x, u\right\rangle + q \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)|$. Thus,
\begin{equation}
    \|\Phi_t(x)\| \leq \|x\| + |q|\|\phi\|_\infty \quad (\forall t \in [0, 1],\; \forall x \in {\mathbb{R}}^d).
\end{equation}
Applying the triangle inequality in $L^d(\rho_0)$ implies $\operatorname{rad}_d(\rho_t) \leq R+|q|\|\phi\|_\infty$, proving (iii). To finish, for the linear part of the kernel we know
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativetracebound1}
    d \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|x\|^2 d\rho_t(x) \leq d \operatorname{rad}_d(\rho_t)^2 \leq d(R+|q|\|\phi\|_\infty)^2.
\end{equation}
For the nonlinear part, we have that
\begin{align}
    \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \kappa_\phi(x, x) d\rho_t(x) &= \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|\Psi_x\|^2_{H^{d/2}(\mathbb{S}^{d-1})} \\&\leq C_d (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} (1+\|x\|)^d d\rho_t(x) \\
    &\leq C_d (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+\operatorname{rad}_d(\rho_t))^d \\
    &\leq C_d (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+R+Q\|\phi\|_\infty)^d
\end{align}
which implies that 
\begin{align}
\label{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativetracebound2}
    \frac{2d^d}{1+M}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\operatorname{tr} (\kappa_\phi(x, x) \1_d) d\rho_t(x) \leq \frac{2d^{d+1}C_d (1+\|\phi\|_{C^m})^2 (1+R+Q\|\phi\|_\infty)^d}{1+M} \leq 1
\end{align}
by definition of $M$. Combining (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativetracebound1}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixnonperturbativetracebound2}) yields (iv).

The final ``in particular" follows by taking $k_{d, \phi} := k_{d,\phi, d^{10000, d^{10000}}}$, observing that $\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle X_t, \theta\right\rangle = 0$ and so $X_T = X_0 + Tu\phi(\left\langle X_0, \theta\right\rangle)$, and applying the result with $q=T$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
This shortcut construction uses the same compress-transport-expand strategy that the optimal transports used in the Gaussian endpoints and linear drift case, see Remark \ref{remark:steinbarronlineargaussiantogaussianmeanmovement}. In that setting it was optimal up to universal constants, but in this nonlinear setting we expect there to be more efficient shortcuts.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixreverseOUsingleindexflows}
    Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be globally-Lipschitz, nonzero, and satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}. Let $u, \theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and $\sigma \in (0, \infty)$, and for each $\varepsilon > 0$ define
    \begin{equation}
        \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}} := \operatorname{Law}(X_1), \quad \dot{X}_t = \varepsilon\sigma u \phi(\left\langle X_t, \theta\right\rangle), \quad X_0 \sim \gamma_d.
    \end{equation}
    Then, it holds that
    \begin{equation}
        \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left({
        \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}
        }\right)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}})} \geq \frac{\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c)}{2}
    \end{equation}
    where $c := \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle$ and we define the quantity
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:proofmathfrakflow}\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c) := \int_0^1 \left\|u Q_r(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)+ \theta \left\langle \cdot, u\right\rangle Q_r'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle) - c \theta Q_r''(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} dr
    \end{equation}
    for the function 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofdefofQr}
        Q_r(t) := \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}\left[\phi\left(rt + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right].
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
Note that by rotational invariance, the expression in (\ref{eqn:proofmathfrakflow}) depends only on $c = \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle$.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Let us denote
   \begin{equation}
       w(x) := \sigma u\phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle), \quad f_\varepsilon := \frac{\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}}{\gamma_d}, \quad c := \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle,
   \end{equation}
   where we know that $\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}$ is absolutely continuous since the flow generated by $w$ is bi-Lipschitz (due to Lipschitzness of $w$). By the continuity equation, for each $\varphi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we have
   \begin{equation}
       \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\right|_{\varepsilon = 0} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi d\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}} = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle \nabla \varphi, w\right\rangle d\gamma_d = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \varphi h d\gamma_d,
   \end{equation}
   where we use Gaussian integration by parts and denote the function 
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofappendixdefofhforflowlowerbound}
       h(x) := \left\langle x, w(x)\right\rangle - \operatorname{div}w(x) = \sigma \left(\left\langle x, u\right\rangle \phi(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - c\phi'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right).
   \end{equation}
   Hence, $f_\varepsilon = 1 + \varepsilon h + o(\varepsilon)$ in the sense of distributions. For each fixed $\tau > 0$, the linear growth of $w$ and OU regularization\footnote{Letting $K_\tau$ denote the Mehler kernel (which is smooth with Gaussian decay of all its derivatives) and $T_\varepsilon$ the flow map for time $\varepsilon$, since $P_\tau f_\varepsilon = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} K_\tau (\cdot,T_\varepsilon(y)) d\gamma_d(y) $ and $T_\varepsilon(y) = y + \varepsilon w(y) + o(\varepsilon)$, we may differentiate under the integral to get local uniform convergence of derivatives.} turn this into $P_\tau f_\varepsilon = 1 + \varepsilon P_\tau h + o(\varepsilon)$ in $C^1_{\operatorname{loc}}$, or in other words
   \begin{equation}
       \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \nabla \log P_\tau f_\varepsilon = \nabla P_\tau h \quad \text{uniformly on compact sets}.
   \end{equation}
   By lower-semicontinuity of the Barron norm w.r.t. local uniform convergence (Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixbarronnormlscunderlocaluniformconvergence}) and Fatou's lemma, we find
   \begin{equation}
       \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}})}{\varepsilon} = \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int_0^\infty \left\|\frac{1}{\varepsilon} \nabla \log P_\tau f_\varepsilon\right\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} d\tau \geq \int_0^\infty \|\nabla P_\tau h\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}d\tau.
   \end{equation}
   We now compute the right hand side. With $r = e^{-\tau}$, by (\ref{eqn:proofappendixdefofhforflowlowerbound}) and the Mehler formula we have
    \begin{align}
        (P_\tau h)(x) &= \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d} \left[h\left(rx + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right] \\
        &= \sigma r \left\langle x, u\right\rangle \mathbb{E}\left[\phi\left(r \left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle\right)\right] \\&\quad + \sigma \sqrt{1-r^2} \mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle \xi, u\right\rangle \phi\left(r\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle\right)\right]\\&\quad  - \sigma c \mathbb{E}\left[\phi'(r\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle)\right].
    \end{align}
    Now, by Gaussian integration by parts we know
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}[\left\langle \xi, u\right\rangle F(\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle)] = \left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle \mathbb{E}[F'(\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle)] \quad (\forall F \in W^{1,2}(\gamma_1)).
    \end{equation}
    We apply this with $F(z) = \phi(r \left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}z)$ and $F'(z) = \sqrt{1-r^2}\phi'(r\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}z)$ to get that
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle \xi, u\right\rangle \phi\left(r\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle\right)\right] = c \sqrt{1-r^2} \mathbb{E}\left[\phi'(r\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle)\right],
    \end{equation}
    which we plug into our earlier expression to find
    \begin{align}
        \frac{1}{\sigma} (P_\tau h)(x) &= r \left\langle x, u\right\rangle Q_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) -cr^2 \mathbb{E}\left[\phi'(r\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle + \sqrt{1-r^2}\left\langle \xi, \theta\right\rangle)\right] \\
        &= r \left\langle x, u\right\rangle Q_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - cr Q_r'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle).
    \end{align}
   Differentiating, we find that
   \begin{equation}
       (\nabla P_\tau h)(x) = \sigma r \left(u Q_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) + \theta \left\langle x, u\right\rangle Q'_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - c\theta Q_r''(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)\right)
   \end{equation}
   and therefore that
   \begin{equation}
       \int_0^\infty \|\nabla P_\tau h\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} d\tau = \sigma \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c).
   \end{equation}
    Since the flow defining $\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}$ is admissible we know that $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{flow}}) \leq 2\sigma \varepsilon$ (where the factor of 2 accounts for the weight $1 + \|\theta\|$ in the bounded-activation Barron definition), yielding the claim.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixbarronnormlscunderlocaluniformconvergence}
Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfy Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}, and 
    let $(w_n)_{n \in {\mathbb{N}}} \subseteq \mathcal{B}_\phi$ and $w \in C_{\operatorname{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^d; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ be s.t. $w_n \to w$ uniformly on compact sets. Then,
    \begin{equation}
        \|w\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \liminf_{n \to \infty}\|w_n\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Set $\hat{\Theta} := {\mathbb{R}}^d \times {\mathbb{R}}$ to be the parameter space. If $\phi$ is bounded, let $\Theta := \hat{\Theta} \cup \{\infty\}$ be its one-point compactification and define
   \begin{equation}
       \psi_{a,b}(x) := \frac{\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b)}{1 + \|a\| + |b|}, \quad \psi_\infty(x) := 0.
   \end{equation}
   The map $\theta \mapsto \psi_\theta$ is continuous from $\Theta$ into $C_{\operatorname{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$: for $\theta \in \hat{\Theta}$ we get continuity at $\theta$ from continuity of $\phi$, while for continuity at $\theta = \infty$ we use that for each compact $K$ we have 
   \begin{equation}
       \sup_{x \in K}|\psi_{a,b}(x)| \leq \frac{\|\phi\|_\infty}{1 + \|a\| + |b|} \to 0
   \end{equation}
   as $\|a\| + |b| \to \infty$ . Similarly, if $\phi$ is positively $s$-homogeneous we define
   \begin{equation}
       \Theta := \{(a, b) \in \hat{\Theta}:\; \|a\| + |b| = 1\}, \quad \psi_{a, b}(x) := \phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b).
   \end{equation}
   This $\Theta$ is compact, and again $\theta \mapsto \psi_\theta$ is a continuous map from $\Theta$ into $C_{\operatorname{loc}}({\mathbb{R}}^d)$. Hence, in either case the Barron norm admits the equivalent representation
   \begin{equation}
       \|u\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \inf\left\{\|\nu\|_{\operatorname{TV}}:\; u(x) = \int_\Theta \psi_\theta(x) d\nu(\theta)\right\} \quad (\forall u \in \mathcal{B}_\phi)
   \end{equation}
   with $\nu$ ranging over finite ${\mathbb{R}}^d$-valued measures on the compact Polish space $\Theta$.

   With this, let $L := \liminf_{n \to \infty}\|w_n\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$ and assume without loss of generality that $L < \infty$. Passing to a subsequence, assume $\|w_n\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \to L$ and choose $\nu_n$ s.t.
   \begin{equation}
       w_n(x) = \int_\Theta \psi_\theta(x) d\nu_n(\theta), \quad \|\nu_n\|_{\operatorname{TV}} \leq \|w_n\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} + \frac{1}{n}.
   \end{equation}
   Since $\Theta$ is compact and Polish, $C(\Theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$ is separable and $\mathcal{M}(\Theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d) = C(\Theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)^*$ is the space of signed vector-valued measures equipped with the TV norm.
Since $(\nu_n)_{n \in {\mathbb{N}}}$ is bounded in $\mathcal{M}(\Theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$, by Banach-Alaoglu we may pass to a subsequence satisfying $\nu_n \rightharpoonup \nu$ weak-* for some $\nu \in \mathcal{M}(\Theta; {\mathbb{R}}^d)$. Since $\theta \mapsto \psi_\theta(x)$ is bounded continuous for every $x$, we know
   \begin{equation}
       w(x) = \lim_{n \to \infty}w_n(x) = \int_{\Theta} \psi_\theta(x) d\nu(\theta)
   \end{equation}
   and so $\nu$ represents $w$. Since $\|\nu\|_{\operatorname{TV}} \leq \liminf_{n \to \infty}\|\nu_n\|_{\operatorname{TV}} \leq L$ by lower-semicontinuity of the dual norm under weak-* convergence, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixreverseOUsingleindextilts}
Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be globally-Lipschitz, nonconstant, bounded below, and suppose it satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} and $\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi'(\xi)] \neq 0$.  Fix $\theta \in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and define
\begin{equation}
    \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}} := (1 + \varepsilon h_\phi) \gamma_d , \quad h_\phi(x) := {\phi}(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi(\xi)]
\end{equation}
for $\varepsilon > 0$ small enough that $1 + \varepsilon h_\phi \geq 0$. Then, it holds that
\begin{equation}
    \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left({\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}}}\right)}{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}})} \leq \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} \cdot \frac{\min\left\{\|\phi\|_\infty, \; \max\left\{|\phi(0)|, \; \operatorname{Lip}(\phi)\right\}\right\}}{\left|\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi'(\xi)]\right|}
\end{equation}
where $Q_r$ is as in (\ref{eqn:proofdefofQr}) and we define the quantity
\begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofmathfraktilt}\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} := \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int_0^1 \left\|\theta \frac{Q_r'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)}{r(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle) - \varepsilon \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi(\xi)])}\right\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}dr.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Let us denote 
    \begin{equation}
        m_\phi := \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi(\xi)], \quad f_\varepsilon := \frac{\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}}}{\gamma_d} = 1 + \varepsilon h_\phi.
    \end{equation}
    For $r = e^{-\tau}$, by the Mehler formula we know
    \begin{equation}
        (P_\tau f_\varepsilon)(x) = 1 + \varepsilon (Q_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - m_\phi)
    \end{equation}
    and therefore that for $r \in (0, 1)$ we have
    \begin{equation}
        (\nabla \log P_\tau f_\varepsilon)(x) = \varepsilon \theta \frac{Q_r'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - \varepsilon m_\phi}.
    \end{equation}
    Using $d\tau = -dr / r$ and integrating,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixinsgleindextiltSteinupperbound}
        \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\left({\pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}}}\right)}{\varepsilon} = \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}}.
    \end{equation}
    
    For the Barron transport distance lower bound, we use an argument similar to that of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixwassersteinandKLcontrol} adapted for unbounded $\phi$. Denote the quantities
    \begin{equation}
        L := \operatorname{Lip}(\phi), \quad C_0 := \max\{|\phi(0)|, \; L\}, \quad M := \|\phi\|_\infty, \quad C_\phi := \min\{M, C_0\}
    \end{equation}
    with $M = +\infty$ for unbounded $\phi$. We claim that for every $w \in \mathcal{B}_\phi$ and every $\rho \in \mathcal{P}_1({\mathbb{R}}^d)$ we have
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixW1estimatetoprove}
        \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\|w(x)\| d\rho(x) \leq (C_0 + LW_1(\gamma_d, \rho)) \|w\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}.
    \end{equation}
    To prove this, note that since $\phi$ is $L$-Lipschitz then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixinequalitycausephiisLlipschitz}
        \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d} \left|\phi\left(\left\langle a, \xi\right\rangle + b\right)\right| \leq |\phi(0)| + L \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_d}|\left\langle a, \xi\right\rangle + b| \leq |\phi(0)| + L(\|a \| + |b|).
    \end{equation}
    Since $\phi(0) = 0$ for positively one-homogeneous $\phi$, if we define
    \begin{equation}
        \omega(a, b) := \begin{cases}
            1 + \|a\| + |b| & \phi \text{ bounded},
            \\ \|a\| + |b| & \phi \text{ positively one-homogeneous}
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    then (\ref{eqn:proofappendixinequalitycausephiisLlipschitz}) implies that
    \begin{equation}
       \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d}\left|\phi\left(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b\right)\right|d\gamma_d(x) \leq C_0 \omega(a, b).
    \end{equation}
    Since $x \mapsto |\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b)|$ is $L\|a\|$-Lipschitz and $\|a\| \leq \omega(a, b)$, by Kantorovich-Rubinstein we have
    \begin{align}
        \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b)|d\rho(x)  &\leq \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} |\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b)|d\gamma_d(x) + L\|a\|W_1(\gamma_d, \rho) \\
        &\leq \left(C_0 + LW_1(\gamma_d, \rho)\right) \omega(a, b).
    \end{align}
    Integrating this over any vector measure representing $w$ and taking the infimum over such representations proves (\ref{eqn:proofappendixW1estimatetoprove}). 

    We now claim that 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixinsgleindextiltDblowerbound}
        \liminf_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \frac{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_\varepsilon^{\operatorname{tilt}})}{\varepsilon} \geq \frac{\left| \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \phi'(\xi)\right|}{C_\phi},
    \end{equation}
    which would yield the main result after combining with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixinsgleindextiltSteinupperbound}).
   To prove this, let $\varepsilon_n \downarrow 0$ be any sequence realizing the $\liminf$, let $(v_t^n, \rho_t^n)_{t \in [0, 1]}$ be any admissible transport from $\gamma_d$ to $\pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}$ with
   \begin{equation}
       \ell_n := \int_0^1 \|v_t^n\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}dt \leq D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}) + \varepsilon_n^2,
   \end{equation}
   and define
    \begin{equation}
        A_n(t) := \int_0^t \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \|v_s^n(x)\| d\rho_s^n(x) ds.
    \end{equation}
    Assume that $\lim_{n \to \infty }D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}) / \varepsilon_n < \infty$  (since (\ref{eqn:proofappendixinsgleindextiltDblowerbound}) holds trivially otherwise), 
in which case $\ell_n \leq \sqrt{\varepsilon_n}$ for all large enough $n$.
    By the standard continuity equation estimate (i.e. the length of an absolutely continuous curve in $(\mathcal{P}_1({\mathbb{R}}^d), W_1)$ upper bounds the $W_1$ distance) we know
$
        W_1(\gamma_d, \rho_t^n) \leq A_n(t)
$. Applying (\ref{eqn:proofappendixW1estimatetoprove}) yields that
\begin{equation}
    A'_n(t) \leq (C_0 + LA_n(t)) \|v_t^n\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}
\end{equation}
for a.e. $t$, after which Grönwall's inequality implies
\begin{equation}
    A_n(1) \leq \frac{C_0}{L}\left(e^{L\ell_n} - 1\right),
\end{equation}
where $L > 0$ since $\phi$ is nonconstant. If $\phi$ is bounded, then we may instead use that $W_1(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}) \leq M D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}) \leq M\ell_n$ (see Proposition \ref{prop:wassersteinkllowerbound}). Hence, in either case we find
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixW1estimatetoprove234}
    W_1(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}) \leq \ell_n \cdot \min\left\{M, \; C_0 \frac{e^{L\ell_n} -1}{L\ell_n}\right\}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, applying Kantorovich-Rubinstein with the $1$-Lipschitz function $x \mapsto \left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle$ implies 
\begin{align}
W_1(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}) &\geq \left|\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle x, \theta \right\rangle d\pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}(x) - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle x, \theta \right\rangle d\gamma_d(x)\right| = \left|\varepsilon_n\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^d} \left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle h_\phi(x) d\gamma_d(x)\right| \\
&= \left|\varepsilon_n \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\xi (\phi(\xi) - m_\phi)\right]\right| = \left|\varepsilon_n \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\xi \phi(\xi) \right]\right| \\
&= \varepsilon_n\left| \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \phi'(\xi)\right|
\end{align}
by Gaussian integration by parts. Combining this with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixW1estimatetoprove234}) yields
\begin{equation}
    \frac{\ell_n}{\varepsilon_n} \geq \frac{\left| \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \phi'(\xi)\right|}{\min\left\{M, \; C_0 \frac{e^{L\ell_n} - 1}{L\ell_n }\right\}}.
\end{equation}
Taking an infimum over transports from $\gamma_d$ to $\pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}}$ and using that $\ell_n \leq \sqrt{\varepsilon_n}$ for all large enough $n$ implies that
\begin{equation}
    \frac{D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi_{\varepsilon_n}^{\operatorname{tilt}})}{\varepsilon_n} \geq \frac{\left| \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \phi'(\xi)\right|}{\min\left\{M, \; C_0 \frac{e^{L\sqrt{\varepsilon_n}} - 1}{L\sqrt{\varepsilon_n} }\right\}} - \varepsilon_n
\end{equation}
for all $n$ large enough. In particular, as $n \to \infty$ we know 
\begin{equation}
    \min\left\{M, \; C_0 \frac{e^{L\sqrt{\varepsilon_n}} - 1}{L\sqrt{\varepsilon_n} }\right\} \to \min \{M, \; C_0\} = C_\phi \quad \text{since $\varepsilon_n \downarrow 0$}
\end{equation}
and so (\ref{eqn:proofappendixinsgleindextiltDblowerbound}) is proved.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixtiltdenominatorremoval}
    If $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$ and $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ or $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$, then 
    \begin{equation}
        \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{r}\left\|\theta Q_r'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}dr.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
We will show that for $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ and $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$ it holds that if
   \begin{equation}
       F_{r,\varepsilon}(t) := \frac{Q_r'(t)}{r(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t))} - \frac{Q'_r(t)}{r} = -\varepsilon \frac{Q_r(t)Q_r'(t)}{r(1+\varepsilon Q_r(t))} = \frac{1}{r} \frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac{\log(1 + \varepsilon Q_r)}{\varepsilon} - Q_r\right],
   \end{equation}
   then there is the scalar Barron norm estimate
   \begin{equation}
       \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int_0^1 \left\| F_{r,\varepsilon} \right\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} dr = 0,
   \end{equation}
   after which the main claim follows by the reverse triangle inequality.

   For $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$, we may use $\sin(a+b) = \sin(a) \cos(b) + \cos(a) \sin(b)$ to find
   \begin{align}
       Q_r(t) &= \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\sin\left(\lambda r t + \lambda \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right] \\
       &= \sin(\lambda rt) \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\cos\left(\lambda \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right] + \cos(\lambda rt)\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\sin\left(\lambda \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right] 
       \\ &= \sin(\lambda rt) \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\cos\left(\lambda \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right]
       \\&= A_r \sin(\lambda r t),
   \end{align}
   where $A_r := \exp(-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}(1-r^2)) \leq 1$. In particular,
   \begin{equation}
       F_{r,\varepsilon} (t) = -\varepsilon \lambda A_r^2 \frac{\sin(\lambda rt) \cos(\lambda r t)}{1 + \varepsilon A_r \sin(\lambda rt)} = -\varepsilon \lambda A_r^2\sum_{j=0}^\infty (-\varepsilon A_r)^j \sin(\lambda r t)^{j+1} \cos(\lambda r t),
   \end{equation}
   where for the second equality we take $\varepsilon < 1$ and use geometric series $\frac{1}{1-x} = \sum_{j=0}^\infty x^j $. Denoting 
   \begin{equation}
       h_j(x) := \sin(x)^{j+1}\cos(x) = \frac{1}{2^{j+2}i^{j+1}} (e^{ix} - e^{-ix})^{j+1} (e^{ix} + e^{-ix}) = \sum_{n = -(j+2)}^{j+2} a_{j,n}\sin(nx + b_{j,n})
   \end{equation}
   where $|b_{j,n}| \leq \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\sum_{n}|a_{j,n}| \leq 1$. Hence,
   \begin{equation}
       \|h_j(\lambda r \cdot)\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \sum_{n=-(j+2)}^{j+2} |a_{j,n}| \left(1 + r|n| + \frac{|b_{j,n}|}{\lambda}\right) \leq 1 + r(j+2) + \frac{\pi}{2\lambda}.
   \end{equation}
   Since $F_{r,\varepsilon}(t) = -\varepsilon \lambda A_r^2 \sum_{j=0}^\infty (-\varepsilon A_r)^j h_j(\lambda r t)$, we find
   \begin{align}
       \|F_{r,\varepsilon}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} &\leq \varepsilon \lambda A_r^2 \sum_{j=0}^\infty (\varepsilon A_r)^j \left(1 + r(j+2) + \frac{\pi}{2\lambda}\right) \\
       &\leq \varepsilon \lambda  \sum_{j=0}^\infty \varepsilon^j \left(j+3 + \frac{\pi}{2\lambda}\right) \\
       &\leq (8\lambda + \pi) \varepsilon
   \end{align}
   for all $r \in (0, 1)$ and $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/2)$. Hence, $\int_0^1 \|F_{r,\varepsilon}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} dr \to 0$.

    For $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$ we apply a deconvolution argument with the Fourier convention $\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(x) e^{-2\pi ix\xi}dx$ (note that this is different than the rest of the paper). If we denote
    \begin{equation}
        G_{r,\varepsilon}(z) := \frac{\log(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(z/r))}{\varepsilon} - Q_r(z/r)
    \end{equation}
    then $F_{r,\varepsilon}(t) = G_{r,\varepsilon}'(rt)$ and so for each $j$ we have
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixfouriertransformofFprime}
        \partial_\xi ^j \widehat{F_{r,\varepsilon}'}(\xi) = r^{-j}\widehat{(-2\pi ix)^j G_{r,\varepsilon}''}\left(\frac{\xi}{r}\right).
    \end{equation}
    Fix any $a \in (\frac{\pi}{8\lambda}, \frac{\pi}{2\lambda})$. We claim there are $D_{\lambda, a}, \varepsilon_{\lambda, a} \in (0, \infty)$ s.t. for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_{\lambda, a})$ and all $r \in (0, 1)$ the function $G_{r,\varepsilon}$ is holomorphic on an open neighborhood of $|\operatorname{Im}(z)| \leq a$ with the estimate
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixstripholomorphicsecondderivativeestimate}
      \sup_{|y| \leq a} |x+iy|^j \left|G_{r,\varepsilon}''(x+iy)\right| \leq \frac{D_{\lambda, a}\varepsilon}{1 + x^2} \quad (\forall x \in {\mathbb{R}})
    \end{equation}
    for $j \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. To see this, we write $u = \lambda x$, $v = \lambda y$ and start from the identities
    \begin{equation}
        |\cosh(u+iv)|^2 = \sinh(u)^2 + \cos(v)^2, \quad |\sinh(u+iv)|^2 = \sinh(u)^2 + \sin(v)^2.
    \end{equation}
    For $z = x + iy$ with $|y| \leq a$ we know $|v| \leq \lambda a < \pi / 2$ and so
    \begin{align}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixcoshboundheedeheedee}
        |\cosh(u+iv)|^2 \geq \cos(v)^2 (\sinh(u)^2 + 1) = \cos(v)^2 \cosh(u)^2 \geq \cos(\lambda a)^2 \cosh(u)^2
    \end{align}
    and also
    \begin{equation}
        |\sinh(u+iv)|^2 \leq \sinh(u)^2 + 1 = \cosh(u)^2.
    \end{equation}
    Dividing these two, 
    \begin{equation}
        |\tanh(\lambda z)| = \frac{|\sinh(u + iv)|}{|\cosh(u+iv)|} \leq \sec(\lambda a).
    \end{equation}
    Also, taking the reciprocal of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixcoshboundheedeheedee}) yields
    \begin{equation}
        |\operatorname{sech}(\lambda z)|^2 = \frac{1}{|\cosh(u+iv)|^2}  \leq \sec(\lambda a)^2 \operatorname{sech}(\lambda x)^2 \leq 4 \sec(\lambda a)^2 e^{-2\lambda |x|},
    \end{equation}
    where we used that $\operatorname{sech}(t)^2 = \frac{4}{(e^t + e^{-t})^2} \leq 4e^{-2|t|}$. Now, we know
    \begin{equation}
       (\tanh (\lambda z))' = \lambda \operatorname{sech}(\lambda z)^2, \quad (\tanh (\lambda z))'' = -2\lambda^2 \tanh(\lambda z)\operatorname{sech}(\lambda z)^2.
    \end{equation}
    and so if we define $q_r(z) := Q_r(z/r) = \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\tanh(\lambda z + \lambda \sqrt{1-r^2} \xi)]$ and differentiate under the expectation then
    \begin{equation}
        |q_r(z)| \leq \sec(\lambda a), \quad |q_r'(z)| \leq 4\lambda \sec(\lambda a)^2 \mathbb{E}[e^{-2\lambda |x + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi|}]
    \end{equation}
    and similarly
    \begin{equation}
        |q_r''(z)| \leq 8\lambda^2 \sec(\lambda a)^3\mathbb{E}[e^{-2\lambda |x + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi|}].
    \end{equation}
Note that $|x + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi| \geq |x| - \sqrt{1-r^2}|\xi| \geq |x| - |\xi|$ and so
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[e^{-2\lambda |x + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi|}] \leq e^{-2\lambda |x|} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[e^{2\lambda |\xi|}].
\end{equation}
    Hence, if we define the constant \begin{equation}C_{\lambda, a} := \sec(\lambda a) + \left(4\lambda \sec(\lambda a)^2 + 8 \lambda^2 \sec (\lambda a)^3\right) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[e^{2\lambda |\xi|}]\in (0, \infty)\end{equation} then for all $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$, $y \in [-a, a]$, and $r \in (0, 1)$ we have
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixboundsonq_rblahblah}
        |q_r(x+iy)| \leq C_{\lambda, a }, \quad |q_r'(x+iy)| + |q_r''(x+iy)| \leq C_{\lambda, a} e^{-2\lambda |x|}.
    \end{equation}
    Take $ 0 < \varepsilon \leq \min \{1,\; 1/(2C_{\lambda, a})\} =: \varepsilon_{\lambda, a}$. Since
    \begin{equation}
        G_{r,\varepsilon} = \frac{\log(1+\varepsilon q_r)}{\varepsilon} - q_r,
    \end{equation}
    and throughout $|y| \leq a$ we have
$        |\varepsilon q_r(x+iy)| \leq  \frac{1}{2}$, 
    we know that the principal branch of the logarithm is holomorphic on a neighborhood of the strip $|\operatorname{Im}(z)| \leq a$ and therefore so too is $G_{r,\varepsilon}$. Furthermore, we compute
    \begin{equation}
        G_{r,\varepsilon}'' = -\varepsilon \frac{(q_r')^2 + q_rq_r''}{1 + \varepsilon q_r} + \varepsilon^2 \frac{q_r(q_r')^2}{(1+\varepsilon q_r)^2}
    \end{equation}
    after which we apply the bound (\ref{eqn:proofappendixboundsonq_rblahblah}) to get
    \begin{align}
        |G_{r,\varepsilon}''(x+iy)| &\leq 2\varepsilon \left(|q'_r(x+iy)|^2 + |q_r(x+iy)||q_r''(x+iy)| \right)+ 4\varepsilon^2 |q_r(x+iy)| |q_r'(x+iy)|^2 \\
        &\leq 4\varepsilon (C_{\lambda, a}^2 + C_{\lambda, a}^3)  e^{-2\lambda|x|}.
    \end{align}
    If we define
    \begin{equation}
        \widetilde{C}_{\lambda, a} := \max_{j \in \{0, 1, 2\}} \sup_{x \in {\mathbb{R}}}(1+x^2)(|x| + a)^j e^{-2\lambda |x|} < \infty
    \end{equation}
    then we have shown (\ref{eqn:proofappendixstripholomorphicsecondderivativeestimate}) with $D_{\lambda, a} := (2\pi)^24(C_{\lambda, a}^2 + C_{\lambda, a}^3 )\widetilde{C}_{\lambda, a}$. Since the map $z \mapsto (-2\pi i z)^j G_{r,\varepsilon}''(z)$ is holomorphic in the strip and satisfies the decay estimate (\ref{eqn:proofappendixstripholomorphicsecondderivativeestimate}), we get the exponential Fourier decay
    \begin{equation}
       \left| \widehat{(-2\pi i x)^jG''_{r,\varepsilon}}(\xi)\right| \leq \pi D_{\lambda, a}  \varepsilon e^{-2\pi a |\xi|} \quad (\forall \xi \in {\mathbb{R}}, \; \forall j \in \{0, 1, 2\}),
    \end{equation}
    see e.g. Theorem 2.1 of Chapter 4 in \cite{steinshakarchi2003complex}.
    In light of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixfouriertransformofFprime}), this implies that
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixboundsonFouriertransformofFprime1335}
        \left|\partial_\xi^j \widehat{F_{r,\varepsilon}'}(\xi)\right| \leq r^{-j}\pi D_{\lambda, a} \varepsilon e^{-2\pi a |\xi| / r} \quad (\forall \xi \in {\mathbb{R}},\; \forall j \in \{0, 1, 2\})
    \end{equation}
    for all $r \in (0, 1)$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,  \varepsilon_{\lambda, a}]$. Let us now define
    \begin{equation}
        k_r(t) := \tanh(4\lambda r t), \quad \widehat{k_r'}(\xi) = \frac{\pi^2 \xi / (2\lambda r)}{\sinh(\pi^2 \xi / (4\lambda r))},
    \end{equation}
    which implies the estimate
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixboundsonFouriertransformofFprime1336}
        \left|\partial_\xi^j  \frac{1}{\widehat{k_r'}(\xi)}\right| \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi^2}{4\lambda r}\right)^j e^{\pi^2 |\xi| / (4\lambda r)} \quad (\forall \xi \in {\mathbb{R}},\; \forall j \in \{0, 1, 2\})
    \end{equation}
    To see this, note that $\frac{\sinh(x/2)}{x} = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 \cosh(\frac{tx}{2}) dt$ and so differentiating under the integral yields
    \begin{equation}
        \left|\frac{d^j}{dx^j} \frac{\sinh(x/2)}{x}\right|  \leq \frac{1}{2^{j+1}} \int_0^1 t^j e^{|x|/2}dt \leq 2^{-j-1}e^{|x|/2}.
    \end{equation}
If we define the function
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixfouriernnonsesedefinitionformreps}
    \widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}(\xi) := \frac{\widehat{F'_{r,\varepsilon}}(\xi)}{\widehat{k_r'}(\xi)} \quad (\forall \xi \in {\mathbb{R}}),
\end{equation}
then by (\ref{eqn:proofappendixboundsonFouriertransformofFprime1335}), (\ref{eqn:proofappendixboundsonFouriertransformofFprime1336}) and the product rule, if we denote $M_{\lambda, a} :=\frac{\pi}{2} D_{\lambda, a} \max_{j \in \{0, 1, 2\}} (1 + \frac{\pi^2}{4\lambda})^j$ then
\begin{equation}
    \left|\partial_\xi^j \widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}(\xi)\right| \leq M_{\lambda, a} \varepsilon r^{-j} e^{-\left(2\pi a - \frac{\pi^2}{4\lambda}\right) |\xi|/r} \quad (\forall \xi \in {\mathbb{R}}, \; \forall j \in \{0, 1, 2\}).
\end{equation} Note that $2\pi a - \frac{\pi^2}{4\lambda} > 0$ since $a > \frac{\pi}{8\lambda}$. The important consequence is that if we denote $c_{\lambda, a} := \frac{M_{\lambda, a}}{\sqrt{2\pi a - \frac{\pi^2}{4\lambda}}} $ then we have
\begin{equation}
    \left\|\partial_\xi^j\widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}\right\|_{L^2(d\xi)} \leq c_{\lambda, a} \cdot \varepsilon r^{\frac{1}{2} - j} \quad (\forall j \in \{0, 1, 2\})
\end{equation}
for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_{\lambda, a})$ and $r \in (0, 1)$. Hence, we may apply Fourier inversion to define $m_{r,\varepsilon}: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$, and so by Plancherel
\begin{align}
    \left\|m_{r,\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^2(dx)} &= \left\|\widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}\right\|_{L^2(d\xi)} \leq c_{\lambda, a} \varepsilon r^{1/2}, \\ \left\|x m_{r,\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^2(dx)} &= \frac{1}{2\pi}\left\|\partial_\xi\widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}\right\|_{L^2(d\xi)} \leq \frac{c_{\lambda, a}}{2\pi} \varepsilon r^{-1/2}, \\ \left\|x^2m_{r,\varepsilon}\right\|_{L^2(dx)} &= \frac{1}{4\pi^2}\left\|\partial_\xi^2\widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}\right\|_{L^2(d\xi)}\leq \frac{c_{\lambda, a}}{4\pi^2} \varepsilon r^{-3/2}.
\end{align}
Furthermore, by Cauchy-Schwarz
\begin{align}
    \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + r|x|)|m_{r,\varepsilon}(x)| dx &\leq \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{(1+r|x|)^2}{(1+r^2x^2)^2}dx\right)^{1/2} \cdot \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+r^2x^2)^2 |m_{r,\varepsilon}(x)|^2 dx\right)^{1/2} \\
    &= \sqrt{\frac{\pi+2}{r}} \cdot \left(\|m_{r,\varepsilon}\|_{L^2(dx)}^2 + 2r^2\|xm_{r,\varepsilon}\|_{L^2(dx)}^2 + r^4 \|x^2m_{r,\varepsilon}\|_{L^2(dx)}^2 \right)^{1/2}\\
    &\leq \sqrt{\frac{\pi + 2}{r}} \cdot c_{\lambda, a}\varepsilon \cdot \left(r + \frac{2r^2}{4\pi^2 r} + \frac{r^4}{16 \pi^4 r^3}\right)^{1/2}
    \\ &= \sqrt{\pi + 2} \cdot \left(1 + \frac{1}{4\pi^2}\right) \cdot c_{\lambda, a}\varepsilon,
\end{align}
where the second line used that $\int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{(1+r|x|)^2}{(1+r^2x^2)^2}dx = \frac{1}{r} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{(1+|y|)^2}{(1+y^2)^2}dy = \frac{\pi+2}{r}$. 
Now, by  (\ref{eqn:proofappendixfouriernnonsesedefinitionformreps}) and the convolution theorem we know $F_{r,\varepsilon}' = k_r' * m_{r,\varepsilon}$ and therefore that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixfouriernonsenseconvolutionrepresentation}
    F_{r,\varepsilon} = k_r * m_{r,\varepsilon} + C
\end{equation}
for some constant $C \in {\mathbb{R}}$. Since $F_{r,\varepsilon} = -\varepsilon \frac{Q_r Q_r'}{r(1 + \varepsilon Q_r)}$ and $\|Q_r\|_\infty < \infty$ while $\lim_{|t| \to \infty }Q_r'(t) = 0$, we know that $\lim_{|t| \to \infty} F_{r,\varepsilon}(t) = 0$. Since $\|k_r\|_\infty < \infty$ and $m_{r,\varepsilon} \in L^1(dx)$, by dominated convergence
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{t \to \infty} (k_r * m_{r,\varepsilon})(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} m_{r,\varepsilon}(x) dx = \widehat{m_{r,\varepsilon}}(0) = \frac{\widehat{F'_{r,\varepsilon}}(0)}{\widehat{k'_r}(0)} = \frac{F_{r,\varepsilon}(\infty) - F_{r,\varepsilon}(-\infty)}{2} = 0.
\end{equation}
Thus, $C = 0$ and so (\ref{eqn:proofappendixfouriernonsenseconvolutionrepresentation}) reads
\begin{equation}
    F_{r,\varepsilon}(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \phi(4rt - 4rx) m_{r,\varepsilon}(x) dx. 
\end{equation}
This is a representation of $F_{r,\varepsilon}$ as a mixture of neurons, and so
\begin{align}
    \|F_{r,\varepsilon}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} &\leq \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + 4r + 4r|x|) |m_{r,\varepsilon}(x)| dx \leq 5 \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+r|x|) |m_{r,\varepsilon}(x)| dx \\&\leq 5 \sqrt{\pi + 2} \cdot \left(1 + \frac{1}{4\pi^2}\right) \cdot c_{\lambda, a}\varepsilon.
\end{align}
This holds for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_{\lambda, a})$ and all $r \in (0, 1)$, which yields the claim.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:appendixreverseOUsingleindexflowsandtiltsactivations}
    Let $\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}$ and $\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}}$ be as in (\ref{eqn:proofmathfrakflow}) and (\ref{eqn:proofmathfraktilt}), respectively. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{(Sinusoidal activation).} If $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ for some $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$, then it holds that
        \begin{equation}
          \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c) = +\infty  \quad (\forall c \in [-1, 1]), \quad \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} \leq 1 + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} + \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}.
        \end{equation}
\item \textbf{(Tanh activation).} If $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$ for some $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$, then it holds that
        \begin{equation}
          \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c) = +\infty  \quad (\forall c \in (-1, 1)), \quad \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} \leq 1 + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} + \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}.
        \end{equation}
        \item \textbf{(ReLU activation).} If $\phi(z) = \max\{0, z\}$, then it holds that
        \begin{equation}
          \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c) = +\infty  \quad (\forall c \in (-1, 1)), \quad \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} \leq 9 + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} + \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}.
        \end{equation}
    \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
First we will show that $\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{flow}}(c) = +\infty$ in the stated cases, for which we denote
    \begin{equation}
        V_r(x) := u Q_r(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) + \theta \left\langle x, u\right\rangle Q_r'(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle) - c\theta Q_r''(\left\langle x, \theta\right\rangle).
    \end{equation}
    If $|c| < 1$ and we take $v := \frac{u - c\theta}{\sqrt{1 - c^2}}$ then $\left\langle v, \theta\right\rangle = 0$ while $\left\langle v, u\right\rangle = \sqrt{1-c^2} > 0$. Hence,
    \begin{equation}
        V_r(av) = u Q_r(0) + a \cdot \theta \sqrt{1-c^2} Q_r'(0) - c\theta Q_r''(0) \quad (\forall a > 0).
    \end{equation}
    In the cases $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ and $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$ we know $\|\phi\|_\infty, \|\phi'\|_\infty, \|\phi''\|_{\infty} < \infty$ and so $\|Q_r\|_\infty, \|Q_r'\|_\infty, \|Q_r''\|_{\infty} < \infty$ for all $r \in (0, 1)$. For $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ we know from the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtiltdenominatorremoval} that
    \begin{equation}
        Q'_r(0) = \lambda r A_r \cos(0) > 0 \quad (\forall r \in (0, 1))
    \end{equation}
    and for $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$ we directly compute
    \begin{equation}
        Q'_r(0) = r \lambda \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[\operatorname{sech}\left(\lambda \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)^2\right] > 0 \quad (\forall r \in (0, 1]).
    \end{equation}
    Hence, $a \mapsto V_r(av)$ is unbounded. Since $\|V_r\|_\infty \leq \|\phi\|_\infty \|V_r\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}$, this implies $\|V_r\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \infty$ for all $r \in (0, 1)$. If instead $|c| = 1$ then $u = c\theta$ in which case
    \begin{equation}
        V_r(a \theta) = u Q_r(a) + au Q_r'(a) - u  Q_r''(a) \quad (\forall a > 0).
    \end{equation}
    In the case $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ we know $ a \mapsto a Q_r'(a) = \lambda r A_r \cdot a \cos(\lambda r a)$ is unbounded, and $\|V_r\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}=+\infty$ is true even when $|c| = 1$. Lastly, in the case $\phi(z) = \max\{0, z\}$ and $|c| < 1$ we again define $v := \frac{u - c\theta}{\sqrt{1-c^2}}$ to get
    \begin{equation}
       \left\langle  V_r(av + b\theta), \theta\right\rangle = c Q_r(b) + \left(a\sqrt{1-c^2} + bc\right) Q_r'(b) - cQ_r''(b) \quad (\forall a, b > 0).
    \end{equation}
    Hence, comparing with $b=0$ gives
    \begin{equation}
        \left\langle V_r(av+b\theta) - V_r(av), \theta\right\rangle = \left(a \sqrt{1-c^2}\right) \left(Q_r'(b) - Q_r'(0)\right) + C_{r,b,c}
    \end{equation}
    for some constant $C_{r,b,c}$ independent of $a$. Hence,
    \begin{align}
        \frac{\|V_r(av+b\theta) - V_r(av)\|}{\|(av+b\theta) - av\|} &= \frac{\|V_r(av+b\theta) - V_r(av)\|}{b} \geq \frac{\left| \left\langle V_r(av+b\theta) - V_r(av), \theta\right\rangle\right|}{b}  \\
        &\geq \frac{a\sqrt{1-c^2}}{b} \left|Q_r'(b) - Q'_r(0)\right| - \frac{|C_{r,b,c}|}{b}.
    \end{align}
    For ReLU, $Q_r'(b) = r\Phi(\frac{rb}{\sqrt{1-r^2}})$ is strictly increasing and so $Q_r'(b) - Q'_r(0) \neq 0$, which means this quantity can be made as large as possible (by taking $a$ large with $b$ fixed). Hence, $V_r$ cannot be globally-Lipschitz; since $\|\phi'\|_{L^\infty} < \infty$ this means that $\|V_r\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} = \infty$ as desired.

    We now bound the energy of the tilts. For any Lipschitz $\phi$ we know
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{1}{r}Q_r'(t) = \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}\left[\phi'\left(rt + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}\left[\xi \phi\left(rt + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)\right]
    \end{equation}
    by Gaussian integration by parts. This is a valid Barron representation, and so
    \begin{align}
        \frac{1}{r} \|\theta Q_r'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} &\leq \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \left[|\xi| \left(1 + r + \sqrt{1-r^2}|\xi|\right)\right] \\
        &= \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\frac{1+r }{\sqrt{1-r^2}} + 1.
    \end{align}
    Using that $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}dr = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\int_0^1 \frac{r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}dr = 1$, we find
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:proofappendixthedenominatorfreeupperboundtilt}
        \int_0^1 \frac{1}{r} \|\theta Q_r'(\left\langle \cdot, \theta\right\rangle)\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} dr \leq \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + 1\right) + 1.
    \end{equation}
    The tilt bounds then follow for the $\phi(z) = \sin(\lambda z)$ and $\phi(z) = \tanh(\lambda z)$ cases from Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtiltdenominatorremoval}. 
    
    For the ReLU case $\phi(z) = \max\{0, z\}$, we use the fact that if $f : {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is $C^2$ with \begin{equation}
        \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -\infty} f'(x) = 0, \quad \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + |x|) |f''(x)|dx < \infty
    \end{equation}
    then there is the representation
    \begin{equation}
        f(x) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \max\{0, x - a\}f''(a) da.
    \end{equation}
   This comes from the identification of $\phi$ as the Green's function of the 1D Laplacian, i.e. \begin{equation}
    \partial_x^2 \phi(x - a) = \partial^2_x \left[\max\{0, x-a\}\right] = \partial_x \left[\1_{x > a}\right] = \delta_{x-a}\end{equation}
   in the sense of distributions. In particular, we have
   \begin{equation}
       \|f\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + |a|) |f''(a)| da.
   \end{equation}
    Hence, if we note that $\mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)} \max\{0, \xi\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and we define the remainder
    \begin{align}
        R_{r,\varepsilon}(t) &:= \frac{Q'_r(t)}{r \left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)} - \frac{Q_r'(t)}{r}
        \\&= \frac{Q'_r(t)}{r} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}} - 1\right),
    \end{align}
    then the same argument of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthedenominatorfreeupperboundtilt}) yields
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eqn:proofappendixfuckingbullshitRrepsnonsense}\mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}  + 1 + \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int_0^1 \int_{\mathbb{R}}(1 + |a|) |R_{r,\varepsilon}''(a)|da dr,
    \end{equation}
    where we use that $\lim_{t \to -\infty}R_{r,\varepsilon}(t) = \lim_{t \to -\infty}R'_{r,\varepsilon}(t)  = 0$ since $Q_r(t), Q'_r(t), Q''_r(t) \to 0$ as $t \to -\infty$ by dominated convergence.
    By the product rule,
    \begin{equation}
        R'_{r,\varepsilon}(t) = \frac{Q''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}} - 1\right) - \frac{Q'_r(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon Q'_r(t)}{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2}
    \end{equation}
    and similarly
    \begin{align}
        R''_{r,\varepsilon}(t) &= \frac{Q'''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}} - 1\right)  - \frac{Q''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon Q'_r(t)}{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2} \\ &\quad - \frac{Q''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon Q'_r(t)}{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2}\\&\quad  - \frac{Q'_r(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2 \varepsilon Q''_r(t) - 2\varepsilon^2 (Q_r'(t))^2 \left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right) }{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^4} \\
        &= \frac{Q'''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}} - 1\right) - \frac{3Q''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon Q'_r(t)}{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2} \\
        &\quad + \frac{2\varepsilon^2 (Q_r'(t))^3}{r\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^3}.
    \end{align}
    This splits $R_{r,\varepsilon}''$ into three terms.
    Using that $Q_r(t) \geq 0$ and so $1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \geq \frac{1}{2}$ for $\varepsilon \leq \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}$, we find that
    \begin{align}
        \left|\frac{Q'''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}} - 1\right)\right| &= \left|\frac{Q_r'''(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} - Q_r(t)\right)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right| \\&\leq \frac{2\varepsilon}{r}\cdot  |Q_r'''(t)| \cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} + Q_r(t)\right)
    \end{align}
    and that 
    \begin{equation}
       \left|\frac{3Q''_r(t)}{r} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon Q'_r(t)}{\left(1 + \varepsilon Q_r(t) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2}\right| \leq \frac{12 \varepsilon}{r} \cdot \left|Q_r''(t)\right| \cdot \left|Q_r'(t)\right|
    \end{equation}
For $\phi(z) = \max\{0, z\}$ we may compute that
\begin{equation}
    Q_r'(t) = r \Phi\left(\frac{rt}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}\right), \quad Q_r''(t) = \frac{r^2}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \varphi\left(\frac{rt}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}\right),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
    Q_r'''(t) = -\frac{r^4 t}{(1-r^2)^{3/2}} \varphi\left(\frac{rt}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}\right), \quad Q_r(t) \leq r|t| + \frac{\sqrt{1-r^2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\end{equation}
for $\Phi$ and $\varphi$ the Gaussian CDF and PDF, respectively. 
Hence,
\begin{equation}
   \frac{1}{r} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|t|) \left( |Q_r'''(t)| \cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} + Q_r(t)\right) + |Q_r''(t)| \cdot |Q_r'(t)| \right)dt \leq C \left(1 + r + \frac{r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} + \sqrt{1 - r^2}\right)
\end{equation}
and since $\int_0^1 \frac{r}{\sqrt{1-r^2}}dr < \infty$ we find
    \begin{equation}
    \int_0^1\frac{1}{r}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(1+|t|)\left( |Q_r'''(t)| \cdot \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} + Q_r(t)\right) + |Q_r''(t)| \cdot |Q_r'(t)| \right)dtdr < \infty.
    \end{equation}
    This implies that the first two terms in the expansion of $R''_{r,\varepsilon}$ stay first order in $\varepsilon$, and do not contribute to (\ref{eqn:proofappendixfuckingbullshitRrepsnonsense}), i.e.
    \begin{equation}
        \mathfrak{F}_\phi^{\operatorname{tilt}} \leq \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} + 1 + \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}  \int_0^1 \frac{2\varepsilon^2}{r}\int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + |a|) \cdot \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 dadr.
    \end{equation}
    Now, since $Q_r' > 0$ for $r \in (0, 1)$ and $Q_r(-\infty) = 0$, $Q_r(\infty) = \infty$, we may substitute $u = Q_r(a) - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ (with $du = Q'_r(a) da$) to find that
    \begin{align}
        \int_{\mathbb{R}} \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 da &\leq r^2 \int_{\mathbb{R}} \frac{Q_r'(a) }{\left|1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right|^3}da \\&= r^2 \int_{ - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}^\infty \frac{1}{(1 + \varepsilon u)^3}du
        \\&= r^2 \frac{1}{2\varepsilon \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^2} \\
        &\leq \frac{2r^2}{\varepsilon},
    \end{align}
    where we used that $Q_r'(a) \leq r$ and $\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \leq \frac{1}{2}$.
    In particular, 
    \begin{equation}
        \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}  \int_0^1 \frac{2\varepsilon^2}{r}\int_{\mathbb{R}}  \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 dadr \leq \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int_0^1 4\varepsilon r dr = 0.
    \end{equation}
    We split the remaining integral into $a < 0$ and $a \geq 0$. Indeed, by using $0 \leq Q_r'(a) \leq r$ and lower bounding the denominator we have
    \begin{equation}
        \int_{-\infty}^0 |a| \cdot \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 da \leq -8r^2 \int_{-\infty}^0 aQ_r'(a) da = 8r^2 \int_{-\infty}^0 Q_r(a) da
    \end{equation}
    using integration by parts. We calculate
    \begin{align}
        \int_{-\infty}^0 Q_r(a) da &= \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}\left[\1_{\xi > 0}\int_{-\sqrt{1-r^2}\xi / r}^0 \left(ra + \sqrt{1-r^2}\xi\right)da\right] \\&=\frac{1-r^2}{2r} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}\left[\xi^2 \1_{\xi > 0}\right]\leq \frac{1}{4r},
    \end{align}
    which means that 
    \begin{equation}
         \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}  \int_0^1 \frac{2\varepsilon^2}{r}\int_{-\infty}^0  |a| \cdot \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 dadr \leq \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int_0^1 4\varepsilon^2 dr = 0
    \end{equation}
    and so the only contribution comes from $a \geq 0$. 
  If $a \geq 0$ then we know $Q_r(a) \geq ra$ and so
  \begin{equation}
 |a| \cdot \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 \leq  \frac{a r^3}{\left(1 + \varepsilon ra - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^3} \leq  \frac{a r^3}{\left(\frac{1}{2} + \varepsilon r a\right)^3} \leq  \frac{8ar^3}{(1+\varepsilon ra)^3}
  \end{equation}
  since $0 \leq Q_r'(a) \leq r$ and $\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \leq \frac{1}{2}$. Hence,
  \begin{align}
         \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}  \int_0^1 \frac{2\varepsilon^2}{r}\int_0^\infty  |a| \cdot \left|\frac{Q_r'(a)}{1 + \varepsilon Q_r(a) - \frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi}}}\right|^3 dadr &\leq \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int_0^1 16\varepsilon^2 r^2 \int_0^\infty \frac{a}{(1+\varepsilon r a)^3}da dr \\
         &= \limsup_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0} \int_0^1 16\varepsilon^2 r^2 \cdot \frac{1}{2\varepsilon^2r^2}dr\\
         &= 8.
    \end{align}
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
We combine Lemmas \ref{lemma:appendixreverseOUsingleindexflows} and \ref{lemma:appendixreverseOUsingleindextilts} with Proposition \ref{prop:appendixreverseOUsingleindexflowsandtiltsactivations} to find that if $|\left\langle u, \theta\right\rangle |<1$ the flow ratios are infinite and the tilt ratios are always bounded above by
    \begin{equation}
        \left(9 + \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} + \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi'(\xi)]\right|}
    \end{equation}
    since $\phi(0) = 0$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(\phi) \leq 1$ for $\phi(z) = \sin(z)$, $\phi(z) = \tanh(z)$, and $\phi(z) = \max\{0, z\}$. In either case, we may confirm that $\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{N}(0, 1)}[\phi'(\xi)]\right| \geq \frac{1}{2}$, from which the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Fix $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and let $\psi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $\Psi: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable. Using coordinates $(z, u) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ with $z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $u \in {\mathbb{R}}$, we define the induced {\em triangular shear measure} $\pi^{\psi, \Psi} \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})$ by
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:appendixshearstructurerepresentation}
    \pi^{\psi, \Psi} := \operatorname{Law}(Z, \psi(U) + \Psi(Z)), \quad (Z, U) \sim \gamma_{n+1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
Fix $\psi, \Psi$ and define $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}, b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ as above.  Then, the following hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] If $\Psi \in C^5_b({\mathbb{R}}^n)$ and $\psi$ is increasing and equal to the identity on $[-2\|\Psi\|_\infty, 2\|\Psi\|_\infty]$, then
        \begin{equation}
            \|\partial_1^3 s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_\infty \gtrsim \|\partial_1^3 \Psi\|_\infty \quad \text{ for all $0 < \tau \lesssim \frac{\|\partial_1^3\Psi\|_\infty}{n \|\Psi\|_{C^5}}$}.
        \end{equation}
        In particular, if $\phi \in C^3_b({\mathbb{R}})$ then $\inf_{R > 0}R^2\|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi^R} \gtrsim \|\partial_1^3 \Psi\|_\infty$, while if $\phi$ is positively $3$-homogeneous then $\|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\gtrsim \|\partial_1^3 \Psi\|_\infty $. The implied constants depend only on $\|\Psi\|_\infty$.
        \item[(ii)] Let $\Psi$ be bounded and $L$-Lipschitz and $\psi$ linear with positive slope, and fix $\tau \geq 0$, $\varepsilon > 0$. If $\hat{s}_\tau$ is a two-layer neural network of width $m$, then \begin{equation}\|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \leq \varepsilon \implies 
        m \geq m_\Psi(Q(\varepsilon + L^2\tau), \tau),
        \end{equation}
        where $m_\Psi$ is defined in Definition \ref{def:appendixhermitewidthenvelope} using the Hermite decomposition of $\Psi$ and $Q$ is a constant depending only on $\|\Psi\|_\infty$ and $\psi$. In such cases, for any $\phi$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} we have
        \begin{equation}
            \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \gtrsim \varepsilon \sqrt{m_\Psi(Q(2\varepsilon + L^2\tau), \tau) -1}
        \end{equation}
        with implied constant depending on $\phi, \|\Psi\|_\infty,\psi$.
    \end{enumerate}
    These statements also hold with $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
Fix $\psi, \Psi$ and define $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}, b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ as above.  Then, the following hold:
     \begin{enumerate}
         \item[(i)] If $\Psi(z) = \sum_{r=1}^M \Phi_r(P_{E_r}z)$ for subspaces $E_r \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^n$ with $\Phi_r \in C^\infty_c(E_r)$ and $\psi$ is a smooth increasing diffeomorphism with $\psi(u) \sim u^p$ outside of a compact set for some $p > 2$, then $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} \in \mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^s}$ for any $s \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and all $\tau \geq 0$.
         \item[(ii)] For any $\psi, \Psi$, any $\varepsilon, \tau  > 0$, and any nonpolynomial activation $\phi$, there is some two-layer neural network $\hat{s}_\tau$ of finite width which uses activation $\phi$ and satisfies $\|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \leq \varepsilon$.
     \end{enumerate}
     This first statement also holds with $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$, and the second statement does if $\pi^{\psi, \Psi} \in \mathcal{P}_2({\mathbb{R}}^d)$.
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised}
    Let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$, fix $\Psi \in C^5_b({\mathbb{R}}^{n}; {\mathbb{R}})$, and let  $\beta, D \in (0, \infty)$ be  s.t. $D> 1$ and
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixassumptionsonPsiforrepresentation}
        \|\Psi\|_\infty \leq \beta, \quad \|\partial^\alpha \Psi\|_\infty \leq D^{|\alpha|} \quad (\forall 1 \leq |\alpha| \leq 5).
    \end{equation}
   Fix $\psi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ measurable and nondecreasing s.t. $\psi(u) = u$ for all $u \in [-2\beta, 2\beta]$.
    Then, there is some $L_{\beta} \in (0, \infty)$ s.t. for every $\eta \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ we have
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:appendixlemmathirdderivativelowerbound}
       \|\partial_1^\eta s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{\infty} \geq \frac{ \|\partial_1^\eta \Psi\|_\infty}{2} \quad \left(\forall \tau \in \left(0, \;L_\beta \frac{ \|\partial_1^\eta \Psi\|_\infty}{nD^{\eta+2}}\right]\right).
    \end{equation}
    This also holds with $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
Since $Z \sim \gamma_n$ is rotation-invariant, the same bound follows if every $\partial_1$ is replaced by any other coordinate derivative $\partial_i$.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
Such a result holds for all derivative orders $\eta$. However, in the natural case $\Psi$ has frequency $D$, i.e. $\|\partial_1^\eta\Psi\|_\infty \asymp D^\eta$, we would get a lower bound of $D^{\eta - 2}$
on the integrated score norms. Hence, only when $\eta \geq 3$ does this argument provide a growing lower bound in the regime where $D$ is large; this is why we focus on the third derivative.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Denote by $\varphi_{a^2}$ the density of $\mathcal{N}(0, a^2)$ w.r.t. Lebesgue and by $q_\tau$ the density of $e^{-\tau} \psi(U) + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}H$ for $U, H \sim \gamma_1$ i.i.d. If we denote $\sigma := \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}$ then
\begin{equation}
    q_\tau(w) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \varphi_1(u) \varphi_{\sigma^2}(w - e^{-\tau}\psi(u)) du.
\end{equation}
Since $e^{-\tau} U + \sigma H \sim \gamma_1$ we know
\begin{equation}
    \varphi_1(w) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \varphi_1(u) \varphi_{\sigma^2}(w - e^{-\tau}u) du
\end{equation}
and hence for $j \in \{0, \ldots, 4\}$ we have
\begin{equation}
    q_\tau^{(j)}(w) - \varphi_1^{(j)}(w) = \int_{|u| > 2\beta} \varphi_1(u)\left[\varphi_{\sigma^2}^{(j)}(w-e^{-\tau}\psi(u)) - \varphi_{\sigma^2}^{(j)}(w-e^{-\tau}u)\right]du.
\end{equation}
If $\tau \in (0, 1/2]$ (and so $\tau \leq \sigma^2 \leq 2\tau$) and $|t| \geq \beta / 2$ then for all $j \in \{0, \ldots, 4\}$ we claim that
\begin{align}
\label{eqn:proofappendixboundonderivativesofgaussianpdf}
    \left|\varphi^{(j)}_{{\sigma^2}}(t)\right| \leq \frac{E_\beta}{2} \tau, \quad E_\beta := 200 \left(\frac{112}{e\beta^2}\right)^{7/2}.
\end{align}
This follows from the observation $|\varphi_1^{(j)}(x)| \leq 10 (1+|x|^4)e^{-x^2/2} \leq 100 e^{-x^2/4}$ and therefore $|\varphi_{\sigma^2}^{(j)}(t)|\leq 100 \sigma^{-(j+1)}e^{-t^2/(4\sigma^2)} \leq 100\tau^{-5/2}e^{-\beta^2/(32\tau)}$. Combining this with the elementary calculus bound $\sup_{\tau \leq 1/2} \tau^{-7/2}e^{-\beta^2/(32\tau)} \leq (112/(e\beta^2))^{7/2}$
yields (\ref{eqn:proofappendixboundonderivativesofgaussianpdf}) and consequently
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendix1dboundonqtauderivatives}
    \max_{0 \leq j \leq 4} \sup_{|w| \leq e^{-\tau}\beta} \left|q_\tau^{(j)}(w) - \varphi^{(j)}_1(w)\right| \leq E_\beta \tau \quad (\forall  \tau \in (0, 1/2]),
\end{equation}
where we note that $|w| \leq e^{-\tau}\beta$ implies that $\min\{|w-e^{-\tau}\psi(u)|, |w-e^{-\tau}u|\} \geq e^{-\tau} \beta \geq \beta / 2$ by monotonicity of $\psi$ and $|u| > 2\beta$.

Now, with $\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} = P_\tau^* \pi^{\psi, \Psi} \in \mathcal{P}({\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})$ the Mehler formula implies that $\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} = \operatorname{Law}\left((Z_\tau, U_\tau)\right)$ for the random variables
\begin{equation}
Z_\tau := e^{-\tau}Z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}} G, \quad U_\tau := e^{-\tau}\left(\psi(U) + \Psi(Z)\right) + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}} H,
\end{equation}
where $Z, G \sim \gamma_n$ and $U, H \sim \gamma_1$ are all independent. Since $\operatorname{Law}(Z_\tau) = \gamma_n$ we have the joint density
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentaitonlowerboundjointdensity}
    \rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u) = \gamma_n(z) F_\tau(z, u),
\end{equation}
where we define $F_\tau(z, \cdot)$ to be the density of $\operatorname{Law}(U_\tau \mid Z_\tau = z)$. Now, we know $Z \mid \{Z_\tau = z\} \sim \mathcal{N}(e^{-\tau}z, (1-e^{-2\tau})\1_n)$ by Gaussian regression and so
\begin{equation}
    F_\tau(z, u) = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} \left[q_\tau\left(u - e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}} G)\right)\right]
\end{equation}
since $q_\tau$ is the density of $e^{-\tau}\psi(U) + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}H$. Let us also define the Gaussian comparator
\begin{equation}
    \bar{F}_\tau(z, u) := \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} \left[\varphi_1\left(u - e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}G)\right)\right]
\end{equation}
For $\ell \in \{0, 1\}$ we have
\begin{equation}
    \left|\partial_u^\ell (F_\tau - \bar{F}_\tau)(e^{\tau}z, 0)\right| = \left|\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}\left[(q_\tau^{(\ell)} - \varphi_1^{(\ell)})(-e^{-\tau}\Psi(z+\sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}G))\right]\right|.
\end{equation}
Differentiating three times in the first coordinate of $e^{\tau}z$ and applying (\ref{eqn:proofappendixassumptionsonPsiforrepresentation}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendix1dboundonqtauderivatives}) yield
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundblabla5}
     \sup_{z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n} \max_{\ell \in \{0, 1\}}\left|\partial_1^k\partial_u^\ell (F_\tau - \bar{F}_\tau)(e^{\tau}z, 0)\right| \leq 5E_\beta D^k \tau \quad (\forall k \in \{0, \ldots, 3\},\; \forall \tau \in (0, 1/2]).
\end{equation}
Next, for $k \in \{0, \ldots, 3\}$ and $\ell \in \{0, 1\}$, each summand of $\partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell \bar{F}_\tau(e^\tau z, 0)$ has the form
\begin{equation}
   ce^{-a\tau} \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} \left[f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z + \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\tau}} G)\right], \quad f_{j,\alpha, \tau}(y) :=  \varphi_1^{(j)}\left(-e^{-\tau} \Psi(y)\right)\prod_{i=1}^m \partial_1^{\alpha_i} \Psi(y),
\end{equation}
where $0 \leq a \leq 6$, $j \in \{0, \ldots, 4\}$, $\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i = k$, and the sum of $|c|$ across all the summands is $\leq 5$. Note the Laplacian bound
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentaitonlowerboundblahblah4}
    \|\Delta f_{j,\alpha,\tau}\|_\infty \leq n B (2+2m+m^2)D^{k+2} \leq 17BnD^{k+2},
\end{equation}
where we denote $B := \max_{0 \leq j \leq 6} \|\varphi_1^{(j)}\|_\infty \leq 20000$. Consequently, the difference between corresponding summands of $\partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell \bar{F}_\tau(e^\tau z, 0)$ and $\partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell \bar{F}_0( z, 0)$ is upper bounded in absolute value by
\begin{align}
|ce^{-a\tau} \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} &\left[f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z + \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\tau}} G)\right] - c f_{j,\alpha,0}(z)| \leq  \\
    &\quad |c|e^{-a\tau} \left|\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} \left[f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z + \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\tau}} G)\right] - f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z)\right| + \\&\quad |c| \left|e^{-a \tau} f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z) - f_{j,\alpha,0}(z)\right|.
    \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundblahblah3}
\end{align}
We know that
\begin{align}
     \left|e^{-a\tau}\varphi_1^{(j)} (-e^{-\tau}\Psi(z)) - \varphi_1^{(j)}(-\Psi(z))\right| &\leq (1-e^{-a\tau})\|\varphi_1^{(j)}\|_\infty  +   \left|\varphi_1^{(j)} (-e^{-\tau}\Psi(z)) - \varphi_1^{(j)}(-\Psi(z))\right| \\
     &\leq (1-e^{-a\tau}) \|\varphi_1^{(j)}\|_\infty  + \|\varphi_1^{(j+1)}\|_\infty (1-e^{-\tau}) |\Psi(z)|  \\
     &\leq B(a + \beta) \tau
\end{align}
and therefore the second term in (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundblahblah3}) is bounded by
\begin{equation}
    \left|e^{-a \tau} f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z) - f_{j,\alpha,0}(z)\right| \leq  B(6 + \beta) \tau D^k.
\end{equation}
For the first term, we use the heat semigroup identity 
\begin{align}
    \left|\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} \left[f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z + \sqrt{1 - e^{-2\tau}} G)\right] - f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z)\right| &= \left|\frac{1}{2} \int_0^{1-e^{-2\tau}} \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n} \left[\Delta f_{j,\alpha,\tau}(z + \sqrt{t}G)\right]dt\right|
    \\ &\leq \frac{1-e^{-2\tau}}{2}\|\Delta f_{j,\alpha, \tau}\|_\infty \\ &\leq \frac{1-e^{-2\tau}}{2}(17BnD^{k+2}) \\
    &\leq 17BnD^{k+2}\tau,
\end{align}
where for the third line we plugged in (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentaitonlowerboundblahblah4}). Summing over the summands, 
we find that
\begin{align}
    \sup_{z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n} \max_{\ell \in \{0, 1\}}\left|\partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell \bar{F}_\tau(e^\tau z, 0) - \partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell \bar{F}_0(z, 0)\right| &\leq 5 \cdot (B(6 + \beta) \tau D^k + 17BnD^{k+2}\tau) \\&\leq B(115 + 5\beta) nD^{k+2}\tau.
\end{align}
Combining with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundblabla5}), we find that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundmainestimate}
     \sup_{z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n} \max_{\ell \in \{0, 1\}}\left|\partial_1^k\partial_u^\ell F_\tau(e^\tau z, 0) - \partial_1^k\partial_u^\ell F_0(z, 0)\right| \leq J_\beta nD^{k+2} \tau 
\end{equation}
for every $k \in \{0, \ldots, 3\}$ and $\tau \in (0, 1/2]$, where we define $J_\beta := B(115 + 5\beta) + 5E_\beta$ and the Gaussian comparator $F_0(z, u) := \bar{F}_0(z, u) = \varphi_1(u-\Psi(z))$.

Armed with this stability along the OU flow, we note that the last coordinate of the score satisfies
\begin{equation}
   S_\tau := (s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi})_{n+1} = \partial_u \log \rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} = \frac{\partial_u F_\tau}{F_\tau}
\end{equation}
due to the joint density (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentaitonlowerboundjointdensity}). Denote also the comparator
$S_0(z, u) := \Psi(z) - u$. 
By the quotient rule, for any $S = \frac{\partial_u F}{F}$ we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundquotientrule1}
