    \partial_1 S = \frac{F_{1u}}{F} - \frac{F_1F_u}{F^2}, \quad \partial_1^2 S = \frac{F_{11u}}{F} -\frac{2F_{1u}F_1 + F_uF_{11}}{F^2} + \frac{2F_uF_1^2}{F^3},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundquotientrule2}
    \partial_1^3 S = \frac{F_{111u}}{F} - \frac{3F_{11u}F_{1} + 3F_{1u}F_{11} + F_{u}F_{111}}{F^2} + \frac{6F_{1u}F_1^2 + 6F_uF_{1}F_{11}}{F^3} - \frac{6F_uF_{1}^3}{F^4}.
\end{equation}
Denoting $m_\beta := \varphi_1(\beta)$, from here on we fix $nD^2 \tau \leq \frac{m_\beta}{2J_\beta}$. Applying (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundmainestimate}) with $k = \ell = 0$ implies that 
\begin{equation}
    F_\tau(e^\tau z, 0) \geq F_0(z, 0) - J_\beta nD^2 \tau \geq \frac{m_\beta}{2}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, since we have $F_0(z, u) = \varphi_1(u-\Psi(z))$ the chain rule implies
\begin{equation}
    \max_{\ell \in \{0, 1\}} \left|\partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell F_0(z, 0)\right| \leq 5BD^k \quad (\forall k \in \{0, \ldots, 3\}),
\end{equation}
after which another application of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundmainestimate}) yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundmainestimate2}
     \max_{\ell \in \{0, 1\}} \left|\partial_1^k \partial_u^\ell F_\tau(e^\tau z, 0)\right| \leq 5BD^k + J_\beta nD^{k+2}\tau \leq J_\beta D^k \quad (\forall k \in \{0, \ldots, 3\}).
\end{equation}
For any term in (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundquotientrule1}), (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundquotientrule2}) of the form $c \frac{\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F}{F^q}$ with $\sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i = k$ and $\ell_i \in \{0, 1\}$ we have the bound
\begin{align}
    \left|\frac{\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_\tau}{F_\tau^q} - \frac{\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_0}{F_0^q}\right| &\leq \frac{1}{F_\tau^q} \left|\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_\tau - \prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_0\right| \\&\quad + \left|\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_0\right| \cdot \left|\frac{1}{F_\tau^q} - \frac{1}{F_0^q}\right|,
\end{align}
where we recall that the $F_\tau$ terms take $e^\tau z$ as their argument while the $F_0$ terms use $z$.
If we apply the telescoping bound
\begin{equation}
   \left| \prod_{i=1}^m a_i - \prod_{i=1}^m b_i\right| \leq \sum_{i=1}^m |a_i - b_i| \prod_{j \neq i} \max\{|a_j|, |b_j|\},
\end{equation}
then by applying (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundmainestimate}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundmainestimate2}) we find
\begin{equation}
    \left|\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_\tau - \prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_0\right|  \leq m J_\beta^m n D^{k+2}\tau.
\end{equation}
Furthermore, we may apply $|\frac{1}{a^q} - \frac{1}{b^q}| \leq \frac{q}{\min\{a,b\}^{q+1}}|a-b| $ for $a, b > 0$ to find 
\begin{equation}
    \left|\frac{1}{F_\tau^q} - \frac{1}{F_0^q}\right| \leq q \left(\frac{2}{m_\beta}\right)^{q+1} |F_\tau - F_0| \leq q J_\beta \left(\frac{2}{m_\beta}\right)^{q+1} nD^2 \tau,
\end{equation}
after which we use that $\left|\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_0\right| \leq J_\beta^m D^k$ to find
\begin{equation}
    \left|\frac{\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_\tau}{F_\tau^q} - \frac{\prod_{i=1}^m\partial_1^{\alpha_i}\partial_u^{\ell_i}F_0}{F_0^q}\right| \leq \left(mJ_\beta^m \left(\frac{2}{m_\beta}\right)^q + qJ_\beta^{m+1} \left(\frac{2}{m_\beta}\right)^{q+1}\right) nD^{k+2}\tau.
\end{equation}
In particular, from (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundquotientrule1}), (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationlowerboundquotientrule2}) we see that $|c| \leq 6$ and so
\begin{equation}
   \sup_{z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n} \left|\partial_1^\eta S_\tau(e^\tau z, 0) - \partial_1^\eta S_0(z, 0)\right| \leq K_\beta n D^{\eta + 2}\tau \quad (\forall \eta \in \{1, 2, 3\})
\end{equation}
for all $\tau \leq \frac{1}{K_\beta nD^2}$, where we define the constant
\begin{equation}
    K_\beta := \frac{2J_\beta}{m_\beta} + \frac{60J_\beta^2}{m_\beta^2} + \frac{400J_\beta^3}{m_\beta^3} + \frac{960J_\beta^4}{m_\beta^4} + \frac{768J_\beta^5}{m_\beta^5} \geq \frac{2J_\beta}{m_\beta}. 
\end{equation}
Since we have $\partial_1^\eta S_0 = \partial_1^\eta \Psi$, we find that
\begin{equation}
    \|\partial_1^\eta s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_\infty \geq {\|\partial_1^\eta\Psi\|_\infty} - K_\beta nD^{\eta + 2} \tau,
\end{equation}
from which the claim follows. Since $(b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} = (s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} + u$, the $\partial_1$ derivatives of the last coordinate are unchanged if we replace $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ with $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.

It remains to find a more explicit upper bound for $K_\beta$. Since $J_\beta \geq 115B$ we know $J_\beta \geq m_\beta$, and so
\begin{equation}
    K_\beta \leq 2190 \left(\frac{J_\beta}{m_\beta}\right)^5.
\end{equation}
Since $J_\beta \leq 20000(115 + 5\beta) + 1000 \left(\frac{112}{e\beta^2}\right)^{7/2} \leq 4.5 \cdot 10^8 (1 + \beta + \beta^{-7})$ and there are the inequalities $(1+\beta + \beta^{-7}) \leq 2e^{\beta^2/2}(1+\beta^{-7})$, $(1+\beta^{-7})^5 \leq 16 (1+\beta^{-35})$, we may use $m_\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\beta^2 / 2}$ to find that
\begin{equation}
    K_\beta \leq 10^{52}e^{5\beta^2} (1+\beta^{-35}).
\end{equation}
Defining $L_\beta := 10^{-52}e^{-5\beta^2} (1+\beta^{-35})^{-1} / 2$ yields the claim.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{corollary:representationlowerbound}
Let $\psi, \Psi$ be as in Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised} and define $D,L_\beta$ accordingly. Then, the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] Let $\phi \in C^3({\mathbb{R}})$ be bounded with $\|\phi'''\|_\infty < \infty$  and let $\mathcal{B}_\phi^R$ be its Barron space with input weights bounded by $R$ (see Definition \ref{def:barronspaces}). Then,
    \begin{equation}
       \inf_{R \in (0, \infty)} R^2 \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi^R}(\pi^{\psi, \Psi}) \geq \frac{L_\beta}{2nD^5} \cdot \max_{i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}}{\|\partial_i^3 \Psi\|_\infty^2}.
    \end{equation}
    \item[(ii)] Let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be positively 3-homogeneous (e.g. $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$) and let $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ be its Barron space (see Definition \ref{def:barronspaceshomogeneous}). Then,
     \begin{equation}
       \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi^{\psi, \Psi})\geq \frac{L_\beta}{2nD^5} \cdot \max_{i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}}{\|\partial_i^3 \Psi\|_\infty^2}.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
The lower bound in Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised} holds for any coordinate $i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$.
If $\phi$ is as in (i) then any Barron function $v(x) = \sum_{j}\mu_j \phi(\left\langle a_j, x\right\rangle + b_j) $  has \begin{equation}|\partial_1^3 v(x)| \leq \|\phi'''\|_\infty \sum_j \|\mu_j\| \|a_j\|^3 \leq \|\phi'''\|_\infty R^2 \|v\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi^R}.\end{equation}
If instead $\phi$ is $3$-homogeneous as in (ii), then the same argument works since $\|\phi'''\|_{L^\infty} < \infty$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixcylindricalschwartz}
    Let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and $\lambda \in (0, \infty)$. We define $\mathcal{C}_\lambda$ to be the class of functions $f: {\mathbb{R}}^n \times {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ which can be written as a finite sum
    \begin{equation}
        f(z, u) = \sum_{r=1}^M F_r(P_{E_r}z, u)
    \end{equation}
    where each $E_r \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a linear subspace (with orthogonal projection $P_{E_r}$) and each $F_r: E_r \times {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfies the seminorm bounds
    \begin{equation}
        |\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j F_r(x, u)| \lesssim_{\alpha, j, N} (1+\|x\|)^{-N} (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j}
    \end{equation}
    for all $N \in {\mathbb{N}}$, all multi-indices $\alpha$, and all $j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$. 
    
    The class $\mathcal{C}_\lambda$ is an algebra which is closed under smooth composition and OU smoothing, i.e. the following properties hold:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] If $f, g \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$, then $fg \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ with seminorms controlled by those of $f,g$ and the angles between the involved subspaces.
        \item[(ii)] If $f \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ and $\eta \in C^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ satisfies $\eta(0) = 0$ and all derivatives of $\eta$ are bounded, then $\eta \circ f \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ with seminorms controlled by those of $f$, the derivative bounds on $\eta$, and the angles between the involved subspaces.
        \item[(iii)] If $f \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ and $g(z, u) = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}[f(az + b G, u)]$ for some $0 < a_- \leq a \leq a_+ < \infty$ and $0 \leq b \leq b_+ < \infty$, then $g \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ with seminorms controlled by those of $f$ with constants depending only on $a_-, a_+, b_+$, and subspace dimensions.
    \end{enumerate}
    
    Furthermore, for any $s  \in {\mathbb{N}}$ with $\phi(t) = \max\{0, t\}^s$ the $\operatorname{ReLU}^s$ activation and $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ its associated Barron space of functions from ${\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ (using the scalar version of Definition \ref{def:barronspaceshomogeneous}), we have $\mathcal{C}_\lambda \subseteq \mathcal{B}_{\phi}$ with Barron norm controlled by the $\mathcal{C}_\lambda$ seminorms.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
For any profile $F: E \times {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$, we denote the seminorm
    \begin{equation}
        [F]_{\alpha, j, N} := \sup_{x \in E,\; u \in {\mathbb{R}}} (1+\|x\|)^N (1+|u|)^{\lambda + j} |\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j F(x, u)|.
    \end{equation}
    
    \textbf{(i).} For this, it suffices to consider two summands
    \begin{equation}
        f(x, u) = F(P_Ex, u), \quad g(x, u) = G(P_Vx, u).
    \end{equation}
    Denote the subspace $W := E + V$ and write $H(x, u) := F(P_Ex, u) G(P_Vx, u)$. Then, $(fg)(x, u) = H(P_Wx, u)$. The linear map $W \ni x \mapsto (P_Ex, P_Vx)$ is injective, and hence by finite-dimensionality $\|x\| \leq C_{E,V} (\|P_Ex\| + \|P_Vx\|)$ and so \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixcylindricalschwartzlemmapart1}
    1 + \|x\| \lesssim (1+\|P_Ex\|)(1+\|P_Vx\|).\end{equation} By the product rule, $\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^jH(x, u)$ is a finite sum of products $(\partial_x^{\alpha_1}\partial_u^{j_1}F)(P_Ex, u)(\partial_x^{\alpha_2}\partial_u^{j_2}G)(P_Vx, u)$ with $\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 = \alpha$ and $j_1 + j_2 = j$. Using (\ref{eqn:proofappendixcylindricalschwartzlemmapart1}),
    \begin{equation}
        |\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^jH(x, u)| \lesssim_{\alpha, j, N} (1+\|x\|)^{-N}(1+|u|)^{-2\lambda - j} \lesssim (1+\|x\|)^{-N}(1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j} 
    \end{equation}
    since $\lambda > 0$. Hence, $fg \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ with controlled seminorms. The result extends to $f, g$ being any finite sums by linearity and the triangle inequality.

    \textbf{(ii).} Write $f(z, u) = \sum_{r=1}^M F_r(P_{E_r}z, u)$ and define $B := \sum_{r=1}^M \|F_r\|_\infty$. We use the anchored multivariate fundamental theorem of calculus: if 
    \begin{equation}
        \Theta(y_1, \ldots, y_M) := \eta\left(\sum_{r=1}^M y_r\right)
    \end{equation}
    then $\Theta(0) = \eta(0) = 0$ and 
    \begin{equation}
        \Theta(y) = \sum_{\emptyset \neq J \subseteq \{1, \ldots, M\}} \left(\prod_{r \in J}y_r\right) \int_{[0, 1]^{|J|}} \eta^{(|J|)} \left(\sum_{r \in J} t_r y_r\right)dt.
    \end{equation}  
    Substituting in $y_r = F_r(P_{E_r}z, u)$ gives a finite decomposition of $\eta \circ f$. Fix a nonempty $J \subseteq \{1, \ldots, M\}$ and define the subspace $E_J := \sum_{r \in J} E_r \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^n$. The corresponding term in $\eta \circ f$, denoted $H_J$, has 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixcylindricalschwartzlemmapart2}
        H_J(x, u) = \prod_{r \in J} F_r(P_{E_r}x, u) \int_{[0, 1]^{|J|}} \eta^{(|J|)} \left(\sum_{r \in J}t_r F_r(P_{E_r}x, u)\right)dt
    \end{equation}
    for every $x \in E_J$. Since the arguments of $\eta^{(|J|)}$ lie in $[-B, B]$, all derivatives of the integral factor are bounded due to the assumed bounds on $\eta$, Faà di Bruno, and the seminorm bounds on $F_r$. As before, the map $E_J \ni x \mapsto (P_{E_r}x)_{r\in J}$ is injective and therefore
    \begin{equation}
        1+\|x\| \lesssim_J \prod_{r \in J}(1+\|P_{E_r}x\|).
    \end{equation}
    Differentiating (\ref{eqn:proofappendixcylindricalschwartzlemmapart2}) and applying Faà di Bruno, each resulting term is a product of finitely many derivatives of $F_r(P_{E_r}x, u)$ multiplied by a bounded derivative of $\eta$. Due to the prefactor, every such term contains at least one value or derivative of $F_r(P_{E_r}x, u)$ for each $r \in J$. Hence, using the seminorm definition of each $F_r$ implies
    \begin{equation}
        |\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j H_J(x, u)| \lesssim_{\alpha, j, N} (1+\|x\|)^{-N}(1+|u|)^{-|J|\lambda - j}.
    \end{equation}
    Since $J$ is nonempty and $\lambda > 0$, this proves the second claim. 

    \textbf{(iii).} By linearity, it suffices to consider a single summand $f(z, u) = F(P_Ez, u)$. Since $P_EG \sim \gamma_E$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        g(z, u) = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}[F(P_E(az + bG), u)] = \widetilde{F}(P_Ez, u), \quad \widetilde{F}(x, u) := \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_E}[F(ax + b\xi, u)].
    \end{equation}
    Hence, $g$ is cylindrical on the same subspace. Furthermore, by differentiating under the expectation we find
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixcylindricalschwartzlemmapart3}
        \partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j \widetilde{F}(x, u) = a^{|\alpha|} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_E} [\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^jF(ax+b\xi, u)].
    \end{equation}
    Since $a \geq a_-$ and $b \leq b_+$ we know that
    \begin{equation}
        \|x\| = a^{-1}\|ax\| \leq a_{-}^{-1} \|ax + b\xi\| + a_-^{-1} b_+\|\xi\|
    \end{equation}
    by the triangle inequality, and so
    \begin{equation}
        (1+\|x\|)^N \lesssim_{N, a_-, b_+} (1+\|ax+b\xi\|)^N (1+\|\xi\|)^N.
    \end{equation}
    Combining this with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixcylindricalschwartzlemmapart3}) and $a \leq a_+$, we get
    \begin{align}
        (1+\|x\|)^N (1+|u|)^{\lambda + j}| \partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j \widetilde{F}(x, u)| &\lesssim a_+^{|\alpha|} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_E}\left[(1+\|\xi\|)^N (1+\|ax+b\xi\|)^N (1+|u|)^{\lambda + j}| \partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j {F}(ax+b\xi, u)|\right] \\
        &\lesssim_{\alpha, N, a_-, a_+, b_+} [F]_{\alpha, j, N} \mathbb{E}_{\xi \sim \gamma_E}[(1+\|\xi\|)^N]. 
    \end{align}
    Since the Gaussian has all moments finite, this implies $g \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ with the claimed seminorm control. 

    \textbf{(Barron embedding).} We will apply a global Sobolev-to-Barron embedding, whose proof we defer to Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixsobolevtobarron}. By the triangle inequality, it suffices to consider a single summand $f(z, u) = F(P_Ez, u)$. Write $D = \dim(E)$ and identify $E$ with ${\mathbb{R}}^D$. Fix $N > D+s$ and $A_F := \sum_{|\alpha| + j \leq D+s+2}[F]_{\alpha, j, N}$. Choose a radial cutoff $\chi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$ equal to 1 on $[-1, 1]$ and supported in $[-2, 2]$, and set
    \begin{equation}
        \zeta(u) := \chi(u/2) - \chi(u).
    \end{equation}
    Then, $\zeta$ is supported on $1 \leq |u| \leq 4$ and 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixbarronembeddingupperboundpartitionofunity}
        1 = \chi(u) + \sum_{q = 0}^\infty \zeta(2^{-q}u) \quad (\forall u \in {\mathbb{R}}).
    \end{equation}
    Using this, we define
    \begin{equation}
        F_q(x, u) := \zeta(2^{-q}u) F(x, u), \quad F_{-1}(x, u) = \chi(u)F(x, u) \quad (\forall q \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}).
    \end{equation}
    For $q \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$ we rescale the last coordinate
    \begin{equation}
        \widetilde{F}_q(x, u) := F_q(x, 2^qu) = \zeta(u) F(x, 2^qu).
    \end{equation}
    By the product and chain rules in the $u$ coordinate,
    \begin{equation}
        \partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j \widetilde{F}_q(x, u) = \sum_{\ell = 0}^j {j \choose \ell} \zeta^{(j - \ell)} (u)2^{q\ell}(\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^\ell F)(x, 2^q u).
    \end{equation}
    Now, on the support of $\zeta^{(j - \ell)}$ we have $|u| \geq 1$, in which case $2^{q\ell}(1 + 2^q|u|)^{-\lambda - \ell} \leq 2^{-q \lambda}$. This means that for all $|\alpha| + j \leq D+s+2$ we have
    \begin{align}
        \left|\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j \widetilde{F}_q(x, u)\right| \lesssim_{D,s} A_F 2^{-q\lambda} (1+\|x\|)^{-N}
    \end{align}
    and these derivatives vanish for $|u| > 4$. Since $N > D+s$, we find
    \begin{align}
        \sum_{|\alpha| + j \leq D+s+2} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D \times {\mathbb{R}}} (1+\|(x, u)\|)^s \left|\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j \widetilde{F}_q(x, u)\right| dxdu &\lesssim_{D,s,N} A_F 2^{-q\lambda} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+\|x\|)^{s-N}dx \\
        &\lesssim_{D,s,N} A_F 2^{-q\lambda}.
    \end{align}
    Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixsobolevtobarron} yields 
    \begin{equation}
        \|\widetilde{F}_q\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \lesssim_{D,s,N} A_F2^{-q\lambda}.
    \end{equation}
    Now, since $F_q(x, u) = \widetilde{F}_q(x, 2^{-q}u)$ we may obtain a Barron representation of $F_q$ from that of $\widetilde{F}_q$ by replacing $\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + a' u + b)$ with $\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + 2^{-q}a'u + b)$. This can only decrease the Barron cost, and so
    \begin{equation}
        \|F_q\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \lesssim_{D,s,N}A_F 2^{-q\lambda}. 
    \end{equation}
    A similar application of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixsobolevtobarron} yields that
    \begin{equation}
        \|F_{-1}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \lesssim_{D,s,N} A_F.
    \end{equation}
    We may apply (\ref{eqn:proofappendixbarronembeddingupperboundpartitionofunity}) to find that
    \begin{equation}
        F_{-1}(x, u) + \sum_{q=0}^Q  F_q(x, u) = \chi(2^{-Q-1}u) F(x, u)
    \end{equation}
    and so they converge locally uniformly to $F$ as $Q \to \infty$. By lower-semicontinuity of the Barron norm under local uniform convergence (\ref{lemma:appendixbarronnormlscunderlocaluniformconvergence}) and the triangle inequality,
    \begin{align}
        \|F\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \|F_{-1}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} + \sum_{q=0}^\infty \|F_q\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \lesssim_{D,s,N} A_F \left(1 + \frac{1}{1-2^{-\lambda}}\right) < \infty.
    \end{align}
    This gives a Barron representation on $E \times {\mathbb{R}} \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^n \times {\mathbb{R}}$, which extends to one on the whole space without changing the parameter norms (since the neurons only see $E \times {\mathbb{R}}$).
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixsobolevtobarron}
Fix any $D,s  \in {\mathbb{N}}$ with $\phi(t) = \max\{0, t\}^s$ the $\operatorname{ReLU}^s$ activation and $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ its associated Barron space of functions from ${\mathbb{R}}^{D} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ (using the scalar version of Definition \ref{def:barronspaceshomogeneous}). 

Then, there is some $C_{D,s} \in (0, \infty)$ s.t. for any $f \in W^{D+s+1,1}({\mathbb{R}}^D)$ if we choose its continuous representative we have
\begin{equation}
    \|f\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\phi}} \leq C_{D,s} \sum_{|\alpha| \leq D+s+1} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+|x|)^s |\partial^\alpha f(x)| dx.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
First, suppose that $D$ is odd and $f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^D)$. Write its Radon transform by
    \begin{equation}
        Rf(\theta, t) := \int_{\theta^\perp} f(t\theta + y)dy.
    \end{equation}
    By the odd-dimensional Radon inversion formula (see (27) and (28) of \cite{parhi2021banach}), we have
    \begin{equation}
        f(x) = c_D \int_{\mathbb{S}^{D-1}} (\partial_t^{D-1} Rf)(\theta, \left\langle \theta, x\right\rangle) d\theta, \quad c_D = \frac{(-1)^{(D-1)/2}}{2(2\pi)^{D-1}}.
    \end{equation}
    We have seen that for every $g \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$, repeated integration by parts gives
    \begin{equation}
        g(v) = \frac{1}{s!}\int_{\mathbb{R}} \max\{0, v-t\}^s g^{(s+1)}(t) dt.
    \end{equation}
    Applying this to $g(\cdot) = \partial_t^{D-1}Rf(\theta, \cdot)$ gives the global representation
    \begin{equation}
        f(x) = \frac{c_D}{s!} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{D-1}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \max\{0, \left\langle \theta, x\right\rangle - t\}^s (\partial_t^{D+s} Rf)(\theta, t) dtd\theta.
    \end{equation}
    By differentiating under the integral, there is the Radon transform identity
    \begin{align}
        (\partial_t^k Rf)(\theta, t) &= \int_{\theta^\perp} \partial_t^k [f(t\theta + y)] dy \\
        &= \int_{\theta^\perp} (\theta \cdot \nabla)^k f(t\theta + y) dy \\
        &= R[(\theta \cdot \nabla)^k f](\theta, t),
    \end{align}
    where $(\theta \cdot \nabla)^k f$ is the $k^{th}$ directional derivative of $f$ in direction $\theta$.
    Since $\partial_t^{D+s}Rf = R[(\theta \cdot \nabla)^{D+s}f]$, the homogeneous Barron cost of this representation is 
    \begin{align}
        \|f\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} &\leq \frac{|c_D|}{s!} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{D-1}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|t|)^s |R[(\theta \cdot \nabla)^{D+s}f](\theta, t)| dtd\theta  \\&=  
        \frac{|c_D|}{s!} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{D-1}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|t|)^s \left|\int_{\theta^\perp} (\theta \cdot \nabla)^{D+s} f(t\theta + y)dy\right|dtd\theta 
        \\
        &\leq \frac{|c_D|}{s!} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{D-1}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_{\theta^\perp} (1+|t|)^s \left|(\theta \cdot \nabla)^{D+s}f(t\theta + y)\right| dy dt d\theta \\
        &= \frac{|c_D|}{s!} \int_{\mathbb{S}^{D-1}}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+|\left\langle \theta, x\right\rangle|)^s \left|(\theta \cdot \nabla)^{D+s}f(x)\right| dx d\theta,
\end{align}
    where the last line fixes $\theta$ and uses the change of coordinates $x = t\theta + y$ (which has Jacobian 1).
    By the multinomial formula, we know
    \begin{equation}
        (\theta \cdot \nabla)^{D+s}f = \sum_{|\alpha| = D+s} \frac{(D+s)!}{\prod_j \alpha_j!} \theta^\alpha \partial^\alpha f.
    \end{equation}
    Since $|\theta^\alpha| \leq 1$, $|\left\langle \theta, x\right\rangle| \leq \|x\|$, and $\prod_j \alpha_j! \geq 1$, we find that
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixsobolevtobarronoddD}
        \|f\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\leq  \frac{|c_D| \cdot |\mathbb{S}^{D-1}| (D+s)!}{s!} \sum_{|\alpha| = D+s}  \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+\|x\|)^s |\partial^\alpha f(x)|dx.
    \end{equation}
    Setting $C_{D,s} := \frac{|c_D| \cdot |\mathbb{S}^{D-1}| (D+s)!}{s!}$ yields the claim for odd $D$ and $f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^D)$. 

    Letting now $D$ be even and $f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^D)$, we fix $\eta \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$ with $\eta(0) = 1$ and define
    \begin{equation}
        F(x, u) := f(x) \eta(u).
    \end{equation}
    Restricting any Barron representation of $F$ to $u = 0$ gives a Barron representation of $f$ with no increase in parameter norm, since each $\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + a' u + b)$ becomes $\phi(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle + b)$. Hence,
    \begin{equation}
        \|f\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \|F\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}.
    \end{equation}
    Let us define for even $D$ the constant
    \begin{equation}
        C_{D,s} := C_{D+1,s} \max_{0 \leq j \leq D+s+1}\int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|u|)^s |\eta^{(j)}(u)| du
    \end{equation}
    for the fixed $\eta$ (which we will use for all $f: {\mathbb{R}}^D \to {\mathbb{R}}$).
    Using that $D+1$ is odd, we apply (\ref{eqn:proofappendixsobolevtobarronoddD}) along with the product rule to see that
    \begin{align}
        \|F\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} &\leq C_{D+1, s} \sum_{|\alpha| + j = D + s + 1} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + \|(x, u)\|)^s |\partial^\alpha f(x)| |\eta^{(j)}(u)| du dx \\
        &\leq C_{D+1, s} \sum_{|\alpha| + j = D+s+1} \left(\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+\|x\|)^s |\partial^\alpha f(x)| dx\right)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|u|)^s |\eta^{(j)}(u)| du\right) \\
        &\leq {C}_{D,s} \sum_{|\alpha| \leq D+s+1}\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+\|x\|)^s |\partial^\alpha f(x)| dx,
    \end{align}
    where we used that $1 + \|(x, u)\| \leq (1+\|x\|)(1+|u|)$. Hence, the claim holds for any $D\in {\mathbb{N}}$ and any $f \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^D)$.
    For general $f$ with finite right hand side, we take $f_j \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}}^D)$ s.t. $f_j \to f$ locally uniformly and
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{|\alpha| \leq D+s+1} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^D} (1+|x|)^s |\partial^\alpha (f_j - f)(x)| dx \to 0
    \end{equation}
    using cutoff and mollification. By lower-semicontinuity of the Barron norm w.r.t. local uniform convergence (Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixbarronnormlscunderlocaluniformconvergence}), the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixrepresentationupperbound}
    Fix $s  \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and let $\phi(t) = \max\{0, t\}^s$ be the $\operatorname{ReLU}^s$ activation with $\mathcal{B}_\phi$ its associated Barron space (see Definition \ref{def:barronspaceshomogeneous}).
     Let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and suppose $\Psi(z) = \sum_{r=1}^M \Phi_r(P_{E_r}z)$, where each $E_r \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a linear subspace (with orthogonal projection $P_{E_r}$) and $\Phi_r \in C^\infty_c(E_r)$.
     Let $\psi \in C^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ be a strictly increasing diffeomorphism and choose $a_\pm, R \in (0, \infty)$, $b_\pm \in {\mathbb{R}}$, and $p > 2$ s.t.
    \begin{equation}
        \psi(u) = a_+ u^p + b_+ \quad (\forall u \geq R), \quad \psi(u) = -a_- (-u)^p + b_- \quad (\forall u \leq -R).
    \end{equation}
    Then, $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}, b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} \in \mathcal{B}_\phi$ for all $\tau \geq 0$ with
    \begin{equation}
      \sup_{\tau \in [0, T]} \max\left\{\| s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}, \| b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}\right\} < \infty \quad (\forall T \in [0, \infty)).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Fix $T > 0$ and let $q_\tau$ be the density of $e^{-\tau}\psi(U) + \sigma H$ for $U, H \sim \gamma_1$ independent and $\sigma := \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}$ (as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised}).  Denote its score by $h_\tau := q_\tau ' / q_\tau$. Since $\psi$ is exactly a power function of exponent $p$ outside of a compact set, the change of variables formula gives that
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves1000}
       q_0(u) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}pa_+^{1/p}} (u-b_+)^{-(p-1)/p} \exp\left(-\frac{a_+^{-2/p}}{2}(u-b_+)^{2/p}\right)
   \end{equation}
  for $u$ large and therefore if $\lambda := 1-\frac{2}{p}$ we have
   \begin{equation}
       h_0(u) = -\frac{a_+^{-2/p}}{p}(u-b_+)^{-\lambda} - \frac{p-1}{p(u-b_+)}.
   \end{equation}
   The analogous formula holds on the negative tail. Hence, for every $j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$ we have
   \begin{equation}
       |h_0^{(j)}(u)| \lesssim_j (1+|u|)^{-\lambda -j}.
   \end{equation}
   We claim that this estimate persists under OU smoothing, i.e. that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves}
       \sup_{\tau \in [0, T]} \sup_{u \in {\mathbb{R}}} (1+|u|)^{\lambda + j} |h_\tau^{(j)}(u)| < \infty \quad (\forall j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}).
   \end{equation}
Indeed, since $q_\tau(\cdot) = e^\tau q_0(e^\tau \cdot) * \varphi_{\sigma^2}$ we may denote $ \tilde{q}_\tau(u) :=  e^\tau q_0(e^\tau u)$ and write
\begin{equation}
    q_\tau(u) = \tilde{q}_\tau(u) G_\tau(u),\quad G_\tau(u) := \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\ell_\tau(u - \sigma H) - \ell_\tau(u)\right)\right],  \quad \ell_\tau := \log \tilde{q}_\tau.
\end{equation}
From (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves1000}) we know that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves101}
    |\ell_\tau^{(j+1)}(u)| \lesssim_{j,T} (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j}
\end{equation}
uniformly for $\tau \in [0, T]$.
Since $\|\ell_\tau'\|_\infty \leq C_T$ is uniformly bounded for $\tau \in [0, T]$ we know $G_\tau(u) \leq \mathbb{E}[e^{C_T|H|}] < \infty$. Similarly, we know $G_\tau(u) \geq e^{-C_T}\mathbb{P}(|H| \leq 1) \gtrsim_T 1$, and therefore
\begin{equation}
    G_\tau(u) \asymp_T 1
\end{equation}
uniformly for $\tau \in [0, T]$.
 On the event $|\sigma H| \leq |u|/2$, by the mean value theorem and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves101}) we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreservesmeanvaluenonsense}
\left|\ell_\tau^{(j)}(u-\sigma H) - \ell_\tau^{(j)}(u)\right| \lesssim_{j,T}|H|(1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j}  \quad (\forall j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}),
\end{equation}
 By Faà di Bruno, for $j \in {\mathbb{N}}$ on this event we know that
\begin{align}
    |\partial_u^j e^{\ell_\tau(u-\sigma H) - \ell_\tau(u)}| &\lesssim_{j,T} e^{C_T |H|} \sum_{\substack{m, r_1, \ldots, r_m \in {\mathbb{N}} \\ r_1 + \ldots + r_m = j}}|H|^m (1+|u|)^{-m\lambda - j}\\
    &\lesssim_{j,T} e^{C_T |H|} (1+|H|)^j (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j},
\end{align}
where the second inequality uses $\lambda > 0$. On the other hand, the bound (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves101}) implies that
\begin{equation}
     |\partial_u^j e^{\ell_\tau(u-\sigma H) - \ell_\tau(u)}| \lesssim_{j,T} e^{c_T|H|} (1+|H|)^j,
\end{equation}
and since
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\left[e^{C_T|H|} (1+|H|)^j \1_{|\sigma H| > |u|/2}\right] \lesssim_{j,T}e^{-c_T u^2}
\end{equation}
for some constant $c_T$ we find that
\begin{equation}
    |G_\tau^{(j)}(u)| \lesssim_{j,T} (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j} \quad (\forall j \in {\mathbb{N}}).
\end{equation}
Since $G_\tau \asymp_T 1$, we find that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves102}
     |\partial^j \log G_\tau(u)| \lesssim_{j,T} (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j} \quad (\forall j \in {\mathbb{N}}).
\end{equation}
However, since $\log q_\tau = \ell_\tau + \log G_\tau$ and so $h_\tau^{(j)} = \ell_\tau^{(j+1)} + \partial^{(j+1)} \log G_\tau$, we may apply (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves102}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves101}) to show the claim (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves}).

Moving on, (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves}) implies that $(1+|u|)^s |h_\tau^{(s+1)}(u)| \lesssim (1+|u|)^{-1 - \lambda}$ and so
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves2}
       \sup_{\tau \in [0, T]} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|u|)^s |h_\tau^{(s+1)}(u)|du < \infty.
   \end{equation}
   The bound (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves}) also implies that $h_\tau^{(j)} \to 0$ as $u \to -\infty$, and so repeated application of the fundamental theorem of calculus yields
   \begin{equation}
       h_\tau(v) = \frac{1}{s!} \int_{\mathbb{R}} h_\tau^{(s+1)}(u) \max\{0, v-u\}^s du.
   \end{equation}
   This is a valid Barron representation, and so (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves2}) yields $\sup_{\tau \in [0, T]}\|h_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^s}}<\infty$.

Next, using the notation from the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised} we have the density
   \begin{equation}
       \rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u) = \gamma_n(z) F_\tau(z, u), \quad F_\tau(z, u) = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}[q_\tau(u - e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}G))].
   \end{equation}
   If we define the quantity
   \begin{equation}
       R_\tau(z, u) := \frac{F_\tau(z, u)}{q_\tau(u)}, \quad S_\tau := \nabla \log R_\tau,
   \end{equation}
   then using that
   \begin{equation}
    \log \rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u) = \log \gamma_n(z) + \log q_\tau(u) + \log R_\tau(z, u)
   \end{equation}
   we find that the scores satisfy
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves3}
       s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u) = \begin{bmatrix}
           -z \\ h_\tau(u)
       \end{bmatrix} + S_\tau(z, u), \quad b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} = \begin{bmatrix}
           0 \\ u + h_\tau(u)
       \end{bmatrix} + S_\tau(z, u).
   \end{equation}
   We claim that affine vector fields are in $\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^s}$; to see this, note that for any $r_0, \ldots, r_s$ distinct we have that $t \mapsto (t+r_0)^s, \ldots, t\mapsto (t+r_s)^s$ span the space of polynomials of degree at most $s$ (since the coefficient matrix is Vandermonde and therefore invertible). Hence, every affine map is a linear combination of these $t \mapsto (t+r_j)^s$ polynomials. However, since
   \begin{equation}
       (t+r)^s = \max\{0, t+r\}^s + (-1)^s \max\{0, -t-r\}^s
   \end{equation}
   we can apply it coordinatewise to find that affine vector fields are Barron. In light of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves3}) it remains to show that $\sup_{\tau \in [0, T]}\|S_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^s}} < \infty$.

To this end, if we denote $B := \sum_{r=1}^M \|\Phi_r\|_\infty$ and $K_\tau(u, c) := q_\tau(u-c) / q_\tau(u)$ then by definition we have
\begin{equation}
    R_\tau(z, u) = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}[K_\tau(u, e^{-\tau} \Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sigma G))].
\end{equation}
Differentiating under the expectation, for $\alpha \neq 0$ every term $\partial_z^\alpha \partial_u^j R_\tau(z, u)$ has the form
\begin{equation}
    Ce^{-(|\alpha| + k)\tau} \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}\left[(\partial_c^k \partial_u^j K_\tau) (u, e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sigma G)) \prod_{\ell = 1}^k \partial^{\beta_\ell}\Psi(e^{-\tau }z + \sigma G)\right]
\end{equation}
with $k \geq 1$, $|\beta_\ell| \geq 1$, and $\sum_\ell \beta_\ell = \alpha$. For $\alpha = 0$, we use instead that
\begin{equation}
    \partial_u^j (R_\tau - 1) = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}[\partial_u^j (K_\tau(u, e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sigma G))-1)].
\end{equation}
Now, since we have
\begin{equation}
    \log K_\tau(u, c) = \log q_\tau(u - c) - \log q_\tau(u) = -\int_{u-c}^u h_\tau(v) dv,
\end{equation}
the estimate (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundOUsmoothingpreserves}) on $h_\tau$ implies that $K_\tau(u, c) \asymp_T 1$ uniformly in $|c| \leq B$ and furthermore
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixderivativeestimatesonK_tau}
    |\partial_c^k \partial_u^j K_\tau(u, c)| \lesssim_{k,j,T} (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j} \quad (\forall k + j \geq 1)
\end{equation}
uniformly in $|c| \leq B$.
Since $K_\tau(u, 0) = 1$, the fundamental theorem of calculus in the $c$ coordinate implies that for all $j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$ we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperboundestimatesonKtau}
    |\partial_u^j (K_\tau(u, c) - 1)| \lesssim_{j,T} |c|(1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j}.
\end{equation}
We define the new function $A_\tau: {\mathbb{R}}^n \times {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
\begin{equation}
    A_\tau(z, u) := K_\tau(u, e^{-\tau}\Psi(z)) - 1.
\end{equation}
Apply the anchored fundamental theorem of calculus, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixcylindricalschwartz}(ii), to $(y_1, \ldots, y_M) \mapsto K_\tau(u, e^{-\tau}\sum_{r=1}^M y_r) - 1$. This function vanishes at $y=0$ (since $K_\tau(u, 0) = 1$) and so
\begin{equation}
    A_{\tau}(z, u) = \sum_{\emptyset \neq J \subseteq \{1, \ldots, M\}} H_{\tau, J}(P_{E_J}z, u), \quad E_J := \sum_{r \in J}E_r,
\end{equation}
where for $x \in E_J$ we define
\begin{equation}
    H_{\tau, J}(x, u) := e^{-|J|\tau} \left(\prod_{r \in J}\Phi_r(P_{E_r}x)\right) \int_{[0, 1]^{|J|}} (\partial_c^{|J|}K_\tau)\left(u, e^{-\tau}\sum_{r\in J} t_r \Phi_r(P_{E_r}x)\right)dt.
\end{equation}
For each $J$ the support of $H_{\tau, J}$ in the $x$ coordinate is contained in the set
\begin{equation}
\{x \in E_J:\; P_{E_r}x \in \operatorname{spt}(\Phi_r) \; \forall r \in J\},
\end{equation}
which is compact (since $\|x\| \lesssim_J \sum_{r \in J}\|P_{E_r}x\|$). Since we know $|e^{-\tau}\sum_{r \in J}t_r \Phi_r(P_{E_r}x)| \leq B$ (and so the estimate (\ref{eqn:proofappendixderivativeestimatesonK_tau}) applies), by the product and chain rule each derivative of $H_{\tau, J}$ is a finite sum of products of values/derivatives of $\Phi_r$ with those of $K_\tau$ with the $u$ derivatives only applying to $K_\tau$ and therefore
\begin{equation}
    |\partial_x^\alpha \partial_u^j H_{\tau, J}(x, u)| \lesssim_{\alpha, j,J,T} (1+|u|)^{-\lambda - j}.
\end{equation}
Since $H_{\tau, J}$ is compactly-supported in $x$, we find that $A_\tau \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ uniformly over $\tau \in [0, T]$.

 Next, since $R_\tau(z, u) - 1 = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_n}[A_{\tau}(e^{-\tau}z + \sigma G, u)]$ we apply Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixcylindricalschwartz}(iii) to find that $r_\tau := R_\tau - 1 \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$ uniformly over $\tau \in [0, T]$. Next, since $K_\tau(u, c) \asymp_T 1$ uniformly in $|c| \leq B$ we also have $R_\tau(z, u) \asymp_T 1$. Hence, if $\eta \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$ is s.t. $\eta(0) = 0$ and
\begin{equation}
    \eta(t) := \frac{1}{t+1}- 1 \quad
\end{equation}
for all $t$ in a neighborhood of the image of $r_\tau$ for all $\tau \in [0, T]$ (which is possible since $1+r_\tau = R_\tau$ is bounded above and away from 0 uniformly for $\tau \in [0, T]$), then by Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixcylindricalschwartz}(ii) we know $\eta \circ r_\tau \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda$. Furthermore, each coordinate of $\nabla r_\tau$ is also in $\mathcal{C}_\lambda$ since taking derivatives only helps with the $u$ decay. Finally, since
\begin{equation}
    S_\tau = \nabla \log R_\tau = \frac{\nabla R_\tau}{R_\tau} = \nabla r_\tau + \nabla r_\tau \left(\frac{1}{R_\tau} - 1\right) = \nabla r_\tau + \nabla r_\tau (\eta \circ r_\tau),
\end{equation}
by the algebra property in Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixcylindricalschwartz}(i) we find that each coordinate of $S_\tau$ is in $\mathcal{C}_\lambda$, uniformly in $\tau \in [0, T]$. The claim follows by applying the Barron embedding statement of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixcylindricalschwartz} coordinatewise.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
For each $n, m \in {\mathbb{N}}$, we define the class $\mathcal{R}_m^{(n)}$ of sums of at most $m$ square-integrable ridge functions on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$, i.e.
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{R}_m^{(n)} := \left\{g: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}:\; g(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m f_j(\left\langle x, \theta_j\right\rangle) \text{ with } f_j \in L^2(\gamma_1) \text{ and } \theta_j \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}\right\} \subseteq L^2(\gamma_n).
    \end{equation}
    The functions $f_j: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ encode both the activations and the output weights of each neuron.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:appendixhermitewidthenvelope}
    Let $\Psi: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be s.t. $\Psi \in L^2(\gamma_n)$.
         Define the function $a_\Psi: {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\} \times [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ by the envelope
     \begin{equation}
        a_\Psi(m, \tau) :=  \left(\sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{-2(k+1)\tau}\sum_{j={m+1}}^{n^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}} \sigma_j(M_k(\Psi))^2\right)^{1/2}.
     \end{equation}
    It is nonincreasing in its first argument, and we define $m_\Psi: (0, \infty) \times [0, \infty) \to {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0,\infty\}$ to be its generalized inverse, i.e.
     \begin{equation}
         m_\Psi(\delta, \tau) := \inf \{m \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}:\; a_\Psi(m, \tau) \leq \delta \}
     \end{equation}
     with the convention that $\inf \emptyset = \infty$.
     We call $m_\Psi$ the {\em Hermite width envelope} of $\Psi$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:appendixdaapproximationlowerbound}
     Let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$, fix $\Psi: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ bounded and Lipschitz, and let $\beta, L \in (0, \infty)$ be s.t.
     \begin{equation}
         \|\Psi\|_\infty \leq \beta,\quad \operatorname{Lip}(\Psi) \leq L.
     \end{equation}
     Fix $\psi(u) = \sigma u$ for some $\sigma \in (0, \infty)$.
     
     Fix any $\tau \in [0, \infty)$ and $\varepsilon \in (0, \infty)$, and suppose that there is some $\hat{s}_\tau: {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ for which $\left\langle e_{n+1}, \hat{s}_\tau(\cdot)\right\rangle \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n+1)}$ for some width $m \in {\mathbb{N}}$ (such as a two-layer neural network of width $m$) and
     \begin{equation}\|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \leq \varepsilon.\end{equation} 
     Then, there is some $Q_{\beta, \sigma} \in (0, \infty)$ depending only on $\beta, \sigma$ s.t.
    \begin{equation}
         m \geq m_\Psi\left(Q_{\beta, \sigma}  (\varepsilon + L^2 \tau),\; \tau\right).
    \end{equation}
    Moreover, for any nonzero $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} there is some $ K_{\phi, \beta, \sigma} \in (0, \infty)$ s.t.
    \begin{equation}
        \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \geq K_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}  \cdot  \varepsilon\sqrt{\max\left\{0,\; m_\Psi(Q_{\beta, \sigma} (2\varepsilon + L^2\tau), \;\tau) - 1\right\}}
    \end{equation}
    These statements also hold with $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixhermiteranklowerbound}
For every $\Psi \in L^2(\gamma_n)$ and every $m \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and $\tau \in [0, \infty)$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \inf_{g \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n)}} \|e^{-\tau} P_\tau \Psi - g\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)} \geq a_\Psi(m, \tau).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Fix some $g(\cdot) = \sum_{j=1}^m f_j (\left\langle \cdot, \theta_j\right\rangle) \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n)}$, where each $f_j \in L^2(\gamma_1)$. With $h_k := \operatorname{He}_k / \sqrt{k!}$ the orthonormalized Hermite basis of $L^2(\gamma_1)$, write $\hat{f}_j(k) := \left\langle f_j, h_k\right\rangle_{L^2(\gamma_1)}$ so that
    \begin{equation}
        f_j = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \hat{f}_j(k) h_k \text{ in $L^2(\gamma_1)$} \quad (\forall j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}).
    \end{equation}
    Since $\theta_j \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$, the defining property of the multivariate Hermite tensors gives
    \begin{equation}
        h_k(\left\langle x, \theta_j\right\rangle) = \left\langle \frac{\mathbf{He}_k(x)}{\sqrt{k!}}, \theta_j^{\otimes k}\right\rangle_F.
    \end{equation}
    Hence, $T_k(f_j(\left\langle\cdot, \theta_j\right\rangle)) = \hat{f}_j(k) \theta_j^{\otimes k}$ and therefore
    \begin{equation}
        T_k(g) = \sum_{j=1}^m \hat{f}_j(k) \theta_j^{\otimes k}.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, $\operatorname{rank}(M_k(g)) \leq m$ for every $k \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$. Since the OU semigroup $P_\tau$ acts on the $k^{th}$ Wiener chaos as multiplication by $e^{-k\tau}$, we find that
    $T_k(e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi) = e^{-(k+1)\tau} T_k(\Psi)$ and so
    \begin{align}
        \|e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi - g\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)}^2 &= \sum_{k=0}^\infty \|e^{-(k+1)\tau} T_k(\Psi) - T_k(g)\|_F^2 \\
        &= \sum_{k=0}^\infty \|e^{-(k+1)\tau}M_k(\Psi) - M_k(g)\|^2_F \\
        &\geq \sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{-2(k+1)\tau} \sum_{j=m+1}^{n^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}}\sigma_j(M_k(\Psi))^2 \\
        &= a_\Psi(m, \tau)^2,
    \end{align}
    where the inequality is due to Eckart-Young and the fact $\operatorname{rank}(M_k(g)) \leq m$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
Fix $R > 0$.
    Let $F: {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ be a measurable vector field. Using coordinates $(z, u) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ with $z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $u \in {\mathbb{R}}$, assume that $F_{n+1}(z, \cdot)$ is integrable w.r.t. $\gamma_1$ on $[-R, R]$ for a.e. $z$, and
    define $\mathcal{A}_RF: {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
    \begin{equation}
        (\mathcal{A}_RF)(z) := \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \gamma_1}[F_{n+1}(z, U) \mid |U| \leq R].
    \end{equation}
    We call $\mathcal{A}_R$ the {\em averaging operator with truncation $R$}.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixaveragingoperator}
    Fix $\sigma, \beta, L , R\in (0, \infty)$, let $\psi(u) = \sigma u$, and let $\Psi: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfy $\|\Psi\|_\infty \leq \beta$ and $\operatorname{Lip}(\Psi) \leq L$.
    Then, for every $\tau \in [0, \infty)$ and every measurable $F: {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ for which $\mathcal{A}_RF$ is defined and in $L^2(\gamma_n)$, it holds that
    \begin{align}
        \| s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - F\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \geq  \alpha_{R,\beta, \sigma} \cdot \left(\|e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi - c_{\sigma, \tau}\mathcal{A}_RF\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)} - C_{R,\beta, \sigma} L^2 \tau\right)
    \end{align}
    where we define the explicit constants
    \begin{align}
        \alpha_{R, \beta, \sigma} &:= \sqrt{\gamma_1([-R, R])} \max\{1, \sigma\}^{-5/2} \exp\left(-\frac{R\beta + \beta^2/2 + R^2\max\{0, 1-\sigma^2\}/2}{2\min\{1, \sigma\}^2}\right),
        \\  C_{R, \beta, \sigma}  &:= \frac{2(R+\beta)}{\min\{1, \sigma\}^2} \exp\left(\frac{(R+\beta)^2}{2\min\{1, \sigma\}^2}\right),\\
        c_{\sigma, \tau} &:= e^{-2\tau} \sigma^2 + 1 - e^{-2\tau}.
    \end{align}
    The same is true with $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
The claim follows directly from the following two estimates on $\mathcal{A}_R$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmasecondthingtoprove}
    \|e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi - c_{\sigma, \tau}\mathcal{A}_R s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{\infty} \leq C_{R, \beta,\sigma} L^2 \tau.
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmafirstthingtoprove}
    \|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - F\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \geq \alpha_{R,\beta, \sigma} c_{\sigma, \tau}\|\mathcal{A}_R s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \mathcal{A}_R F\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)},
\end{equation}
The same will be true for $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$, after which the result will follow from the reverse triangle inequality.

To show these claims, let us denote $q_- := \min\{1, \sigma\}$, $q_+ := \max\{1, \sigma\}$, $c = c_{\sigma, \tau}$ and observe that $q_-^2 \leq c \leq q_+^2$. For each $z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ we define
\begin{equation}
    \eta_z := e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}X), \quad X \sim \gamma_n.
\end{equation}
Note that $|\eta_z| \leq \beta$ and $\mathbb{E}[\eta_z] = e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi(z)$. If we denote
\begin{equation}
    \widetilde{\eta}_z(u) := \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\eta_z \exp\left(-\frac{(u-\eta_z)^2}{2c}\right)\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{(u-\eta_z)^2}{2c}\right)\right]}
\end{equation}
then we claim that
\begin{equation}
    (s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} = \frac{\widetilde{\eta}_z(u) - u}{c}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, as was the case in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised}, by Gaussian regression we know that conditionally on the first $n$ coordinates being equal to $z$ the last coordinate under $\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ has the same law as
\begin{equation}
    \sqrt{c}W + \eta_z, \quad W \sim \gamma_1 \text{ independently of $\eta_z$}.
\end{equation}
The conditional density of the last coordinate is therefore $p_z(u) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi c}} \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{(u-\eta_z)^2}{2c}\right)\right]$, and so
\begin{align}
    (s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} = \partial_u \log p_z(u) = \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{u-\eta_z}{c} \exp\left(-\frac{(u-\eta_z)^2}{2c}\right)\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(-\frac{(u-\eta_z)^2}{2c}\right)\right]} = \frac{\widetilde{\eta}_z(u) - u}{c}.
\end{align}
This also implies that $(b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} = \frac{\widetilde{\eta}_z(u) - u}{c}+u$, and since the standard Gaussian conditioned on $[-R, R]$ is centered we find
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixvalueoftheaveragingoperator}
    (c\mathcal{A}_R s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi})(z) = (c\mathcal{A}_R b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi})(z) = \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \gamma_1}[\widetilde{\eta}_z(U) \mid |U| \leq R],
\end{equation}
and in particular $\mathcal{A}_R s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} = \mathcal{A}_R b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$. We now compare $\widetilde{\eta}_z(u)$ and $\mathbb{E}[\eta_z]$. For $u, y \in {\mathbb{R}}$ we let
\begin{equation}
    w_u(y) := \exp\left(-\frac{(u-y)^2}{2c}\right)
\end{equation}
to see that $\widetilde{\eta}_z(u) = \mathbb{E}[\eta_z w_u(\eta_z)] / \mathbb{E}[w_u(\eta_z)]$ and therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmacovarianceequality}
    \widetilde{\eta}_z(u) - \mathbb{E}[\eta_z] = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_z, w_u(\eta_z))}{\mathbb{E}[w_u(\eta_z)]}.
\end{equation}
Now, since $|\eta_z| \leq \beta$ and $|u| \leq R$ we know that
$\mathbb{E}[w_u(\eta_z)] \geq \exp\left(-\frac{(R+\beta)^2}{2c}\right)$.
Furthermore, for $y \in [-\beta, \beta]$ we know
$|w'_u(y)| = \frac{|u-y|}{c} w_u(y) \leq \frac{R+\beta}{c}$. 
Hence, the covariance inequality $|\operatorname{Cov}(Y, f(Y))| \leq \operatorname{Lip}(f) \operatorname{Var}(Y)$ implies that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmaupperboundintermsofvariance}
    \sup_{u \in [-R, R]}\left|\widetilde{\eta}_z(u) - \mathbb{E}[\eta_z]\right| \leq \frac{R+\beta}{c} \exp\left(\frac{(R+\beta)^2}{2c}\right) \operatorname{Var}(\eta_z).
\end{equation}
However, the function $x \mapsto e^{-\tau}\Psi(e^{-\tau}z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}x)$ is $Le^{-\tau}\sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}$-Lipschitz and so the Gaussian Poincaré inequality yields
\begin{equation}
    \operatorname{Var}(\eta_z) \leq L^2 e^{-2\tau} (1-e^{-2\tau}) \leq 2L^2 \tau.
\end{equation}
Combining this with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmaupperboundintermsofvariance}) and $c \geq q_-^2$ and using $\mathbb{E}[\eta_z] = e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi(z)$, we find
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n}\sup_{u \in [-R, R]}  \left|\widetilde{\eta}_z(u) - e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi(z)\right| \leq C_{R, \beta, \sigma}L^2 \tau.
\end{equation}
Averaging over $u$ and using (\ref{eqn:proofappendixvalueoftheaveragingoperator}) gives the estimate (\ref{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmasecondthingtoprove}) for both $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ and $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.

To prove the second estimate (\ref{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmafirstthingtoprove}), we note that the density of $\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ is given by
\begin{equation}
    \rho_{\tau}^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u) = \gamma_n(z) p_z(u)
\end{equation}
since the first $n$ coordinates have marginal law $\gamma_n$ and the last coordinate has density $p_z$ conditioned on the event where the first $n$ coordinates equal $z$. Therefore,
\begin{align}
    \|s_{\tau}^{\psi, \Psi} - F\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})}^2 &\geq \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^n} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \left|(s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} - F_{n+1}(z, u)\right|^2 p_z(u) du d\gamma_n(z) \\
    &\geq \kappa_{R,\beta, \sigma} \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^n} \int_{-R}^R \left|(s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(z, u))_{n+1} - F_{n+1}(z, u)\right|^2 d\gamma_1(u)d\gamma_n(z),
\end{align}
where we use that
\begin{equation}
    \frac{p_z(u)}{\gamma_1(u)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{c}} \mathbb{E}\left[\exp\left(\frac{c-1}{2c}u^2 + \frac{u\eta_z}{c} - \frac{\eta_z^2}{2c}\right)\right] \geq \kappa_{R, \beta, \sigma}
\end{equation}
for all $|u| \leq R$ and we denote
\begin{equation}
    \kappa_{R, \beta, \sigma} := \frac{1}{q_+} \exp\left(-\frac{R\beta + \beta^2 / 2 + R^2\max\{0, 1-\sigma^2\}/2}{q_-^2}\right).
\end{equation}
Hence, by applying Jensen's inequality under the conditional law $\gamma_1(\cdot \mid [-R, R])$ we find
\begin{align}
    \|s_{\tau}^{\psi, \Psi} - F\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})}^2 &\geq \kappa_{R, \beta, \sigma} \gamma_1([-R, R]) \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^n}\left|(\mathcal{A}_Rs_\tau^{\psi, \Psi})(z) - (\mathcal{A}_R F)(z)\right|^2 d\gamma_n(z)  \\
    &= \kappa_{R, \beta, \sigma} \gamma_1([-R, R])\| \mathcal{A}_R s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \mathcal{A}_RF\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)}^2.
\end{align}
Using $\kappa_{R,\beta,\sigma}\gamma_1([-R, R]) / c^2 \geq \alpha_{R, \beta, \sigma}^2$, we get (\ref{eqn:proofappendixaveraginglemmafirstthingtoprove}). The same argument applies to $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixeaveragingoperatorpreserveswidth}
    Fix $m \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and let $F : {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ be measurable s.t. its last coordinate satisfies $F_{n+1} \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n+1)}$. Then, $\mathcal{A}_RF \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n)}$ for all $R > 0$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Let us express
   \begin{equation}
       F_{n+1}(z, u) = \sum_{j=1}^m f_j(\left\langle z, v_j\right\rangle + b_j u)
   \end{equation}
   for $f_j \in L^2(\gamma_1)$ and $\|v_j\|^2 + |b_j|^2 = 1$. Choose $\theta_j \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ s.t. $v_j = \|v_j\| \theta_j$ (where if $\|v_j\| = 0$ then we choose arbitrary $\theta_j$) and define
   \begin{equation}
       \widetilde{f}_j(t) := \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \gamma_1}[f_j(\|v_j\|t + b_j U) \mid |U| \leq R].
   \end{equation}
    Naturally, this means that
    \begin{equation}
        (\mathcal{A}_R F)(z)  = \sum_{j=1}^m \widetilde{f}_j(\left\langle z, \theta_j\right\rangle).
    \end{equation}
    It remains to check that $\widetilde{f}_j \in L^2(\gamma_1)$. With $Y, U \sim \gamma_1$ i.i.d. we have
    \begin{align}
        \|\widetilde{f}_j\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)}^2 &\leq \mathbb{E}[f_j(\|v_j\|Y + b_j U)^2 \mid |U| \leq R] \\&\leq \frac{1}{\gamma_1([-R, R])} \mathbb{E}[f_j(\|v_j\|Y + b_j U)^2 ]\\
        &= \frac{1}{\gamma_1([-R, R])} \|f_j\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)}^2,
    \end{align}
    where the first line is Jensen and the third is because $\operatorname{Law}(\|v_j\|Y + b_jU ) = \gamma_1$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Letting $q_-,q_+$ be as before, we choose $R := \frac{q_-^2}{\beta + q_-}$, and so $R \leq q_- \leq 1$, $\frac{\beta R}{q_-^2} \leq 1$, and $\frac{R^2}{q_-^2} \leq 1$. We first show that
\begin{equation}
    Q_{\beta, \sigma} := 9 (1+\beta) \frac{\max\{1, \sigma\}^{5/2}}{\min\{1, \sigma\}^2} \exp\left(\frac{\beta^2}{2\min\{1, \sigma\}^2}\right)   \geq \max\{\alpha_{R, \beta, \sigma}^{-1}, C_{R, \beta, \sigma}\}.
\end{equation}
Since $R \leq 1$ we know $\gamma_1([-R, R]) \geq 2Re^{-1/2}/\sqrt{2\pi} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi e}} R$, and so
\begin{align}
    \alpha_{R, \beta, \sigma}^{-1} &= \gamma_1([-R, R])^{-1/2} q_+^{5/2} \exp\left(\frac{R\beta + \beta^2 / 2 + R^2 \max\{0, 1-\sigma^2\}/2}{2q_-^2}\right)\\
    &\leq e\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1/4} R^{-1/2} q_+^{5/2} \exp\left(\frac{\beta^2}{4q_-^2}\right) \\
    &\leq  e\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)^{1/4} \frac{1+\beta}{q_-^2} q_+^{5/2} \exp\left(\frac{\beta^2}{2q_-^2}\right) \\
    &\leq Q_{\beta, \sigma}.
\end{align}
Similarly, we have
\begin{align}
    C_{R, \beta, \sigma} 
    &= \frac{2(R+\beta)}{q_-^2} \exp\left(\frac{\beta^2}{2q_-^2} + \frac{\beta R}{q_-^2} + \frac{R^2}{2q_-^2}\right) \\
    &\leq 2e^{3/2} \frac{1+\beta}{q_-^2} \exp\left(\frac{\beta^2}{2q_-^2}\right)\\
    &\leq Q_{\beta, \sigma}.
\end{align}
We now prove the width lower bound. Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixaveragingoperator} to $F = \hat{s}_\tau$ gives
\begin{equation}
    \varepsilon \geq \alpha_{R, \beta, \sigma} \left(\|e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi - c_{\sigma, \tau} \mathcal{A}_R \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)} - C_{R, \beta, \sigma}L^2\tau\right)
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}
    \|e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi - c_{\sigma, \tau} \mathcal{A}_R \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)} \leq \alpha_{R, \beta, \sigma}^{-1}\varepsilon + C_{R, \beta, \sigma}L^2\tau \leq Q_{\beta, \sigma}(\varepsilon + L^2 \tau).
\end{equation}
Since $(\hat{s}_\tau)_{n+1} \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n+1)}$, Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixeaveragingoperatorpreserveswidth} ensures that $c_{\sigma, \tau}\mathcal{A}_R \hat{s}_\tau \in \mathcal{R}_m^{(n)}$. By Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermiteranklowerbound}, we know that
\begin{equation}
    a_\Psi(m, \tau) \leq Q_{\beta, \sigma}(\varepsilon + L^2 \tau)
\end{equation}
and therefore $m \geq m_\Psi(Q_{\beta, \sigma}(\varepsilon + L^2\tau), \tau)$. 

It remains to prove the Barron lower bound.
Let $\mathcal{H} := L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi})$, denote
\begin{equation}
    \kappa_s := (\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}|G|^{2s})^{1/(2s)} = \left(\frac{2^s \Gamma(s+1/2)}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^{1/(2s)},
\end{equation}
and define the constant
\begin{equation}
    \Lambda_{s,\beta,\sigma} := \begin{cases}
        \left((\kappa_sq_+)^{2s} + \max\{1,\beta\}^{2s}\right)^{1/2} & 0 < s < 1/2,\\
        \max\{\kappa_s q_+ + \beta, 1\}^s & s \geq 1/2.
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Finally, set
\begin{equation}
    A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma} := \begin{cases}
\|\phi\|_\infty & \text{$\phi$ bounded},
\\ \max\{|\phi(1)|, |\phi(-1)|\} \Lambda_{s, \beta, \sigma} & \text{$\phi$ positively $s$-homogeneous.}
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
We show that every normalized neuron has $\mathcal{H}$-norm at most $A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}$. If $\phi$ is bounded then obviously
\begin{equation}
    \left\|\frac{\phi(\left\langle \cdot, a\right\rangle + b)}{1 + \|a\| + |b|}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}} \leq \frac{\|\phi\|_\infty}{1 + \|a\| + |b|} \leq A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}.
\end{equation}
Suppose now that $\phi$ is positively $s$-homogeneous. 
Let $X_\tau \sim \rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ so that 
\begin{equation}
    X_\tau = e^{-\tau} (Z, \sigma U + \Psi(Z)) + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}} G
\end{equation}
for $Z \sim \gamma_n$, $U \sim \gamma_1$, $G \sim \gamma_{n+1}$ independent. For parameters $a = (v, t) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \times {\mathbb{R}}$ and $b \in {\mathbb{R}}$, write
\begin{equation}
    \left\langle X_\tau, a\right\rangle + b = H_a + D_{a,b}
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}
    H_a := e^{-\tau} (\left\langle Z, v\right\rangle + \sigma t U) + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}} \left\langle G, a\right\rangle
\end{equation}
is centered Gaussian and 
\begin{equation}
    D_{a,b} := e^{-\tau}t\Psi(Z) + b.
\end{equation}
Since we have
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}[H_a^2] = \|v\|^2 + c_{\sigma, \tau} t^2 \leq q_+^2 \|a\|^2
\end{equation}
we find that $\|H_a\|_{L^{2s}} \leq \kappa_s q_+ \|a\|$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
    |D_{a,b}| \leq |t|\beta + |b| \leq \beta \|a\| + |b|.
\end{equation}
Suppose first that $s \geq 1/2$. Since $|\phi(w)| \leq \max\{|\phi(1)|, |\phi(-1)|\} |w|^s$ we have
\begin{align}
    \|\phi(\left\langle X_\tau, a\right\rangle + b)\|_{L^2} &\leq \max\{|\phi(1)|, |\phi(-1)|\} \cdot  \|H_a + D_{a,b}\|_{L^{2s}}^s
    \\ &\leq \max\{|\phi(1)|, |\phi(-1)|\} \cdot (\kappa_s q_+ \|a\| + \beta\|a\| + |b|)^s 
    \\&\leq A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}(\|a\| + |b|)^s.
\end{align}
If we instead have $0 < s < 1/2$ we know $|x+y|^{2s} \leq |x|^{2s} + |y|^{2s}$ and so
\begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}|H_a + D_{a,b}|^{2s} &\leq \mathbb{E}|H_a|^{2s} + \mathbb{E}|D_{a,b}|^{2s} \\
    &\leq (\kappa_s q_+)^{2s}\|a\|^{2s} + (\beta \|a\| + |b|)^{2s}
    \\&\leq \Lambda_{s, \beta, \sigma}^2 (\|a\|+|b|)^{2s}.
\end{align}
Hence, in either case we know that
\begin{equation}
    \left\|\frac{\phi(\left\langle \cdot, a\right\rangle + b)}{(\|a\| + |b|)^{s}}\right\|_\mathcal{H} \leq A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}.
\end{equation}
We finish by noting that if $\mathcal{N}_{\phi,k}^{(n+1, n+1)}$ denotes the class of vector-valued two-layer neural networks of width at most $k$ with activation $\phi$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep}
    \inf_{G \in \mathcal{N}_{\phi,k}^{(n+1, n+1)}} \|\hat{s}_\tau - G\|_\mathcal{H} \leq \frac{A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma} \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}}{\sqrt{k}} \quad (\forall k \in {\mathbb{N}}).
\end{equation}
Indeed, given a Barron representation $\hat{s}_\tau(\cdot) = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \times {\mathbb{R}}} \phi(\left\langle \cdot, a\right\rangle + b) d\mu(a, b)$ with \begin{equation}B_\mu := \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \times {\mathbb{R}}} w(a, b) d\mu(a, b) \leq \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} + \delta, \quad w(a, b) := \begin{cases}
    1 + \|a\| + |b| & \text{$\phi$ bounded},
    \\
    (\|a\| + |b|)^s & \text{$\phi$ $s$-homogeneous},
\end{cases}\end{equation}
we normalize $\mu$ to a probability measure, sample $k$ i.i.d. normalized neurons $Y_j := \frac{\phi(\left\langle \cdot, a_j\right\rangle + b_j)}{w(a_j, b_j)}$, and take
\begin{equation}
    \hat{G}(\cdot) := \frac{B_\mu}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k Y_j.
\end{equation}
We may calculate that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}\|\hat{s}_\tau - \hat{G}\|_\mathcal{H}^2 = \frac{B_\mu^2}{k} \mathbb{E}\|Y_1 - \mathbb{E}Y_1\|^2_\mathcal{H} \leq \frac{B_\mu^2A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}^2}{k} \leq \frac{A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}^2 (\|\widehat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} + \delta)^2}{k},
\end{equation}
after which taking $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves (\ref{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep}). Define
\begin{equation}
    M := m_\Psi(Q_{\beta, \sigma}(2\varepsilon + L^2\tau), \tau).
\end{equation}
If $M \leq 1$ then the claim is trivial, so we suppose $M \geq 2$. For every $k < M$, the width lower bound we already proved implies
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep1}
    \inf_{G \in \mathcal{N}_{\phi,k}^{(n+1, n+1)}} \|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - G\|_\mathcal{H} \geq 2\varepsilon
\end{equation}
since the last coordinate satisfies $G_{n+1} \in\mathcal{R}^{(n+1)}_k$ for all $G \in \mathcal{N}_{\phi,k}^{(n+1, n+1)}$. On the other hand, by the triangle inequality and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep}) we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep2}
    \inf_{G \in \mathcal{N}_{\phi,k}^{(n+1, n+1)}} \|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - G\|_\mathcal{H} \leq \|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \hat{s}_\tau\|_\mathcal{H} + \inf_{G \in \mathcal{N}_{\phi,k}^{(n+1, n+1)}} \|\hat{s}_\tau - G\|_\mathcal{H} \leq \varepsilon + \frac{A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}\|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}}{\sqrt{k}}
\end{equation}
for every $k < M$.
Combining (\ref{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep1}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixpropositionapproximationtheBarronstep2}) implies that
\begin{equation}
    \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \geq \frac{\varepsilon \sqrt{k}}{A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}} \quad (\forall k < M).
\end{equation}
Taking $k = M-1$ (or $k \uparrow \infty$ if $M = \infty$) and setting $K_{\phi, \beta, \sigma} = 1/A_{\phi, \beta, \sigma}$ yields the claim.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:appendixapproximationupperbound}
    Let $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and $\psi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$, $\Psi: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be measurable, and let $\phi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be nonpolynomial and satisfy Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}. 
    Then, for any $\varepsilon, \tau \in (0, \infty)$ there is some $m \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and neural network $\hat{s}_\tau: {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ of the form $\hat{s}_\tau(x) = \sum_{j=1}^m u_j \phi(\left\langle x, a_j\right\rangle + b_j)$ with $u_j, a_j \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ and $b_j \in {\mathbb{R}}$ for which $\|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}<\infty$ and
    \begin{equation}
        \|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \leq \varepsilon.
    \end{equation}
    If $\pi^{\psi, \Psi} \in \mathcal{P}_2({\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})$, then the same statement holds with $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Let us write the OU interpolant by \begin{equation}
    X_\tau := e^{-\tau} X + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}} Z, \quad X \sim \pi^{\psi, \Psi}, \; Z \sim \gamma_{n+1}
\end{equation}
with $X, Z$ independent. Fix $\tau > 0$.
    By the Tweedie formula (\ref{eqn:prelimtweedie}) we have $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}(x) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}} \mathbb{E}[Z \mid X_\tau = x]$. Conditional Jensen implies that
    \begin{align}
        \|s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})}^2 = \frac{1}{1-e^{-2\tau}} \mathbb{E}\left[\|\mathbb{E}[Z \mid X_\tau]\|^2\right] \leq \frac{\mathbb{E}\|Z\|^2}{1-e^{-2\tau}} = \frac{n+1}{1-e^{-2\tau}} < \infty
    \end{align}
    and hence $s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} \in L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}) $. If $\phi$ is nonconstant and bounded, then \cite[Theorem 1]{hornik1991approximation} directly implies the result. If $\phi$ is instead positively $s$-homogeneous for $s \in {\mathbb{N}} $, then the $(s+1)^{th}$ discrete derivative of $\phi$ is bounded, nonconstant (since $\phi$ is nonpolynomial), and representable using $s+2$ neurons, so the same universal approximation statement applies at the cost of increasing the width. Lastly, if $\pi^{{\psi, \Psi}}$ has finite second moment then $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} = s_\tau^{\psi, \Psi} + \operatorname{Id}$ is also in $L^2(\rho_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})$, and so we may apply the same argument.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixtriangularearlystoppingerrorTVW1}
    Let $n \geq 2$ and $\Psi\in L^1(\gamma_n)$ and define
    \begin{equation}
        \pi := \pi^{\operatorname{Id}, \Psi} = \operatorname{Law}(Z, U + \Psi(Z)), \quad \rho_\tau := P_\tau^* \pi,
    \end{equation}
    with $Z \sim \gamma_n$ and $U \sim \gamma_1$ independent. If we denote $M_\Psi := \mathbb{E}_{Z \sim \gamma_n}[\Psi(Z)^2 e^{-\Psi(Z)^2/4}]$ then
    \begin{equation}
        \min\left\{\operatorname{TV}(\pi, \rho_\tau), \; W_1(\pi, \rho_\tau)\right\} \geq \frac{M_\Psi}{4\sqrt{2}} (1-e^{-2\tau}) \quad (\forall \tau \geq 0).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
Since $\Psi \in L^1(\gamma_n)$, both $\pi$ and $\rho_\tau$ have finite first moments. Consider
\begin{equation}
    f(z, u) := e^{-u^2/2}.
\end{equation}
We know $0 \leq f \leq 1$ and $\|\nabla f\|_\infty = \sup_{u \in {\mathbb{R}}} |u|e^{-u^2/2} \leq 1$. So, by the dual characterizations of total variation and $W_1$, we know
\begin{equation}
     \min\left\{\operatorname{TV}(\pi, \rho_\tau), \; W_1(\pi, \rho_\tau)\right\}  \geq \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}} f d\rho_\tau - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}} f d\pi.
\end{equation}
The last-coordinate marginal of $\rho_\tau$ has law equal to $\operatorname{Law}(U + e^{-\tau}\Psi(W))$ for $U \sim \gamma_1$ independent of $W \sim \gamma_n$. Using the fact that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \gamma_1} \left[e^{-(U+a)^2/2}\right] = \frac{e^{-a^2/4}}{\sqrt{2}},
\end{equation}
we obtain that
\begin{equation}
    \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}} f d\rho_\tau - \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}} f d\pi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \mathbb{E}_{Z \sim \gamma_n}\left[e^{-e^{-2\tau}\Psi(Z)^2/4} - e^{-\Psi(Z)^2/4}\right].
\end{equation}
Since $e^x - 1 \geq x$ for $x \geq 0$, pointwise we have
\begin{equation}
    e^{-e^{-2\tau} \Psi(z)^2 / 4} - e^{-\Psi(z)^2/4} = e^{-\Psi(z)^2/4} \left(e^{(1-e^{-2\tau}) \Psi(z)^2/4} - 1\right) \geq \frac{1-e^{-2\tau}}{4} \Psi(z)^2 e^{-\Psi(z)^2/4},
\end{equation}
from which the claim follows by taking an expectation.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixtriangularearlystoppingerrorKL}
Let $\Psi, \pi, \rho_\tau$ be as in Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtriangularearlystoppingerrorTVW1}, and assume further that $\|\Psi\|_\infty \leq \beta$. Let $D_\tau$ denote either $\operatorname{KL}(\rho_\tau \| \pi)$ or $\operatorname{KL}(\pi \| \rho_\tau)$. Then,
\begin{equation}
    \sqrt{D_\tau} \geq \frac{1}{\sqrt{2(1+\beta^2)}} \max_{m \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}} \left\{ (1-e^{-\ell_n(m) \tau}) a_\Psi(m, 0)\right\} \quad (\forall \tau \geq 0),
\end{equation}
where we denote $\ell_n(m) := 1 + 2\lceil \log(m+1)/\log(n)\rceil$.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
The claim is immediate for $\tau = 0$, so fix $\tau > 0$. 
Both $\pi$ and $\rho_\tau$ have first-coordinate marginal $\gamma_n$, and conditional on the first coordinate being $z \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ the last coordinate under $\pi$ has law $\mathcal{N}( \Psi(z), 1)$ and under $\rho_\tau$ has law
\begin{equation}
    \operatorname{Law}\left(W + e^{-\tau} \Psi\left(e^{-\tau}z + \sqrt{1-e^{-2\tau}}G\right)\right)
\end{equation}
with $W \sim \gamma_1$, $G \sim \gamma_n$ independent; this can be shown via Gaussian regression, see the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised}. In particular, both conditional laws are a standard Gaussian plus an independent shift supported on $[-\beta, \beta]$. Thus, with $U$ a random variable drawn from the conditional law of the last coordinate under either $\pi$ or $\rho_\tau$ we know
\begin{equation}
    \log \mathbb{E} e^{t(U - \mathbb{E}U)} \leq \frac{1+\beta^2}{2}t^2 \quad (\forall t \in {\mathbb{R}}),
\end{equation}
where the bounded shift contributes $\beta^2 t^2/2$ by Hoeffding's lemma and the Gaussian contributes $t^2/2$. Now, we know the variational inequality that for probability measures $P, Q$ on ${\mathbb{R}}$ we have
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{KL}(P \| Q) &\geq \sup_{f \text{ Lipschitz}}\left\{ \mathbb{E}_P[f] - \log \mathbb{E}_Q\left[e^f\right]\right\}
    \\ &\geq \sup_{t \in {\mathbb{R}}} \left\{t(\mathbb{E}_PY - \mathbb{E}_QY) - \log \mathbb{E}_Q e^{t(Y - \mathbb{E}_QY)}\right\} ,
\end{align}
where we apply the first line with $f(y) = t(y - \mathbb{E}_Q[y])$ to get the second. Thus, with $P$ and $Q$ the distributions of the last coordinate under $\pi$ and $\rho_\tau$ conditioned on the first being $z$, we have
\begin{equation}
    \operatorname{KL}(P \| Q) \geq \sup_{t \in {\mathbb{R}}} \left\{t(\mathbb{E}_PY - \mathbb{E}_QY) - \frac{1+\beta^2}{2}t^2\right\} = \frac{\left|\mathbb{E}_PY - \mathbb{E}_QY\right|^2}{2(1+\beta^2)} = \frac{|\Psi(z) - e^{-\tau}P_\tau \Psi(z)|^2}{2(1+\beta^2)}.
\end{equation}
The same argument works with $P$ and $Q$ swapped. Since the marginals of the first coordinates coincide, by the chain rule for relative entropy we find
\begin{equation}
    D_\tau \geq \frac{\|\Psi - e^{-\tau} P_\tau \Psi\|_{L^2(\gamma_n)}^2}{2(1+\beta^2)} = \frac{1}{2(1+\beta^2)} \sum_{k=0}^\infty (1 - e^{-(k+1)\tau})^2 \|M_k(\Psi)\|_F^2,
\end{equation}
where we expand in Hermite chaoses. For each $m \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$, by definition of $\ell_n(m)$ we know $k+1 < \ell_n(m) \implies n^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor} \leq m$. Hence,
\begin{align}
    D_\tau &\geq \frac{1}{2(1+\beta^2)} \sum_{k=0}^\infty (1-e^{-(k+1)\tau})^2 \sum_{j=m+1}^{n^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}} \sigma_j(M_k(\Psi))^2 \\ &\geq \frac{(1-e^{-\ell_n(m)\tau})^2}{2(1+\beta^2)} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \sum_{j=m+1}^{n^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor}} \sigma_j(M_k(\Psi))^2 \\&= \frac{(1-e^{-\ell_n(m)\tau})^2}{2(1+\beta^2)} a_\Psi(m, 0)^2.
\end{align}
Taking square roots and maximizing over $m$ proves the claim. Since $a_\Psi(m, 0) \to 0$ as $m \to \infty$, this maximum is attained at a finite $m$.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{definition:triangularresnet}
Fix an activation $\varphi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $n,W, L \in {\mathbb{N}}$. 
Choose scalar functions $g, \chi \in \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, W}$. For each $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}$, choose $ h_\ell \in \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, W}$ and input/output features $ a_\ell, b_\ell \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ with $\left\langle a_\ell, b_\ell\right\rangle = 0$. Choose also a readout direction $v \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$.
Using these choices, we define a ResNet:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item With $(z^{(0)}, u^{(0)}) \in {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ the input, the first stage of $L$ layers is
    \begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}[c]
z^{(\ell)}
  &= z^{(\ell-1)}
     + b_\ell g\left(
       \left\langle z^{(\ell-1)}, a_\ell\right\rangle
     \right), \\
u^{(\ell)}
  &= u^{(\ell-1)}
     + h_\ell\left(u^{(\ell-1)}\right),
\end{aligned}
\qquad
(\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}).
\end{equation}

\item The middle readout stage is 
    \begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}[c]
z^{(L+1)}
  &= z^{(L)}, \\
u^{(L+1)}
  &= u^{(L)}
     + \chi\left(\left\langle z^{(L)}, v\right\rangle\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\item Denoting $\ell := L+1-j$, the third stage of $L$ layers is
    \begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}[c]
z^{(L+j+1)}
  &= z^{(L+j)}
     - b_\ell g\left(
       \left\langle z^{(L+j)}, a_\ell\right\rangle
     \right), \\
u^{(L+j+1)}
  &= u^{(L+j)},
\end{aligned}
\qquad
(j \in \{1, \ldots, L\}).
\end{equation}

\end{enumerate}
Denoting the parameters by $\theta := \left(g, \chi, (h_\ell, a_\ell,b_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L,v\right)$, we write
$\operatorname{TResNet}_{\theta}: {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ to represent the mapping sending $(z^{(0)}, u^{(0)}) \mapsto (z^{(2L+1)}, u^{(2L+1)})$. 

We also denote the Gaussian pushforward by $\pi^\theta := (\operatorname{TResNet}_\theta)_\# \gamma_{n+1}$, the OU flow by $\rho_\tau^\theta := P_\tau^* \pi^\theta$, and the Lebesgue and Gaussian scores respectively by $s_\tau^\theta := \nabla \log \rho_\tau^\theta$ and $b_\tau^\theta := \nabla \log \frac{\rho_\tau^\theta}{\gamma_{n+1}}$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
Let $\theta = \left(g, \chi, (h_\ell, a_\ell,b_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L,v\right)$. Then,
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{TResNet}_\theta(z, u) = (z, \psi_\theta(u) + \Psi_\theta(z))
    \end{equation}
    where we define $\psi_\theta: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
    $\psi_\theta := (\operatorname{Id} + h_L) \circ \cdots \circ (\operatorname{Id} + h_1)$
    and $\Psi_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
    \begin{equation}
        \Psi_\theta(z) := \chi(\left\langle G_L(z), v\right\rangle), \quad G_\ell(z) := G_{\ell-1}(z) + b_\ell g \left(\left\langle G_{\ell - 1}(z), a_\ell\right\rangle\right), \quad G_0(z) := z.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, $\pi^\theta = \pi^{\psi_\theta, \Psi_\theta}$, $s_\tau^\theta = s_\tau^{\psi_\theta, \Psi_\theta}$, and $b_\tau^\theta = b_\tau^{\psi_\theta, \Psi_\theta}$.
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Defining the map $S_\ell(x) := x + b_\ell g(\left\langle x, a_\ell\right\rangle)$, since $\left\langle a_\ell, b_\ell\right\rangle = 0$ we know that
    \begin{equation}
        S_\ell^{-1}(x) = x - b_\ell g(\left\langle x, a_\ell\right\rangle). 
    \end{equation}
    Since $G_\ell = S_\ell \circ \cdots \circ S_1$, the claim follows by construction.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixrepresentationlowerboundresnets}
Fix $\omega \in C^5_b({\mathbb{R}}) \cap \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, W}$ s.t.
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationconditionsonomega}
    \omega(0) = 0, \quad \omega'(0) > 0, \quad \omega''(0) = 0, \quad \omega'''(0)\neq 0.
\end{equation}
Then, there is a constant $\Lambda_\omega \in (0, \infty)$ depending only on $\omega$ for which the following holds. 
    Let $\theta = \left(g, \chi, (h_\ell, a_\ell,b_\ell)_{\ell=1}^L,v\right)$ satisfy the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] We have $g = \Lambda_\omega \omega$ and $\chi = \omega$.
        \item[(ii)] For every $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}$, $\operatorname{Id} + h_\ell$ is increasing with $h_\ell = 0$ on $[-2\|\omega\|_\infty, 2\|\omega\|_\infty]$.
        \item[(iii)] For every $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}$ we have $\|a_\ell\| = \|b_\ell\| = 1$ and $\left\langle a_\ell, b_\ell\right\rangle = 0$. Also, $a_{\ell + 1} = b_\ell$ for every $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L-1\}$  along with $b_L = v$. 
    \end{enumerate}
    Then, there are constants $B_\omega \in (0, \infty)$, $c_\omega, C_\omega \in (1, \infty)$ depending only on $\omega$ s.t. $C_\omega / c_\omega \geq 2$ and \begin{equation}
       6\|s_\tau^{\theta}\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^3}}  \geq  \|\partial_{a_1}^3 s_\tau^{\theta}\|_{\infty} \geq B_\omega C_\omega^{L} \quad \left(\forall \tau \in \left(0, {B_\omega}{c_\omega^{- L}}\right]\right).
    \end{equation}
    The same statement holds for $b_\tau^{\theta}$. In particular, $\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^3}}(\pi^{\theta}) \geq B_\omega^2 2^L$ and if $\phi \in C^3({\mathbb{R}})$ satisfies Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} with $\|\phi\|_\infty, \|\phi'''\|_\infty < \infty $ then $\inf_{R > 0} R^2 \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi^R}(\pi^\theta) \geq B_\omega^2 2^L / \|\phi'''\|_\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
In the case $\{a_1, \ldots, a_L, v\} \subseteq \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ is an orthonormal set, due to the chaining in assumption (iii) this construction has the particularly clean form
    \begin{align}
        \Psi_\theta(z) &= \omega\left(\left\langle z, v\right\rangle + \Lambda_\omega \omega\left(\left\langle z, a_L\right\rangle + \Lambda_\omega \omega\left( \cdots + \Lambda_\omega \omega\left(\left\langle z, a_1\right\rangle\right)\right)\right)\right).
    \end{align}
    One can choose $(h_\ell)_{\ell = 1}^L$ to produce $\psi_\theta = (\operatorname{Id} + h_L) \circ \cdots \circ (\operatorname{Id} + h_1)$ with complicated behavior outside $[-2\|\omega\|_\infty, 2\|\omega\|_\infty]$, but inside this region $\psi_\theta$ is the identity by assumption (ii).
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
Let us denote $\kappa_1 := \omega'(0)$, $K_\omega := 52(1 + \|\omega\|_{C^5})$, and
    \begin{equation}
        \Lambda_\omega := \max\left\{1,\; \frac{6}{\kappa_1}, \; \frac{1458K_\omega^5}{\kappa_1^6}\right\}.
    \end{equation}
    We also set $C_\omega := (\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega-2)^3$ and $c_\omega := 2K_\omega^5 (1+\Lambda_\omega)^5 / C_\omega$ as well as
    \begin{equation}
        B_\omega := |\omega'''(0)| \min\left\{\frac{1}{2},\; \frac{L_\beta}{K_\omega^5}\right\}
    \end{equation}
    where $\beta := \|\omega\|_\infty$ and $L_\beta$ is the constant from Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised}. Since $\kappa_1\Lambda_\omega \geq 6$ and $\Lambda_\omega \geq 1$ we know 
    $ \kappa_1\Lambda_\omega - 2 \geq \frac{2}{3}\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega$ and $1 + \Lambda_\omega \leq 2\Lambda_\omega$. Hence,
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{C_\omega}{c_\omega} = \frac{(\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega - 2)^6}{2K_\omega^5(1+\Lambda_\omega)^5} \geq \frac{\kappa_1^6 \Lambda_\omega}{729K_\omega^5} \geq 2.
    \end{equation}
    Also, $K_\omega \geq \kappa_1$ and so $K_\omega(1+\Lambda_\omega) > \kappa_1\Lambda_\omega > \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega - 2 \geq 4$. Thus,
    \begin{equation}
        c_\omega = \frac{2K_\omega^5 (1+\Lambda_\omega)^5}{(\kappa_1\Lambda_\omega - 2)^3} > 2(\kappa_1\Lambda_\omega - 2)^2 \geq 32
    \end{equation}
    and so $1 < c_\omega \leq C_\omega / 2$. Now, choose an orthonormal basis of ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ whose first vector is $a_1$ and set
    \begin{equation}
        D := K_{\omega }^{L+1}(1+\Lambda_\omega)^L.
    \end{equation}
    By Faà di Bruno applied inductively to the recursion defining $G_\ell$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        \|\partial^\alpha G_\ell\|_\infty \leq (K_\omega (1 + \Lambda_\omega))^{\ell |\alpha|} \quad (1 \leq |\alpha| \leq 5,\; \forall \ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}),
    \end{equation}
    since the number of partitions of a set of at most 5 elements is $\leq 52$. Applying this formula once more to $\Psi_\theta(z) = \omega(\left\langle G_L(z), v\right\rangle)$ gives
    \begin{equation}
        \|\Psi_\theta\|_\infty \leq \beta, \quad \|\partial^\alpha \Psi_\theta\|_\infty  \leq D^{|\alpha|} \quad (1 \leq |\alpha| \leq 5).
    \end{equation}
    It remains to lower bound $\|\partial_{a_1}^3 \Psi_\theta\|_\infty$. For this, we denote
    \begin{equation}
        w_0 := a_1, \quad w_\ell := b_\ell,\quad J_\ell := \1_n + \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega w_\ell w_{\ell - 1}^\top
    \end{equation}
    for $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}$. For $0 \leq i < j \leq L$ we define
    \begin{equation}
        P_{i,j} := \left\langle w_j, J_j \cdots J_{i+1}w_i\right\rangle, \quad P_{i,i} := 1.
    \end{equation}
    We claim that
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixresnetpushforwardrepresentationinductionpropagation}
        P_{i,j} \geq (\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega - 2)^{j-i}.
    \end{equation}
