    Indeed, starting from $u_i := w_i$ we recursively set $u_k := J_k u_{k-1}$ for $k \in \{i+1, \ldots, j\}$ and $A_k := \left\langle w_{k-1}, u_{k-1}\right\rangle$ for $k \in \{i+1, \ldots, j+1\}$. We prove inductively that $A_k > 0$ and $\|u_{k-1}\| \leq 2A_k$. For $k = i+1$ this is trivial, and since
    \begin{equation}
        u_k = u_{k-1} + \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega A_k w_k
    \end{equation}
    we have that
    \begin{align}
        A_{k+1} &= \left\langle w_k, u_k\right\rangle = \left\langle w_k, u_{k-1}\right\rangle + \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega A_k \geq -\|u_{k-1}\| + \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega A_k \geq (\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega - 2) A_k > 0.
    \end{align}
    Moreover, 
    \begin{align}
        \|u_k\| \leq \|u_{k-1}\| + \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega A_k \leq (\kappa_1\Lambda_\omega + 2)A_k \leq 2(\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega - 2)A_k \leq 2A_{k+1},
    \end{align}
    where the second to last inequality uses that $\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega \geq 6$. This closes the induction, and hence $(\kappa_1\Lambda_\omega - 2)A_k \leq A_{k+1}$ for all $k$. Since $A_{j+1} = P_{i,j}$, (\ref{eqn:proofappendixresnetpushforwardrepresentationinductionpropagation}) follows. 

    Now, let us define \begin{equation}
        F(t) := \left\langle w_L, G_L(tw_0)\right\rangle.
    \end{equation}
From the recursion defining $G_\ell$, we know that
    \begin{equation}
        G_\ell(tw_0) = G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0) + \Lambda_\omega w_\ell \omega(\left\langle w_{\ell - 1}, G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right\rangle). 
    \end{equation}
    Since $G_\ell(0) = 0$ (due to $\omega(0) = 0$), differentiating once at $t = 0$ yields
    \begin{equation}
        \left.\frac{d}{dt}G_\ell(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} = J_\ell \left.\frac{d}{dt}G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right|_{t=0}
    \end{equation}
    which we iterate to find that
    \begin{equation}
        F'(0) = \left\langle w_L, J_L \cdots J_1 w_0\right\rangle = P_{0,L}.
    \end{equation}
    Similarly, differentiating the recursion twice yields
    \begin{equation}
        \left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}G_\ell(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} = J_\ell \left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} + \Lambda_\omega w_\ell \omega''(0) \left\langle w_{\ell - 1}, \left.\frac{d}{dt}G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right|_{t=0}\right\rangle^2.
    \end{equation}
    Since $\omega''(0) = 0$ and $G_0(tw_0) = tw_0$ has zero second derivative at $t=0$, by induction we find $ \left.\frac{d^2}{dt^2}G_\ell(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} = 0$ for each $\ell$ and therefore $F''(0) = 0$. Differentiating a third time, all terms involving $\omega''(0)$ or a second derivative of $G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)$ vanish. Thus,
    \begin{align}
         \left.\frac{d^3}{dt^3}G_\ell(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} &= J_\ell \left.\frac{d^3}{dt^3}G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} + \Lambda_\omega w_\ell \omega'''(0) \left\langle w_{\ell - 1}, \left.\frac{d}{dt}G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right|_{t=0}\right\rangle^3 \\
         &= J_\ell \left.\frac{d^3}{dt^3}G_{\ell - 1}(tw_0)\right|_{t=0} + \Lambda_\omega w_\ell \omega'''(0) P_{0,\ell - 1}^3.
    \end{align}
    By iterating this and then projecting onto $w_L$, we find that
    \begin{equation}
        F'''(0) = \Lambda_\omega \omega'''(0) \sum_{\ell = 1}^LP_{0,\ell - 1}^3 P_{\ell, L}
    \end{equation}
    since the cubic term $w_\ell P_{0,\ell-1}^3$ is propagated by $J_L \cdots J_{\ell + 1}$. Finally, since $\Psi_\theta(tw_0)  = \omega(F(t))$ we apply the chain rule to find
    \begin{equation}
        \frac{d^3}{dt^3} \omega(F(t)) = \omega'''(F(t))F'(t)^3 + 3\omega''(F(t)) F'(t) F''(t) + \omega'(F(t)) F'''(t).
    \end{equation}
    At $t = 0$ we have $F(0) = F''(0) = \omega''(0) = 0$ and $\omega'(0) = \kappa_1$, and so
    \begin{equation}
        \partial_{a_1}^3 \Psi_\theta(0) = \omega'''(0) F'(0)^3 + \kappa_1 F'''(0) = \omega'''(0) \left(P_{0,L}^3 + \kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega \sum_{\ell = 1}^L P_{0, \ell-1}^3 P_{\ell,L}\right).
    \end{equation}
    Since all terms in the parentheses are positive, there is no cancellation and so
    \begin{equation}
        \|\partial_{a_1}^3 \Psi_\theta\|_\infty \geq |\partial_{a_1}^3 \Psi_\theta(0)| \geq |\omega'''(0)| P_{0,L}^3 \geq |\omega'''(0)| (\kappa_1 \Lambda_\omega - 2)^{3L} = |\omega'''(0)|  C_\omega^L,
    \end{equation}
    where we applied (\ref{eqn:proofappendixresnetpushforwardrepresentationinductionpropagation}). By assumption (ii) we know that $\psi_\theta$ is increasing and the identity on $[-2\beta, 2\beta]$.
    By Lemma \ref{lemma:stupidnonsenserevised}, we have that \begin{equation}\|\partial_{a_1}^3 s_\tau^\theta\|_\infty \geq \frac{|\omega'''(0)|}{2}C_\omega^L \geq B_\omega C_\omega^L\end{equation} whenever $\tau \leq L_\beta \frac{|\omega'''(0)| C_\omega^L}{(L+1)D^5}$. Note that $\Psi_\theta$ depends on a subspace of dimension at most $L+1$ and so we replace $n $ with $L+1$ for this application (since the OU semigroup tensorizes).
    Since $L+1 \leq 2^L$, we find that
    \begin{align}
         L_\beta \frac{|\omega'''(0)| C_\omega^L}{(L+1)D^5}  &= L_\beta \frac{|\omega'''(0)|}{(L+1)K_\omega^5} \cdot \left(\frac{C_\omega}{K_\omega^5 (1+\Lambda_\omega)^5}\right)^L \\&\geq L_\beta \frac{|\omega'''(0)| }{K_\omega^5} \cdot \left(\frac{C_\omega}{2K_\omega^5 (1+\Lambda_\omega)^5}\right)^L 
         \\ &= L_\beta \frac{|\omega'''(0)|}{K_\omega^5} \cdot c_\omega^{-L} \\&\geq B_\omega c_\omega^{-L}.
    \end{align}
    The rest of the result follows from the proof of Corollary \ref{corollary:representationlowerbound}.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
Note that this obstruction is proved only for exponentially-small OU times. We create small but very rapid variations, which amplify the third derivative but become hidden under a small amount of noise.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixrepresentationupperboundresnets}
    Assume the setting of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationlowerboundresnets}. Assume further that $\omega \in C^\infty_c \cap \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, W}$ and that $\psi := (\operatorname{Id} + h_L) \circ \cdots \circ (\operatorname{Id} + h_1)$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism with
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixresnetrepresentationupperboundtailcondition}
       \psi(u) = \begin{cases}
            -a_- (-u)^p + b_- & u \leq -R \\
            a_+ u^p + b_+ & u \geq R
        \end{cases}
    \end{equation}
    for some $a_\pm \in (0, \infty)$, $b_\pm \in {\mathbb{R}}$, $R > 2\|\omega\|_\infty$, and $p > 2$. Then, $s_\tau^\theta \in \mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^s}$ for all $\tau \geq 0$ and $s \in {\mathbb{N}}$ with the uniform bound
    \begin{equation}
        \sup_{\tau \in [0, T]}\|s_\tau^\theta\|_{\mathcal{B}_{\operatorname{ReLU}^s}} < \infty \quad (\forall T \in (0, \infty)).
    \end{equation}
    The same statements hold with $s_\tau^\theta$ replaced by $b_\tau^\theta$.
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
We know that $\psi_\theta = \psi$. By the assumed tail behavior, we know that $\psi_\theta$ satisfies the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationupperbound}. It remains to verify the assumptions on $\Psi_\theta$. We first show that if $f(z) = F(P_Ez)$ is a cylindrical function with $F \in C^\infty_c(E)$ and $S(z) := z + bg(\left\langle a, z\right\rangle)$ is a single-index field (with $a, b \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$) then $f \circ S$ is a sum of two cylindrical functions which are $C^\infty_c$ on their active subspaces. Indeed, with $V := E + \operatorname{span}\{a\}$ we define for $x \in V$ the function
\begin{equation}
    H(x) := F(P_Ex + P_E b g(\left\langle a, x\right\rangle)) - F(P_Ex)
\end{equation}
and so $f(S(z)) = F(P_Ez) + H(P_Vz)$. Clearly, $H$ is smooth, and since $\|x\| \lesssim_{E, a} \|P_Ex\| + |\left\langle a, x\right\rangle|$ we find that $H \in C^\infty_c(V)$. 
By linearity, if $f$ is a finite sum of cylindrical functions, each of which is $C^\infty_c$ on its active subspace, then the same is true for $f \circ S$.

Now, in the present construction we have $g, \chi \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$ and $\Psi_\theta = f_0 \circ S_L \circ \cdots \circ S_1$ with $f_0(z) = \omega(\left\langle v, z\right\rangle)$. Since shears preserve the finite structure of being a sum of smooth cylindrical functions, $\Psi_\theta$ satisfies the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationupperbound}.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{prop:appendixrepresentaitonupperlowerbounds}
Let  $\phi(t) = \max\{0, t\}^3$ be the $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ activation, and define $\varphi = \phi * \eta$ using some nonnegative even $\eta \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$ with $\int_{\mathbb{R}} \eta = 1$ which is supported in $[-\delta, \delta]$ for some $\delta \in (0, 1/4)$. 

Then, for each $d \geq 4$ there exists a $\operatorname{TResNet}_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ of depth $2d-3$ and width $16$ with two-layer blocks using activation $\varphi$ s.t. 
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi^\theta) \gtrsim 2^d, \quad D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi^\theta) \lesssim d, \quad \text{and } s_\tau^\theta, b_\tau^\theta \in \mathcal{B}_\phi \quad (\forall \tau \geq 0),
\end{equation}
where the implied constants depend only on $\eta$.
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
By mollification, if we denote $m_2 := \int_{\mathbb{R}} r^2 \eta(r) dr \leq \delta^2$ then $\varphi(t) = 0$ for all $t \leq -\delta$, while for $t \geq \delta$ we have
\begin{align}
    \varphi(t) &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} (t-r)^3 \eta(r) dr \\&= t^3 \int_{\mathbb{R}} \eta(r) dr - 3t^2 \int_r r \eta(r) dr + 3t \int_{\mathbb{R}} r^2\eta(r) dr - \int_{\mathbb{R}} r^3 \eta(r) dr \\
    &= t^3 + 3tm_2
\end{align}
since $\eta$ is even. 
We define the scalar function $\omega \in \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, 10}$ using 10 neurons in the following way:
    \begin{equation}
        \omega(t) := B\left(t - \frac{1}{2}\right) - B\left(t + \frac{1}{2}\right), \quad B(t) := \frac{1}{6}\sum_{j=0}^4 (-1)^j {4 \choose j} \varphi(t + 2 - j).
    \end{equation}
    Note that $\omega \in C_c^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$ (since $B(\cdot)$ is a mollification of the discrete fourth derivative of $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$, which is compactly supported), and in particular $\|\omega\|_\infty < \infty$. Furthermore, since the unsmoothed discrete derivative equals $\frac{5}{4}t - t^3$ near zero, convolution with the even mollifier implies that 
    \begin{equation}
        \omega(t) = \left(\frac{5}{4} - 3m_2\right)t - t^3 \quad \left(\forall |t| < \frac{1}{2}- \delta\right). 
    \end{equation}
Thus, $\omega(0) = 0$, $\omega'(0) = \frac{5}{4} - 3m_2 > 0$, $\omega''(0) = 0$, and $\omega'''(0) = -6 \neq 0$, i.e. $\omega$ satisfies (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationconditionsonomega}). 

 Now, take $R := 2\|\omega\|_\infty + 1> 2\|\omega\|_\infty + \delta$ and set
 \begin{equation}
     \sigma := \sqrt{\frac{23}{3}R^2 - 4m_2}, \quad r = \frac{R+\sigma}{2}.
 \end{equation}
 Define the scalar function $h \in \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, 6}$ using 6 neurons in the following way:
 \begin{equation}
 \label{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofh1forconcreterepresentationresnet}
     h(u) := \frac{G(u) - G(-u)}{3R\sigma}, \quad G(u) := 2\varphi(u-r) - 3\varphi(u-r-R) + \varphi(u-r-2R).
 \end{equation}
 Since $\sigma > R$ we have $r > R$, which means for every $|u| \leq 2 \|\omega\|_\infty$ we know $G(u) = 0$ and so $h(u) = 0$. Also, since $G'$ is the mollification of \begin{equation}3(2\max\{0, u-r\})^2 - 3\max\{0, u-r-R\}^2 + \max\{0, u-r-2R\}^2),\end{equation} 
 which is everywhere nonnegative, we know $G' \geq 0$. For $u \geq r + 2R + \delta$ we know $G(-u) = 0$ and we may expand the cubic tails to find that if $v = u-r$ then
 \begin{align}
     G(u) &= 2v^3 + 6vm_2 - 3(v-R)^3 - 9(v-R)m_2 + (v-2R)^3 + 3(v-2R)m_2 \\
     &= 2v^3 - 3(v-R)^3 + (v-2R)^3 + 3m_2 (2v - 3(v-R) + (v-2R)) \\
     &= 3Rv^2 + 3R^2v - 5R^3 + 3m_2 R\\
     &= 3R\left((u-r)^2 + R(u-r) - \frac{5}{3}R^2 + m_2\right)
     \\&= 3R(u^2 - \sigma u),
 \end{align}
 where we used that $2r-R = \sigma$ and $r^2 -Rr = \frac{5}{3}R^2 - m_2$. By oddness, this implies
 \begin{equation}
    u + h(u) = \frac{u|u|}{\sigma}  \quad (\forall |u| \geq r+2R + \delta).
 \end{equation}


    We take $n = d-1$, $L = d-2$, and choose ResNet parameters $\theta = (g, \chi, (h_\ell, a_\ell, b_\ell)_{\ell = 1}^L, v)$ according to the following:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] We take $g = \Lambda_\omega \omega$ and $\chi = \omega$, where $\Lambda_\omega$ is defined in Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationlowerboundresnets}. Note that $\omega \in C^\infty_c({\mathbb{R}})$ satisfies (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationconditionsonomega}) and can be made with 10 neurons with activation $\varphi$, i.e. $\omega \in \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, 10}$.
        \item[(ii)] For each $\ell \in \{3, \ldots, L\}$ we take $h_\ell = 0$, and we take $h_1 = h_2 = h$ as defined in (\ref{eqn:proofappendixdefinitionofh1forconcreterepresentationresnet}); this can be made with 6 neurons with activation $\varphi$, i.e. $h_1,h_2 \in \mathcal{N}_{\varphi, 6}$. Note that $(\operatorname{Id} + h_2)\circ (\operatorname{Id} + h_1)$ is an increasing $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism which satisfies the tail condition (\ref{eqn:proofappendixresnetrepresentationupperboundtailcondition}) with $p=4$.
        \item[(iii)] For each $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}$ we take $a_\ell = e_\ell$ and $b_\ell = e_{\ell +1}$, along with $v = e_{L+1}$.
    \end{enumerate}
    The resulting map $\operatorname{TResNet}_\theta: {\mathbb{R}}^d \to {\mathbb{R}}^d$ is a ResNet of depth $2L+1 = 2d-3$ which uses two-layer blocks with activation $\varphi$: the first two have width 16, and all subsequent ones have width 10. The assumptions of Lemmas \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationlowerboundresnets} and \ref{lemma:appendixrepresentationupperboundresnets} are both satisfied, and so $\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\pi^\theta) \geq B_\omega^2 2^L = \frac{B_\omega^2}{4}2^d \gtrsim 2^d$ while $s_\tau^\theta, b_\tau^\theta \in \mathcal{B}_\phi$ for all $\tau \geq 0$ (uniformly on compact OU time intervals). 

    We finish by constructing a Barron flow transporting $\gamma_d$ to $\pi^\theta$ which realizes $D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_d, \pi^\theta) \lesssim d$. Since the ResNet layers in the $z$ coordinate which compute $\Psi^\theta$ are orthogonal shears (as is the readout layer), we can represent them by an ODE with drifts given by the layers themselves at cost $\lesssim d$; this flow computes $\Psi^\theta$, writes the readout, and uncomputes $\Psi^\theta$. Since we can prepend a Barron flow on the $u$ coordinate before this, the claim follows if we can show that
    \begin{equation}
        D_{\mathcal{B}_\phi}(\gamma_1, \psi_\# \gamma_1) < \infty, \quad \psi := (\operatorname{Id} + h) \circ (\operatorname{Id} + h).
    \end{equation}
    It suffices to exhibit a finite-cost flow implementing $F = \operatorname{Id} + h$, which we will run twice. To start, note that the ODE 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperlowerboundsflowdefiningC}
        \dot{u} = -\frac{1}{2}u^3
    \end{equation}
    has a time-1 map $C: {\mathbb{R}} \to (-1, 1)$ given by the smooth increasing diffeomorphism
    \begin{equation}
        C(u) = \frac{u}{\sqrt{1+u^2}}.
    \end{equation}
    If we choose a smooth cutoff $0 \leq \zeta \leq 1$ which vanishes on $(-\infty, 1/4]$ and equals 1 on $[1/2, \infty)$ and define the velocity
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperlowerboundsflowdefiningE}
        v(u) := u^2 (\zeta(u) - \zeta(-u)),
    \end{equation}
    then the ODE $\dot{u} = v(u)$ has a time-1 map $E: (-1, 1) \to {\mathbb{R}}$ which is an odd increasing diffeomorphism with
    \begin{equation}
        E(u) = \frac{u}{1-u} \quad (\forall u \in [1/2, 1)).
    \end{equation}
    Indeed, on this region the ODE is $\dot{u} = u^2$ which is well-posed (since the blowup time is $1/u > 1$), and for other $u \in [0, 1/2)$ comparison with $\dot{u} = u^2$ ensures existence through time 1. By oddness, the same is true for negative initial conditions. Now, we define the smooth increasing diffeomorphism $K := E^{-1} \circ F \circ C^{-1}: (-1, 1) \to (-1, 1)$. For $u$ sufficiently close to 1, the quadratic tails of $F$ give
    \begin{equation}
        F(C^{-1}(u)) = \frac{u^2}{\sigma(1-u^2)}, \quad K(u) = \frac{u^2}{\sigma + (1-\sigma)u^2}. 
    \end{equation}
    Hence, $K$ extends smoothly to 1 with $K(1) = 1$ and $K'(1) = 2\sigma > 0$. By oddness, the same holds at $-1$. Thus, $K(\pm 1) = \pm 1$ and $\min_{[-1, 1]}K' > 0$. Defining the linear interpolation
    \begin{equation}
        K_t(u) := (1-t)u + tK(u), \quad w_t(u) := (K - \operatorname{Id})(K_t^{-1}(u)),
    \end{equation}
    we find that $\partial_t K_t(u) = w_t(K_t(u))$ and that $w_t(u)$ is jointly smooth in $(t, u)$ with fixed compact support. In particular, using the $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ representation
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperlowerboundsflowdefiningstuff}
        f(u) = \frac{1}{6}\int_{\mathbb{R}} \phi(u-a) f^{(4)}(a) da
    \end{equation}
    for $f$ which vanish on some $(-\infty, u_0]$ with compactly supported fourth derivative, we may extend $w_t$ to all of ${\mathbb{R}}$ in a way that
    \begin{equation}
        \sup_{t \in [0, 1]}\|w_t\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \leq \frac{1}{6}\sup_{t \in [0, 1]} \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1+|u|)^3 |\partial_u^4 w_t(u)|du < \infty.
    \end{equation}
    The flow (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperlowerboundsflowdefiningC}) defining $C$ has the $\operatorname{ReLU}^3$ representation $\frac{\phi(-u) - \phi(u)}{2}$. Lastly, the flow (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperlowerboundsflowdefiningE}) defining $E$ has $v(u) = q(u) - q(-u)$ with $q(u) := u^2 \zeta(u)$. Therefore, $q(u) =  0$ for $u \leq 1/4$ and $q(u) = u^2$ for $u \geq 1/2$, which means $q^{(4)}$ is smooth and supported on $[1/4, 1/2]$. Using the representation (\ref{eqn:proofappendixrepresentationupperlowerboundsflowdefiningstuff}), this implies that $q$ has finite Barron norm which means $v$ does too. Since $F = E \circ K \circ C$, the result follows by concatenating these Barron flows.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixhermitebranchinglemma}
    Let $g: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be Lipschitz, centered (i.e. $\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1} [g(G)] = 0$), and non-affine in $L^2(\gamma_1)$ (i.e. $\|g\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)} > |\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1} [Gg(G)]|$). Let $\chi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be bounded and Lipschitz. Fix $L \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and an orthonormal basis $\{e_0, \ldots, e_L\}$ of ${\mathbb{R}}^{L+1}$, and define $F_L: {\mathbb{R}}^{L+1} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationresnetthreelayernetworksofthetype}
        F_L(z) := \chi\left(z_0 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}} \sum_{\ell = 1}^L g(z_\ell)\right).
    \end{equation}
    For positive integers $K_1 \leq K_2$ we define the quantity
   \begin{equation}
    \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K_1, K_2) := \sum_{j=K_1}^{K_2} \frac{1}{j!}\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1} \left[\chi(\sqrt{\lambda_g}G) \operatorname{He}_j(G)\right]^2, \quad \lambda_g := {1 + \|g\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)}^2}.
   \end{equation}
   Then, there are some $b_g, c_g \in (0, \infty)$ and $K_g \in {\mathbb{N}}$ (depending only on $g$) s.t. for any $K_g \leq K_1 \leq K_2$ there is some $L_0 = L_0(g, \chi, K_1, K_2)$ s.t.
   \begin{equation}
       a_{F_L}(m, \tau) \geq \frac{1}{2}e^{-b_g K_2\tau} \sqrt{\mathcal{V}_{\chi, g} (K_1, K_2)}
   \end{equation}
   for every $L \geq L_0$, every $\tau \geq 0$, and every integer $0 \leq m \leq L^{c_g K_1}$.
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{corollary:approximationlowerbound}
    Let $g, \chi: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ satisfy the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermitebranchinglemma}. 
   Suppose further that there are constants $c, K_0 \in (1, \infty)$ and a function $V: {\mathbb{N}} \to (0, \infty)$ for which
   \begin{equation}
       \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K, \lfloor cK\rfloor) \geq V(K) \quad (\forall K \geq K_0).
   \end{equation}
    For every $\varepsilon > 0$, we denote the quantity
    \begin{equation}
        K(\varepsilon) := \max\left\{K \geq K_0:\; V(K) \geq C_{\chi, g} \varepsilon^2\right\},
    \end{equation}
    where $C_{\chi, g} := 64 Q_{\|\chi\|_\infty, 1}^2 \left(1 + \operatorname{Lip}(\chi)^2 (1 + \operatorname{Lip}(g)^2)\right)^2$ and our convention here is that $\max \emptyset = 0$.
   
   Then, there are constants $\varepsilon_0, c_1, c_2 \in (0, \infty)$ depending only on $g, \chi,V,c,K_0$ s.t. the following holds: for each $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_0]$ there is some $L_0 = L_0(g, \chi, \varepsilon)$ s.t. for every $L \geq L_0$, every $\tau \in [0, c_1 \min\{\varepsilon, 1/K(\varepsilon)\}]$, and every two-layer neural network $\hat{s}_\tau: {\mathbb{R}}^{L+2} \to {\mathbb{R}}^{L+2}$ of width $m$ with
   \begin{equation}\|s_{\tau}^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L} - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2\left(\rho_\tau^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}; {\mathbb{R}}^{L+2}\right)} \leq \varepsilon\end{equation}  we must have \begin{equation}
       m \geq L^{c_2 K(\varepsilon)} \quad \text{and} \quad \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \geq D_{\phi, \chi} \varepsilon L^{c_2 K(\varepsilon)/2} \quad \forall \phi \text{ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton}},
   \end{equation} 
   where $D_{\phi, \chi}>0$ is a constant depending only on $\phi$ and $\chi$.
   
   The same statements hold with $s_\tau^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}$ replaced by $b_\tau^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}$. Moreover, if we set $n=L+1$ and $\theta = (g, \chi, (h_\ell, a_\ell, b_\ell)_{\ell = 1}^L, v)$ is s.t.
   \begin{equation}
   \label{eqn:proofappendixcorollarylowerboundconstraintsontheta}
       \{a_1, \ldots, a_L, v\} \subseteq {\mathbb{R}}^n \text{ is orthonormal}, \quad b_\ell = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}v, \quad h_\ell = 0 \quad (\forall \ell \in \{1, \ldots, L\}),
   \end{equation}
  then the same statements hold with $s_\tau^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}$ replaced by either of $s_\tau^\theta$, $b_\tau^\theta$ and $\rho_\tau^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}$ replaced by $\rho_\tau^\theta$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
Since $\Psi_\theta = F_L$ and $\psi_\theta = \operatorname{Id}$ under (\ref{eqn:proofappendixcorollarylowerboundconstraintsontheta}), it suffices to prove the claim for $F_L$.
    Denote $Q := Q_{\|\chi\|_\infty, 1}$ for $Q_{\beta, \sigma}$ from Proposition \ref{prop:appendixdaapproximationlowerbound} along with $\Lambda := \operatorname{Lip}(\chi) \sqrt{1 + \operatorname{Lip}(g)^2}$. Then, for every $L$ by the chain rule we have 
    \begin{equation}
        \|F_L\|_\infty \leq \|\chi\|_\infty, \quad \operatorname{Lip}(F_L) \leq \Lambda. 
    \end{equation}
    Choose $\varepsilon_0$ sufficiently small that $K(\varepsilon) \geq \max\{K_g, \lceil K_0\rceil\}$ for all $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_0]$, which is possible since $V$ is strictly positive. For any $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_0]$ by definition of $K(\varepsilon)$ we have
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K(\varepsilon), \lfloor cK(\varepsilon)\rfloor) \geq V(K(\varepsilon)) \geq C_{\chi, g} \varepsilon^2 = 64 Q^2 (1+\Lambda^2)^2 \varepsilon^2.
    \end{equation}
    Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermitebranchinglemma} with $K_1 = K(\varepsilon)$ and $K_2 = \lfloor cK(\varepsilon)\rfloor$, we obtain some $L_0 = L_0(g, \chi, \varepsilon)$ s.t. for all $L \geq L_0$ and all integers $0 \leq r \leq L^{c_g K(\varepsilon)}$ we have
    \begin{equation}
        a_{F_L}(r, \tau) \geq \frac{1}{2}e^{-b_g cK(\varepsilon) \tau}\sqrt{\mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K(\varepsilon), \lfloor cK(\varepsilon)\rfloor)} \geq 4Q(1+\Lambda^2) e^{-b_g cK(\varepsilon)\tau}\varepsilon.
    \end{equation}
    Choosing $c_1 \leq \min\{1, \log(2)/(b_g c)\}$, if $\tau \in [0, c_1 \min\{\varepsilon, 1/K(\varepsilon)\}]$ then $e^{-b_gcK(\varepsilon)\tau} \geq 1/2$ and $\tau \leq \varepsilon$. This means that
    \begin{equation}
        a_{F_L}(r, \tau) \geq 2Q(1+\Lambda^2) \varepsilon.
    \end{equation}
    Since $Q(2\varepsilon + \Lambda^2 \tau) \leq 2Q(1+\Lambda^2)\varepsilon$, it follows from the definition of the Hermite width envelope (see Definition \ref{def:appendixhermitewidthenvelope}) that
    \begin{equation}
        m_{F_L}\left(Q(\varepsilon + \Lambda^2 \tau), \; \tau\right), m_{F_L}\left(2Q(\varepsilon + \Lambda^2 \tau), \; \tau\right) \geq  \lfloor L^{c_g K(\varepsilon)}\rfloor.
    \end{equation}
    Applying Proposition \ref{prop:appendixdaapproximationlowerbound} with $\psi = \operatorname{Id}$, $\Psi = F_L$, and $n = L+1$, we find that the width lower bound holds with $c_2 = c_g$ and that for any $\phi$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption:activationfunciton} we have
    \begin{equation}
        \|\hat{s}_\tau\|_{\mathcal{B}_\phi} \geq K_{\phi, \|\chi\|_\infty, 1} \varepsilon \sqrt{ \lfloor L^{c_g K(\varepsilon)}\rfloor} 
    \end{equation}
    with the same holding for $b_\tau^{\psi, \Psi}$.
    Increasing $L_0$ if needed, we may take $\lfloor L^{c_g K(\varepsilon)}\rfloor \geq L^{c_g K(\varepsilon)}/2$, in which case the Barron norm claim holds with $D_{\phi, \chi} =  K_{\phi, \|\chi\|_\infty, 1} / \sqrt{2}$.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixhermitedecayforapproximation}
Let $g: {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be centered with $\lambda_g := 1 + \|g\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)}^2 < \infty$. Then, there is some $K_0 \in (0, \infty)$ depending only on $\lambda_g$ s.t. $\mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K, 2K) \geq V(K)$ for all $K \geq K_0$, where we define $V: {\mathbb{N}} \to (0, \infty)$ as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] If $\chi(t) = \frac{\max\{0, t\} - \max\{0, t-a\}}{a}$ for some fixed $a \in (0, \infty)$ then we take $V(K) = bK^{-3/2}$ for some $b \in (0, \infty)$ depending on $\lambda_g, a$.
    \item[(ii)] If $\chi(t) = \tanh(t)$ then we take $V(K) = be^{-\pi \sqrt{K / \lambda_g}}$ for some $b \in (0, \infty)$ depending on $\lambda_g$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
In particular, for (i) we get $K(\varepsilon) \asymp \varepsilon^{-4/3}$ while for (ii) we have $K(\varepsilon) \asymp \log(1/\varepsilon)^2$.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- proof-53: body_md -->
Fix $\lambda > 0$ (which we take as $\lambda = \lambda_g$), and let us denote $\alpha_j := \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}[\chi(\sqrt{\lambda }G) \operatorname{He}_j(G)] / \sqrt{j!}$. 

For the ReLU difference, we simply apply \cite[Lemma A.3]{fu2023singleattention} to see that 
\begin{equation}
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{j!}}\mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1} \left[\max\{0, G-w\} \operatorname{He}_j(G)\right] = \frac{e^{-w^2/2} \operatorname{He}_{j-2}(w)}{\sqrt{2\pi j!}} \quad (\forall j \geq 2)
\end{equation}
for any $w \in {\mathbb{R}}$. By homogeneity and linearity, for every $j \geq 2$ 
this gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixReLUdifferencehermitescaling}
    \alpha_j = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda} }{a\sqrt{2\pi j!}} \left[\operatorname{He}_{j-2}(0) - e^{-a^2/(2\lambda)} \operatorname{He}_{j-2}\left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\right)\right].
\end{equation}
If we denote $u(t) := e^{-t^2/4} \frac{\operatorname{He}_n(t)}{\operatorname{He}_n(0)}$ for an even $n \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$, then the Hermite equation $\operatorname{He}_n'' - t \operatorname{He}_n' + n \operatorname{He}_n = 0$ implies that
\begin{equation}
    u''(t) + \left(n + \frac{1}{2}-\frac{t^2}{4}\right)u(t) = 0, \quad u(0) = 1, \quad u'(0) = 0.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for all $t \geq 0$ we have
\begin{align}
    \frac{d}{dt} \left[u'(t)^2 + \left(n + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{t^2}{4} \right)u(t)^2\right] &= 2 u'(t) \left(u''(t) + \left(n + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{t^2}{4}\right) u(t)\right)- \frac{t}{2}u(t)^2 \\&= -\frac{t}{2}u(t)^2 \leq 0.
\end{align}
Hence,
\begin{equation}
   \left(n + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{t^2}{4}\right)u(t)^2  \leq  u'(t)^2 + \left(n + \frac{1}{2} - \frac{t^2}{4}\right)u(t)^2 \leq n + \frac{1}{2}
\end{equation}
and so whenever $n + 1/2> t^2/4$ we have 
\begin{equation}
    \left|\frac{e^{-t^2/2} \operatorname{He}_{n}(t)}{\operatorname{He}_{n}(0)}\right| \leq e^{-t^2/4} \sqrt{\frac{n+\frac{1}{2}}{n+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{t^2}{4}}}.
\end{equation}
Therefore, as $n = j-2\to \infty$ we find that
\begin{equation}
    \limsup_{\substack{j \to \infty\\ j \text{ even}}} \left|\frac{e^{-a^2/(2\lambda)} \operatorname{He}_{j-2}(a/\sqrt{\lambda})}{\operatorname{He}_{j-2}(0)}\right| \leq e^{-a^2/(4\lambda)} < 1.
\end{equation}
In particular, as $j \to \infty$ with $j = 2r + 2$ even we have the asymptotic
\begin{equation}
    \alpha_j^2 \asymp_{\lambda, a} \frac{\operatorname{He}_{j-2}(0)^2}{j!} = \frac{{2r \choose r}}{4^r (2r + 1) (2r+2)} \asymp \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi r} (2r+1)(2r+2)} \asymp j^{-5/2},
\end{equation}
where we used that ${2r \choose r} / 4^r \asymp 1/\sqrt{\pi r}$ as $r \to \infty$. Hence, $\alpha_j^2 \asymp j^{-5/2}$ for $j$ large and even. Summing over a band gives
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K, 2K) \gtrsim_{\lambda, a} \sum_{\substack{K \leq j \leq 2K \\ j \text{ even}}} j^{-5/2} \asymp K^{-3/2}.
\end{equation}
Note that by (\ref{eqn:proofappendixReLUdifferencehermitescaling}) we know that $|\alpha_j| > 0$ for all $j \geq 2$ even, and so by decreasing $b$ our result holds even up to $K_0 =2$.

    For $\tanh$, we replicate the argument of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtanhhermitescaling}. Note that $\alpha_j = 0$ for even $j$. By the same Fourier transform formula as in Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtanhhermitescaling} we have
    \begin{equation}
        \widehat{(\tanh(\sqrt{\lambda} \cdot))'}(\xi) = \frac{\pi \xi / \sqrt{\lambda}}{\sinh(\pi \xi / (2 \sqrt{\lambda}))},
    \end{equation}
    and so the same integration by parts and Parseval argument implies that for odd $j$
    \begin{equation}
        \alpha_j = \frac{(-1)^{(j-1)/2}}{\sqrt{\lambda j!}} \int_0^\infty \frac{\xi^j e^{-\xi^2/2}}{\sinh(\pi \xi / (2\sqrt{\lambda}))}d\xi.
    \end{equation}
    We again set $F(\xi) := j \log \xi - \frac{\xi^2}{2} - \frac{\pi \xi}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}$. Splitting at $\xi = 1$, we find that as odd $j \to \infty$ there is the asymptotic
    \begin{equation}
        \log |\alpha_j| = -\frac{1}{2}\log(\lambda j!) + \log \int_1^\infty e^{F(\xi)}d\xi + O_\lambda(1).
    \end{equation}
    The same Taylor estimates as in Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtanhhermitescaling} (with $2q$ replaced by $j$) apply because $F'(\sqrt{j}) = -\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}$ and $F''(\xi) = -\frac{j}{\xi^2} - 1 \leq -1$ for all $\xi$. In particular, \begin{equation}
        \log\left(\int_1^\infty e^{F(\xi)}d\xi\right) = F(\sqrt{j}) + O_\lambda(1)
    \end{equation}
    and consequently
    \begin{equation}
        \log |\alpha_j| = \frac{j}{2}\log j - \frac{j}{2} - \frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}\sqrt{j} - \frac{1}{2}\log(\lambda j!) + O_\lambda(1).
    \end{equation}
    Applying Stirling, we get
    \begin{equation}
        \log |\alpha_j| = -\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt{\lambda}}\sqrt{j} - \frac{1}{4}\log j + O_\lambda(1)
    \end{equation}
    or in other words that
    \begin{equation}
        \alpha_j^2 \asymp_\lambda j^{-1/2} e^{-\pi \sqrt{j/\lambda}} \quad (j\to \infty  \text{ odd}).
    \end{equation}
    We sum over the band to find that
    \begin{equation}
        \mathcal{V}_{\tanh, g}(K, 2K) \asymp_\lambda \sum_{\substack{K \leq j \leq 2K \\ j \text{ odd}}} j^{-1/2} e^{-\pi \sqrt{j/\lambda}} \asymp_\lambda e^{-\pi \sqrt{K/\lambda}},
    \end{equation}
    where the last asymptotic is due to the integral equality
    \begin{equation}
        \int_K^{2K} x^{-1/2}e^{-\pi \sqrt{x/\lambda}}dx = \frac{2\sqrt{\lambda}}{\pi} \left(e^{-\pi \sqrt{K/\lambda}} - e^{-\pi \sqrt{2K/\lambda}}\right).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proof-53 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
Note that for any $\varepsilon, \tau > 0$ and any $\theta$ there is an approximate score network $\hat{s}_\tau$ s.t. $\|s_\tau^\theta - \hat{s}_\tau\|_{L^2(\rho_\tau^\theta; {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1})} \leq \varepsilon$, see Proposition \ref{prop:appendixapproximationupperbound}. The lower bounds in this subsection say that any such approximate score network must have large width and Barron norm.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{lemma:appendixearlystoppingforresnets}
    Assume the setting of Corollary \ref{corollary:approximationlowerbound}. Then, for every $a \in (0, \infty)$ there exist constants $\varepsilon_0, b_1, b_2 \in (0, \infty)$ s.t. for every $\varepsilon \in (0, \varepsilon_0]$ there is an $L_0(\varepsilon)$ for which the following holds:

    For every $L \geq L_0(\varepsilon)$ and every $\tau_0 \geq a \min\{\varepsilon, 1/K(\varepsilon)\}$, if we denote $\pi = \pi^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}$ and $\rho_{\tau_0} = \rho_{\tau_0}^{\operatorname{Id}, F_L}$ then we have the lower bounds
    \begin{align}
        \min\left\{\operatorname{TV}(\pi, \rho_{\tau_0}), \; W_1(\pi, \rho_{\tau_0})\right\} &\geq b_1  \min\{\varepsilon, 1/K(\varepsilon)\},\\
        \min\left\{\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}(\pi \|\rho_{\tau_0})}, \; \sqrt{\operatorname{KL}( \rho_{\tau_0} \| \pi)}\right\} &\geq b_2 \varepsilon.
    \end{align}
    The constants depend only on $a, g, \chi, c, K_0, V$.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
In light of Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermitedecayforapproximation}, if $\chi$ is the difference of two ReLUs then $\operatorname{TV}, W_1 \gtrsim \varepsilon^{4/3}$ while if $\chi = \tanh$ then $\operatorname{TV}, W_1 \gtrsim \varepsilon$. In both cases, $\sqrt{\operatorname{KL}} \gtrsim \varepsilon$.
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- proof-54: body_md -->
Choose $\varepsilon_0 \leq 1$ sufficiently small that $K(\varepsilon) \geq K_g$. Applying Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixhermitebranchinglemma} at time 0, both to the band $[K(\varepsilon), \lfloor cK(\varepsilon)\rfloor]$ and to one fixed admissible band with positive mass, gives
    \begin{equation}
        a_{F_L}(\lfloor L^{c_gK(\varepsilon)}\rfloor, 0) \gtrsim \varepsilon, \quad a_{F_L}(0, 0) = \|F_L\|_{L^2(\gamma_{L+1})} \gtrsim 1
    \end{equation}
    for $L \geq L_0(\varepsilon)$. Here and below, the implied constants are independent of $\varepsilon, L, \tau_0$. Since $\|F_L\|_\infty \leq \|\chi\|_\infty$, we have
    \begin{equation}
        M_{F_L} \geq e^{-\|\chi\|^2_\infty / 4}\|F_L\|_{L^2(\gamma_{L+1})}^2 \gtrsim 1,
    \end{equation}
    and for $L \geq 2$ we know
    \begin{equation}
        \ell_{L+1}(\lfloor L^{c_gK(\varepsilon)}\rfloor) \geq 2c_g K(\varepsilon) \frac{\log L}{\log(L+1)} \geq c_g K(\varepsilon).
    \end{equation}
    Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtriangularearlystoppingerrorTVW1} therefore implies that
    \begin{align}
        \min\{\operatorname{TV}(\pi, \rho_{\tau_0}), W_1(\pi, \rho_{\tau_0})\} &\gtrsim 1-e^{-2\tau_0} \\&\geq 1-e^{-2 a \min\{\varepsilon, 1/K(\varepsilon)\}} \\&\geq (1-e^{-2a}) \min\{\varepsilon, 1/K(\varepsilon)\}.
    \end{align}
    Similarly, Lemma \ref{lemma:appendixtriangularearlystoppingerrorKL} implies that with $D_{\tau_0}$ as the KL in either direction,
    \begin{align}
        \sqrt{D_{\tau_0}} &\gtrsim \max\left\{1-e^{-\tau_0},\; \varepsilon\left(1-e^{-c_g K(\varepsilon) \tau_0}\right)\right\}.
    \end{align}
    If $\varepsilon \leq 1/K(\varepsilon)$ then $1-e^{-\tau_0} \geq 1-e^{-a\varepsilon} \geq (1-e^{-a})\varepsilon$, while if $\varepsilon > 1/K(\varepsilon)$ then we have that $1-e^{-c_g K(\varepsilon) \tau_0} \geq 1-e^{-c_ga}$. In either case, $\sqrt{D_{\tau_0}} \gtrsim \varepsilon$.
<!-- end proof-54 -->
<!-- proof-55: body_md -->
Let us denote $V_g := \|g\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)}^2$ and $\beta_j := \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}[g(G) h_j(G)]$ for $j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$, where $h_j := \operatorname{He}_j / \sqrt{j!}$ are the $L^2(\gamma_1)$-orthonormal Hermite polynomials. Because $g$ is centered we know $\beta_0 = 0$ and therefore $V_g = \sum_{j \in {\mathbb{N}}} \beta_j^2$. Moreover, since $\beta_1 = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}[Gg(G)]$ then
\begin{equation}
    0 < \mathfrak{v}_g := \frac{\sum_{j \geq 2} \beta_j^2}{8\lambda_g} \leq \frac{1}{8}, \quad \lambda_g := 1+V_g,
\end{equation}
since $g$ is non-affine in $L^2(\gamma_1)$. The heart of this proof is to show that for all $ \lceil 4/\mathfrak{v}_g\rceil \leq K_1 \leq K_2$, we have the estimate 
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixthehermitebranchinglemmamainestimate}
    \liminf_{L \to \infty} \sum_{k=K_1}^{\lceil B_g K_2\rceil} \;\sum_{j > L^{\lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2 \geq \frac{13}{48} \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K_1, K_2)
\end{equation}
where $M_k(F_L)$ are the balanced matricizations of the Hermite tensor coefficients of $F_L$ (see Definition \ref{def:appendixhermitewidthenvelope}) and we denote
\begin{equation}
    B_g := \frac{8 (1 + \operatorname{Lip}(g))^2}{\lambda_g}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, from (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthehermitebranchinglemmamainestimate}) we find an $L_0=L_0(g, \chi, K_1, K_2)$ s.t. 
\begin{equation}
    \sum_{k=K_1}^{\lceil B_g K_2\rceil} \;\sum_{j > L^{\lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2 \geq \frac{1}{4} \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K_1, K_2) \quad (\forall L \geq L_0).
\end{equation}
Moreover, $K_1 \geq \lceil 4/\mathfrak{v}_g\rceil$ implies $\lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor - 1 \geq  \mathfrak{v}_g  K_1 - 2 \geq c_g K_1$ with $c_g :=  \mathfrak{v}_g /2$, and so for every $m \leq L^{c_g K_1}$ and $\tau \geq 0$ we find
\begin{equation}
    a_{F_L}(m, \tau)^2 \geq \frac{1}{4}e^{-2(\lceil B_g K_2\rceil + 1)\tau} \mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K_1, K_2).
\end{equation}
Taking $b_g := B_g + 1$ yields the claim.
The proof of (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthehermitebranchinglemmamainestimate}) proceeds in the following high-level steps:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item For each $k \in {\mathbb{N}}$, we fix a balanced cut $S_k \subseteq \{1, \ldots, k\}$ with $|S_k| = \lfloor k / 2\rfloor$ to define the matricization $M_k(F_L)$. 
    We show that our Hermite spectral tail of interest is controlled by the elements of the Hermite tensor coefficients whose indices cross the cut. More precisely, for any integer $R > 1$ we show that
     \begin{equation}
        \liminf_{L \to \infty} \sum_{j > L^{R-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2 \geq \liminf_{L \to \infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 \quad (\forall k \in {\mathbb{N}}),
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathcal{I}_k \subseteq \{0, \ldots, k\}^k$ is a certain collection of $k$-tuples, $C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p})$ denotes the number of distinct positive entries of $\mathbf{p}$ appearing on both sides of the cut $S_k$, and $d_{\mathbf{p}, L}$ is proportional to the Hermite coefficient tensor entry $T_k(F_L)[\mathbf{p}]$. 

    \item By tensor symmetry, the fraction of entries satisfying the crossing condition can be computed using a uniformly random balanced cut. Using this, we show that
    \begin{equation}
        \lim_{L \to \infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 = \sum_{J =1}^k \alpha_J^2 \cdot \mathbb{P}_J(N=k, \; C_S \geq R) \quad (\forall k \in {\mathbb{N}})
    \end{equation}
    with the notation
    \begin{equation}
         \alpha_J := \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}\left[\chi(\sqrt{\lambda_g}G)h_J(G)\right].
    \end{equation}
    Here, $\mathbb{P}_J$ is an auxiliary probability law describing the Hermite degrees and uniformly random balanced cut, and under $\mathbb{P}_J$ we denote by $N$ the total degree and by $C_S$ the crossing count for a uniformly random balanced cut $S$. Note that $\mathcal{V}_{\chi, g}(K_1, K_2)  = \sum_{J=K_1}^{K_2}\alpha_J^2$.
    
    \item  By simple probabilistic estimates and plugging in our quantities, we show that \begin{equation}\mathbb{P}_J(N \leq  B_g K_2 , \;C_S\geq  \mathfrak{v}_g K_1)\geq\frac{13}{48} \quad (\forall K_1 \leq J \leq K_2).\end{equation}
    Combining this with the prior steps proves the main estimate (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthehermitebranchinglemmamainestimate}). 
\end{enumerate}
\textbf{(Step 1).} Fix $k \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and let $L > k$. Choose a subset $S_k \subseteq \{1, \ldots, k\}$ of size $|S_k| = \lfloor k/2\rfloor$; $S_k$ defines the row indices of the balanced matricization and $S_k^c$ defines the column indices. 
    For each tuple $\mathbf{i} = (i_1, \ldots, i_k) \in \{0, \ldots, L\}^k$, we denote $\mathbf{i}_{S} = (i_r)_{r \in S}$ and observe that by symmetry of $T_k(F_L)$ we have
    \begin{equation}
         M_k(F_L)[\mathbf{i}_{S_k}, \mathbf{i}_{S_k^c}] = T_k(F_L)[\mathbf{i}] = \sqrt{\frac{\prod_{\ell = 0}^L \nu_\ell(\mathbf{i})!}{k!}} \mathbb{E}_{Z \sim \gamma_{L+1}}\left[F_L(Z) \prod_{\ell = 0}^L h_{\nu_\ell(\mathbf{i})}(Z_\ell)\right],
    \end{equation}
    where we denote $\nu_\ell(\mathbf{i}) = \#\{r:\; i_r = \ell\}$.
    We define the crossing quantity
    \begin{equation}
        C_S(\mathbf{i}) := \left|\{i_r:\; r \in S\}\cap \{i_r:\; r \in S^c\} \cap \{1,\ldots, L\}\right|
    \end{equation}
    to be the number of distinct coordinate labels (other than 0) which appear in both the row and column indices for a balanced cut $S$. Now, let $\mathcal{I}_k\subseteq\{0,\ldots,k\}^k$ be the set of tuples whose distinct positive labels, listed in order of first appearance, are $\{1, 2, \ldots, s\}$ for some $s \leq k$. Equivalently, we require that the distinct nonzero values of $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k$ are $\{1, 2, \ldots, s\}$ and 
    \begin{equation}
        \min\{r:\; p_r = 1\} < \min\{r:\; p_r = 2\} < \ldots < \min\{r:\; p_r = s\}.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, a positive entry may repeat a previously introduced label or introduce the next unused label, but it cannot skip a label.\footnote{By this, we mean tuples like $(0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 2, 3)$ or $(0, 1, 2, 1, \ldots)$ but not $(0, 2, \ldots)$.} Note that $s$ depends on $\mathbf{p}$. For every $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k$ we define two matrices of the same dimensions as $M_k(F_L)$ by
    \begin{equation}
        U_{\mathbf{p}, L}[\mathbf{i}_{S_k}, \mathbf{i}_{S_k^c}] := L^{-s/2} \sum_{\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_s = 1}^L \;\prod_{r = 1}^k \1_{i_r = \ell_{p_r}}, \quad U_{\mathbf{p}, L}^{\neq}[\mathbf{i}_{S_k}, \mathbf{i}_{S_k^c}] := L^{-s/2} \sum_{\substack{\ell_1, \ldots, \ell_s = 1\\ \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_s \text{ distinct}}}^L \;\prod_{r = 1}^k \1_{i_r = \ell_{p_r}},
    \end{equation}
    where we denote $\ell_0 := 0$. Thus, $U_{\mathbf{p},L}^{\neq}$ enforces exactly the coordinate equalities specified by $\mathbf{p}$ whereas $U_{\mathbf{p}, L}$ also permits different positive labels of $\mathbf{p}$ to receive the same coordinate. 
    We set
    \begin{equation}
        d_{\mathbf{p}, L} := L^{s/2} T_k(F_L)[\mathbf{p}].
    \end{equation}
    Because $F_L$ is invariant under permutations of the coordinates $1, \ldots, L$, tuples whose nonzero entries are equivalent up to relabeling have the same tensor coefficients. Hence,
    \begin{equation}
        M_k(F_L) = \sum_{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k} d_{\mathbf{p}, L} U_{\mathbf{p}, L}^{\neq}.
    \end{equation}
    Fix an integer $R > 1$. We decompose $M_k(F_L) = A_{k,L} + H_{k,L} + E_{k,L}$ using the matrices
    \begin{equation}
        A_{k,L} := \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) < R}}d_{\mathbf{p}, L} U_{\mathbf{p}, L}, \quad H_{k,L} := \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}}d_{\mathbf{p}, L} U_{\mathbf{p}, L}, \quad E_{k,L} := \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k}}d_{\mathbf{p}, L}( U_{\mathbf{p}, L}^{\neq} -  U_{\mathbf{p}, L}).
    \end{equation}
    We will now prove some bounds on these matrices. 
    If we denote $a_t := \#\{r\in S_k:\; p_r = t\}$ and $b_t := \#\{r \in S_k^c:\; p_r = t\}$, then we find
    \begin{equation}
        U_{\mathbf{p},L} = \left(e_0^{\otimes a_0} (e_0^{\otimes b_0})^\top\right) \otimes \bigotimes_{t=1}^s D_t, \quad D_t := \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}} \sum_{\ell = 1}^L e_\ell^{\otimes a_t} (e_\ell^{\otimes b_t})^\top
    \end{equation}
    up to row and column permutations,
    with $e_\ell^{\otimes 0} := 1$. These permutations preserve rank and singular values. Now, if $a_t, b_t \geq 1$ then both families $\{e_\ell^{\otimes a_t}\}_{\ell = 1}^L$ and $\{e_\ell^{\otimes b_t}\}_{\ell = 1}^L$ are orthonormal, and so the displayed expression for $D_t$ is an SVD with all singular values equal to $1/\sqrt{L}$. If either $a_t = 0$ or $b_t = 0$, then $D_t$ is a row or column vector of norm 1 (since its squared norm is $\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell = 1}^L 1 = 1$). It therefore has one nonzero singular value equal to 1, as does the term $e_0^{\otimes a_0} (e_0^{\otimes b_0})^\top$.
    We also have
    \begin{equation}
        C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) = \#\{t \in \{1, \ldots, s\}:\; a_t,b_t > 0\}.
    \end{equation}
    Since the nonzero singular values of a Kronecker product are all the possible products of those of the factors, we find that $U_{\mathbf{p},L}$ has exactly $L^{C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p})}$ nonzero singular values which are all equal to $L^{-C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p})/2}$. Hence,
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{rank}( U_{\mathbf{p}, L}) = L^{C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p})}, \quad \|U_{\mathbf{p}, L}\|_{\operatorname{op}} = L^{-C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p})/2}.
    \end{equation}
    Next, we claim that 
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationHermitebranchinglemmaboundondpL}
        |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}| \leq \|\chi\|_\infty V_g^{s/2}  \leq \|\chi\|_\infty \max\{1, V_g^{k/2}\} =: B_k.
    \end{equation}
    To show this, denote $j := \nu_0(\mathbf{p})$ and $q_t := \nu_t(\mathbf{p}) \geq 1$. We start from the fact that if $Z = (Z_0, \ldots, Z_L) \sim \gamma_{L+1}$ then
    \begin{equation}
        d_{\mathbf{p}, L} = L^{s/2} \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \mathbb{E}\left[F_L(Z) h_j(Z_0)\prod_{t = 1}^sh_{q_t}(Z_t) \right].
    \end{equation}
    If we define $Q_j(y) := \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}[\chi(G+y) h_j(G)]$ and differentiate the convolution, we find
    \begin{equation}
        Q_j^{(s)}(y) = \sqrt{\frac{(j+s)!}{j!}} \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}[\chi(G+y)h_{j+s}(G)]
    \end{equation}
    and therefore $\|Q_j^{(s)}\|_\infty \leq \|\chi\|_\infty \sqrt{\frac{(j+s)!}{j!}} $. If we define $(\Delta_uQ)(y) := Q(y+u) - Q(y)$, then repeated application of the fundamental theorem of calculus yields
    \begin{equation}\label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationHermitebranchinglemmaboundondpL10000}
        (\Delta_{u_1} \cdots \Delta_{u_s}Q)(y) = \left(\prod_{t=1}^s u_t\right) \int_{[0,1]^s} Q^{(s)}\left(y + \sum_{t=1}^su_tv_t\right)dv,
    \end{equation}
    which we apply to $Q_j$ to find that
    \begin{equation}
        \|\Delta_{u_1} \cdots \Delta_{u_s}Q_j\|_\infty \leq \|Q_j^{(s)}\|_\infty \prod_{t=1}^s |u_t| \leq \|\chi\|_\infty \sqrt{\frac{(j+s)!}{j!}} \prod_{t=1}^s |u_t|.
    \end{equation}
    On the other hand, denoting $Y_L := \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{\ell = s+1}^L g(Z_\ell)$ and integrating over $Z_0$ yields
    \begin{align}
        d_{\mathbf{p}, L} &= L^{s/2} \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \mathbb{E}\left[\chi\left(Z_0 + Y_L + \sum_{t=1}^s \frac{g(Z_t)}{\sqrt{L}} \right)h_j(Z_0) \prod_{t=1}^s h_{q_t}(Z_t)\right] \\
        &= L^{s/2} \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \mathbb{E}\left[Q_j\left(Y_L + \sum_{t=1}^s \frac{g(Z_t)}{\sqrt{L}}\right)\prod_{t=1}^s h_{q_t}(Z_t)\right].
        \label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationlowerbounddpLnonsense2}
    \end{align}
    Now, use the finite differences identity $(\Delta_{u_1} \cdots \Delta_{u_s}Q)(y) = \sum_{A \subseteq \{1, \ldots, s\}} (-1)^{s-|A|} Q(y + \sum_{t \in A}u_t)$ along with the fact
    \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}\left[Q_j\left(Y_L + \sum_{t \in A} \frac{g(Z_t)}{\sqrt{L}}\right)\prod_{t=1}^s h_{q_t}(Z_t)\right] = 0 \text{ if $A \subsetneq \{1, \ldots, s\}$},
    \end{align}
    which is true since for any $t \notin A$ we may integrate over $Z_t$ and use $\mathbb{E}[h_{q_t}(Z_t)] = 0$. So, only the $A = \{1, \ldots, s\}$ term of the finite differences identity survives, which we plug into (\ref{eqn:proofappendixapproximationlowerbounddpLnonsense2}) to find that
    \begin{align}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationlowerbounddpLnonsense3}
        d_{\mathbf{p}, L} &= L^{s/2} \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\Delta_{g(Z_1)/\sqrt{L}}\cdots \Delta_{g(Z_s)/\sqrt{L}}Q_j\right)(Y_L) \prod_{t=1}^s h_{q_t}(Z_t)\right]
        \end{align}
        and therefore
        \begin{align}
        | d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|
       & \leq \|\chi\|_\infty  \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}}  \sqrt{\frac{(j+s)!}{j!}} \prod_{t=1}^s \mathbb{E}\left[|g(Z_t)h_{q_t}(Z_t)|\right]  \\
        &\leq \|\chi\|_\infty  \sqrt{\frac{(j+s)! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}}  \|g\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)}^s \\
        &\leq \|\chi\|_\infty V_g^{s/2},
    \end{align}
    where we use Cauchy-Schwarz and that $\|h_{q_t}\|_{L^2(\gamma_1)} = 1$ in the second line and that $\sqrt{\frac{(j+s)! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \leq 1$ in the third. This proves (\ref{eqn:proofappendixapproximationHermitebranchinglemmaboundondpL}).

    Now, since $|\mathcal{I}_k| \leq (k+1)^k$ we find that
    \begin{equation}
        \operatorname{rank}(A_{k,L}) \leq (k+1)^k L^{R - 1}, \quad \|H_{k,L}\|_{\operatorname{op}} \leq (k+1)^kB_k L^{-R/2}.
    \end{equation}
    Also, since $U_{\mathbf{p},L} - U_{\mathbf{p},L}^{\neq}$'s nonzero entries come from exactly the assignments with a repeated coordinate label we find
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormboundneq}
        \|U_{\mathbf{p},L} - U_{\mathbf{p},L}^{\neq}\|_F^2 = L^{-s} \left(L^s - L(L-1)\cdots (L-s+1)\right) \leq \frac{{s \choose 2}}{L} \leq \frac{{k \choose 2}}{L}.
    \end{equation}
   In particular, $\|E_{k,L}\|_F^2 \leq (k+1)^{2k}B_k^2 {k \choose 2} /L = O_k({L^{-1}})$. If we define $d_m(B) := \sqrt{\sum_{j > m} \sigma_j(B)^2}$ and observe that this is a distance to the set of matrices of rank at most $m$ (w.r.t. Frobenius norm), then by the triangle inequality we have that
   \begin{equation}
      d_m(B)^2 \leq (1+\eta)d_m(B+E)^2 + (1+\eta^{-1})\|E\|_F^2.
   \end{equation}
   Therefore, taking $B = A_{k,L} + H_{k,L}$ and $E = E_{k,L}$ gives
\begin{equation}
    \sum_{j > L^{R - 1}} \sigma_j(M_k(F_L))^2 \geq \frac{1}{1+\eta}\sum_{j > L^{R - 1}} \sigma_j(A_{k,L} + H_{k,L})^2 - O_{k,\eta}(L^{-1}).
\end{equation}
    Using the elementary inequality
    \begin{equation}
        \sum_{j > m} \sigma_j(A + H)^2 \geq \|H\|_F^2 - (m+\operatorname{rank}(A)) \|H\|_{\operatorname{op}}^2 \quad \left(\forall A, H \in {\mathbb{R}}^{M \times M'}, \; \forall M,M' \in {\mathbb{N}}\right),
    \end{equation}
 if we take $m = L^{R - 1}$ along with $A = A_{k,L}$ and $H = H_{k,L}$ then
    \begin{align}
        \sum_{j > L^{R - 1}} \sigma_j(M_k(F_L))^2 \geq \frac{1}{1+\eta}\|H_{k,L}\|_F^2 - O_{k,\eta}(L^{-1}).
    \end{align}
   Taking $L \to \infty$, we find that
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep1}
         \liminf_{L \to \infty} \sum_{j > L^{R-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2  \geq \liminf_{L \to \infty} \frac{1}{1+\eta}\|H_{k,L}\|_F^2.
    \end{equation}
     By (\ref{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormboundneq}), replacing $U_{\mathbf{p},L}$ by $U_{\mathbf{p},L}^{\neq}$ in $H_{k,L}$ changes the matrix by at most $O_k(L^{-1/2})$ in Frobenius norm. Since the matrices $U_{\mathbf{p},L}^{\neq}$ have disjoint entry supports for distinct $\mathbf{p}$, we find
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationlowerbounddpLnonsense500}
        \|H_{k,L}\|_F^2 = \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 \frac{L(L-1)\cdots (L-s+1)}{L^s} + o(1)
    \end{equation}
    with $s = \max_r p_r$. Combining this with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep1}), taking $\eta \downarrow 0$, and noting that $L(L-1) \cdots (L-s+1) / L^s \to 1$ yields
    \begin{equation}
    \label{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep1NEW}
        \liminf_{L \to \infty} \sum_{j > L^{R-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2 \geq \liminf_{L \to \infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 .
    \end{equation}
    \textbf{(Step 2).} 
We first fix $\mathbf{p}$ and compute the limit of $d_{\mathbf{p}, L}$. Recalling our notation $j = \nu_0(\mathbf{p})$, $q_t = \nu_t(\mathbf{p})$, and $Y_L = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{\ell = s+1}^L g(Z_\ell)$ for $Z = (Z_0, \ldots, Z_L) \sim \gamma_{L+1}$, we start from (\ref{eqn:proofappendixapproximationlowerbounddpLnonsense3}) and the finite difference integral representation (\ref{eqn:proofappendixapproximationHermitebranchinglemmaboundondpL10000}) to get that
    \begin{align}
        d_{\mathbf{p}, L} &= \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\int_{[0, 1]^s} Q^{(s)}_j \left(Y_L + \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{t=1}^s g(Z_t)v_t\right)dv\right)\prod_{t=1}^s g(Z_t)h_{q_t}(Z_t)\right].
    \end{align}
    Noting that $Q_j^{(s+1)}$ is bounded (and so $Q_j^{(s)}$ is Lipschitz), $g$ is Lipschitz, and the $h_{q_t}$ are polynomials of fixed degree, we find that
    \begin{align}
 d_{\mathbf{p}, L} &= \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\int_{[0, 1]^s} Q^{(s)}_j \left(Y_L\right)dv\right)\prod_{t=1}^s g(Z_t)h_{q_t}(Z_t)\right] + O_k(L^{-1/2}) \\
         &= \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \cdot \mathbb{E}\left[Q^{(s)}_j \left(Y_L\right)\right] \cdot \prod_{t=1}^s \beta_{q_t} + O_k(L^{-1/2}), 
    \end{align}
    where the second line uses that $Y_L$ is independent of $\sigma(Z_1, \ldots, Z_s)$. 
    Since $g$ is centered with finite Gaussian moments, by the central limit theorem we know that $\operatorname{Law}(Y_L) \to \mathcal{N}(0, V_g)$ narrowly as $L \to \infty$. Since $Q_j^{(s)}$ is bounded and continuous, we find that
\begin{align}
    \lim_{L \to \infty} d_{\mathbf{p}, L} = \sqrt{\frac{j! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1} \left[ Q_j^{(s)} (\sqrt{V_g}G )\right] \cdot \prod_{t=1}^s \beta_{q_t}.
\end{align}
Convolving the two Gaussians (whose variances add to $\lambda_g = 1 + V_g$) implies that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1} \left[ Q_j^{(s)} (\sqrt{V_g}G )\right] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{j!}} \left.\frac{d^{j+s}}{dy^{j+s}} \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}[\chi(\sqrt{\lambda_g}G + y)]\right|_{y=0} = \sqrt{\frac{(j+s)!}{j!}} \lambda_g^{-(j+s)/2} \alpha_{j+s},
\end{equation}
and therefore with $J := j+s$ we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixresnetapproximationbranchinglemmastep2limofdpL}
    \lim_{L \to \infty} d_{\mathbf{p}, L} = 
    \alpha_J \lambda_g^{-J/2}
    \sqrt{\frac{J! \prod_{t=1}^s q_t!}{k!}}\prod_{t=1}^s \beta_{q_t}.
\end{equation}
Now, for each integer $J \in {\mathbb{N}}$ we assign to integer configurations $j \in {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$, $(m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}} \subseteq {\mathbb{N}} \cup \{0\}$ satisfying $j + \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}m_q = J$ the probabilities
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixapproximationloweroundhermitebranchingpdfofJ}
    \mathbb{P}_J\left(j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right) := \frac{J!}{j! \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}m_q!} \left(\frac{1}{\lambda_g}\right)^j \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\left(\frac{\beta_q^2}{\lambda_g}\right)^{m_q}.
\end{equation}
These sum to 1 by the multinomial formula, since $\frac{1}{\lambda_g} + \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}} \frac{\beta_q^2}{\lambda_g} = \frac{1+V_g}{\lambda_g} = 1$. For each configuration drawn from $\mathbb{P}_J$, we set \begin{equation}
    s := \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}m_q, \quad N := j + \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}qm_q,
\end{equation}
choose $q_1 \leq \ldots \leq q_s$ with exactly $m_q$ occurrences of each $q$, and form the tuple 
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{i} := (\underbrace{0, \ldots, 0}_{j}, \underbrace{1, \ldots, 1}_{q_1}, \ldots, \underbrace{s, \ldots, s}_{q_s}) \in \mathcal{I}_N.
\end{equation}
Choose $S \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\}$ uniformly at random among subsets of size $\lfloor N /2 \rfloor$ and define
\begin{equation}
    C_S := C_S(\mathbf{i}) = |\{i_r:\; r \in S\} \cap \{i_r:\; r \in S^c\} \setminus \{0\}|.
\end{equation}
To identify (\ref{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep1NEW}) probabilistically, fix any configuration $j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}$ with $N = k$. There are
\begin{equation}
    \frac{k!}{j! \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}(q!)^{m_q}}
\end{equation}
distinct permutations of the tuple $\mathbf{i}$. Each canonical tuple $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k$ with these multiplicities arises from exactly $\prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}m_q!$ such permutations, as labels with equal multiplicities can be arbitrarily permuted without changing their canonical representative $\mathbf{p}$. Hence, the number of canonical $k$-tuples with the fixed multiplicities $(m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}$ is equal to
\begin{equation}
        \frac{k!}{j! \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}(q!)^{m_q} m_q!}.
\end{equation}
Let $\pi$ be a uniformly random permutation of $\{1, \ldots, k\}$. 
By the above counting argument, the canonical representative of $(i_{\pi(1)}, \ldots, i_{\pi(k)})$ produces a uniformly random canonical tuple $\mathbf{p}_\pi \in \mathcal{I}_k$ with the given multiplicities.
Note that relabeling preserves crossing counts, i.e.
\begin{equation}
  C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}_\pi) = C_{S_k}(i_{\pi(1)}, \ldots, i_{\pi(k)}) = C_{\pi(S_k)}(\mathbf{i}).
\end{equation}
Since $\pi(S_k)$ is a uniformly random balanced cut, the fraction of canonical tuples $\mathbf{p}_\pi$ satisfying $C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}_\pi) \geq R$ is exactly $\mathbb{P}_J(C_S \geq R \mid j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}})$. From (\ref{eqn:proofappendixresnetapproximationbranchinglemmastep2limofdpL}) we know that
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{L \to \infty} |d_{\mathbf{p}_\pi, L}|^2 = \frac{\alpha_J^2 J!}{k! \lambda_g^J} \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}(q! \beta_q^2)^{m_q}, \quad J = j + \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}m_q.
\end{equation}
Hence, averaging over $\pi$ for a fixed configuration $j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}$ with $N=k$ yields
\begin{align}
 \frac{j! \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}(q!)^{m_q} m_q!} {k!}\sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k,
 \nu_0(\mathbf{p}) = j \\
\#\{1 \leq t \leq s:\;  \nu_t(\mathbf{p}) =q\} = m_q \; \forall q \in {\mathbb{N}} \\
 C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} \lim_{L \to \infty} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 = \frac{\alpha_J^2 J!}{k! \lambda_g^J} \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}(q! \beta_q^2)^{m_q} \mathbb{P}_J\left(C_S \geq R \mid j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right)
\end{align}
or in other words that
\begin{align}
    \sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k,
 \nu_0(\mathbf{p}) = j \\
\#\{1 \leq t \leq s:\;  \nu_t(\mathbf{p}) =q\} = m_q \; \forall q \in {\mathbb{N}} \\
 C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} \lim_{L \to \infty} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 &= \frac{\alpha_J^2 J!}{j! \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}m_q!} \left(\frac{1}{\lambda_g}\right)^j \prod_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}} \left(\frac{\beta_q^2}{\lambda_g}\right)^{m_q} \\&\quad \cdot \mathbb{P}_J\left(C_S \geq R \mid j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right) \\
 &= \alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J\left(j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right)\cdot \mathbb{P}_J\left(C_S \geq R \mid j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right),
\end{align}
where the second line applied the definition of $\mathbb{P}_J$ in (\ref{eqn:proofappendixapproximationloweroundhermitebranchingpdfofJ}). 
We exchange the limit and the finite sum and then sum over all configurations for which $N=k$ (which includes summing over $J$). However, since $J \leq N$ we need only consider $J \leq k$, which yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep2}
    \lim_{L \to \infty}\sum_{\substack{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{I}_k \\ C_{S_k}(\mathbf{p}) \geq R}} |d_{\mathbf{p}, L}|^2 = \sum_{J =1}^k\alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(N=k,\; C_S \geq R).
\end{equation}
\textbf{(Step 3).} Under $\mathbb{P}_J$, let $B := \sum_{q \geq 2}m_q$ be the number of positive labels occurring at least twice (i.e. the number of nonlinear factors). Because the probability mass function of $\mathbb{P}_J$ from (\ref{eqn:proofappendixapproximationloweroundhermitebranchingpdfofJ}) is a multinomial law, we find that $B \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(J, 8\mathfrak{v}_g)$ (since $\sum_{q \geq 2}\beta_q^2 / \lambda_g = 8 \mathfrak{v}_g$). Moreover, since $g$ is Lipschitz we know that
\begin{equation}
    \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}} q\beta_q^2 = \mathbb{E}_{G \sim \gamma_1}|g'(G)|^2 \leq \operatorname{Lip}(g)^2,
\end{equation}
which implies that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}_J[N] = \mathbb{E}_J \left[j + \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}qm_q\right] = \frac{J}{\lambda_g} \left(1 + \sum_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}q \beta_q^2\right) \leq \frac{JB_g}{8}. 
\end{equation}
By Markov's inequality, we find that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}_J(N > B_g J) \leq \frac{1}{8}.
\end{equation}
Next, by the binomial Chernoff bound we know
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}_J(B < 4 \mathfrak{v}_gJ) \leq e^{-\mathfrak{v}_gJ},
\end{equation}
and so a union bound gives that for $J \geq K_g$ we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixhermitebranchingchernoffconsequence}
    \mathbb{P}_J(N \leq B_g J, \; B \geq 4 \mathfrak{v}_gJ) \geq 1 - \frac{1}{8} - e^{-\mathfrak{v}_g J} \geq \frac{13}{16},
\end{equation}
where we denote $K_g := \lceil 4/\mathfrak{v}_g\rceil$. Now, condition on a configuration $j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}$ with $B \geq 1$. For each positive label occurring at least twice, select two positions carrying that label. A uniformly balanced random cut separates these positions with probability $\geq \frac{1}{2}$, which implies
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}\left[C_S  \mid j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right] \geq \frac{B}{2}.
\end{equation}
Next, we know that
\begin{equation}
   C_S = C_S \1_{C_S < B/4} + C_S \1_{C_S \geq B/4} \leq \frac{B}{4} + \frac{3B}{4} \1_{C_S \geq B/4},
\end{equation}
where we use that $0 \leq C_S \leq B$ (since any pair contributing to $C_S$ must also contribute to $B$). Taking conditional expectations,
\begin{equation}
    \frac{B}{2} \leq \mathbb{E}\left[C_S  \mid j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right] \leq \frac{B}{4} + \frac{3B}{4}\mathbb{P}_J\left(C_S \geq B/4 \mid  j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right).
\end{equation}
Since $B > 0$, we rearrange to find that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{P}_J\left(C_S \geq B/4 \mid  j, (m_q)_{q \in {\mathbb{N}}}\right) \geq \frac{1}{3}.
\end{equation}
For a configuration with $B=0$ this holds trivially, and therefore it always holds. Combining with (\ref{eqn:proofappendixhermitebranchingchernoffconsequence}) gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep3}
    \mathbb{P}_J(N \leq B_gJ, \; C_S \geq \mathfrak{v}_g J) \geq \frac{13}{48}.
\end{equation}

We now finish the proof of the main claim (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthehermitebranchinglemmamainestimate}). Combining the estimates (\ref{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep1NEW}) and (\ref{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep2}) from steps 1 and 2, respectively, gives
\begin{align}
     \liminf_{L \to \infty} \sum_{j > L^{R-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2 &\geq  \sum_{J =1}^k\alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(N=k,\; C_S \geq R).
\end{align}
For $K_g \leq K_1 \leq K_2$, summing over $K_1 \leq k \leq \lceil B_gK_2\rceil$ and taking $R = \lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor$ gives
\begin{align}
    \liminf_{L \to \infty}\sum_{k=K_1}^{\lceil B_gK_2\rceil} \sum_{j > L^{\lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor-1}} \sigma_j (M_k(F_L))^2 &\geq \sum_{k=K_1}^{\lceil B_gK_2\rceil} \sum_{J =1}^k\alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(N=k,\; C_S \geq \lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor)
    \\ &= \sum_{J=1}^{\lceil B_gK_2\rceil} \alpha_J^2\sum_{k = \max\{K_1, J\}}^{\lceil B_gK_2\rceil} \mathbb{P}_J(N=k,\; C_S \geq \lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor)
    \\ &= \sum_{J=1}^{\lceil B_gK_2\rceil} \alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(K_1 \leq N\leq \lceil B_gK_2\rceil, \; C_S \geq \lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor) \\
    &\geq\sum_{J=K_1}^{K_2} \alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(K_1 \leq N\leq \lceil B_gK_2\rceil, \; C_S \geq \lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor) \\
    &= \sum_{J=K_1}^{K_2} \alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(N\leq \lceil B_gK_2\rceil, \; C_S \geq \lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor)\\
&\geq \sum_{J=K_1}^{K_2} \alpha_J^2 \mathbb{P}_J(N\leq B_gJ, \; C_S \geq \mathfrak{v}_g J)\\
    &\geq \frac{13}{48} \sum_{J=K_1}^{K_2}\alpha_J^2,
\end{align}
where the third and fifth lines use that $N \geq J$ almost surely, the fourth uses that $V_g = \operatorname{Var}(g) \leq \operatorname{Lip}(g)^2$ and so $B_g \geq 1$, the sixth uses that $\lceil B_g K_2\rceil \geq B_g J$ and $\lfloor \mathfrak{v}_g K_1\rfloor \leq \mathfrak{v}_g J$, and the last uses (\ref{eqn:proofappendixappromxiationResnetfrobenisunormstep3}) from step 3. This is exactly the claim (\ref{eqn:proofappendixthehermitebranchinglemmamainestimate}).
